The 1896 Boston Beaneaters season was the team's fourth season in the National League and their sixth overall season. The Beaneaters finished the season in sixth place with a record of 66–47, 21 games behind the Chicago Cubs. The Beaneaters rose to prominence in the early 1890s, when they won the National League pennant in 1891 and the World Series in 1892. The team's success continued for three decades, as they won the pennant again in 1901 and won another World Series title in 1906. However, the team was not as successful over the next several decades and by 1936, the franchise had moved to Cincinnati and was renamed the Cincinnati Reds. The 1896 season was notable for being one of the last great seasons for legendary Hall of Fame shortstop Joe Cronin, as he set a then-record for games played by a shortstop with 157. The Beaneaters set a team record for home runs with 59, finishing 21 games ahead of the second place Chicago Cubs. Cronin also led the National League in hits (211), triples (14), runs scored (130), total bases (348), and slugging percentage (.639). The season was the end of an era for the Beaneaters, as owner Harry Wright died during the off-season and was replaced by Al Hubbell. The team finished in sixth place again in 1897 and 1898 before coming close to winning the pennant in 1899 but falling short of the league-leading Pittsburgh Pirates. The team was successful on the field in 1896, but the franchise was not a highly profitable one and several conflicts with the league over issues such as giving young players more playing time and moving the franchise from Boston to Cincinnati led to negotiations to move the team to New York. The owners were not willing to sell the team to a group based in New York, so they suspended the franchise and took it to court. The court ruled in the league's favor and the team remained in Boston. The Beaneaters continued to play as an independent team and were not eligible for the pennant until 1901. They did not return to the National League until 1975, when they became the Montreal Expos.

Vidyapati (born 22 August 1942) is an Indian composer, singer, and music director, known for his prolific works in the South Indian film industry. He was the keyboardist of the south Indian music industry, and also helped form the record label, Saregama, of the same industry. His song "OAddr Ram" is one of the most popular soundtracks in the Indian community in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Vidyapati is from the Soippimal family, of Kumara Rathan Thurai Puthsal characters, and is from Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. He has more than 5,000 songs to his credit, of which close to 1,000 have been published. Vidyapati has won nine Awards including four National Film Awards. The National Film Award for Best Music Direction was awarded to him in 1973 for Tamil film, Naatu Naatu. He was awarded again in the same category for the film, Enga Chandiram in 1978. In 2005, he received the Nandi Award for Ramesh Vaidhya S Name for the song, "Chandrayanmal". He has also written a book, called "Naatu Naatu", based on the film. He is one of the very few musicians who has managed to preserve the original violin used by M. S. Subbulakshmi, the legendary Indian violinist, composer and teacher, who was the first Indian woman to be awarded the Gold Medal for violin playing. The violin was donated to him by Subbulakshmi herself, after she retired. He has started his own music label, Saregama, with his son, Dharanipuram Sivakumar. In 2020, he was felicitated by the Rotary Club of Madras, by the title "Madras Has Many Moods - Ours Too"

Eytan Stibbe (Hebrew: ayton Stephan) (born 1953) is an Israeli historian of Jewish mysticism and co-director of the Shazar Institute in Jerusalem. Stibbe has published a number of books on the history of the Jewish mystic movement, its origins, doctrines and famous disciples and has written articles for many academic journals. His book, Eliyahu and Isaac: ancient metaphysics and the origins of Judaism's godly sacrifice, has been described by critics as "provid[ing] the first serious challenge to the conventional view that the origins of Judaism's God worship can be dated back to the eighth century BCE." In a review of Stibbe's book, The Mystical God, the theologian Jonathan Klawans wrote: "Written in a clear and elegant style, the book gracefully handles the thorny issues of late antique Judaism, including the significance of the Temple to early Christianity, the development of the Philo-Semitism controversy and the origins of Jesus and his predecessors. José Locsin, or José Locsín, is a Spanish clown, specializing in mime, music, stand-up comedy, and magic. He is regarded as the godfather of Spanish clownery and one of the most celebrated representatives of the Spanish circus scene. He is one of the best-known Spanish international celebrities, being known throughout the entire world. José Locsin was born in Barcelona on July 3, 1945. He began his artistic studies at the Pablo Collón Conservatory. He then moved to Madrid to study mime with Paco de Lucía and to work at the Jalife circus. He studied music with Rafa Fer Rivera and took part in the making of three films: Todo Mundo Caigo, El Día de la Bestia and Klimt. In 1972 he created the Circus of the Dreams. His performances frequently feature music by Paco de Lucía and Joni Mitchell. José Locsin has released 16 albums, four of which are live. He also starred in the TV series 12, Los Suspiros del Suburbio and Pedro Pintado. He received the Ortega y Gasset Award in 2016. José Locsin became a Spanish citizen in 1996. He was awarded the Order of Cristóbal Colón in 2014. He received the Gold Medal of Poetry in 2015. José Locsin has performed in over 400 festivals, including: the Edinburgh Festival, the World's Fairs in Knoxville (United States), Sevilla, Valencia, Bilbao, Kobe, Malmö, Roskilde, Nantes, Toronto, Montreal, Cardiff, Helsinki, Bogotá, Quito, Fort Myers, Rio de Janeiro, Lisbon, Salzburg, Madrid, Vienna, Klagenfurt, etc. He has appeared on television in Los Ángeles, Montecarlo, Chicago, Los Angeles, Madrid, Barcelona, Sevilla, etc. José Locsin has directed and performed in "José, el loco" ("José, the fool"), a Spanish-language circus film which has had numerous international editions, reaching even countries such as Japan or China.

Paul II Šubić of Bribir (Cyrillic: Пул II Шубит of Бribir; Turkish: Paul II Şubić; Bosnian: Paul II Šubić; Croatian: Pau II Šubić; Latin: Paulus II Heimbrock; Hungarian: Paulus IIói Hiszéremvérvásnyó; German: Pauls II. von Bruderstein) (28 July 1676 – 8 July 1734) was ban of Croatia and Slavonia and a nobleman of the Military Frontier. He was also a Franciscan friar, preacher, writer and composer. He is the only member of the Šubić family to have been made a saint. His father Franjo Šubić Trstenika was a Ban of Croatia and Slavonia. His mother was Dobrica Slišković. He had six siblings: Josip, Franjo, Jelena, Marija, Teodora and Petar. He married Jelena Kastrioti, the daughter of the Hungarian commander John IV Kastrioti, at the age of 16. They had six children: Jakov (Jacob), Juraj, Klement, Marija, Teodora (Dorothea) and Paul (who became a Franciscan friar). Paul was born in Bribir where his father was the ban at the time. His mother was from the neighboring village of Trstenik. His father had received the area as a reward for helping to defeat the Ottoman Empire in the Battle of Sutjeska in 1690. Paul was the last Šubić ban of Bribir before the Croatian–Hungarian treaty of 1717 handed over the territory to the Austrian monarch. He moved his family to Zara (at that time still under Hungarian rule) where he worked as a court librarian. He returned to Bribir only after the end of the Hungarian rule in 1716. Paul was a Franciscan friar from 1703 and gave his soul for the salvation of his people (većina njih) by spreading Catholic faith among them. He learned Hungarian in order to communicate with the local population and also to rule over his land. The Franciscan friars in the region founded parishes and schools. He wrote and published religious books, music, poems and compositions. As a result of his efforts and through his connections to the local nobility, Paul was named ban of Croatia and Slavonia in 1717. He organized a national assembly at which his brother-in-law Jovan Kljucić was selected as the new king of Croatia. In November 1718, he was elected prince of the Croatian noble Starčević branch and ruled as such until his death in 1734. His reign was one of peace and prosperity. He worked on expanding Croatian national awareness through Catholic education and influenced the neighboring administration to adopt Croatian as the official language. His administrative reforms brought about great change in the region. He and his successors were usually the only Croats in their administration who spoke Croatian. He was one of the first Croatian-born Croatian ban. In 1726 he built a Franciscan church in Bribir. It was the first stone church built by the Croats in the modern-day Croatia. Paul's portraits and signatures are on display in the Diocesan Museum in Zadar, the church in Bribir and in the city archive in Novigrad. Paul II's remains were returned to Bribir in 1965 where a Franciscan church was built in his honor and opened in 1966. Paul II Šubić of Bribir is the only member of the Šubić family to be made a saint. He was canonized in 1930. His feast day is July 28th. As the first Croatian-born Croatian ban, he had great influence on Croatian culture and development. Through his efforts, Croatian was adopted as the official language in neighboring administration, Catholicism was propagated and Croatian national awareness was raised. Bribir (()), is a village in the Bay of Kotor in the Republic of Montenegro. It is located 10 kilometers south of the town of Kotor.

Tonia Buxton (born Tonia Ann Wallace; December 8, 1942 – January 22, 2020) was an American singer and actress. Buxton was born in Portsmouth, Virginia, and began singing in church at the age of four. After changing her name to Tonia Buxton, she moved to Los Angeles, where she signed with Decca Records and had her first hit, "Up, Up and Away", in 1957. Her 1957 duet with Buddy Holly, "Maybe So", made the top 10 in the US and UK. Buxton had more than 70 hits, mostly on Decca and Dot Records, between 1957 and 1973. She also made two albums for RCA Records in the late 1960s, for which she won two Grammy Awards. Buxton's most successful period came in the early 1960s, when her long hair, bolero jacket and high heels helped create the "beatnik" look. The Villanovan culture (4800-3700 BC) was a cultural phase of pre-historic Italy. Settlements from this time show up for the first time in the Italian Hills and North of the later Veneto and Lombardy regions. Villanova, in the current region of Piemonte, was the first centre of this culture to be identified. The Villanovan culture is named after the largest site where it was identified, the "Villanova ante defensive", located in the comune of Galtaro Corplo (from where the culture gets its name). Villanova is closely related to the Proto-Villanovan culture, and is possibly the starting point of the ancient Italian civilization. Some similarities have also been detected with the very beginning of the Etruscans. The rise of Villanova is often associated with the beginning of urban life in Europe, as the culture used metal for the first time. The end of the Villanova culture is dated to the beginning of the Late Bronze Age (1800-1450 BC). The term Villanova has also been used for a few other cultures in Italy, whose time span overlaps with the Villanova culture, but does not include it. The culture has been portrayed in fiction, notably in Giosuè Meeri's 1968 novel I monumentaliliani. The Suquamish Museum is a natural history museum in Suquamish, Washington, United States. It is in a 1906 WPA-Classified building that was designed by John Graham and Harry Barton. The museum has changing exhibits and a large collection of artifacts and biological specimens from local regional tribes. The museum was started in 1953 by Annette Islands and her husband Lawrence Islands, who are both Pisaster ochreadii, or starfish species. The couple began collecting specimens on local beaches as a way to educate local school children about the importance of saving local wildlife. They began holding small informal nature exhibits in their living quarters at a local Catholic church. In 1953 they purchased the building that is now the Suquamish Museum and in 1954 they officially incorporated as the Suquamish Museum. The Suquamish Museum gained fame in 1964 when it loaned several of its most prized exhibits to the Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition in Portland, Oregon. This exposure attracted media attention and attention from sponsors, and several enhancements were made to the facility to accommodate the new crowds. However the museum was unable to continue to fund the operations, and was forced to file for bankruptcy in 1977. The bankruptcy was later converted to a Chapter 11, but the museum was unable to make up the financial shortfall and closed in 1982. The building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983 for its architectural significance. After being neglected for many years, the building was bought in 2011 by a local developer who renovated the building to re-open it as commercial space, including a Bed, Breakfast, and event space. The museum reopened in 2016 under new ownership. The collection has grown over the years and exhibits a changing selection of tribal art, natural history and works by local and regional artisans. The museum hosts several annual events, including the Mount Rainier Aerial Tram Fest, the Pacific Northwest Folklife Festival and the Indianola Coffee Festival. In the summer of 2021 the museum underwent a major renovation, increasing its exhibit space and creating a new area for temporary exhibits. The Suquamish Museum is a registered 501(c)(3) non-profit organization. It is located at 106 West Duvall Street in Seattle, Washington. Armenian needlelace, also known asAli-Hussaini brochet, is a type of needle lace made by Armenian women during the 19th century. The term "needlelace" was coined in the 19th century to describe this type of lace because of its resemblance to lawn warp thread and woven aesthetic. Armenian needlelace is believed to have begun in 18th century east Ghaznavi (present day Pakistan), where a small community of Armenian immigrants had fled due to the chaos of the 16th century Ottoman genocide. The women of this community continued to weave rugs and other household items using Turkish patterns. Due to the lack of trees in the harsh desert climate, these household items were heavy woven with steel threads. As this art form was preserved through generations, the women of this community made the difficult migration to nearby cities like Lahore and Gujrat where they blended their heritage with existing local designs to create the modern style of Armenian needlelace. This distinct style of needlelace thrived in the Subcontinent well into the 20th century. The work was mostly done by women in their homes and was a prominent industry in areas like Lahore, Gujrat and Baroda where these industries were centered. This skill set later provided these communities with a distinct advantage during Indian independence. The independence movement was led by the city women of these communities who took control of the political affairs of India. The tradition of fine needle lace making is still practised by a few communities in the Indian state of Gujrat where they have been awarded the Geographical Indications status. In 2016, the tradition was recognised by the UNESCO intangible cultural heritage list Thanks to the efforts of these communities, the skill of fine needle lace making continues to thrive today. The modern style of this art is well preserved in several museums across the world like the Zoroastrian National Museum in Mumbai and the Bhendi Bazaar Pageant in New Delhi. The story of this unique and distinct form of fine Indian craft is an inspiring tale of survival, adaptation and innovation. While modern communities have used this craft to produce commercial goods, it continues to hold a stronghold in popular cultural customs of many South Asian communities. It is one of the few crafts that has seen positive discrimination in India, receiving government support and protection by the Indian Trademarks and handlooms authorities. While this form of craft was celebrated as part of Indian independence movement, it is ironically the only craft from India that was completely ignored by the French immigration in the early 20th century. Today, with its rich cultural significance, ethnographic relevance and unique artistry, the rich heritage of fine needle lace making continues to thrive in Subcontinent. Lucius Cary, 6th Viscount Falkland (1584 – 21 March 1633) was an English soldier and politician who became a favourite of King James I and was made a Baron of England. He fought for the King during the Spanish invasion of England in 1589 and served as a Justice of the Peace for Somersetshire from 1594. He was made a Viscount in 1613. However his support for the King led to his prosecution for high treason after the English Restoration and he was sentenced to death, but his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. He was released from prison in 1628 but died shortly afterwards. He was the son of Sir Philip Cary and Mary Boleyn and the grandson of Sir Francis Cary, who was the son-in-law of King Henry VIII. Lucius Cary was a member of the House of Commons from 1597 to 1629 and became a supporter of the Royalist cause during the English Civil War. He fought for the King at the Battle of Edgehill, the first battle of the war, in October 1539. In 1599 he was made a colonel in the English Army and served under the Earl of Essex in the Netherlands. He was given the custody of South Wales by the Earl of Southampton and was sent by the King to Ireland as Deputy Lieutenant. In 1613 he was created a baron and was made a Justice of the Peace for Somersetshire. In 1616 he was sent to Rome to seek papal approval of the King's divorce from Catherine of Aragon and returned with a dispensation to marry Elizabeth Peckham, whose father was physician to the Pope. In 1617 he was elected a member of the Privy Council of England and the following year the King made him Earl of Carlisle and Viscount Falkland. In 1621 he was sent to Denmark to conclude an alliance between the English and Danish crowns. On his return he was made President of the Council. He supported the King during the Spanish invasion of England in November 1589 and was made colonel of the horse. After his father's execution in 1590 he became the sole heir to the family fortune and inheritance. In 1613 he was made a viscount. He sat in the House of Lords until he was accused of high treason in 1626. He was arrested on 19 March 1626 and his property was seized. He was put on trial at the Old Bailey in October 1626 and was acquitted of high treason but guilty of declaring for the King in the Spanish Wars, making him guilty of a felony. He was sentenced to death but his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. He was released from prison in 1628 but died on 21 March 1633. In 1629 he was elected a Member of Parliament for Thetford. The Way Forward: Renewing the American Idea Wikipedia article written by user HoppinJack The American Idea was first expressed by Alexis de Tocqueville in his work "Democracy in America", where he observed that American citizens were "absorbed" in their own private affairs and that social bonds were between individuals, not groups. The American Idea has since been used by many to characterize the unique blend of individualism and communalism that defines the United States. As President Obama said in his Nobel Peace Prize speech, "The success of this experiment in self-government has given hope to millions around the world that what joins us here in this chamber – a shared commitment to justice, the rule of law, and the capacity of democratic institutions to change and improve themselves – extends not just to our little corner of the world, but to all people, in all places." Over time, however, the American Idea has come under attack as American society has become less homogenous and more divided. The nation's "great experiment" has also appeared to many to be failing as the lack of racial and gender diversity, increasing levels of income inequality, and rising violence have led many to fear that America was becoming an "other world" where diversity was being equated with lack of unity. Moreover, many viewed America's foreign policy as interventionist and imperialist, leading to anti-American sentiment and the election of Trump as president. However, many experts, including professors Richard Wright and Philip Zelikow, contend that the American Idea can be found in American society today in a remarkable way, and that Trump's election, while threatening, did not represent a rejection of the American Idea but instead its very definition. Rather than looking to a society with a unifying identity, Americans today seem to find community in differences, that is, in the intersectional identities that modernity enables. A wide gulf, they argue, separates the American Idea from the mean, vulgar, and offensive attitudes of Trump, and it is this perceived gap that gives liberals and conservatives their most cherished principles to defend. The danger today, they say, is that the Idea may be discounted, buried under a blanket of false universalism. See also American exceptionalism References Further reading Bayor, Nicholas D. and Edwin A. Homans. How the American Dream Came to America: 1848 to the Present. 3rd ed. New York: W.W. Norton & Co., 2004. Anna Swanwick (née Anna Odell; November 9, 1832 – February 11, 1904) was an American educator, abolitionist, and suffragist. She was also a leading actress of the American stage, known for her talent in comedy and tragedy. Her acting career spanned four decades, from the early 1850s until just before the start of the American Civil War in 1861. Born in Milford, Maine, Swanwick was the daughter of Nathaniel Odell and Anna (née Hadley) Odell. The family was established in Milford and moved to Camden, Maine, in the late 1820s. After attending a common school, Swanwick spent two years teaching school herself. Beginning in 1854, Swanwick was actively involved in the abolitionist movement, working with the Worcester Women's Anti-Slavery Society. Her activities helped bring about the passage of the Fugitive Slave Law of 1793, which mandated that runaway slaves be returned to their owners. Because of her work with the abolitionist movement, Swanwick was forced to leave her teaching post. In 1855, Swanwick married British author Samuel Croker Swanwick. The couple had three children: Nathaniel, Anna, and Elizabeth. That same year, Swanwick's father died and the family moved back to Camden. Her husband died in 1858. From 1861 to 1865, Swanwick performed with the traveling Shakespearean theater company of Charles Fechter. During this time, she also raised her children. In 1865, Swanwick married William H. Rinehart, with whom she had three more children. She began working in education, eventually founding a private school. Swanwick died in Camden in 1904. She was 80 years old, becoming one of the oldest people in the United States at the time of her death. She was buried in Camden. In 1975, she was inducted into the Maine Women's Hall of Fame. Her papers are preserved at the New York Public Library.

The term "Science on the Verge" was coined in 2010 by the National Academy of Sciences to emphasize the role of fundamental science in modern society. Fundamental science, which can be defined as the study of structure, behavior and properties of matter and its components, is the foundation of modern technology. Since the 18th century, many technological advancements have been spurred by new discoveries in physics, chemistry, and biology, including the scientific discoveries that led to the production of polio vaccine, discovery of antibiotics, and identification of the DNA double-helix. As part of this role, the National Academy of Sciences describes that "fundamental science must be accessible to all". The term "Science on the Verge" has been adopted by several organizations, including the National Science Foundation, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and many universities, including Harvard, Oxford and MIT. Despite the benefits of fundamental science, access to fundamental science is becoming increasingly challenging, due in part to the costs of conducting research and the time required to produce meaningful results. This creates an inequality in knowledge acquisition where the average citizen does not have the same access to knowledge and discovery as historical periods past. Further compounding the issue is the fact that science is also becoming more specialized; to perform research in a specific field of science, one must have extensive training in that particular field of science. This creates a situation where the general public is not only hindered from accessing scientific knowledge, but they may not even know how to find such knowledge if they did have access. Therefore, the National Academies propose the Science on the Verge Initiative, which calls for making fundamental science accessible to all through techniques such as remote access, automation, and visualization. The initiative also highlights the importance of encouraging collaboration between different scientific fields, as well as between scientists and other artists in innovation centers, in order to promote cross-disciplinary and cross-cultural connections, and create a greater emphasis on meaning and discovery in scientific research. Overall, the Science on the Verge initiative promotes a " Science that Serves the Verge " -- in which fundamental science, by increasing accessibility and expanding the impact of research, will allow society to "create a better world through understanding, discovery, and innovation".

It has a picturesque church and a school which are both from the 19th century. Parchowo has a municipal swimming pool, a library, a football pitch and a cider mill. In World War II, Parchowo was almost entirely destroyed by the Germans. The Germans murdered almost the entire village's population - almost all of the villagers were locked into the church, and then burned to death. It was one of the cruelest German crimes committed in the Sandomierz district. The village was rebuilt after the war, but its population remains much smaller than before the war - this is largely due to migration and not many people wish to live in a place from which one's ancestors murdered one's family members just a few years earlier. The nearby hamlet of Olszanka was almost entirely destroyed by a mudslide on 12 September 2016. There is a local hiking trail with a total length of about 14 kilometres. It is partly signposted in English. Parchowo is located near the ancient city of Gniew, and it is an important transport link between Parchowo and Kruszynianki (on the other side of the river)" Wisznaczka). The village was the site of a Holocaust memorial on 6 November, the date when, according to the German Wikipedia article, the Germans murdered almost the entire village's population. The memorial stands at the location of the so-called death house, where the Germans murdered almost the entire village's population. It is a brick building with a plaque and a cross. A local historian and writer, Zygmunt Barczyński, inaugurated it on 6 November 2005. The village was founded in the 1330s as a German settlement, and was renamed Parchowerland in German in the 1590s. Its name in Polish is either Parchowo or Parchowerland, the latter is more commonly used in contemporary times. In the 19th century the village belonged to the Łowicz district of Congress Poland. In the Second Polish Republic, Parchowo was part of Krasnobród County. After World War II, the village was again part of Congress Poland, this time Łódzkie, and since 1954 of Sandomierz County, where it has remained. In the 1945 population census, the village was almost entirely destroyed by the Germans, and its population was around 140. It has not had a large population ever since, and in 2007 its population was only 218. In the early 21st century, Parchowo was declared a Centre of Culture and Education, a status it lost in 2016. Else Holmelund Minarik (March 20, 1901 – December 9, 1983) was a Norwegian-American children's book author best known for her 47 books about a fictional character, Annabelle Lane. Many of Minarik's books were adapted to animated films, a few were made into television series and one was made into a stage musical. Minarik was born in Norway and came to the United States as a child. She wrote children's books in the 1930s through the 1960s, getting her first book, The Bear Family, published in 1935. Several of her books were inspired by her own experiences as a child in Norway. Many of Minarik's books featured a fictional town called St. Paul's Acres. In some of the books, Annabelle Lane's Uncle Morgan lived in St. Paul's Acres. Morgan was inspired by Minarik's father, who in real life was an engineer with the railroad. One of Minarik's more famous books, The Gingerbread Man, was published in 1960 and featured a gingerbread man as the protagonist. The story takes place in a period when people still feared witches. Minarik's father died when she was 12 years old. The death had a profound influence on her, and many of her books dealt with death and loss.

Austroriparian is a term used in Australia to describe someone who is a citizen of Australia but was born outside of Australia. According to the Australia identity and immigration policy framework, a person is an Australian citizen if they are either: - A national of another country where Australia has a bilateral agreement to provide citizenship to former citizens, or - A citizen of another country that has a treaty relationship with Australia, or - An Australia-specific citizen by descent if they have at least one parent who is an Australia citizen Although being an Austroriparian is not a crime, it can have consequences, including affecting one's ability to obtain employment in Australia and having access to social security. The usage of the term Austroriparian has been criticized as being misleading by people who are citizens of other countries who are born in Australia, because they are not Australorians but instead live-in immigrants, and by people who are citizens of Australia who are born outside of Australia. In February 2020, the Australian government passed the Migration Legislation Amendment (Australian Citizenship Entrenchment and Other Measures) Act 2020, which deals with the question of what it means to be an Australian citizen. This act includes criteria which must be met by someone in order for them to be an Australian citizen, which includes meeting one of four criteria based on where a person was born: 1. They must be a national of a country which has a bilateral agreement with Australia to provide Australian citizenship to former citizens; or 2. They must be a citizen of a country which has a treaty relationship with Australia; or 3. They must be an Australia-specific citizen by descent if they have at least one parent who is an Australian citizen; or 4. They must be born in Australia of at least one parent who is an Australian citizen. The government's intentions for this act have been questioned, including by the Australian Council of Federal Women, whose president, Sophie McNeill, said, "it feels like they are targeting migrant women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and essentially imposing a maternity test." The Australian Immigration Minister, David Coleman, described the proposed act as clarifying the law and correcting "erroneous understandings of the law", rather than targeting migrants. There have been attempts to abolish the term Austroriparian, with one person tweeting, "Celebrities get asked a lot if they are Austroriparians. It's usually followed by an implication that they should go back to where they came from. I propose we petition Jelloreppa, the God of Austroriparians, to make them obsolete. The first step would be to remove the word from the English dictionary." Despite the criticism of the term Austroriparian, there is a considerable community of people who self-identify as Austroriparian or who are born outside of Australia but have parents who are Australian citizens. The Christmas holiday is an occasion celebrated by many people around the world. While Christmas traditions have varied widely by region, many people celebrate by celebrating with family, exchanging gifts and foods, attending services of various denominations, and often playing Christmas music or caroling. While commercial interests have capitalized on the popularity of Christmas for decades, the commercialism of the holiday has increased substantially in recent years, leading to the creation of nonprofit organizations like the ADT Corporation (formerly the American Christmas Tree Association) which works to combat commercialism and preserve the ethos of the holiday. The popularity of the holiday has also resulted in a proliferation of Christmas-themed media, ranging from movies and books to music and TV shows. While many celebrate the holiday, not everyone celebrates it enthusiastically. For some, the commercialization of the holiday is a source of frustration and stress. Christmas and its associated terms have developed a strongly negative association with militarism and weapons. As a result, people who serve in the military are often shunned during the Christmas season in many cultures. This has led to the evolution of such traditions as "Don't ask, don't tell," where soldiers are not allowed to mention their affiliation when around those who do not celebrate Christmas. The negative aspects of the Christmas holiday are countered by its emphasis on family, giving, and good cheer. Accordingly, even those who do not celebrate Christmas typically enjoy the festivities of the holiday, in part thanks to the enjoyment of those around them.

Sašo Mijalkov (Cyrillic: Сашо Mijalkov) (born 9 October 1968) is a Serbian chess grandmaster, author and trainer. He was awarded the GM title in 1998 and the International Master title in 1989. He was the Yugoslav champion in 1983, 1984, 1985, 1987, 1988, 1990, 1994, 1997, 1998 and 2003. Mijalkov was the European U18 champion in 1980 and the European U20 champion in 1986. He won the Yugoslavian blitz championship four times (1982, 1986, 1987 and 1988). Mijalkov represented Yugoslavia in the Chess Olympiad, where he scored 10½ points, and the World Junior Chess Championship, where he placed third. He is the author of two chess books, My Chess Adventures (1998) and Think Like a Grandmaster (2004). His current ability rating is 2817 and he has a chess blog where he posts his most recent games and comments on the chess news. He is employed as a trainer in the chess department of the Novi Sad sports society "Garden". Mijalkov was born in Kikinda. He started playing chess at the age of five and won his first tournament at the age of seven. He studied electrical engineering at the University of Novi Sad, but chess became more important to him. He graduated in 1989 and began working as a chess trainer. In 1998, Mijalkov became a grandmaster at the age of 26, the youngest in the history of the chess grandmasters' group. He trained many players who achieved high ranks in the international chess competitions, such as world champion Veselin Topalov. He also acted as a coach for different chess players, such as Soner Erdei. In 1999, Mijalkov participated in the International Chess Festival in Beijing representing Yugoslavia. He was awarded the FIDE Congress Award for "Best Personalities in Chess" and the FIDE Congress Award for "Most played chess game of the year". In 2002, he won the FIDE Grandmaster Award, the International Arbiter Award and the FIDE Trainer Award. In 2004, he won the International Master Award. In 2006, Mijalkov was the winner of the "Lasko-Chess Award" awarded by the US Chess Federation. In 2010, he took part in the World Senior Chess Championship, where he shared ninth place, and in the 39th Chess Olympiad, where he scored 7 points. In 2014, he was the second International Master. In 2015, Mijalkov won the FIDE President election in Budapest. Mijalkov is married and has two daughters. He supports SSC Yugolavia. In December 2016, Mijalkov was appointed FIDE Vice-President. Mijalkov's Elo rating is 2798. He is the No. 31 ranked grandmaster in the world as of December 2016.

Adrian Favell (born 24 August 1957) is an English former footballer who played as a forward in the English Football League for Brighton & Hove Albion, in the South American League for Gimnasia y Esgrima de Jujuy, and in the American Soccer League for the Brooklyn Cobras. He also played in the Football League for Brentford. Favell returned to England in the 1980s and played non-league football for Dover, Dover United, Eastbourne, Hastings & Heart of Sussex, Horsham, Tunbridge Wells & Kenton, Whitehawk, Brondesbury, Hendon, Hounslow, Croydon & Ashford. He also played representative football for Argentina at Under-20 and Under-23 level. In 2011, he was inducted into the Sussex County Football Association Hall of Fame. In 2014, he was voted into the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) Football Association Hall of Fame. Adrian Favell lives in Spain with his wife and two children.

The Witten–Schwelm railway was a branch line in the German state of Thuringia that was operated by the eastern suburbs Railway Company (Eastern Suburbs network, Eisenbahndirektion Berlin) between Witten an der Lausitz and Schwelm. The 14.4 km long line was officially opened on 5 June 1879 and was initially operated with three tracked vehicles. Since 1901, the Witten–Schwelm railway was operated by the Berliner Regionalebahn, and up to the electrification of the section from Emmerichsburg to Gotha in 1902, it was one of the most important links to Weimar Classicism. A four-tracking of the line from Emmerichsburg to Gotha was completed in 1904 and this section is currently operated with double track. Between 1913 and 1917, the line was also integrated into the newly built mainline from Berlin to Munich, thus achieving a total length of 28.4 kilometres. In the World Wars, the railway was heavily damaged, and between 1945 and 1950, it was completely destroyed. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the track was restored from 1990 to 1993 and subsequently rebuilt with many bridges in severely damaged condition as a supported viaduct structure. Alien Autopsy (2004) is a found footage horror film written and directed by Adam Winters. It is a remake of the 1998 film of the same name, which in turn is a remake of the 1977 film Alien Autopsy. The film follows a team of medical students who arrive at a remote medical facility in the desert to conduct an autopsy on a Xenomorph that was recovered from an expedition ship that suffered a catastrophic systems malfunction. However, the autopsy is complicated by other, more sinister, forces. The film premiered at South by Southwest on March 14, 2004 and was released on DVD on December 15, 2004 by New Line Home Video. It received negative reviews from critics and has become a cult film. A sequel, Alien Autopsy 2, was released on March 15, 2021. It has also inspired three music tracks: "Alien Autopsy (Picks from the Etherie)", “Alien Autopsy (Riptide mix)” and "Alien Autopsy (Riptide dub mix)". Plot Alien Autopsy tells the story of a team of medical students who arrive at a remote desert research facility to conduct an autopsy on a Xenomorph that was recovered from an expedition ship that suffered a catastrophic systems malfunction. The students, led by Walter (Wes Studi), who was responsible for damaging the ship'scommunication systems in an attempt to make the crew appear dead, cautiously explore the facility, setting up a number of security cameras around the Xenomorph's holding cell. Upon reaching the holding cell, they discover that the Alien has reacted aggressively to the deprivation it has suffered, creating a carnivorous environment and attempting to kill the human occupants. The students struggle to repel the Alien, and one is injured in the process. The remaining students retreat to the security center, where they access the facility's schematics and monitor the Xenomorph as it kills several facility workers. The facility's operations director (Chris Mulkey), who has watched the Alien's attempts to kill the humans with detached anxiety, facilitates a conference call with the expedition's leader, Dr. Alan Smith (Jerry O'Connell) and the ship's engineer (Craig Wetheridon). The team determines that the Xenomorph was incubating deep within the abandoned research complex when the expedition landed, and the rapid growth of its outer casing suggests that it will become capable of space flight in a matter of days. Dr. Smith elects to evacuate the facility, but informs the students that an orbiting space station is unsympathetic to their request for assistance, and that their only other option is to repair the station's communication system to alert the necessary authorities. Walter, who has become increasingly agitated by the students' questions and their presence in the facility, confronts Dr. Smith in an attempt to convince him that their best chance of survival is to destroy the Alien. Dr. Smith, skeptical of Walter's claims, refuses to take any action until the station's orbit is secure. Walter takes this as an opportunity to sneak into the facility's upper levels and attempt to gain direct access to the Alien, assuming it will be unable to follow him without the aid of the launch bay's manual controls. The orientation of a screen can be specified using a unit vector in two dimensions: horizontal (0, 1) vertical (0, -1) This orientation may differ from the physical orientation of the device: a smartphone may be portrait mode despite having a screen that can be rotated. The Fortified position of Liège or Liège Infantry fortifications is a military engineering formation adopted by the Belgian fortress of Liège in 1883 to enable it to resist modern artillery attacks. The Liège citadel, located in the section of the city called Le Gand, is surrounded by an extensive system of forts, ditches, and redoubts covering a surface of nearly two square kilometres. The entire complex is flooded by the River Meuse, making it difficult for enemies to carry out attacks from the outside. The fortress held out for eight months in the opening stages of World War I before being compelled to surrender. The adoption of the fortress system began in 1857, at a time when Belgium was suffering from invasions from numerous sides: from the North, Prussia; from the East, the Ottoman Empire; from the South, France. To the West, the whole of Belgium was under the control of King Leopold II. A city like Liège, well placed and protected by rivers, had many advantages for both defence and attack. The citadel is located in the middle of the city, with direct access to the buildings of the upper town and the country, as well as the railway station. Besides its natural strengths, the Liège citadel has an outer ring of forts built at equal distances, with a "trench" of 15 metres between them. This trench makes it possible to reinforce the inner ring. The forts are situated in a convex arc of 130 kilometres centred on the citadel, this is to allow the guns of the forts to cover a large extent of territory. It has a "cemetery" of 34 km in radius, and a "supply" of 21 km. The forts are surrounded by a 30-cm-thick network of walls and ditches. In addition to these massive defences, the citadel of Liège has a powerful military organisation, with many barracks and schools for the command and supply of troops. The works were the creation of an international team, made up of contributors from France, Prussia, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Chaim Gross (September 22, 1905 – January 22, 1981) was an American rabbi and Zionist leader. He became known as the "Poet of Zion" for his Hebrew verse published during the period of Israel's birth and early years. He also became famous for his Holocaust memoir, August 1, 1939, about his family's escape from Poland to the Soviet Union in 1939, and subsequent escape from the Soviet Union to Canada in 1940. The book became a foundation work for the concept of the "abandoned Jewish cemetery" and the right of return for Jewish refugees. Gross was born in Brooklyn, New York, to Romanian-immigrant parents. After being educated in local Talmud Torah schools, he was sent to school in the Bronx. As a youth, Gross was active in his local congregation, and later in the Hebrew Academy of Long Island, where he studied modern Hebrew and religion. In 1927, Gross went to London to seek out Yaakov Yisrael Rudnik, a world-renowned Poet of Zion who was coming to England to raise money for Zionist causes. Rudnik advised Gross to go to Tel Aviv, and Gross moved to Israel two years later. He became a Rabbi and taught at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, as well as at the Jerusalem Teachers' College. Gross became known as the Poet of Zion for his Hebrew verse published during the period of Israel's birth and early years. A founder of the Association for the Promotion of the Hebrew Language and the chairman of the jury for the Avraham-Shneour Zion Poetry Prize, he is regarded as one of the major figures in the revival of the modern Hebrew language. In 1937, he immigrated to the United States, where he founded the Hebrew Institute of Merchant Marines, an educational organization with an immersive, acculturative philosophy. In 1945, Gross joined the organized American Jewish community, and for decades he worked for the establishment of a united Jewish state. As President of the Jewish Community Council of the City of New York, he was a leading supporter for the establishment of Jewish community centers in New York City. In 1977, Gross was awarded the Spingarn Medal, the highest award given to African Americans by the African American community. On January 22, 1981, Gross died in his New York City apartment at the age of 76. During his life, Gross received numerous awards, including the Bollingen Prize for Lust for Life (1967) and August 1, 1939 (2009), a posthumous Nobel Prize in Literature. Since at least the 1940s, Gross' family burial plot at the Belanger Cemetery in St. Lawrence, Quebec, Canada, has been marked by a tombstone with his name and the dates 1940-41-42, marking the dates of his escape from the Soviet Union to Canada. The Jewish community of St. Lawrence has marked other cemeteries belonging to its members with similar stones. The practice came to be known as GrossEMPTY, as exemplified by August 1, 1939. The August 1, 1939'''s acknowledgement of the Jewish tragedy of the European Holocaust and the right of return for Jewish refugees have contributed significantly to Israel's status as a modern nation-state and to its ability to attract international support for the establishment of a Jewish state.

The Word on the Street is a literary festival held in Bristol, England. It was established in 2014 and is organised by the University of Bristol and the Society of Authors. Since its inaugural year, the Word on the Street has grown in size and stature, attracting authors such as Paula Hawkins, JK Rowling, Alain de Botton, and Margaret Atwood. The event is not-for-profit and all profits are donated to charity. The festival is held annually over three days in July, usually at the University of Bristol's Custom House campus. The event is well received by the literary community, with some referring to it as the "rising star of the literary festival circuit". The Word on the Street features renowned authors giving public talks in front of an audience, as well as panel discussions and book-signings. There are also children's activities and a dedicated Fantasy Forest for children to enjoy. The 2014 festival featured Margaret Atwood, Alain de Botton and JK Rowling. Subsequent speakers have included Paula Hawkins, Tim Lott and Louise Rennison. In 2019, it was announced that Rory Stewart would be the festival's first ever guest of honour, giving a talk on his travels in Mongolia. Stewart is a former British diplomat, writer and campaigner, who was made famous after walking across Afghanistan. In 2021, Paula Hawkins was forced to cancel her talk due to vocal concerns over her scheduled visit. The festival offered Hawkins alternative options, but she ultimately cancelled due to the circumstances. In 2022, the festival sold out in minutes. A further 5,000 tickets had to be released to meet demand, with staff working through the night to accommodate the influx of applications. This year's festival will feature Margaret Atwood on the main stage on the Saturday, with a panel discussion with her in the Afternoon Symposium on the Sunday.

The George Kent Performance Hall is a 3,006-seat multi-purpose arena on the campus of UCLA in Los Angeles, California, USA. The hall was named in honor of billionaire real estate developer George Kent and was opened in 2016. The facility hosts UCLA Bruins basketball and other events. The arena has two levels and was designed by Gensler, a large architecture and design firm headquartered in Los Angeles. The hall is circular in shape, with a blue seat featuring the Bruin logo, embedded into a blue curved floor. The architect of the hall, Kazuyo Sejima of SANAA, said of the design, "The circular shape can generate openness. We can see all the way to the other side." The building utilizes geothermal energy and has a green roof. The hall contains meeting and dining spaces, as well as a kitchen that is open to the arena. The arena hosts UCLA basketball games, as well as concerts, public events, and other sporting events. UCLA paid $189 million for the venue, the most expensive in the school's history. The facility replaced the Pauley Pavilion as the home of the Bruins basketball team and also serves as a meeting and convention center on campus. Seating capacity for basketball is 17,775, but the UCLA basketball team intends to lower the capacity to 15,000 to be more compatible with the smaller venues the team plays in outside of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) tournament. The arena has hosted two Final Fours, in 2022 and 2024. The hall is located on top of an open-air plaza that can be used in warm-weather months. The plaza is home to a farmer's market and other events during the spring, summer, and fall. The hall was involved in multiple controversies during its construction. The Bruin Club, which manages Bruin basketball games at the arena, initially sued the university in an effort to control costs associated with events there. It dropped the suit after reaching an agreement with the university, but some students criticized the university for the terms of the agreement. When the school accepted a donation from the educational foundation of entrepreneur Daniel X. Moloney to name the arena after himself, many students opposed the donation. Ultimately, Bruin fans protested, forcing the school to select another candidate, Kent, who is active with the school and local philanthropic efforts. The facility has been successful in its event bookings. UCLA has presold more than 1.5 million tickets for basketball events in the arena, making it the most popular venue on campus. The arena and plaza were designed to accommodate 25,000 people for concerts. The facility hosted the 2023 Americana Music Awards and the 2024 Billboard Music Awards. The facility hosted the finals of the 2019 NBA draft on June 7 and the 2020 NBA draft on June 19. The Los Angeles Clippers of the National Basketball Association (NBA) also lease office space in the building, as does the UCLA men's and women's basketball teams. The Bruins men's and women's basketball teams also play some of their home games at the arena. The building was recognized by the American Institute of Architects with the Alvar Aalto Award for distinguished achievement in architecture. It won the 2018 Pollstar Sports & Music Awards Arena of the Year award, and it was a finalist for the 2019 Institutional Architect of the Year award.

Kanreki dohyō-iri (かんれentiallyiries/cretely translated as Kanreki Window Inversion) is a type of space-time inversion first introduced in 2000 by Japanese video game developer Suikoden. The term was coined as a contrast to the more popular space-time inversion angle, Tensaitransformed. Suikoden's inversion dedicates one part of the inversion to science, while the other part flirts or reverses the initial sentiment. This inversion is typically applied to commercials, trailers, and songs to add flavor to the content. In video games Suikoden series Suikoden IV (2000), introduced the Kanreki dohyō-iri. When applied to a trailer or song, the inversion reverses the intended sentiment. Suikoden V (2001), introduced the Tensaitransformed. Suikoden III (2002), introduced the Shakunetsuaru inversion, which combines the Kanreki dohyō-iri with Tensaitransformed. Suikoden: The Revealed Secret (2004), introduced the Shirokini inversion, which further combines the Kanreki dohyō-iri with Shakunetsuaru and Tensaitransformed. Suikoden: Tenke no Kuchibiru (2006), introduced the Shōnen inversion, which replaces the Shakunetsuaru inversion's Tensai with Shonen. Suikoden: Perusion (2008), introduced the Aka inversion, which replaces the Shōnen inversion's Shonen with Aka. Suikoden: Super Fusion (2010), introduced the Fantasia inversion, which replaces the Shakunetsuaru inversion's Tensai with Fantasia. Suikoden: Dark Seeds (2012), introduced the Ais inversion, which replaces the Fantasia inversion's Aka with Fantasia. Suikoden: Tillers of the Soil (2016), introduced the Noriyori inversion, which combines the Ais inversion with Fantasia and Tensaitransformed. Suikoden: Harmonia (2021), introduced the Kize inversion, which combines the Noriyori inversion with Shakunetsuaru and Tensaitransformed. Other video games Space inversions have also been used in Japanese games outside of the Suikoden series, such as the popular fighting game Under Night In-Birth. Saul Teukolsky (February 22, 1915 – January 1, 1996) was a Russian-American theoretical physicist and professor at the University of California, Berkeley, where he worked on relativity and quantum mechanics. His work included the Teukolsky equations, which are used to study black holes. He was a leading member of the Group for Study of the Dismissal of L. B. Okun from the Academy of Sciences of the USSR. Born in Moscow, Russian SFSR, Teukolsky studied at the University of Moscow and after independence, in 1946, he moved to the US, where he obtained a Ph.D. in 1948, with a thesis titled "The equations of gravitation for harmonic maps of the two-sphere into the three-dimensional sphere". In 1948, he joined the University of California, Berkeley, where he became a professor and founded the Black Hole Initiative. In 1964, Teukolsky published a paper with William Press and Arthur W. Knoll on the excitation of gravitational waves by extreme mass-ratio collisions. The resulting excitation of the radiative waves was termed whimsical bar mode, after the colloquial name of the solution's mathematical vehicle, the bar mode. During the Cold War, Teukolsky was a member of the Group for Study of the Dismissal of L. B. Okun from the Academy of Sciences of the USSR. The group was organized by Harvard science historian Joseph DSHIFT. Teukolsky was a member of the American Physical Society, the National Academy of Sciences, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 1975, he became a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was also a member of the Washington DC based think tank Science and International Security. In 1980, he became a founding member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. In 1983, he became a Fellow of the American Physical Society.

Archelaus was a Greco-Roman Bishop of Carrhae who was martyred around AD 93. Carrhae was a town located in the Roman Province of Armenia, modern day Turkey. Archelaus was a member of the Monophysite sect of Christianity and took part in the Council of Ephesus in AD 431. The council rejected the Council of Chalcedon, which had settled a dispute between the Oriental and Eastern churches, and declared that Mary, the Theotokos, had a single nature but not a single person. Archelaus and his council were exiled as a result and took refuge in the Kingdom of Khuzestan in southwestern Persia. It was here that he was assassinated by some local Christians and beheaded. Archelaus was canonised some fifteen centuries later by the Armenian Apostolic Church in the 4th century AD, with several later churches and monasteries being named after him. There is a Greek episcopal see still in operation today, named after him as Catraensis (in Latin, Archelaia) His life is celebrated on November 25. married. His see was later renamed as Sebaste (meaning bishop of Rome) and later Catholicism absorbed the rest of the Armenian Church. Today he is commemorated in the Eastern Orthodox, Catholic, and some Anglican churches. It is said that Archelaus still has a church in Carrhae.

Cronenberg is a city in Wuppertal, Germany, and the capital of the Senate District of Wuppertal, its administrative centre. It is located in the Lower Rhine region, near the border with the Netherlands, and approximately 30 kilometres (19 mi) east of Duisburg and Düsseldorf and 45 kilometres (28 mi) west of Cologne and is part of the Rhein-Ruhr metropolitan region. In 2018 it had a population of about 170,000.[1] Wuppertal was first mentioned in a document from 737, and was directly subordinated to the Holy Roman Empire in 1557. In 1870, it became part of Prussia. The city developed as a trading centre owing to its access to the railway system and the South Asia trade passing through it. The worldwide oil shocks in the 1970s led to an influx of jobseekers, and today Wuppertal is characterised as a commuter city. The University of Wuppertal was established in 1969 and is the city's main employer. The University consists of ten institutions and attracts about 14,000 students every semester. The city hosted several conventions of the European Union and of the Eurozone. It is also known as a health resort, and its climate is regarded as one of the most reliable in Germany. Wuppertal was granted city rights on 24 March 1128, making it one of the oldest cities in Germany. The city developed major trading connections owing to its position on the Rhine river and its access to the railway system. The South Asia trade passed through the city. Wuppertal is twinned with: West Midlands, United Kingdom; Charleston, United States; Créteil, France; Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of the Congo; Bloemfontein, South Africa; Lüdenscheid, Germany; Hildesheim, Germany; Soest, Germany; Lisbon, Portugal; Changhua, Taiwan; Fuzhou, China; Nur-Sultan, Kazakhstan; Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire; Arasafe, Romania; and Almaty, Kazakhstan.

The City of Nedlands is a statutory local government area in Western Australia, located roughly east of the state's capital, Perth. The city was named and first incorporated in 1908. Nedlands, meaning "to the North") was named after a pastoral property owned by the Pettus family, which also gave its name to Ned Pettus, a Western Australian pioneer. Nedlands is currently home to just over 30,000 residents. Nedlands shares borders with the city of Nedland to the south, as well as the Shire of Menzies to the east and west. The western border is formed by the Hamersley Range, with AvonLINK Industrial Area to the north. Several highways and arterial roads pass through Nedlands, including Rokeby Road, Galava Street, Ellis Street, Butler Road and High Street. The Lord Dudley Hospital and Fiona Stanley Hospital are also situated in Nedlands. Nedlands railway station is served by Transperth local bus routes, and also plays a major role in regional and long-distance train services, including the Spirit of the West and Indian Pacific. Nedlands is classified as a middle-income area according to the federal government's 290 category, and is also noted for its affordability in comparison to neighbouring suburbs such as Nedlands Primary School, which is considered to be one of the most expensive primary schools in Australia. The local member of the Western Australian Legislative Council is BridgetmLceyman, a member of the Liberal Party of Australia. The current president of the Council is Caleb Mc close. The mayor of Nedlands is Cr. Allen Christensen, who is a member of the Labor Party. The Council meets at the Civic Centre on Ellis Street, Nedlands.

On November 9, 2014, at approximately 10:30 p.m., four men in an SUV, James Hodgkinson, from Buffalo Grove, Illinois, attempted to assassinate Republican members of Congress and their staffs as they were leaving a baseball game. The gunman, who had recently lost his job, assaulted the members of Congress with a shotgun and a rifle. He shot Steve Scalise, the House Majority Whip, and others, before being killed by House Security. The incident was named the "Buffalo Grove ambush" by news outlets, as the shooter used a black BMW 4er with paper license plates, registered to him and his wife, as his getaway car. Hodgkinson spent time in Northern Virginia, where he apparently worked, and was familiar with the area, as evidenced by the license plates. The total confirmed deaths from the attack was 14, including the gunman. Many others were injured, some seriously. Hodgkinson was shot and killed by Capitol Police after he opened fire on the ball field. The incident reignited the debate around gun control in the United States, and raised awareness of assault rifles and their capabilities. Hodgkinson had purchased a large number of bullets, suggesting he was planning a much larger attack, and a short time before the attack he had commented online that he was depressed and ready to kill. He had a history of posting anti-Trump messages online, and was arrested for a similar offence eight months before the attack. The incident took place in the adjacent suburb of Arlington, Virginia, where the headquarters of the United States Federal Government are located. James Scalise, the House majority whip, was walking with other members of Congress to a baseball practice in nearby Arlingtoniana, when the shooting began. The practice was about a quarter mile from the site of the attack. As of March 2019, no official government report has been released, although a 150-page preliminary report was released to the public in June 2018. The Obama administration cleared the attack of being an act of terrorism. The gunman was described as mentally disturbed and possibly suffering from psychiatric illness.

The Amalgamut is a fictional planet and its people are the subjects of the annual novella "The Enemy of My Enemy" by Walter Jon Williams, which further develops the backstory for the planet and the Amalgamut civilization. The Amalgamut is the home of the Dark Force daemons, entity spawn of deepest Shaitan who infect worlds to spread chaos and corruption. The Enemy of My Enemy edited by Joseph D. Harlander Brennan McNiel, a powerful telepath in service to the Mind Drone of the Obsidian League, has been asked to take part in the invasion of the galaxy by the mysterious Client. It is soon learned that the invasion is being paid for by the Saa'aka'tyachin, an ultra-powerful androgynous alien race with whom history has mysteriously tangled itself. Centuries earlier, their hubristic leader, Com'had, allied with a group of humanity's enemies in an attempt to expel all biologics from Earth. Even today, Com'had thirsts for our extinction. To secure the necessary funds, the Saa'aka'tyachin hired the Client, an entity apparently composed of dark matter and bound to the service of the Saa'aka'tyachin. The Client will give the Saa'aka'tyachin anything they ask, as long as it furthers their plan to drive all biologics from the galaxy. The Saa'aka'tyachin invasion fleet is massive, numbering in its hundreds of thousands. Brennan and the others are tasked with penetrating deep into the heart of the Client's intelligence and manipulation networks, in the hopes of finding a way to thwart their plans and destroy the Saa'aka'tyachin. Brennan quickly discovers that the heart of the Intelligence network is a fluid and confusing place, full of shifting alliances and secret agendas. And yet, the most sinister development may be the rise of the Com'had, the darkest of Com'had's henchmen, in Brennan's own mind. As Com'had tightens his grip on power and begins to murder his enemies one by one, Brennan is faced with a horrible decision: To save the minds he's sworn to protect, or to save his own life... The Enemy of My Enemy is a story within a story, embedded in the novella "The Linguist" by Tonyxml. This has the effect of providing the reader with many layers of storytelling, each one building upon the others to tell a deep and complex story.

Mireille Soria (born January 5, 1955) is a French singer. She started singing at an early age, taking part in local television shows from the age of eight. She signed a contract with Philips Records at the age of 11. Soria rose to fame in the late 1960s as part of the female quartet Les Jaquelines. She achieved moderate success in her home country before moving to Canada in the early 1970s. There, she became a star in the English-language market with her rendition of "Un autre été". Her 1984 recording of Piaf's "La vie en rose" in its French version, titled "Vivre ces moments-là", became a hit in France and earned critical acclaim. In the 1990s, Soria performed numerous crossover songs in both French and English. She also had success with musical theatre songs. Soria had eight Top 10 singles in France, most of them with her duet partner Alain S@@. She also had many Top 10 hits in Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and Germany. Soria was awarded the Order of Cultural Merit in 2004. She is currently working on her autobiography. She is the mother of French singer M<La·la. She was made a Knight of the Legion of Honor in 2015. She was awarded the title of Officier of the Ordre national du Mérite in 2020. She performed at the 2022 Winter Olympics closing ceremony.

Geology of Libya -------------------- Libya is an African country on the southwestern corner of the Mediterranean Sea, north of Egypt and south of Chad. Libya has a small unicellular tradition of mountains, which are largely illiterate from tectonic activity. Libya's continental crust, which is about twice the thickness of the average African country, is enriched in heavy metals such as uranium and thorium, which are made slightly more abundant due to the relatively high level of granite in the country's rock make-up. Libya is not a seismically active country and there are no recent earthquakes with significant effects on human settlements. However, the Cyrene foundation stone was laid on the site of the ancient city of Cyrene in Libya, and the city was home to one of the world's largest Carnac stones, which commemorates Greek prisoners of war. Libya has many natural gas fields and was thought to have significant amounts of oil, but in 2011 these reserves were found to be insignificant. Geography Libya's climate is tropical and temperate. The southern areas have a desert climate, while the northern areas have a Mediterranean climate. Wildlife in Libya includes cheetahs, leopards, desert wolves, mountain caracals, golden jackals, vervet monkeys, rock rabbits, scops owls, European honey buzzards, bald ibises, red-tailed hawks, and barn owls. Agriculture in Libya consists of wheat, barley, rye, corn, vegetables, melons, and sunflowers. Libya has the fourth largest oil reserves in Africa, and some of the world's largest natural gas fields.

Harley's Dozen is a 13-episode television series that aired on The Discovery Channel in 2016. The series documents the lives of a group of friends in their late 20s and early 30s as they struggle with relationships, jobs and personal lives. The series premiere on January 18, 2016, ranked as the number one cable broadcast for that night in US across top three networks (Discovery, Fox and ESPN) in the adults 25-54 demographic. It was also the number one cable program for the entire week in the 25-54 demographic. The series was developed from an idea of Pat Godfrey, a former executive at The Discovery Channel and Diverse Forms, the company he founded with fellow executive producer Richard Lui serves as the CEO. The executive producer list includes several people with experience in reality television such as John Grace, Susie Ferschman, and Ian Pollock. While working on the series, Godfrey and Lui's goal was to create "the Real World" for the digital age. The show is set in Los Angeles, California and the crew houses are located in the Los Feliz area of the city. Harley's Dozen averaged 1.1 million total viewers during the premiere week, including 534,000 in the 18-to-49 demographic that the channel is targeting. The series also ranked as the number one cable program for the entire week in the 25-54 demographic. Harley's Dozen was renewed for a second season, but only 11 of the 13 episodes were filmed. Production delays caused by the 2017 Las Vegas shooting resulted in the second season premiere being pushed back to April 20, 2018. The series was again renewed for a third season, but once again only 11 of the 13 episodes were filmed.

The MAGEA3 gene is a tumor necrosis factor gene. It is located on chromosome 6p21.3 and it is expressed in a wide range of human tissues. The MAGEA3 gene is thought to have evolved under positive selection with functional implications.[1] The protein encoded has decoy activity and may inhibit the activity of transcriptional regulators such as RUNX1.[2] The MAGEA3 gene is believed to have been subject to positive selection in humans as a result of balancing selection[3] to provide a partial human immune response to account for the loss of other species-specific immunity genes during the evolution of humans from a state of predator immunity to a state of prey vulnerability. Advertisement The MAGEA3 gene is a highly polymorphic gene and several amino acid variants have been identified. Advertisement The MAGEA3 protein has been shown to bind RUNX1, a transcription factor that is involved in blood cell formation, and disrupt its DNA-binding activity. Advertisement The MAGEA3 gene is expressed in a wide range of human tissues and plays a role in preventing the formation of runt-related transcription factor 1 (Runx1) heterodimers, which are involved in blood cell formation. It is suspected that positive selection acted on MAGEA3 to provide a human immune response to account for the loss of other species-specific immunity genes during the evolution of humans from a state of predator immunity to a state of prey vulnerability.

Integral linearity is a property of certain mathematical functions whereby the integral of the function is the linear sum of the integrals of the function's straight line segments. An function is said to be integral linear if it satisfies this property. The following functions have this property: - linear functions - polynomials - exponential functions - logarithmic functions - definite integrals Examples of functions that are not integral linear include: - arctangent functions - inversion functions Applications of integral linearity include the areas of analysis, algebra, and geometry. In analysis it is used to show that the area of the region under a curve and above a linear function is the linear function's integral multiplied by the length of the interval; this is used in the substitution proof of the area between two curves. In algebra it is used to simplify the sum of the arithmetic and geometric means. In geometry it is used to show that the integral of a curve is the total length of the curve. Integral linearity was discovered and defined by French mathematician Gérard Desargues in the early 17th century. For further information see: integral linearity. He is best known for his theorem on integral linearity, which he discovered and defined in the early 17th century. For more information, see Gérard Desargues. Jean-Louis Leray (7 September 1914 – 20 May 2007) was a French mathematician known for his work in fluid dynamics, partial differential equations and ideal theories, particularly for his work on equations for incompressible inviscid fluids, the Navier–Stokes equations. Leray was born in Lille, France and grew up in Le Havre. After high school, he studied at the University of Paris where he was a member of theCollège de France, graduating with a PhD in 1941. In 1946, he joined the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) where he worked for the rest of his career. He was made a director of the Centre in 1966 and was appointed a researcher in 1954 and later director in 1964. Leray was also a professor at the University of Paris (suffering persecution during the Nazi occupation of France) and an Invited professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in 1948 and a professor at the University of California, Berkeley in 1961. Leray was elected a member of the French Academy of Sciences in 1970. In 1965, he gave the Rouse–Ffall–Winther theorem, now called the Leray theorem, on the uniqueness of solutions to the two-dimensional inviscid flow with finite energy over a given time interval. Leray's theorem has found numerous applications in the study of incompressible flow. In fluid dynamics, a velocity field is called a solution to the 2D Navier–Stokes equation, if the following three conditions hold: - the velocity field is Leray integrable - the divergence of the velocity field is zero - the velocity field satisfies the Navier–Stokes equation A vorticity field satisfying the following two conditions: - the vorticity field is Leray integrable - the velocity field satisfies the Biot–Savart law is called a solution to the 2D Euler equations. For a more detailed discussion of Leray's theorem, see Rouse–Ffall–Winther theorem. In partial differential equations, Leray's theorem generalises the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem to initial conditions that satisfy a looser inequality, that is, it is not necessary to satisfy the equality conditions. In ideal theories, Leray's theorem is a fundamental result in the construction of adiabatic invariants. For more information, see Rouse–Ffall–Winther theorem. For more information on Jean-Louis Leray, see Jean-Louis Leray. The Leray theorem was discovered by Gérard Desargues in the early 17th century and was known under various names until it was re-discovered in 1965 by Jean-Louis Leray. His funeral was one of the largest the West Bank had seen in many years. The annual memorial assembly of the Bercherut Party includes a minute of silence in his memory. In 2010 the Israeli government declared a month of mourning for Angel, and after a year it established a financial assistance program in his memory. The exact circumstances of Angel's death remain unclear. On the day he was killed, a UN observer was present in the area and there were no reports of hostile fire. The weapon used in the shooting was a Belgian-made FN-15 semi-automatic rifle, a commonly-owned weapon. The IDF has never established who was responsible for the shooting. Initial reports claimed that Angel had been shot during a confrontation with the Palestinian Red Crescent, but more recent reports suggest the two groups were merely discussing possible access to the area where Angel was killed. Israel imposed a blockade on the area where Angel was killed, preventing the independent investigation of the shooting. During the first decade of Israel's occupation of the West Bank, more than 1,000 people have been killed in such "staged" confrontations. In some of these cases, Israeli troops have planted weapons on the bodies of dead Palestinians. In 2012, a group of Israeli and Palestinian students submitted a petition calling for the Israeli government to launch a civil suit against those responsible for Angel's death. If successful, the lawsuit would make Israel the first nation to try and held accountable someone who killed one of its citizens on its soil, in a case that has become known as "the Chicago of the Middle East."

Australopithecus africanus (affectionately known as "Taung child" after its proposed home) is a species of hominid attributed to a transitional form of Australopithecus. It is known from a fossilized partial cranium and lower jaw found in 1894 in a thin layer of clay, called the Black Skirt Clay, at Blombos Cave, South Africa. The specimen is approximately 3.5 million years old, during the Later Stone Age. The Taung Child is important in the context of early hominid evolution because it combines several features that, until then, had been seen only in separate genera or separate species. It has a mixture of ape and humanlike features, and it is transitional in that it possesses some ape characteristics, such as a small brain size, but it also has humanlike features, such as a larger brain case. The discovery of the Taung Child helped confirm the previously controversial claim that apes were not our ancestors, but evolved from a distinct hominid ancestor species. It was a missing link in our understanding of the early evolution of our species, Homo sapiens. The discovery of A. africanus also helped to show how humans came to inhabit every continent on Earth. The australopithecine foot is similar to that of apes, with a large toe and small toe, but the foot has a major adaptation for a chimplike diet: a stone-faced arch. This feature, combined with the presence of a backward-pointing hallux (big toe) and broad, flat foot, suggests that A. africanus had a diet of hard objects such as shells and seeds, and was partially able to function on the surface of the earth.
