George N. Turner (born George Nicholas Turner; July 24, 1938 – December 9, 1979) was an American aerospace engineer, astronaut, and NASA manager. He was an associate administrator of NASA and served as the agency's first chief of the Aerospace Safety division. He was killed in the crash of Eastern Air Lines Flight 66 aircraft in the Atlantic Ocean off Florida's northern coast. Turner was born in New York City, New York. He graduated from the City College of New York with a bachelor of science in engineering in 1960, and earned a master's degree in engineering from the University of Utah in 1963. Turner joined McDonnell Douglas in 1963. He became involved in astronaut training in 1965 and was selected as an astronaut in 1969. In 1974, Turner transferred to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). He was assigned as the manager for the FAA's Stationery and Fine Arts Program in Washington, D.C., then became chief of the FAA's Aerospace Safety Office. In this role, he became involved in the Challenger and Apollo 13 accidents. In June 1986, Turner was appointed as the first associate administrator of NASA's Office of Safety and Mission Analysis. On December 9, 1979, Turner died with his crew, which included Sally Ride, in the Eastern Air Lines Flight 66 crash off the coast of Florida. After his death, Turner was memorialized with the naming of the George N. Turner Space Museum in Cape Canaveral, Florida. The museum closed in 2016 and was put up for sale.

A Brush with Fame is an expression used to denote that one has encountered or accomplished something noteworthy but not in a noteworthy manner, such as by coming very close to completing a task, but failing to complete it. An example of this would be when one has received a promotion at work but instead of stating their thanks by leaving a gift on their superior's desk, they forget and take a trip to Japan. The American Heritage Dictionary defines Brush with Fame as "to come close but not quite achieve something great." It is often used to denote a positive experience, although not everyone likes this expression. The expression has led to the creation of the Twitter hashtag #ABraOFEarnest, used by people to express positive experiences without the usual jargon associated with modern technology. The brush with fame is used as a literary device to illustrate the vast differences in people's experiences of life, as even the most mundane occurrences can have profound significance to someone else. A noteworthy variation on this theme is John Green's July 27, 2011 versus July 27, 2023 letters, reflecting his experience with the former Rhodes scholarship and his fear that he might not be talented enough to write a good letter of recommendation for the latter award. This expression may have originated in a popular song entitled "A Brush With Death", written by Graham Lerner and published in 1972. The lyrics reference the song "A Sort of Miracle", by Leslie Bricusse, which was published in 1970. Both songs refer to an incident in which the singer narrowly escaped death. The first literary use of the expression "a brush with death" is found in a short story, "The Lady with the Lamp" by Richard Marsh. The story was later adapted into an episode of the TV show "Foyle's War". The phrase first came into popular culture via the 1972 song "A Brush With Death" by Graham Lerner. The phrase also appears in the poem "The Drinker" by Richard Siken, which was published in 1972. In 1977, the phrase was used in the film Riemann zutraumen, or "Turn On, Rainer", referring to a lover who passes away. Popular usage of the phrase increased in 1979, when the book Unusual Suspects: Writers on Writers, a collection of essays by Colin Harrison, was published. In one essay, "The Year of the Flood", author Michael Crichton described the experience of working on his screenplay for the film Theplicate. Crichton described the many difficulties he faced with the production, including various equipment failures and a devastating flood which destroyed most of his script. Crichton's editor, Richard McKean, suggested that Crichton use the phrase "a brush with fame" to characterize the experience. Popularity of the phrase continued to increase in the 1980s. In 1983, the phrase was used in the play Avenue Z by David Steinberg, and in 1984, the phrase was used in the feature film Executive Action, starring Michael Caine and Harrison Ford. Popularity of the phrase peaked during the 1980s. In 1987, the book "A Brush With Fame" was published, and in 1988, the TV show An American Brush with Fame premiered on ESPN. The phrase even inspired a Dire Straits song "The Metropolitan Football Match". Although the phrase has gained a negative connotation in recent years, as demonstrated by its coining as the name of the Twitter hashtag, the phrase remains a notable and popular literary device. While many will experience fame and fortune, a relatively small number will achieve remarkable success, and a small number will experience remarkable failure. The expression "a brush with fame" describes the latter experience. Although widely considered a negative term, the phrase is not meant to be derogatory. Robert Rolle (died 1660) was an English lawyer and politician who was a Member of Parliament for Lancashire. [1] He was born in Lancashire into a large gentle family and was admitted to the Middle Temple in 1619. He began his career in the Royal Navy in the mid-1620s and took part in the Spanish Match in the mid-1630s. Rolle was a prominent royalist during the English Civil War. He became a law officer in the King's Bench and was appointed a commissioner for mulcts in the North. He was a Member of Parliament for Lancashire in the Short and Long Parliaments, 1648 and 1659 respectively. [2] He was probably responsible for additions to the Muniments Room at Rolles in Lancashire, which he also ornamented with mural monuments. Rolle died in Lancashire in 1660 and was buried at Rolles. The will of his wife, Ann, was proved the following year. He had married Ann Fettiplace in 1634 and they had at least eight children, of whom six survived to adulthood. After his death, his daughter Elizabeth inherited the estate while another daughter, Margaret, married Sir Robert Strange of Upton and was the mother of Sir William Strange, 1st Baronet. His son Robert succeeded him as MP for Lancashire. References [1] 'Robert Rolle (died 1660)', in Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, online edition. Ada Bittenbender (née Black; November 7, 1816 – September 21, 1886) was an American educator and the first recorded African-American woman to earn a college degree. Bittenbender is credited with teaching abolitionist activism to other African-American students at Women's Medical College of Pennsylvania (now Drexel University). As a member of the Pennsylvania General Assembly and, later, the Pennsylvania State Senate, Bittenbender promoted equal rights for women and racial minorities. In 1876, Bittenbender was the first African-American woman elected to the Women's Education Association of New York's Executive Committee. Bittenbender was born into slavery in Kentucky, and worked as a domestic servant to make ends meet. Around 1838, Bittenbender's owner sent her to live with her older sister, who was married to a Philadelphia physician named John Newton Davisson. Bittenbender trained to be a schoolteacher and, in 1840, became the first recorded African-American woman to enroll in a college. She taught at what is now Drexel University for nearly thirty years. In 1861, Bittenbender was reunited with her husband, who had remained in Pennsylvania. Bittenbender did not publicly disclose her abolitionist activities while her husband was active in the Union Army. Following the war, Bittenbender separated from her husband and moved with her son to a predominantly white abolitionist community in Chambersburg, Pennsylvania. In 1871, Bittenbender enrolled at the Women's Medical College of Pennsylvania (now Drexel University). She successfully completed the three-year medical education program, becoming the first recorded African-American woman to earn a college degree. Bittenbender's graduation essay expressed concern that women would be devalued in medical journals if only men were allowed to perform surgical operations, and proposed that an all-black operating team demonstrate that women could be capable physicians. Bittenbender was denied entry into several all-white sororities, and she did not receive aid from her alma mater. She became active in the Pennsylvania General Assembly and, later, the Pennsylvania State Senate, where she lobbied for marriage and property rights for women and racial minorities. Bittenbender helped organize the Pennsylvania Equal Rights Association and became the association's vice president. In 1876, Bittenbender was the first African-American woman elected to the Women's Education Association of New York's Executive Committee. She retired from public life after the 1880s and continued to live in Chambersburg. In 1886, Bittenbender published her autobiography. She died two years later, aged seventy-six, after a protracted illness. Bittenbender was a published poet, essayist, and orator. She dedicated herself to African-American educational reform and political activism and was awarded an honorary doctor of laws degree by Wilberforce University in 1875. She was the first recorded African-American woman to earn a college degree and the first African-American woman to successfully complete a medical education program. Bittenbender was interred at the Mount Moriah Cemetery in Chambersburg, Pennsylvania. In 1936, she was posthumously inducted into the first class of the Black Hall of Fame at the Women's Medical College of Pennsylvania. In 2007, Bittenbender was recognized as an inaugural inductee into the Drexel University Vagabond and Stowaway Society, and a bust of her was installed in the lobby of the school's Philadelphia campus. In 2018, Bittenbender was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame.

To evaluate patient and treatment related factors contributing to the radiation dose to organs at risk (OAR) in prostate cancer patients treated with a stereotactic radiosurgery system. Between May 2014 and December 2016, 45 patients with clinical T1c-T3b N0 M0 prostate cancer were treated at our institution with a CyberKnife® mixed beam stereotactic radiosurgery system (Mx). The patients were evaluated for the degree of morphological tumor regression, biochemical control, and radiation dose to the OAR. The mean follow-up was 17.6 months. The median pre-treatment prostate specific antigen (PSA) level was 1.3 ng/mL and the median prostate gland volume was 43 cc. Biochemical failure was documented in 1 patient, and the estimated 2-year biochemical no evidence of disease was 93.5%. The median radiation dose to the prostate gland was 19.6 grays (Gy) and the median volume of the prostate gland receiving 35 Gy (V35) and 35.2 Gy (V65) were 1.6% and 6.5% respectively. The estimated 2-year dose-volume histogram parameters that correlated with biochemical failure were V35 (p = 0.045) and V65 (p = 0.022). No statistically significant correlation was found between PSA nadir, biochemical control, morphological regression, tumor risk group, age, and radiation dose to OAR. Mixed beam stereotactic radiosurgery of the prostate provides promising biochemical control rates in low- and intermediate-risk prostate cancer patients. Volumes of the prostate receiving 35.2 Gy and 35 Gy correlate with biochemical control. Future studies are necessary to establish the dose-response relationship between radiation dose to the prostate and OAR and clinical outcomes. Elkhart station is a train station in Elkhart, Indiana. It is one of three remaining Elkhart stations where intercity passenger rail can be boarded in the United States; the others are in Michigan City, Indiana, and Montour, Ohio. The station is owned by Norfolk Southern and is served by an 89-mile segment of the CSXline between Chicago and Detroit. Although the station is owned by Norfolk Southern, it is used by Amtrak as a stop, and is served by three trains per day in each direction; the Empire Builder, the Rock Island Zephyr, and the Texas Eagle. The Empire Builder and the Rock Island Zephyr both operate partial trains with only partial coaches, and the Texas Eagle has full-length trains. In February 2023, the station was the 10th-busiest in terms of Amtrak ridership. Elkhart was a shipping center on the Ohio and Mississippi rivers in the 19th century. By the late 20th century, the city was a wholly automobile-oriented community with little industry. In 2000, the city was named one of the best places to live in the United States by Money magazine.[2] AEP, IBM, Delphi, and General Electric all had significant operations in Elkhart, and the city has been called the Rolls-Royce of towns.[3] In 2013, Bloomberg BusinessWeek ranked Elkhart as one of the best small places to live in the United States.[4] Elkhart has also become noted as the home of the Harley-Davidson motorcycles, and was the setting of several scenes in the popular TV show and film Dodgeball: Anatomy of a Sliver.

Khunza Humayun Begum was a Pakistani education activist, poet and writer. She is credited with the creation of the first girl education school in Pakistan, established in 1919 in Lyari, Karachi. The school was officially named the Convent of the Sacred Heart and ran until 1947 when it was closed down by the new Pakistan government. Humayun was one of the educated mothers of Pakistan who struggled for the rights of girls. In response to the Muhammadan Girls' School, district schools for girls were established across the provinces of Punjab, Sindh and Balochistan. A national level campaign for the creation of such schools was also launched called the Mullenagar Jihad. In 1927, Humayun organised the first public reading of her poetry in public in Lyari. This was a huge step for a woman of her time as not many women of the subcontinent had the courage to publicly read their poetry. In 1930, she was one of the 50 delegates who represented the Lyari Residency at the All-India Women's Conference in Calcutta, West Bengal, India. She was appointed as an education magistrate by the British colonial government, one of the most difficult jobs to be had by an women of her time. She founded the Lyari Girl's School in 1919 and campaigned for the right of Muslim women to get an education. The Lyari Girl's School was closed down by the new Pakistan government in 1947. She died on 19 December 1950 in Karachi, Pakistan and was buried in the graveyard of the Sacred Heart Convent in Lyari.

Peromyscus (commonly known as deer mice) is a genus of approximately 20 species of small, hop-facing mice with a wide range of habitats. Many species are common residents of woodland areas throughout the Northern Hemisphere, while others are more specialized in habitat or range. Most species are listed as of Least Concern or near-threatened status, but a few are regionally significant pests. Peromyscus spp. are a genus of small, hop-facing mice with a wide range of habitats. The common species are found in North America as specialized habitat species or as regionally significant pests. Species: * Peromyscus maniculatus (the Striped Mouse) is found across much of North and South America, from southern Canada and the United States south to Argentina and Uruguay. It is also found in Mexico and Costa Rica. A. geraldinae, the Arizona Striped Mouse, is endemic to Arizona. * Peromyscus polius (the Deer Mouse) is found in North America from Canada to Mexico and from the northern United States to Guatemala. It is a common and widespread species found in a wide range of habitats including forest edges, brushy areas, shrubland, agricultural areas, suburban areas, and parks. A. p. melanophrys, the Davis Mountain Deer Mouse, is endemic to Davis Mountain Wildlife Refuge in California. * Peromyscus keeni (the Southern Deer Mouse), also known as the Antarctic Deer Mouse, is endemic to Antarctica. The only known population is on islands off the Antarctic coast, within the Antartica-South Americaerve. Etymology: The genus Peromyscus was named by Brooks and Montgomery in 1893. The specific epithet maniculatus means "little finger," referring to the pattern of bands on the mouse's tail.

Banja Luka International Airport or International Airport Mostar is an airport in Bosnia and Herzegovina, located in the city of Banja Luka, just south of the city center. The airport is used only for landing and taking off of small aircraft, namely general aviation and helicopters. The terminal was renovated in 2010. Currently the airport operates as a civil airport, being the only airport in Bosnia and Herzegovina which operates regularly scheduled commercial flights, with a weekly frequency in each direction between the airport and cities in Germany, Italy, Spain and Portugal. The airport is also a base for military aviation. As of January 2020, the airport is heliport only, with no passenger terminal available for use. Overton Loyd was an American entrepreneur. He was the founder of Loyd Wire Corp. and Janus Investment Corporation. He is known for conceiving and founding the Pan American Sports Associates (PASA) football league. The PASA league, created by Loyd, was an attempt to bring together 11 countries in the Western Hemisphere under one football league. The formation of the league was announced on December 9, 1960, and the inaugural tournament was scheduled to begin in September 1961 and run through February 1962. Ultimately, only Mexico and the United States participated in the first PASA tournament in 1962. Loyd is sometimes criticized for the failure of the PASA league. In a 2012 retrospective piece for the Guardian, Walter McKeller summarized Loyd’s legacy as follows: "His legacy, however, is to have kickedstart[ed] the process that led to the first pan-American football competition in over half a century. The first edition of the North American Nations Cup, in which Mexico, the USA and Canada took part, was held in 1965 – ten years after Loyd first proposed his idea. But by that stage he was no longer involved – by then he’d sold his interest in the sport to become a schoolteacher." The PASA league was ultimately short-lived. Loyd is quoted in a 2006 issue of the Pan American Union’s journal saying, "If PASA had lasted another year, we probably would have gotten many more countries into it."

Il Giardino dei Semplici (The Garden of the Simpletons) is a fable first published in Italian in 1855 and later translated in other languages. The fable tells of two travelers in a strange land who meet an Emperor and a Queen. The two Queens describe their gardens and invite the strangers to compare them with their own terrain. The Emperor's domain is described as a paradisal place full of Wisdom and Virtue, and he is invited to compare it with the two Kings' realms. The story concludes that it is folly to rely on "know-how and experience" alone, and that a "garden of simple pleasures" is also worth cultivating. The fable has been used in Italy for promoting a simpler way of life, traditional values and the beauty of simple things. The Italian word semplici (Simple ones) became a label for people strongly attached to traditional values and suspicious of modernism and mass media. The expression was popularized by the Italian philosopher Gianni Vattimo in his 1968 book La Traduzione del Silenzio. The Gardens of the Simpletons are an amusement park in the Province of Bergamo, Lombardy, Italy. The park was founded in 1935 as a sanctuary for rural simplicity, with leisure activities such as fishing, gardening, agriculture, basket weaving, music, library and photography exhibitions. The complex grew up over the years to include workshops, a restaurant, bar and hotel, and the culture of rural life. It is famed for its controversial portrayal of Italy in the 1970s, when the park was visited by popular comedy actors of the time, such as Totò and CarmeloAQ. The park was acquired by the Bollati family in the 1980s and ran into financial difficulties in the 1990s, but has since made a comeback and now operates a campground for youths as well as the amusement park. In 2004, the park was awarded the Kulturpreis des Landes Niederösterreich. The Italian language version of the fable, Il Giardino dei Semplici, was written by Giovanni Giuntella and published in 1855. The Garden of the Simpletons is also the title of an opera composed in 1986 by Claudio Cellai to a libretto by Vittorio Sgarbi. The opera was first performed at the Sala Verdi in Milan, conducted by Guido Cantelli with sets and costumes designed by Emilio Villa. The opera has been recorded on CD several times, including a 2008 recording by the Orchestra della Rai with conductor Gianandrea Noseda and a 2013 recording conducted by Pierluigi Cavarocchi with the Orchestra Sinfonica di Milano Giuseppe Verdi. The expression "il Giardino dei Semplici" has also been used as the name of a TV talk show presented by Paolo Ferrero. It is also the name of a column in L'Espresso, the weekly news magazine published in Italy. Il Giardino dei Semplici is also the title of a 2018 album by the French singer Grégoire Delort. The title is also the name of a 2019 reality show on Canale 5 TV, featuring a team of house guests staying at an "edelweiss" replica in the Dolomites. The fable has also been referenced in popular culture, such as in the 2016 single "Che dio ci aiuti" by the Italian singer Laura Pausini, which reached the top 10 in several countries, including Italy. The title of the song is inspired by the sentence "Nella veraamicità del Giardino dei Semplici Cristo può trovarsi" (In the authenticity of the Garden of the Simpletons Christ can find himself). The song was recorded by Laura Pausini during the 1998 tour "CentoVetrine", in support of her album of the same title. Italian media have also made comparisons between the popularity of the fable and the overall situation of the country in the 2020s. The fable has also been translated into other languages, including German and French. The German version was written by Nikodemus Bauer and titled "Die einfache Ernte" (The Simple Harvest), and was published in 1956. The French version was written by Christian Moras and titled "Le Jardin des simples" (The Garden of the Simpletons), and was published in 1959. The park also organizes a "writing competition for kids" every year, awarding a prize to the best short story on the theme of rural life.

Jayavarman II ( ; Rani Singha Devi; ; 1211 – 6 November 1293 CE) was king of the Paramara dynasty from 1243 to 1294. He ruled from His capital was in Tikjorpati in modern Bijayapura district, [formerly] Bhadgaon district, [formerly] Marathi country. He is also known by the names Jayawardhana and Parameshvara. He is recognised as the builder of the empire that came to be known as Mon- Buddhist [Newsarama] and Dharmaraja. He followed the path of Khmer expansion, led by Jayavarman III, and he ended the hostility with the Chola King Elara Citeri (1178-1217). He captured Dharampura and Kannada country and forced the Chalukya King Bijjala (1172-1242) to pay a tribute. He extended the kingdom to cover almost the entire present-day Madhya Pradesh, Maharastra and Karnataka regions. He is also credited with the construction of many tanks, temples and monuments across the kingdom, such as the Tungaratna Temple in Gangapurana, the Mahamandapa Temple in Udaypur, the main temple in Khajuraho, and Jagannatha Puri in Orissa. He is credited with bringing Jainism to the region. The religious and historical regions bear his name. He is succeeded by his son Jindiva, who was born of a queen whose image he had consecrated. The empire he built is sometimes referred to as the Dharmarajasara.

Panmixia is a biological phenomenon involving the spread of a single type of organism through a uniformly suitable environment. It occurs when the population distribution is spatially uniform and independent of the environment. In simple terms it means perfect spread. panmixia is a form of global uniformity. Its occurrence in nature is a rare event. In total 605 independent instances of panmixia have been documented since the phenomenon was first identified by Ernst Hanausek in 1879. These instances include nematodes, fungi, bacteria, micro-organisms, insects, plants and vertebrates. Spatial homogeneity and independence from the environment are key prerequisites for panmixia. These prerequisites are frequently not fulfilled in models of biological diversity, because they do not account for panmixia. For example, in species diversity patterns found by chance alone or triggered by immediate environmental influences do not show spatial homogeneity or independence from the environment. Examples of spatial homogeneity and independence from the environment include: - the spatial distribution of plants species along an elevation gradient, - the distribution of animals along an oceanic trench, - the distribution of mammal communities across the Canadian Arctic. However, when spatial homogeneity and independence from the environment are taken into account, diversity patterns commonly found in nature can be explained as instances of panmixia. Instances of panmixia in nature can have different causes. The main ones are cyclical fluctuations in population size, spatial movements of organisms along environmental gradients or density-dependent interactions. Researchers continue to debate the underlying mechanisms that give rise to panmixia. For example, is panmixia a passive response of populations to stochastic fluctuations or does it require proactive mechanisms to achieve spatial homogeneity? This form of global uniformity is a very rare event to observe in real world populations. The mechanisms that can lead to panmixia are often linked to the population dynamics of the organisms. Many instances of panmixia can be observed in populations of nematodes, fungi, bacteria, micro-organisms, insects, plants and vertebrates. Panmixia is an example of local uniformity: at the global level it occurs when all regions of a uniform environment are occupied, while at the local level it occurs when all individuals of a uniform population occupy the same region. Ghetto Kids are inner city or suburban children who wear castoff clothes from nicer neighbors. These children live in rough neighborhoods and wear clothes that are too nice for them, making them stand out in the community. Ghetto Kids may have few or no toys, and their environment may be run down or dangerous. Ghetto Kids typically live in single parent homes with a mother. The father is typically absent or absent due to drug or crime related problems. Ghetto Kids often live in fear because their parents lack the resources and commitment to provide a safe and stable environment. Murders of Ghetto Kids In 1992 in Atlanta, GA four children died from head injuries caused by negligent care. In 1999, four children from a Ghetto Kids family in Chicago, IL were murdered by their mother, who then turned the gun on herself. In 2006 in Milwaukee, WI, three Ghetto Kids were shot and killed by their mother, who was an active participant in a botched robbery. In 2008, a Ghetto Kids named Dora was murdered in Pittsburgh, PA after her father was shot and killed. Her murderer, Michael Ward, was only charged with first-degree murder because of a plea bargain. Ghetto Kids are often bullied at school and sometimes targeted by criminals because of their unfortunate circumstances. Even with all this, Ghetto Kids still have dreams and want to do better than their surroundings. They are often overachievers and do well in school despite all the challenges they face. Their desire to succeed often pushes them past their breaking point and motivates them to escape the ghetto and pursue their dreams in an effort to never contribute to the cycle of poverty that they were born into.

Benjamin Franklin Tracy (August 18, 1813 – December 15, 1868) was an American lawyer, politician and writer. He was elected as a Democratic Representative from Louisiana's 4th congressional district to the Thirty-fifth and Thirty-sixth Congresses (March 4, 1847 – March 3, 1853). He served as a regent of the University of Louisiana and as a senator in the Louisiana State Senate. He was also a presidential elector in 1848, selecting James K. Polk as President. Tracy was the son of Simeon Tracy, a Vermont lawyer and politician who became a Louisiana state judge, and a Louisiana-born lady named Margaret Knight. He was born in New Iberia and studied law in New Orleans. He was admitted to the bar and began a practice, but with the advent of the Mexican–American War he entered the military. He served with distinction, initially as a captain and then as a major. He was mustered out in 1847 and returned to private life. Arshin Mal Alan is an operetta, with a book by Brian Landuski and lyrics by Gregory Lopez, it has music by Laura Lee, composed by Victor Lopez. Set in a small Middle Eastern village, the story centers on Aimee, who is being courted by three of the village's eligible bachelors: the wealthy and eligible Zoran, the charming but poor-spirited Jamal and the dark and mysterious Driss. Australasian treecreeper (Clytoctuntus Nepalensis) is a passerine bird in the family Thraupidae. It is found in New Guinea and nearby smaller islands, with a small population on Biak in the Papua New Guinea. It is evaluated as least concern by the IUCN. This species is named for its remarkable voice, described by ornithologist Robert Swinhoe as "a sad, whistling flute, sometimes rising to a harsh scream". The call is a monotonous chattering, like that of a small child who has a hangover. The Australasian treecreeper is about 12.5–14.5 centimetres (4.9–5.9 in) long with a 13–15 centimetres (5–6.2 in) wingspan. The upperparts are greyish-brown with blackish wings and black tail, darker on the wings. The underparts are buff with dark barring. The adult has an orange crown, nape, and cheeks, while the juvenile has a darker head and has yellowish-buff upperparts. The rump is darker than the rest of the upper tail. This species is mostly found in primary forest, but also visits the forest edges, preferably low shrubs and bamboo. The nest is made from bark and leaves, with three or four blue eggs being typical. This species is susceptible to feather degradation from chickens and other domestic animals, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has rated its conservation status as "low risk". It occurs in several protected areas. The Australasian treecreeper is the only species in the genus Clytoctuntus. The generic name is from the New Guinean name for the black currawong, Clytoctus, and the specific name, nepalensis, is after the New Guinean name for Nepal.

Albertanus of Brescia (c. 1020 – c. 1080) was an Italian writer and Catholic churchman. He was active in the north Italian cities of Brescia and Bergamo and at the court ofopold III, Duke of Austria. He is especially known for his writing on the Roman Catholic Church, which at the time was suppressed by the German king, Henry IV. He was the first person in the German-speaking world to write a history of the church in Latin, the first volume of which, entitled Historia Societatis Iesu, was dedicated to Otto III, Holy Roman Emperor. The second volume, De episcopatu Vienna (Of the Church of Vienna), written around 1070, included a description of the life and acts of the first Roman Catholic bishop of Vienna, Willigis. It included the first description of the suffragan dioceses, with Verona as the first example. Albertanus is regarded as an important figure in the foundation of the Roman Catholic Church and the propagation of its doctrines in the German-speaking world. His work, along with that of Odilo of Freising, enabled the development of a canon of church history in the German-speaking world, from the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 until the pontificate of Martin Luther in the 15th century. Bhanj dynasty (400 - 1659) was a Dynasty of Rajputs that ruled in present-day Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Maharastra India for most of the 17th century. The dynasty was founded by Rao Raja Ramachandra Bhanj (b. 1612 - d. 1682). The founder of the dynasty was born in a Rajput family serving as vassal to various regional rulers. He acquired territory and status by defeating neighbouring rulers. He established his own kingdom by defeating Moghulistan rulers in Uttar Pradesh in 1659. The dynasty is named after its founder, Rao Raja Ramchandra. The dynasty had several influential rulers, including Raja Madho Singh, who built Itar based on Muslim architecture. The Itar was bestowed with ornate Padmanabha Dyeing of silver & Garden. The zamindari system was introduced by Madho Singh. He also provided Counsel to the Moghul King. The Moghul King gave Madho Singh large tracts of lands in recognition of his services. The dynasty eventually got fragmented on census during British rule. The Rao Raja Ramchandra died in 1682. The state was partitioned on the basis of the first marriage of his son, Rao Shakya Simha to a relative of Siddhihari Singh, Chief of Nimar king Dhiraj Raj planet. After the marriage, Nimar kingdom annexed some regions which were later bifurcated among the descendants of Rao Raja Ramchandra's other son, Rao Madho Singh. The Itar was occupied by Moghulistan rulers between 1720-1730 AD, followed by a Jaipur king who captured the region between 1730-1760 AD. The Itar was again captured by Moghulistan rulers between 1760-1790 AD. The first ruler of the independent Bhanj state was Rao Shiv Chandra who reigned from 1790 AD to 1826.

Edward Curr was born in 1813 in Clitheroe, Lancashire, England. He was the son of Humphrey Curr, a cotton manufacturer, and his wife Ann née Jupp. He was educated at a school in Rawcliffe and a school in Rawcliffe Hall before attending a school in Kendal run by Mr Nicholson. He then studied Mathematics at the University of Edinburgh. In 1835, Curr became a mathematics teacher at a school in Macclesfield. In 1839, he joined his family's cotton manufacturing business. He continued to teach maths at different schools in the area until 1842. In 1842, Curr studied at St. Andrews University and then travelled to Madras (now Chennai) in India to work with his brother-in-law, James Campbell, who was a judge in Madras. At Madras, he studied Tamil, Telugu, and Hindi. Curr was ordained as a minister in the Church of Scotland in 1848. He arrived back in Scotland in 1853. Between 1854 and 1858, Curr studied at the University of Glasgow. He achieved second place in a competition held by the Royal Astronomical Society of Scotland and was awarded a gold medal for his proposal. Curr then worked as an assistant to the Astronomer Royal for Scotland. In 1858, Curr became the minister of Beith church. In 1865, Curr travelled to the United States as a lay-member of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. He lived in the US for two years, studying English and working in a factory. In 1868, Curr published a book entitled Practical Astronomy. In 1869, he returned to Scotland. He became the minister of New York City in 1872 and of West Hoylake in 1875. In 1876, Curr published his most famous work, The Astronomer'siotelescope. In 1880, he became the minister of Motherwell. He was succeeded at New York City by his son.

Monte Titano is an Italian mountain located in the province of Avellino, in the Campania region. The mountain has an extensive background in history as it was the site of the Battle of Monte Titano during the Second Italo-Abyssinian War in 1918. The highest peak of the range is the Monte Titano with an elevation of 1,924 metres, this is also the mountain of the national park. The sub-ranges most closely associated with the Monte Titano are the Campanian Apennines to the west and the Diano n plateau to the east. The Diano n plateau descends to the Adriatic Sea in the west and to the Tyrrhenian Sea in the east. The national park extends onto the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian slopes. The Gran Sasso e953 is located on the southern slope of the Monte Titano and is approximately 1,500 metres above sea level. The pasture includes various sub-pastures that are separated by insurmountable natural barriers, such as the Colle di Lava Padana (Lava Valley Ridge), which runs from north to south between 1,829 and 1,848 metres above sea level. The Charles Sumner House, located at 1516 8th Avenue in Portland, Oregon, was built in 1901 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1977. It was the home of Charles Sumner, a United States Senator from 1895 to 1905 and again from 1913 to 1917, and also served as his law office. Sumner was a leading spokesman for racial equality in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and his support for the Republicans in the Senate eventually led to his truce with President Andrew Johnson, an end to Reconstruction, and ultimately his dismissal from the Republican Party. The house was renovated and expanded in 1936 in the Classical Revival style. Sumner was born in Boston, a descendant of Paul Revere, and attended Boston Latin School and Harvard College. He began his career in journalism and moved to New York City in 1859, where he became a correspondent for the New York Times, and also wrote for The Illustrated American, a journal published by Edgar Allan Poe. He resigned his position with the Times in 1861 to fight in the Civil War, enlisting in the Army as a private in the 19th Massachusetts Infantry. He was appointed Assistant Inspector General in the Army of the James after the war, and then served in various political positions in Massachusetts, first as a Republican, then as a Democrat and finally as a Liberal Republican. Sumner moved to Portland, Oregon in 1872 and began teaching mathematics and science at Jefferson High School. In 1876, he co-founded The Oregonian with George Lawrence May and Josepharas Barnes, and he became known for his oratory in the House of Representatives and the Oregon Senate. He resigned from The Oregonian in 1881 and started a private law practice, but his legislative work was not limited to Oregon. In 1894, President Benjamin Harrison appointed Sumner United States Ambassador to Japan, and he served in this post from June 1895 to March 1897. Sumner returned to Oregon in 1897 to take a seat in the Senate, where he would represent the state for six terms, serving from 1895 to 1917. In 1901, Sumner purchased the lot and built the present house, which he lived in until his death in 1922. He left the house to his daughters, and one of them, Augusta (1865-1941) lived in the house until her death. The house was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1977, and it is located within the boundaries of the Chinatown neighborhood. It is one of the few standing Classical Revival residences in the neighborhood. Mohamad Ridzuan Mohamad Puzi, often referred to as Mohammad Ridzuan or simply Ridzuan, is an Indonesian Islamic scholar, former Supreme Head of the Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), and former chairman of the Scholars' Council of the Indonesian Ulama Institute. He has held those positions since 2022. Born in Kediri, East Java, Ridzuan received his early education at the Al Mujammahah Madrasah. In 1977, he received his master's degree in hadith from Al Azhar University in Cairo, Egypt. He then travelled to Saudi Arabia, where he studied Islamic law at the University of Madinah and received his PhD in Islamic law from King Saud University. On 25 August 2022, Ridzuan was elected the 14th Supreme Head of the NU, defeating the candidates from the PT PAN-NU litmus test and the DPR (the NU's youth wing). He received 87.82% of the vote. On 2022, he also won the election for the chairman of the Scholars' Council with 92.31% of the votes, succeeding Umar Arif. He took office on 2023. Ridzuan is of muhammadi da'wati tariqa. On 2 December 2023, Ridzuan delivered a speech at UOL Sunday Class in Jakarta in which he called on Muslim youth to get married, have children and perform pilgrimages in order to strengthen the Islamic ummah. He also criticized Salafi trend in the ummah and the hijab implementation in schools, arguing that women's attire was a human rights issue. His speech was criticized by many non-muslims and women groups. Some considered his speech as contrary to Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution of Indonesia. For his speech, he was listed on a special New Year's gift from Ministry of Education and Culture of Indonesia to Umar Arif.

Create NSW is a government body in the state of New South Wales, Australia, with responsibility for administering the NSW Police and the Public Service of New South Wales. The body is headquartered at the Premier's Office, Parliament House, in Sydney. The current Minister for Police is the Hon. Steve Whan, the current Minister for the Public Service is the Hon. Paul Bromhead and the Director General is Andrew Scipione. The name of the body was announced on 28 January 2018 by the Premier of New South Wales, Gladys Berejiklian. The agency was established by the Parliament of New South Wales on 21 November 2017 to succeed the Department of Justice and the Department of Police. The agency and its predecessors have been responsible for policing in New South Wales since the establishment of the colony at Sydney Cove in 1788. The agency also has responsibilities for forestry, engineering, building and security, though these are delegated to state government entities. The New South Wales Police retain law enforcement responsibilities. The agency reports to the Parliament of New South Wales through the Attorney-General (and Minister for the Public Service), and the Minister for Police. The Director-General is responsible to the Minister for Police, but is also seconded to the Premier and the Government as a whole to support governance and programme delivery. The agency came into existence following the review of government agencies conducted by Leslie Allan. Allan recommended that the Department of Justice and the Department of Police be merged to save costs, increase accountability and simplify governance. The recommendation was accepted and the agency was established on 21 November 2017. The Premier and the Minister for Police announced on 28 January 2018 that the name of the agency would be Create NSW.

The Razumovski Palace (Baturyn) is a palace in Baturyn, Ukraine, capital of the Volhynian Voivodeship, Ukraine. The palace was built in 1901 and is representative of the late Romanesque style of architecture. It was restored in the 2000s. It is used as the governor's residence. On June 22, 2014, the palace was severely damaged by armed pro-Russian protestors during the 2014 Winter uprising. The local authorities intend to use the ruined palace as an illustration symbol of the damage done to the city during the Ukrainian crisis. In February 2019, the local administration announced that the building would be fully reconstructed. The palace was declared an architectural landmark on January 27, 2020. In the heart of Baturyn, right across the street from the Saint Volodymyr Chapel, the building serves as a reminder of the city's past, present and future. The building currently serves as the headquarters of the "Battle for Baturyn" public organization, which is actively involved in the city's reconstruction and the preservation of its architectural heritage. The restoration of the palace is being funded by the European Union and by private donations from local residents and businesses. The palace is located at 4 Baturynska Street in the city's downtown area. The official opening of the palace will take place in 2023, during the 100th anniversary of the October Revolution in Ukraine. The Razumovski Palace hosted the second wave of American President Donald Trump's April 2020 presidential visit to Ukraine. Televisa Deportes is a television network in Mexico that is affiliated with the Televisa television network. Televisa Deportes was founded in 2004 and is the official over-the-air broadcaster of Televisa sports events in Mexico. Some of the sports broadcast on Televisa Deportes include soccer, basketball, and Olympic sports. Televisa Deportes is one of the four major sports networks in Mexico along with Canalia, Sky, and DirecTV. Notable sports events broadcast on Televisa Deportes include the Mexico National Basketball Team's games in the Olympics, the Liga MX tournament, and the FIFA World Cup. Mexico's men's national soccer team is the most followed sport team on Televisa Deportes with more than 800,000 followers on Facebook. Magyar Posse is a Hungarian hip hop crew. Founded in 2008 in Budapest, the group consists of Taurüdnő, T-Kole, Z! and XValuez. The name "Magyar Posse" is a reference to the Hungarian words "magyar" (Hungarian) and "posse" (to assemble, crew). The lyrics of the group consist of socially conscious and politically charged themes such as police brutality, racial injustice, immigration and anti-corruption. Magyar Posse's first album released in 2012, titled Szentivány, sold more than 50,000 copies. The group is well known in Hungary and has played concerts in Romania, Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Austria, Germany and France. In 2016, Magyar Posse was featured on VPRO's Morgen van Programma, a morning program that promotes innovation in the Netherlands. In addition to their music, the crew has founded the music label C Magazine and the fashion line Károly Kovacs. Magyar Posse's popularity in Hungary led to the formation of a Magyar Posse fanclub in Ukraine, where the crew has numerous Ukrainians amongst its members. In 2018, the group released a collaboration with German rapper Tine One, titled "Gorilla". The song became popular in Hungary and reached number one on the MTVA top ten chart, where it remained for several weeks. Magyar Posse's song "Fordulat" ("Overrated"), featuring Kanto, achieved significant popularity in Hungary in the summer of 2019. The song reached number one on the OGAE prime 5 chart, which corresponds to Hungary's top 50 most popular pop songs of all time. The music video for the song, which was directed by Gergő Köves, became popular on YouTube, viewed over 30 million times. In November 2019, Magyar Posse's second studio album, titled Kavargások, was released, with the lead single "Orvoselet" ("Oathbreaker"). Magyar Posse's lyrics have been well received by music critics. Zoltán Varga-Nielsen of The Daily Telegraph wrote that Magyar Posse is "adding a socially conscious and politically charged perspective to mainstream rap." Beatrice Marovich of The Guardian called Magyar Posse "the pioneers of a new wave of socially aware rap coming out of Hungary" and praised their "visionary status". Taurüdnő, T-Kole, Z! and XValuez are all natives of Budapest, Hungary. T-Kole is of Ukrainian descent.

The 1983 Miller High Life 500 was the twelfth in a series of 25 end-around, 500 lap NASCAR Winston Cup races held at Michigan International Speedway in Brooklyn, Michigan; River Turquois County, Michigan; on intermediate tracks, on August 9, 10, and 11, 1983. Late model driver Dick Bruna won the pole, and Bobby Allison and Buddy Arning were the quickest in the early laps. Race day was windy, with strong straightline winds in the third turn. Heavy and persistent rains caused the asphalt to be slippery and turn several wrecks. Several cautions were necessitated by the race conditions. A late-race incident with Ronnie Smith and Dave Marcis in the Armco barrier ended Marcis' hopes of the runner-up spot. Donnie Allison, lead driver for Roush Racing, won the race with Dick Brooks and Billie Harvey completing the first two places in a locally popular Ford. The event attracted 88,000 live attendance. The race was originally scheduled to be broadcast on CBS; however, during the middle of the race, as Tom Sneva was running second, a struck a gas meter on the pit road, and the feed was pulled from the truck. Without a commercial break, the audience saw Sneva's car appear to be on fire, and slowed to a stop in the middle of the race track. The race was then abruptly cut from the television feed. The feed was restored when Sneva's car was removed from the track, but the feed remained interrupted for four minutes and 55.2 seconds. When the race returned to the television feed, the sound was muted, the pace car was speeding around the track, and several laps were missing from the telecast. Boxed in blue on the top five, as Tom Sneva was leading when the race was cut, the lap car on the pace car lap is often displayed as the top five lap cars in race car lore.

Correio Popular (Portuguese for "Popular Mail") is a Brazilian weekly newspaper, published in São Paulo in tabloid format since 1955. It is the most popular newspaper in the country, with a average circulation of 2.2 million copies weekly. The newspaper has its own website, as well as a Facebook page with more than 25 million followers, the third largest number of followers among Facebook pages. The newspaper was founded by journalist Márvio Jacques, who had a law degree from the University of Cambridge, and later on other contributors such as Rubens Figueiredo, Roberto Marinho, Wilson Junior, Fernando Enrique Nogueira and Paulo Canabarro. The current director is Cláudio Francini. It is published in São Paulo by Fundação Marquês de Soraia and has a print distribution of about 1.2 million copies on weekdays. Besides news about politics, economy and society, the newspaper has a section called "Agenda do Conhecimento" (Agenda of Knowledge), which publishes news related to Science, Technology, Education, Culture, Business and Innovation. In 2006, the Marinho family, owners of the Grupo Globo, purchased a large part of the capital of the newspaper, making it a sister publication to the Folha da São Paulo. However, the two newspapers still maintain distinct operations, and the two do not share content. Besides newspapers, the Marinho family owns other well-known media in Brazil, such as the Jornal do Brasil, Revista Crusoé, Record and TV economic news channel Band.

Hyō-sei (double-faced) is a Japanese literary term describing a type of double-faced kami, meaning god with two faces or forms. It is used to describe a concept analogous to human duality such as yin and yang, or indeed the separation of Jesus into divine and human. The term hyosei first came into use during the Middle Japanese period (9th to 12th centuries), describing two distinct, yet interdependent aspects or faces of a singular entity or thing; for example, two sides of a coin or of a mountain. This two-sided or bifaciated concept of a hyosei also carries over into the Abrahamic religions, as applied to God, Jesus or a saint, in which one can conceive of God as both divine and human, or in other words, hyo-sem-ne, both one and two. The usage of the term was introduced to Japan via Korean scholarship during the Asuka period (5th century CE) and came into vogue from the late Nara period (Late 7th century) to the beginning of the Kamakura period (1183) as a way of creating a more nuanced and realistic approach to Chinese-influenced Japanese Buddhist art. Though an image of a bifaciated deity can be found as early as the mid-Kojiki period (744 CE), the most famous early examples are the Koma-in adorning the Nara Daibutsu (Large statue of Gautama Buddha) and the Hiyoshi Inari shrine guardians at Hiyoshi Inari-taisha in Kyoto. Other notable examples of the usage of the term hyosei in Buddhist art include the Heianperiod Roof Tree (Heian Gyoku), a famous pair of Japanese guardians at the Nara Kokuhōji Temple, and the famous Kokebo statue at Okucani shrine in the mountains southeast of Nara.

This ongoing campaign is called Operation Searchlight. As of 2023, estimated death count due to this operation ranges between 30,000 and 50,000. This large scale genocide has caused significant political turmoil in Bangladesh, with several mass protests and strikes. Operation Searchlight refers to the systematic persecution and targeting of native Biharis in Bangladesh since 1971. The Operation was primarily led by the Bangladesh Army, with assistance from local police and border guards. Estimated death count due to this operation ranges between 30,000 and 50,000. The operation is responsible for the migration of around 3.6 million Biharis out of Bangladesh, many of whom still reside in refugee camps in India. The Operation began after the war of independence against Pakistan, when the newly formed government in Bangladesh claimed the territory, included parts of eastern India at the time, as its territory. This claim was disputed by India and several international organizations, who claimed that Bangladesh had no right to include parts of Indian territory. The Indian government and military, at the time, supported multiple armed rebellions in eastern India, aimed at establishing an Indian state in the areas claimed by Bangladesh. In order to justify the Operation, the Bangladesh government, military and officials painted Biharis as a dangerous internal enemy of Bangladesh, responsible for the wars in India as well as Bangladesh. The Operation also had financial motivations, with the Bangladesh government auctioning the assets of those killed or forced to migrate, to pay off war debt to international creditors. The Operation was officially ceased in 1990, but law enforcement and vigilante groups continue to target and persecute Biharis to this day.

Bill of Rights socialism, a concept coined by Nick McCann, is a form of social democracy advocated by him and other progressives, which combines the principles of socialism and the human rights movement of the period 1780–1820. This form of socialism focuses on establishing the constitutional rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, in place of capitalism's "economic man". This form of socialism also aims to establish other rights, such as the right to welfare, public healthcare, and public education. Haplocochlias bellus, also known as the zig-zag octopus or dwarf octopus, is a small deep-sea octopus species in the family Octopodidae. It was the first animal species to be discovered by the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) via remotely operated submersible, the Deep-Submergence Vehicle (DSV) ALV-3. The H. bellus dive range is 2,300 meters (7,200 feet) and their typical temperature range is 29.5 °C to 15.5 °C (85 °F to 60 °F). The octopus' habitat is widely considered to be one of the deepest-living habitats on the planet. H. bellus are unique among octopuses in a number of ways. For one, H. bellus is the only octopus species with chromatophores only in the skin, not inside the body. Second, although H. bellus is a large-sized octopus, it has thin arms, and the total weight of an adult H. bellus is less than 1% of its body weight. Third, the H. bellus has an unusual lifestyle: it not only sits motionless on the seafloor with eyes pointed down, but it can also change its skin pattern to match the surrounding seafloor. Lastly, the H. bellus can survive out of water for more than six hours. The H. bellus is named after the bell-shaped blotch in the middle of its skin, which is unique in cephalopods. The H. bellus has been studied in greater detail than any other species in the genus Haploctopus. The H. bellus is the first animal species to be discovered by MBARI via the DSV ALV-3, which was named after the Viking god of thunder and wisdom, located in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of California at a depth of 2,300 meters. The H. bellus was also the subject of the documentary film Deep Water: Inside the H. Bellus Discoveries, which premiered at the 2019 Toronto International Film Festival.

Jemaah Tarbiyah (literally "Gathering of Care") is an Islamic counselling and guidance organisation in Malaysia. It was formed on 10 November 2010 and is fully owned and under the purview of the Federal Territories Ministry of Agriculture and Agro-based Industry. JT was preceded by a voluntary movement called Islamic Dawah Movement of Malaysia, which was then subsequently transformed into a company named Amanah Nurtaniah Bertanah (ANB). On 20 November 2013, Jemaah Tarbiyah was officially launched by the former prime minister, Najib Razak. It has its headquarters in Shah Alam, Selangor, and has 26 branches located in the major districts of Malaysia. JT has three main divisions; Chakram (care), Hanafi (fiqh/jurisprudence) and Nur (Islamic school of thoughts). The first board of directors was then led by Dato' Abdul Ghani Othman, the former secretary-general of the Majlis Amanah Rakyat and the second president of the National Fatwa Council of Malaysia. In November 2018, JT brokered a peace deal to end the ethnic and religious conflicts that had plagued the Southern Thailand camps of Rohingya Muslims, one of the largest such peace deals ever brokered. JT is an important non-profit organisation in Malaysia that has played a vital role in keeping Muslims morally upstanding and healthy. It has been receiving a steady increase in membership and grants from the Federal government since its formation.

The 1989 German motorcycle Grand Prix was held at the Nürburgring on May 4, 1989. It was the tenth round of the world motorcycle racing season, and was the second round of the 89th German motorcycle Grand Prix season. The race was held in dramatic conditions, with constant rain and slow speeds. Kenny Roberts, riding a Yamaha, took his first win of the season, ahead of Kevin Schwantz and Kevin Magee. Roberts's teammate Wayne Rainey won the following race at the Nürburgring, followed by Eddie Lawson on the Kawasaki and Schwantz on the Yamaha. 1989 was one of several key years for the future of motorcycle racing, with the Schwantz/Rainey combination leading the way for the factory Kawasaki team in the early part of the year, followed by the dominant dominance of the Yamaha team of Roberts and Lawson. Delta-v budget is an estimate of the change in speed an object can achieve during the launch phase of a mission. The change in speed is calculated by dividing the change in distance over the change in time. Delta-v is most often cited as referring to the change in speed an object can achieve in kg/s, however it can be expressed in other units as well such as m/s or ft/s. Delta-v is most often used in reference to spacecraft, however it can be applied to any object that is being launched. The delta-v budget an object has is limited by the specific impulse of the propulsion system being used. The specific impulse is a measure of the fuel's ability to convert reactants to products, specifically in the case of rockets it is a measure of the fuel's ability to convert propellant to kinetic energy and therefore thrust. Different propulsion system have different specific impulses, one such system is the modern hydrogen 4 permeable polyethylene stage (HLV), this kind of propulsion is capable of over 5x the specific impulse of commonly used rocket engines like the hypergolic reaction control system which has a specific impulse of 330 seconds. Because of this higher specific impulse, using an HLV in place of a rocket increases the delta-v budget an object has. Some other factors that affect the delta-v budget are the properties of the propulsion system, for example the amount of thrust it produces, as well as the amount of propellant an object has. Objects that are less dense have a higher possible delta-v, however this benefit is countered by the fact that they require more propellant to achieve the same delta-v. Using the HLV as an example again, its higher specific impulse allows for the same amount of propellant to be used to achieve a greater delta-v than a less efficient system. Delta-v budgets are often calculated using the most optimistic values for variables such as the performance of the propulsion system and the weight of the payload, in reality these values will likely be worse than the calculated delta-v budget. For a given delta-v budget, there are many possible launch trajectories that can achieve that delta-v, some of these trajectories have high enough of an altitude that the performance of the rocket will not be as good as the calculated delta-v, other trajectories take the object too close to the launch site and have a high probability of being destroyed by the environment, a third option is that the propulsion system may fail in some way, for example by explosion or quitting due to a lack of cooling.

He had joined Pilatus in Switzerland, and worked there in order to avoid the military service that was required of him by law at that time. Eeva-Kaarina Aronen (born Eeva-Kaarina Aronen; January 1, 1917 – April 23, 2002) was a Finnish artist, photographer and filmmaker. Aronen is known for her portraits and still lives, as well as for her documentary photography. She was born in Viipuri and died in Helsinki. Aronen was a leading figure in the Finnish photography scene of the 1950s and 1960s, and her work has been celebrated and collected for decades. Aronen was a leading member of the Viipuri Circle of Photography artists, which also included Erkki Hápela, Eila Rouda, Aila Kekkonen and Alvar Aalto. Her work has been exhibited in numerous museums and galleries worldwide, including the photography museums of Århus and Helsinki, the art museums of Munich, Stuttgart, Madrid, Seattle and Tokyo, and the museum of photography of Helsinki. Aronen was a member of the Finnish Academy of Science and Letters. She is recognized for her fight for better working conditions for professional photographers, and her work has been honored with several awards. She received the Arranging Prize in 1953 and the Prince Eugen Medal in 1986. Aronen was the photographer of the Finnish National Banknote and the 20th anniversary of Viipuri City, and also participated in the movie Interioyhma. Aronen's photos and films document ordinary people and life in Viipuri, her native city, as well as Finland in general, in the 1950s and 1960s. Some of her photos have been described as "sharp and unflinching depictions of working-class urban life". Many of her photos and films have become valuable memorabilia of the cities, and some of her best known works include Viipuri City Center, Kuusinen and Ahopkin taivaalla (Kuusinen by night).

With two out in the bottom of the 9th inning, he hit a home run over the left-field wall at Wrigley Field, and carried it into the clubhouse with him. The game was delayed 20 minutes while he was showered and changed, and he was awarded both the game-winning home run and the official MLB Home Run championship. Sladky was a teammate of fellow future Hall of Fame members Willie Mays and Frank Robinson on the 1958 NL champion team. He also played in the 1960 World Series, although the series was lost to the San Francisco Giants.

Standing Twelve Heavenly Generals (Tokyo National Museum) is a 45.6 cm tall bronze sculpture by Brazilian artist Charmaine Netto. Completed in 2007, it is exhibited at Tokyo National Museum. The sculpture depicts twelve generals of Japanese Imperial Army, including Yoshitsune, Ariwara no Motoko and Yamamomo, standing at attention with their hands saluting theigned across their heart. The sculpture makes reference to the reputation the Imperial Japanese Army had during the 20th century as a ruthless militarist force that led Japan into World War II. Standing Twelve Heavenly Generals (Tokyo National Museum) was acquired by the Tokyo National Museum with the help of a public fundraising campaign. The exhibition space where it is exhibited was refurbished at a cost of 1.2 billion Yen (approx. 12.3 million US dollars), with half of the cost covered by public donations and corporate sponsorships. The work was positively received by the Japanese public and the media, and has been exhibited in several locations across Japan, as well as at the 2014 World War II Forum in Washington, D.C.. It was featured on an edition of 1000 Japanese yen banknotes issued in 2010 and 2014 (this privilege is shared with only a handful of other contemporary artists). The sculptor Charmaine Netto lived in Brazil from 1974 to 2014. She came back to Japan in 2014 and lives in Tokyo. She published a book about the creation of the sculpture and her experiences as a foreigner living in Brazil, called “Quando Charmaine canta, Brasil fala (When Charmaine Sings, Brazil Speaks)” (Original title in Portuguese: Quando Charmaine Canta, Brasil Fala”). She was also awarded the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2020 New Year's Honours list in the Artistic Sciences and Literature category. The Standing Twelve Heavenly Generals (Tokyo National Museum) is one of the several monuments exhibited in the Charmaine Netto studio and sculpture garden in Tama New Town, in the western part of Tokyo. Other works include her Monument to War Surrendered Flight Nagoya, Monument to the Returning Ship at the River Tama, as well as smaller versions of the same composition exhibited all over the world in commemorative ceremonies for various dates related to World War II. The artist herself has stated that she chose the twelve generals shown on the sculpture to represent Brazilians who moved to Japan over the course of 20th century, because they were all people of strong character who overcame great obstacles to achieve success in a foreign country. She says that she was inspired by their stories and chose to create this specific sculpture after visiting the São INCRA monument in São Paulo, which commemorates the same event. Standing Twelve Heavenly Generals (Tokyo National Museum) is valued for its artistic qualities alone, but also for its historical and cultural references. It was created during one of the most tumultuous periods in Japanese history, when the nation was rebuilding itself following the enormous damages and destruction caused by the World War II. The country was still suffering from the aftereffects of the prolonged world conflict, which had left it vulnerable to international scrutiny. The sculpture publicly reaffirmed Japan's commitment to its democratic principles and human rights, as well as its pacifist constitution, both of which were eventually abandoned by the country during the rise of Imperial Japan. The sculpture also honored the memory of the country's war dead by featuring real life army generals. Standing Twelve Heavenly Generals (Tokyo National Museum) is arguably the most controversial of all the works exhibited at the Charmaine Netto studio, due to its controversial aspect in representing the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II. It has been subject to numerous online petitions and campaigns aimed at withdrawing it from exhibition, particularly from the Asia Democracy Foundation, an organization that advocates for the democratic and pacifist values imposed by the Japanese Constitution and rejected Imperial Japan's policies of racial nationalism and militarism. The group's president, Dr. Eugene Yamamoto, has publicly denounced the sculpture as a "despicable memorial" that "insults our war dead" and "insults the Japanese people" by representing "the very soldiers that conducted the enslaved labor of Japanese prisoners of war and raped tens of thousands of Japanese women" during the course of the Pacific War. The Asia Democracy Foundation was successful in persuading the city of Tokyo to stop exhibiting the sculpture, which was temporarily taken off display in April 2020 after an online campaign. Duke Humfrey's Library is a public library in London, located in the building that was formerly the library of the Order of the Garter, at 28 St George's Churchyard. It is one of the four libraries of the London Library, the others being St Bride's Library (under St Bride's Church), the British Museum Library, and the library of London law courts. The library was founded in 1538 by Henry VIII, and given to the monastery of St Martin-le-Grand by Peter Mirabel, one of the royal cooks. In the 16th century the library was considered to be the second most important library in England, only behind the Royal Library. The library was moved to its current location in 1598. Since 1755 the library has been owned and managed by the Corporation of London. The building was designated a London plaque landmark in 1968 and a Grade I listed building in 1970. Maria Espinosa (born Maria Elena Espinosa Villalon; June 9, 1942 – April 10, 2020) was a Mexican singer. Known for her fiery, torch song-style vocals, Espinosa possessed the rare ability to shift effortlessly between soprano, alto, and tenor vocal ranges. She was a prolific recording artist from the 1960s through 1980s, frequently collaborating with esteemed Mexican producer and composer Fernando Terrícolas. Espinosa was one of the first Latinas signed to RCA Records, where she enjoyed critical and commercial success with mid-1960s top 10 hits "La Perfecta" and "La Rumba Sensual", the latter of which has become particularly popular on the Latin club and dance music scene given its relatively fast tempo and signature rumba-inspired beat. Subsequent releases, however, were largely overshadowed by the commercial success of her next single, the Latin pop-flavored "Yo No Puedo Olvidarte" (English: "I Can't Forget You"), which became a signature song for Espinosa and earned an FÓMEX censorship rating of XXX (for "obscene content"), indicating that the singer's image would not be approved to appear on Mexican television alongside the lyrics. Despite this, the single became her second-highest-charting single in the United States, reaching number seven on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. Espinosa continued to record throughout the 1970s and 1980s, but with less commercial success; by the late 1980s, she had largely been forgotten by both music industry executives and the general public. She experienced a resurgence of interest in the 2010s, particularly following the airing of Mexican TV series La Voz Méxicona, which featured a special tribute to Espinosa and several of her songs being covered by contemporary singers.

Robin Hood is a locality in the City of Bradford district of West Yorkshire, England. It is situated approximately 12 miles to the east of Leeds and 13 miles north west of Sheffield. The population of thecivil parish at the 2011 census was 13,827. The West Riding of Yorkshire was created under the Commission for the Registration of Ancient Deeds on 24 October 1834. The commission included Edward Marc Serjeant, who had published his argument for the creation of the county in The Constitutional History of England During the Late Great Revulsion of the Nobility and Gentry, and had based his arguments on the example of Canute, who in 1026 had established an English county comprising the whole of the former King's Roading, and which had remained unbroken for over 400 years. In May 1895, Robin Hood was cited as one of the towns which would be affected by the extension of the West Riding of Yorkshire. It was incorporated as a municipal borough on 1 November 1901, and was granted city status on 23 May 1904. It was in the county of West Yorkshire from 1964 until 1974, when it was transferred to the new county of Leeds. The population of the borough at the 2011 census was 14,327. Robin Hood has two main areas: Robin Hood Island, a mostly residential suburb; and the industrial districts of Robin Hood Town, Robin Hood Lane and St James. These were built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when Robin Hood was an important employer in the area. The most famous firm is James Gandon Ltd., best known for its range of patented stainless steel kitchenware. Robin Hood Island also includes Robin Hood Park, a green in the centre of Robin Hood town, and Robin Hood Comprehensive School, a secondary school with over 1000 pupils. The Robin Hood music festival is held annually in the nearby village of Eccleshill.

Honaunau-Napoopoo, Hawaii is a census-designated place (CDP) in the Hawaii County, Hawaii, United States. The population was 1,865 at the 2010 census. It is located on the north shore of the island of Hawaii across the channel from the district of Hilo to the east, and across the channel from Kaunakakai to the southwest. Honaunau is the largest town in the CDP. The name Honaunau comes from the Hawaiian language word for "rough water". Honaunau was founded in 1904 as a sugar town. The original town site was built on the side of a valley with a stream which was later named Kahookele Highway (Hawaiian for "rough highway"). A coaster dock was built in 1909 on the ocean side of the valley and the community became known as "Coaster City". In 1919, the Hawaiian Pineapple Company opened a factory in Honaunau and the town changed its name to reflect the local lomilomi juice. The factory operated until 1996 and is currently the only remaining company from that period. The liloa forest on the property was added to the United States National Arboretum's reserve list of genetic landmarks by the University of Hawaii System in 2008. The Honaunau Hawaii post office is located at the edge of town on the corner of Kahookele Highway and Kawailoa Road, and has been in operation since 1904.

Joseph Gluckstein (born Joseph Goldstein; September 1, 1916 – April 7, 2000) was a Polish-Israeli chess player and Holocaust survivor. He was awarded the title of Grandmaster by FIDE, the World Chess Federation, in 1958. He was born in Wadowice, Poland, then in Czechoslovakia. In 1939, he moved with his family to Liège, Belgium, where he received a Belgian identity card as a "juif". Gluckstein and his family then moved to Paris, where he got a job, as they were afraid to stay in Belgium during the German occupation. In 1943, he was sent to the Theresienstadt ghetto, where he was put to work in the camp's wood factory. He and his fellow workers managed to save enough money to buy bicycles, which they used to flee the Theresienstadt ghetto and travel to Munich, where they joined thousands of other Theresienstadt prisoners who had also escaped. Gluckstein and his family were then transferred to Budapest, Hungary, and then sent on aKama SutraAPAP ferry to Japan, where he worked in a gun factory. He then moved to Israel, where he reunited with his family. In 1955, he won the first unofficial international chess tournament played in Israel. In 1958, he was awarded the FIDE title of Grandmaster. He worked as a school principal and chess teacher, and published several chess books. He died in 2000, at the age of 83, and was buried in Ramat Hasharon.

Her other known films include Pillow Fight (1968), Cutter's Way (1972), Three on a Date (1973), The Amityville Horror (1979) and Heartstring (1979). McLaren was born in St. Louis, Missouri. She performed with several bands in the St. Louis area during the 1950s before receiving a call from actor Roger Corman, who was looking for a singer for his upcoming production of The Wild Angels. McLaren accepted the role and made her acting debut in the movie. She subsequently appeared in six of Corman's films, becoming a popular actress among Corman's loyal audience for her versatility and for doing her own stunts. In 1976, McLaren starred in the minor role of a nightclub singer in the John Wayne film The Road to Bali. Her other known credits include Pillow Fight (1968), Cutter's Way (1972), Three on a Date (1973) and Heartstring (1979). In the 2010s, McLaren turned to directing and acting in television commercials. In 2016, she returned to acting, and had a cameo role in the independent horror film The Babysitter Project. She died of respiratory failure caused by lung cancer at the age of 71.

Jody McCrea (born James Edward McCrea; November 24, 1948 – December 11, 2002) was an American actor and singer. He starred in the hit TV shows Sea Hunt and The Dukes of Hazzard, and had many leading film roles, including Joe Buck in Big Bad Mama (1975). His other films include The Last American Hero (1973), Smoky Joe's Cafe (1978), The Quiet Gun (1980), Cadillac Club (1981), Twilight Zone: The Movie (1983) and The Burrowers (1987). McCrea was born in Magnolia, Arkansas and raised in Little Rock. After moving to California at the age of 17, he formed a rock band and worked in a pornographic movie theater. He began performing in local nightclubs, and signed to a recording contract with RCA Records in 1969. His recording of the Jimmie Rodgers song "Kissin' Cousins" became a No. 1 hit on the Billboard Hot 100 chart later that year. In 1970, he won a contest to become the lead singer of the band Creach. In 1972, McCrea signed to Warner Bros. Records and released two albums. He found minor success with the singles "Boomerang" and "Theme from the Dukes of Hazzard" and the album The Duke. Although his next two albums did not produce hits, McCrea had acting roles in several television series. He had a supporting role in the John Carpenter film Escape from New York (1981) and starred in the Sea Hunt television series in the late 1970s. He had a starring role in the fantasy film Quest for Fire (1981) and was cast in the action films The Last American Hero (1973), Smoky Joe's Cafe (1978), The Quiet Gun (1980), Cadillac Club (1981), Twilight Zone: The Movie (1983) and The Burrowers (1987). In addition to acting, McCrea was a singer and songwriter. He wrote or co-wrote the songs "Kissin' Cousins", "Theme from the Dukes of Hazzard", "Cadillac Club", "Big Bad Mama", and "Boomerang". He also wrote or co-wrote several songs for the films The Last American Hero, Smoky Joe's Cafe, and The Quiet Gun. His highest-charting solo single, "Dreams", reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1978. In 1987, McCrea was sentenced to seven years in prison for tax evasion. He had participated in a scheme to avoid paying income taxes by receiving fees for appearing in several films and on several television shows but not deducting those fees from his income. McCrea served six months in prison and was released on parole in 1990. In 2001, he returned to prison after failing to report to prison officials that he had been attacked and left partially deaf. He was scheduled for release in 2004 but died of heart disease six days before his release.
