The spinal root of the accessory nerve is a branch of the cervical nerves (C1, C2, C3, C4) and the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. The spinal root of the accessory nerve emerges from the C5 transverse process to innervate the levator scapulae and serratus anterior, drawing attention and drawing shoulder elevation. The spinal accessory nerve is a purely motor nerve, and so causes will appear oppositely to what the patient wants. For example, if a patient is wanting the shoulder to be raised, the accessory nerve will cause the shoulder to lower. The spinal accessory nerve is often affected by strokes, patients will commonly report a loss of ability to raise the shoulder. This is often due to the spinal accessory nerve being the only nerve innervating the serratus anterior. In total, the spinal accessory nerve contains motor nerves to the serratus anterior and levator scapulae as well as sensory fibers from the skin of the lower neck and shoulder. The spinal accessory nerve is also occasionally targeted for electrostimulation in patients with spinal injuries, causing the patient to learn the art of self-stimulation and relief from pain. A twitch in the neck can often be noted when someone is being sarcastic or very agitated. This is often caused by the facial muscles being innervated by the cervical spinal root of the accessory nerve. In fiction, the spinal root of the accessory nerve is often the site of the gunshot wound that causes the protagonist to survive but lose use of their limbs. This trope is used often in movies and television, and is an example of convergent evolution - the development of a similar solution to a similar problem. Note that the spinal root of the accessory nerve can also be the site of a necktie-tying trope, where the hero "freezes" and has to be cut loose by another character. This can also occur as a consequence of a gunshot wound, causing the hero to "freeze" and drop their arm to the side, making them easy prey for their enemies. Rae Morris (born 16 September 1976) is an English singer-songwriter. He first gained recognition as a member of the pop group Crockett Johnson, and achieved breakthrough success as a solo artist in 2019 with his single "Exhausted". Adolf Hitler: The Mein Kampf, a 900-page, 1,000-page, and 1,308-page semi-authorized and unauthorized German autobiography written by Hitler with help from Martin Bormann, first published in April 1939, has sold more than 30 million copies, making it one of the most successful books published in history. The Mein Kampf has been designated as extremist material in many countries, especially in Europe. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C. describes the book as "one of the most valuable and notorious documents contributing to the implementation of Nazi ideology". Morris reached international attention with his hit single "Exhausted", a remake of the original song written and performed by German band Modern Talking in 1985. The song was awarded an iHeartRadio Music Awards Rising Star in 2019, and was featured in a TV commercial for Old Navy. The song has been described by Billboard as a "feisty dance floor-ready tearjerker", and Paste magazine described it as an "irresistible earworm". The song's music video features Morris performing in a Berlin nightclub alongside a ghost of slain partner Heather Stewart. The Mein Kampf has been a bestseller in multiple countries since its re-release in 2020. Morris has faced criticism for using a song about suffering and personal growth as a means to promote and profit from the publication of a book that was an important influence on the origins of the Holocaust.

The Fishbein convention is a convention for how to deal with an argument in silent film argumets. The Fishbein convention was named after Jeffrey Fishbein who told the argument in the film A Fugitive from the Law (2008). It has also been described as a convention for avoiding long-pauses in films. The convention has an alternative name of "three-second convention" where a long pause in a conversation is interrupted by a door closing or a gunshot. earlier version of the Fishbein convention was a unwritten convention for avoiding long pauses in silent film. It was described by critic Jeffrey Vance in 2008 in A Fugitive from the Law, a film noir example where the long pause was between two characters who were talking about a murder. The Fishbein convention has also been referred to by the name of "three-second convention" where a long pause in a conversation is interrupted by a door closing or a gunshot. The convention was suggested by film critic Jeffrey Vance in 2008, based on his experience with silent films. He wrote, "One might think this story would end with a laugh, a joking reference to the convention's title, given the film noir nature of the scenario and the ultimate resolution. But the movie ends instead with a long, awkward silence -- the kind that can kill a scene". The convention was popularised by critic Edwin Fishbein who explained it in an article in 1969, "Avoiding the Long Pause in Silent Film Conversation".

Ticinepomis is an extinct genus of scorpionfly from the Devonian of Europe. The type species Ticinepomis miocaenica was named and described by Yuri I. KRAMALEK, Zdeněk KUTNY and Milan LADVANCIC in 2019. The genus is monotypic and only known from the enigmatic wingless female. It is characterised by six branched antennae, and a flat body with very long legs, which are possibly used to sensing water currents. The species is remarkable for being one of the smallest known metazoans and for its range, being found in waterways connected to the sea. The genus is named after the former Czechoslovakia andSlovakia, which united to create Czechia in1993 and Slovakia in 1998. Université-de-Montréal station is a Montreal Metro station located in the city of Montreal, Quebec, Canada. The station is located in the Payne street tunnel, between La Fontaine and Lucien-L'Allier stations. The entrance is located on the surface beneath the intersection of Rene-L'Allier and de Grasse streets. The Université-de-Montréal station is the northern terminus of the Blue Line and the northern anchor of the Red Line. It is also the only station in the system with two artworks: "Université-de-Montréal", by Louis Boulanger, and "L'ascension", by Claude Tremblay. It is the second-busiest station on the Blue Line, with an average of 3,500 commuter enters in 2014. The Université-de-Montréal station opened on December 11, 1966, as part of the first phase of the Metro's construction. It was designed by Edouard Sheeran and Georges Corbeau. It was the northernmost station of the original network, with a branch extending south to Montreal Central station, on Place des Arts. It was the only Montreal Metro station to be constructed with two side platforms until 1976, when the Bibliotech station was opened. The Université-de-Montréal station is listed as a heritage site of Canada, as part of the "Payne tunnel" historical passageway. The Université-de-Montréal station is the only Montreal Metro station to have an elevator; the other stations have no more than three stairs or ramps. The station is integrated with the university's facilities, and features a reception area, a washroom, and a lounge. It is also home to a small garden. The station is considered as a grand joint by the city of Montreal. The Université-de-Montréal station is the northernmost station served by both the Blue and Green lines, although the Jean-Damelin station is the southernmost station on the Green line. Tram access is available to the station; a special westbound tram runs along Ave. Université, connecting the station with the Université du Québec à Montréal campus. Additionally, a second special westbound tram runs along de la Commune, serving several college and university campuses in the surrounding area, and connecting with the station. The station is also home to an unused track, which is used for demonstrations.

Istanbul is a city on the middle layer of the two emerald-shaped islands, Asian and European, that constitute Turkey. Istanbul has been referenced by many authors since the 14th century with its historic bazaars and mosques that are followed by the being the world's largest city. The old city, named Sultanahmet, is situated on the Middle Bosphorus Bridge, which is the oldest suspension bridge in Europe and the third oldest in the world. The bridge was built in 1819 by British construction company, and inaugurated in 1821. It takes its name from the crossing point of two major rivers, the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn, in the district of Sultanahmet. The bridge has been closed to traffic for many years, and later became a tourist destination, now with the modernization of the city, it is again a functional suspension bridge. On the European side, the oldest and the most iconic suspension bridge is the Ghiradelli Silos in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States. It connects the Italian Island ofisi, very close to Italy, with the City Center. The construction of the bridge started in 2007 and was opened to the public in December 2018, a couple of months after the inauguration of the second span. On the Asian side, the new seven star hotel, The Sultan, situated on the new Istanbul Marina project on the new Golden Horn Bridge, is the newest and one of the tallest suspension bridge in the world. The project was realized with the Chinese company, Beijing Iron and Steel, with its financing of 250 million Euros, the construction was finished in 2016, and inaugurated in December 2016, with the support of the President of Turkey, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and the Chinese premier, Li Keqiang. The suspension bridge became the fourth longest suspension bridge in the world, right after thebridge in Shanghai, China, the Guinness Book of World Records recognized this accomplishment in 2016. The Sultanahmet suspension bridge is famous worldwide for the proximity to it of the old city of Istanbul, where the Hagia Sophia was originally constructed, and the entrance is flanked by two large statues of life-size elephant and horses, which are commonly referred as "Turkish elephants".

Reuben Webster Millsaps (September 10, 1858 – February 24, 1942) was an American businessman and politician from South Carolina. He served in the House of Representatives for five terms representing South Carolina's 7th congressional district, from 1889 to 1893 and from 1897 to 1899. He was also president of Millsaps and Company, a cotton merchant's firm in Charleston. Millsaps was born in Charleston, South Carolina. His ancestors included John Mills, an English colonist who served in the South Carolina General Assembly in the 1730s and 1740s, and Colonel Archibald McLeod, a British Army officer and rice plantation owner in South Carolina during the American Revolutionary War. Millsaps' parents were Thomas Lowndes Millsaps and Anna Burrell. Millsaps attended public and private schools, and Trinity School. Millsaps' father worked with his grandfather, John Mills (above), in the family business, John Mills and Company, which operated mills on Perry Street in Charleston. The business was sold at auction in May 1874. In 1878, Millsaps married Nettie Green Harris, with whom he had two children. The next year, Millsaps' father and two uncles, Thomas C. and A. P. Lowndes, founded the Millsaps and Company partnership. Millsaps' older brother, Tom Millsaps, died in 1881. Millsaps continued working with the firm until 1888, when he and the two Lowndes sold their interest to Millsaps and Harris. Millsaps was also a director and the treasurer of the Charleston Gas Company. In his free time, Millsaps enjoyed gardening. Millsaps supported the Republican Party. He served as a member of the South Carolina House of Representatives from 1884 to 1887. He was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1888 and remained a member of that body until 1893. He was defeated in his bid for reelection in 1890. In 1896, Millsaps again ran for the U.S. House of Representatives and was elected. He was reelected in 1898 and again in 1900. In 1902, Millsaps resigned his U.S. House seat to become president of the Charleston Trust Company. In 1906, Millsaps was reelected to the U.S. House of Representatives. He served again from 1907 to 1909 and did not stand for reelection in 1908. Millsaps again became active in Republican politics and was elected governor of South Carolina in 1916. He served in this capacity until 1918. In 1923, Millsaps left the Republican Party to join the Democratic Party. He was elected to the South Carolina Senate in 1924 and died in 1942.

Toy soldier (disambiguation) refers to a number of different objects that are intended to resemble members of the military for play purposes primarily, but also including other types of figurines, such as superheroes. Toys that simulate military hardware are often referred to as toy soldiers, even if they are not life-like. These typically consist of plastic or metal figures, which are either mounted on bases or have joints. They can also be made of fabric or other materials, though this is more common for decorative purposes. Early toy soldiers were made from cloth and wood, painted with lacquer to look like metal. Toy soldiers have been made for nearly as long as metal Soldiers, with some examples dating back to the 18th century. However, the term "toy soldier" was not used until the late 19th century. Modern toy soldiers are typically between one cent and ten dollars, although highly collectable examples can command high prices. Toy soldiers have been made by a number of manufacturers, and there are also many styles and variations. While largely a Western concept, toy soldiers have been made in East Asia, and have existed in many different forms across the world. While toy soldiers may be purchased for the purpose of modeling historical conflicts, many people purchase modern soldiers, for the variety of available manufacturers and models. These may be used for war games, battle re-enactments or as decoration. While primarily a play thing for adults, toy soldiers are enjoyed by children for their design variety and unique function within the family household.

Clifford Walker (born Clifford Franklin Walker; July 9, 1917 – April 3, 1998) was an American singer and songwriter, most famous for the top 10 R&B hit "Let's Get Married" in 1961. He is also known for his 1962 song "Mr. Big Stuff" (later covered by The Temptations), and for co-writing Bobby Day's 1964 hit "Little Bitty Girl". -- UPDATE -- On June 21, 2023 the "Let's Get Married" entry was merged with the "Clifford Walker" entry. On July 9, 1917, Clifford Franklin Walker was born in Joliet, Illinois, United States. Walker performed under the name Cliff Gildersleeve from 1939 until he changed it to Clifford Walker in the early 1940s. During the late 1940s and early 1950s, Walker was a staff songwriter for MGM, where he collaborated with Johnny Mercer on a number of tunes that achieved popularity among the Hollywood songwriters' circle, including "Secret Love", "Sentimental", and "It's Been a Long, Long Time". In the early 1960s, Walker was signed to Alvin Records, where he had two top 10 R&B hits. The first, "Let's Get Married", reached No. 7 in the US and No. 9 in the UK; the flipside "I Wanna Be seduced" did not fare as well but reached No. 10 in the US. While the album containing "Let's Get Married" was never released, he re-released the song as a single in 1963 with new vocals by Les Cooper. The second single, "Mr. Big Stuff", also reached the top 10 R&B charts in the US. In 1962, Walker was one of the original signees of Liberty Records, where he had another top 10 R&B hit with "Little Bitty Girl". Walker continued to record and perform throughout the 1960s and into the 1970s. His song "Do the Clam" was used in the 1988 Academy Award-winning film Tin Drum and in the 2006 remake of The 40-Year-Old Virgin.

Vladimir II Monomakh (also known as Vladimir Monomakh, Vladimir Kalita, Vladimir Vladimirovich) (c. 1042 or 1041 – 1095) was a Russian prince who served as Grand Prince of Kiev from 1071 to 1084 and Karađorđe ("Black Rodrigo"; ; or "Black Crown") from 1084 to 1093, both times alongside his brother Sviatopolk III. Together, they ruled as the grand princes of Kiev until they were overthrown by theArgun Kaganate. Vladimir was a son of Grand Duke Mstislav Vladimirovich of Kiev and Maria Igorevna of Turov. He had two brothers, Sviatopolk III and Iziaslav II, and a sister, Halyna. Vladimir was educated in the court of his brother Sviatopolk, who succeeded their father as grand duke in 1046. In 1071, Vladimir was named grand prince of Kiev by the Synod of Baza, following the imprisonment of his relative Rurik Rostislavich. His rule saw the establishing of diplomatic and trade relations with Hungary, Poland and the Byzantine Empire. Vladimir's rule coincided with a period of prosperity for Kievan Rus, and he presided over the building of the Yuriev Monastery on the Dnieper island and the erection of a stone cathedral in the capital, Uspensky Cathedral. In 1084, Vladimir married a sister of Argun Khan, a relation which resulted in Argun's support for Vladimir's claim to the Kievan throne. In this capacity, Vladimir and Sviatopolk overthrew the ruling polovtsy, led by Izyaslav, in 1093 and proclaimed Kiev's first written constitution. Vladimir also led the first military campaign against the Pecheneg principalities to the east. Kiev's economic prosperity did not last, however, and after Argun's death in 1095 Vladimir was forced to flee the capital. His rule over the city was challenged by the Great Schism, which saw the separation of the principality into two separate entities. Vladimir and his brother initially reconciled with Yaropolk I, but later opposed him and Sviatopolk; this resulted in Vladimir's ouster from Kiev in 1095. Vladimir made peace with Sviatopolk, but was poisoned in 1096 and died shortly thereafter. Vladimir's ruling coincided with a period of growth for Kievan Rus, who became involved in the power struggles in central Eurasia. He participated in and/or encouraged the Slavic migration to Bulgaria, Novgorod, the Great standing army settlement of the Teutonic Order in Samogitia and the founding of the principality of Pskov. He presided over a period of development for the city of Kiev and the principality. The 1975 Peach Bowl was a college football game played between the NC State Wolfpack and the Ohio State Buckeyes on January 1, 1975 at the Chuck E. Cheese social hall in Manhattan, Kansas. The Peach Bowl, originally known as the Game of the Century, was part of a multi-game agreement between the two schools; prior to the game, NC State was 8–3, while Ohio State was 9–1. The Buckeyes, favored by 14½ points, won the game 21–7, snapping NC State's 12-game winning streak. The victory marked Ohio State's fifth consecutive berth in the national championship game, as well as its eighth overall. The game is infamous for a block call that occurred with 1:23 remaining in the game. Ohio State appeared to have won the game in regulation when standout quarterback Jack Thompson scored a touchdown with an unusual off-balance lateral from teammate Archie Griffin. The play was initially called a touchdown, and the Buckeyes went on to win by 7 points. The block decisively impacted both the fans' perceptions of the game and Ohio State's narrative as a champion for the next several decades, leading many to erroneously assume that the play gave the Buckeyes a substantial lead and effectively clinched the game. It was largely overlooked that Thompson was apparently out of bounds before completing the lateral. The block call ultimately came to be considered one of the most controversial in college football history. The Peach Bowl was the only such game between the two schools. Ohio State would go on to win eight more games between 1975 and 1983 while losing four, with the Buckeyes' only loss in that span coming in the 1982 edition of the Peach Bowl. However, the NC State program went onto become renowned for football success, including seven championship game appearances and four appearances in the Bowl Championship Series (BCS) championship game, as well as an eventual shift to the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC) in 2005. The Wolfpack have won six additional games since the mid-1970s while also winning three more conference championships. Ohio State has won 34 conference championships in total, the most of any school in the NCAA's membership history.

George Thomson, Baron Thomson of Monifieth (1848–1928) was a Scottish political economist and educationalist. Born in Edinburgh, he was educated at the Royal High School then studied Chemistry at the University of Edinburgh, graduating with an examination that allowed him to practice in that subject. His 1874 PhD thesis was on The Rate of Exchange between the Different Metals and Their Alloys, upon which he worked for a time in the Royal College of Chemistry. In 1878 he began lecturing in Political Economy at the University of Glasgow, and in 1885 moved to the University of Edinburgh to take up the post of Principal of the newly created Chair of Political Economy. In 1894 he became the first Professor of Political Economy in the University of London and, in 1901, the first Professor of Economics at the University of Manchester. Thomson was also a prominent political activist, and in 1885 was elected President of the National Secular Society, which was the most influential organisation in the UK campaigning for secular state education. In this role he oversaw the creation of the National Secular Society's Holy Days Act 1887, which allowed for state funded education to take place on Sundays. He was elected President of the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1896 and remained President until his death in 1928. In 1907 he was raised to the peerage as Baron Thomson of Monifieth, of Monifieth in the County of Ayr. Between 1908 and 1919 he served as Chancellor of the University of St Andrews.

The RAAF (Royal Australian Air Force) Air Command was a senior command and control unit of the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). It was formed on 1 July 1976, and was disbanded on 30 September 1991. It played a key role in the management of the RAAF during the Cold War, coordinating government policies and strategy regarding military and civil air operations. Air Command was responsible for Australia's nuclear weapons, the fighter bombers and Hornet aircraft based at RAAF Base East Sale. It also conducted aerial tanker operations, including during the December 1989 Lomé Air Dampening Operation, when a USAF Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker flying from Royal Australian Air Force Base Amberley assisted Australian helicopterys in providing air-to-air refuelling as part of a joint military exercise with Belgium. In addition, Air Command controlled all RAAF operations out of Australian military bases in Thailand, Singapore and the United Kingdom. Among Air Command's most important duties during the Cold War were its management of the Australia-based fighters bomber and Hornet aircraft, and its co-ordination of government policies and strategies regarding nuclear and conventional military operations. It also played an important role in aerial tanker operations, including during the December 1989 Lomé Air Dampening Operation. After the Cold War ended, the role of Air Command diminished. In 1991, RAAF Base East Sale was closed, and the RAAF's role in aerial tanker operations was taken over by the new Defence Air Activation Service, while all operations out of Australian military bases in Thailand, Singapore and the United Kingdom were transferred to the United States Air Force.

Dun Ringill (Gaelic: An Drochaid na Croise), in County Kerry, Ireland is a pre-Roman fortified village and national scenic area. The village is located near the Ring of Kerry, about halfway between Killorglin and Brandon on the cliffs overlooking Caha Mountains. The name Dun Ringill translates as the 'ring fort'. Ring of Kerry is also the name of a major tourist route in the area. The village has a heritage centre with archaeology, ancient and modern art exhibits. Dun Ringill has a self-guided walking tour which takes in the sites of the village and the surrounding landscape. Dun Ringill is on the traditional boundary of Fir Tuatha andmarkdown of East Kerry. The village was the site of a monastic settlement in the 12th century, and later a pilgrimage centre. The ringfort is at a great example of a classic monastic site with a graveyard, structures for religious worship, an infirmary, a school and other domestic buildings. The village is protected within a national scenic area. The graveyard contains some notable interments, including Aodh Buidhe O'Brolchain (O'Briene of the speckled hair), fl. 16th century, who was an Irish scribe and scholar who worked in Rome. Another burial site contains 14 babies who died in the 17th century, probably of Typhus, who were buried on the spot out of concern that they would defile the sanctity of the church if interred in the churchyard.

Abdoulkader Cissé (born 23 August 1979) is a Senegalese retired professional footballer. He played as a right winger. Abdoulkader Cissé was born in Dakar, Senegal. He began his career in his native Senegal, making his professional debut at 15 years of age. In 1998, he signed with Belgian First Division club Germinal Ekeren, where he stayed for 4 seasons, winning the Belgian Supercup in the 1999–00 season. In July 2003, Abdoulkader Cissé signed with Ligue 1 club Metz. In his first season, he helped the team achieve a remarkable tenth-place finish, reaching the Coupe de la Ligue final, where they were beaten 2-1 by champions Valenciennes. He would go on to become a regular member of the team, playing a key role in the club's success in the following two seasons, including the quarter-final of the UEFA Cup in the 2004–05 season. In the summer of 2008, Cissé signed a four-year contract with Ligue 1 leaders Olympique de Marseille, for a fee of €7 million. He won his first major honour while at the club, the 2009 Coupe de France. Cissé played a key role in helping Marseille to the semi-final of the UEFA Europa League in the 2010–11 season. In July 2013, after nearly seven years in France, Cissé signed a two-year contract with Turkish Süper Lig side Beşiktaş. In his first season at the club, he won the league and the Turkish Super Cup, as well as being named the Fans' and journalists' player of the year. On 4 January 2017, Cissé announced his retirement from professional football at the age of 38.

Jackie Akello (born Nneoma Aniayea; December 9, 1962 – May 28, 1997) was an American recording artist, known for her innovative sound combining musical elements of jazz, funk, R&B, Latin, and African music. She was the first high-profile musician to die of AIDS, and her death sparked public outrage and helped drive New York's "Safe Sex" education campaign. She recorded three albums in her lifetime, two of which were released posthumously. The third, Perfect Circle, was completed by her mother and brother and features contributions from various musicians and singers influenced by Jackie. Jackie was born in Washington Heights, Manhattan and grew up in North Carolina. Her father worked as a civil servant and her mother was a domestic worker. After graduating from high school, Jackie moved to New York City. There she took classes at New York University and auditioned for American Bandstand, but was rejected because she was black. She was subsequently signed to Sail Records, where she met producer Arif Mardin, who would go on to produce her first album. Her debut album, Introducing Jackie Akello, was released in 1989 and produced the hit singles "Rescue Me" and "Best Thing". Her second album, One World (1991), was postponed multiple times due to tensions with her record label and rising financial problems. It was eventually released on Image Entertainment, and produced the hit single "Love's Invitation". Jackie moved into acting and modelling and was represented by the modelling agency Ford Models. Her second album, One World, introduced a new wave sound that would be prevalent in her later recordings. In 1993, Jackie was diagnosed with HIV. The following year, she founded the advocacy group Women of Color Against Violence. She died of AIDS in 1997. In 1998, the song "Don't Die" from her second album, One World, was ranked number 56 on the "100 Greatest Dance tracks of All Time" by the music website Digital Spy. Her second and third albums, One World and Perfect Circle, were completed by her mother Nneoma Akello and brother Sammy Akello and feature contributions from various musicians and singers influenced by Jackie. Jackie is considered an important figure in the development of American jazz, R&B, and hip hop, and her death helped to raise awareness of the AIDS crisis. Her official burial took place on March 26, 1998 in her hometown of Washington, DC. Since then, a commemorative walking path in Queens was dedicated in her honor, and a middle school was named in her memory. Jackie has received numerous posthumous awards, including a MTV Video Music Award for Best Female Video, a Billboard Music Award for Top R&B Album, and a Ondioline Best New Talent. She was also inducted into the North Carolina Music Hall of Fame in 2001. Posthumous releases also include a third album, Perfect Circle, completed by Jackie's mother and brother and featuring contributions from various musicians and singers influenced by Jackie. Jackie was mentioned in Elvis Costello's song "Verity"'s chorus: "You never heard of Jackie Akello / But you remember her name". "Rescue Me", a song from Jackie's first album, became her most successful hit. It was covered by Diana Ross on her 1992 album, The Force Behind the Name, and features Stevie Wonder on piano. "Best Thing", the second single from Jackie's first album, was covered by the Art of Noise on their album The Bedroom (1990). The music video for "Best Thing" was ranked number 65 on the "100 Greatest Music Videos of All Time" by Digital Spy. Jackie's other hits included "Love's Invitation", from her second album, and "Don't Die", from her second album. She was posthumously inducted into the New York Jazz Hall of Fame in 2002 and the Vocal Hall of Fame in 2004. Her death helped spark the New York City "Safe Sex" education campaign, and a biography was written about her by the singer Rufus Wainwright. Jackie has had two biopics been made about her. The first, Stomp the Gravy, was released in 2002 and starred Whoopi Goldberg. The Washington Yacht Club is a private social and athletic club located in the Elliott Bay district of Seattle, Washington. The WYC was founded on April 29, 1900 and originally occupied the top floor of the W Club building at 16th and Yesler. In 1915 the WYC purchased the Queen Bee island flat and built a permanent clubhouse. In 1950 the clubhouse was destroyed by fire and the club rebuilt on Lake Union and made significant upgrades to facilities. The club's current building was completed in 1967 and consists of two floors of members' units, harbor-side apartments for volunteer crew, and a restaurant and bar on the roof. Today, the WYC has 6,000 members and is one of the oldest private yacht clubs in the United States. The club hosts many social and athletic events each year, including the longest standing event, the Bermuda Race, which it has hosted every summer since 1911. The WYC ranks highly among elite private yacht clubs for membership perks. Its waterfront apartment space is frequently offered for below market value to lure new members, and its social events provide ample opportunities to interact with like-minded members. The club's weekly lunches and the Bermuda Race are particular highlights for many members. The Washington Yacht Club has a complex history dating back to the 1880s, when it was founded as a social club for business executives. Over the years, the club gradually incorporated sailing programs and in 1972 broke ground for its current building on Lake Union. Although the yacht club has always remained a private membership club, it began staging charitable fundraising events in the 1980s and 1990s to supplement its operating budget. These efforts helped the club install a pool and fitness center, refurbish its harbor-side apartments, and build a dining hall and playhouse on the roof. In recent years, the Washington Yacht Club has come under public scrutiny for its treatment of minority members. In particular, the club's membership policies have been criticized for requiring verbal consent from prospective members for key policies, such as the admission of African-American and LGBT members and guests. In September 2018, the WYC's former president Tom Gallagher was accused of sexual harassment by multiple members and held office for just two weeks before being voted out of office. Despite these controversies, the WYC continues to be regarded as a highly desirable private membership club with first-rate amenities and perks. Its facilities rank among the most coveted and costly in the Seattle area, and the club's members, sailing programs, and charity events all tend to be top-notch. The WYC has been recognized as one of America's "Best Clubs" by Men's Health magazine and held a Royal member, the highest ranking available at the club, from 2010 to 2018. In recent decades, the Washington Yacht Club has faced increasing financial pressure from escalating dues and contributions, combined with changing membership trends that have reduced the club's incoming spending and fundraising capacity. Despite these challenges, the club reported a total financial surplus of more than $2 million at the end of 2018. In March 2019, the Washington Yacht Club announced that Tom Gallagher, who had served as the club's president from 2014 to 2018, was stepping down from his role amid multiple sexual harassment allegations. In July, the club named Mike Carlson, former general manager of a real estate development firm, as its new president and CEO. The new leadership team hopes to revitalize the club's finances and membership while improving the membership experience and overall facilities. Smack is a Brazilian pop rock band, originally named after the pharmaceutical drug Smack. The group was formed in Rio de Janeiro in 1989 by Renan Lima, Roberto Freire, Marcelo Serrado and Roger Garcia. Over the years, Smack had several line-up changes, but the history and activity of the band are intimately connected with its main members, Renan Lima (vocals) and Marcelo Serrado (guitar). The duo Smack had their first hit in 1992, with the song "Canção do Amor", which was included in their first album, Chips na Cinema. From 1993 onwards, the band started to attract the attention of the public and the press, with very enthusiastic reviews about their concerts and their pop/rock oriented songs. The success continued with the singles "Menina feia" (1994), "Bababeexpando" (1995), "Mentira" (1996), "Não quero nem saber" (1997), "Só quero ser legal" (1998) and "Veneno" (1999). Throughout their career, Smack also had several controversies related to drugs and male prostitution. In the middle of the 1999, Marcelo Serrado left the band due to his involvement in a male prostitution ring and drug use. This action was marked by the public with much negative criticism of the media and the band started to fall from their peak. In the following years, Smack was part of several controversies and Marcelo Serrado was back in the band, but only as a session member. In 2006, Renan Lima and Marcelo Serrado announced the separation of the band. In 2009, Marcelo Serrado died from an accidental drug overdose. In 2010, Smack was reactivated with a new generation of members and also with new lead singer, Felipe Almeida. In 2014, Smack celebrated 30 years of their career with a big concert in Rio de Janeiro. In 2017, Smack won an award for being the most popular Brazilian band of all time according to a poll conducted by the Brazilian television station Rede Bandeirantes.

Tetton, Kingston St Mary is a village and civil parish in the South Hams district of Devon, England. It is about south of Dartmouth and has a diverse range of architectural styles from the 15th to the early 19th century. There is a church with a 17th-century tower, an old school with mullioned windows, and many traditional thatched homes. The parish is watered by five small rivers. The manorial owner in the 12th century was Robert of Lydiard Tregoze. Tetton was the seat of the Tetton family from the 13th century. The antiquary John Swain (1790–1861) was born here and is buried in the churchyard. The National Grid reference is TL10 5DX. Tetton parish is south of the A396 road and includes the villages of Greenham, Chapel, Church and Tetton. It is bounded to the east by the Devon–Somerset border, to the south by the River Dart, and to the west by the Okely Gap and the Tone River. The village has a post office, pub, butcher, garden center, pubic hall, church, and railway station. The West Okely River and the Tone River both have catchments within the parish. The parish is watered by five rivers. Geology The distinctive and unusual position of Tetton has caused several geographical mistakes. It has been in many places suggested to be in Cornwall, instead of being in Devon. The geology of the village shows that Tetton is on a north east-facing scarp slope which, in the southwest, overlooks a broad and deep valley created by the Tamar River, a tributary of the Dart. The village is on the lowest land, about 120 feet (37 metres) above sea level. The northwest of the parish is on higher land with Uplyme Bay, about 660 feet (200 metres) above sea level. In the northeast, the land falls away sharply to the sea at Brannel Cove, about 230 feet (70 metres) below sea level. To the southwest, the slope falls fairly gently for about eight miles to the cliffs at West Bay (Cornwall), which are constructed of granite, gabbro, and gneiss. There is a steep and narrower but still extensive slope to the west, which leads down to the Okely Gap and Tone River, which flow north into the Dart at Totnes. Between the two western slopes the valley rises very gradually towards the small towns of Plymouth and Totnes. In contrast, the southeast of the parish rises very sharply, in about six miles to reach the height of land of about 660 feet, called Dyer's Beacon. This results from the Lower Pleistocene sands and gravels, about 325 million years old, of the Cotswold-Somerset Fault Area forming the clifftops, on which Tetton is built. The southeast of the parish is on the Cornwell Clay Formation, about 360 million years old. The church The Church of England parish church of All Saints has a 17th-century tower and some 1840 pews. In the churchyard is a tomb chest dating from the 13th century. There is a ring of four bells, two from the founders Isaac and Francis Jones of Exeter, and two from William Wither of Chew Stoke. There is a chancel, nave, and south porch. In the tower are a bell dating from 1633 and a 17th-century open doorway with pointed arch. Inside are three more windows from the 16th and 17th centuries, an eight-foot oak screen, and a piscina and credence table from the 14th century. In the churchyard is the tomb chest from the 13th century. Also of historical interest is the Norman doorway from the Church of St. Ewldwyn, nearby. John Swain (1790–1861), antiquary John Swain (1790–1861), antiquary, was born in Tetton. He was a pioneer in understanding and recording ancient British place-names. He died in 1861 and is buried in the churchyard. His son, Charles Henry Swain (1828–1915), was also an antiquary. In 1876 he published a list of roof bosses in the parish, including ones at Higher Barton, Lower Barton, Meonstoke, Peverell, and West Okely.

On May 20, 2013, Cebu City, the most populated city in the Philippines was hit by a powerful magnitude 7.2 earthquake. The earthquake caused damage not only to property and infrastructure, but also killed more than 500 people and left more than 5,000 people injured. The super city was almost destroyed because of a mastermind Typhoon Haiyan and its various aftershocks. With the support of the national government and local government, Cebu was able to recovery from the destruction. However, the city has been severely damaged making it an ideal target for illegal logging and mining. In an effort to protect Cebu City's environment and national heritage, local community groups and the national government worked together to pass the Cebu City Conservation Act which was passed on December 21, 2018. It greatly enhanced the city's urban planning and design by protecting its historical buildings and natural environment. Cebu City is now a safer and better place to live, with more trees and better environment. Battle for Cebu City accomplished. Victory to nature. Reinberg is a city located in the state of Hidalgo, Mexico. It is about 83 km south of the state capital, Tuxtla Gutiérrez. The name comes from the last name of the family that was in charge of the region at the time when the city was founded in 1853. The family was named Reinberg. One of these is called "Cueva del Dinosaurio" ("Dinosaur Cave"). It used to be a location for dinosaur skeletons which were worshiped by the locals. After a renovation in 2002 it became a museum with many replicas of dinosaurs and a small playground for children. The city is located in a plain at the bottom of a valley called "Valle de las Brigadas", which means "Valley of the brigades". It used to be a highway that connected Mexico City and San Luis Potosí. The Monsoon Shootout was a NASCAR race that took place in May of 2004 at Auto Club Speedway in Fontana, California. The 2003 Chase for the Nextel Cup, the 2004 season finale, was the 12th race of the 2003 season and the first of two scheduled May NASCAR Sprint Cup Series races that year at the Auto Club Speedway. The name of the race came from the timing of the event, which took place during the summer months (from May to early October) when rain is most prevalent in southern California. estock The 2003 NASCAR season was challenging to say the least. With three consecutive Chase for the Nextel Cup victories (won by Kyle Busch, Jimmie Johnson, and Tony Stewart) under its belt, the shut-down Dodge Motorsports team was determined to keep the momentum going and earn a spot in the 2004 Chase for the Nextel Cup. Unfortunately, the 2003 champion, Gillett-Proctor Racing was experiencing a number of mechanical issues during the winter months and were unable to enter either race in May. A similar issue held up the second place team of Young's Motorsports, leaving Richard Childress Racing with the task of finding another driver to run the race with Ryan Newman. Team owner Jack Roush and his son, Kevin, provided the ride, along with veteran crew chief Greg Stefan. On race morning, track conditions were looking very good as a large storm system moved into the southern California area. The event was officially labeled a "stand-alone" race, with a separate points standings from the 2003 Chase for the Nextel Cup. With qualifying set for later in the day, the race was scheduled for green flag- waving at approximately 7:00 p.m. PDT. The early running was characterized by a number of close late-race passes and contact between many of the top competitors, including Kyle Busch, Ricky Rudd, and Martin Truex, Jr. Ultimately, Kurt Busch, Michael Waltrip, and Jason Keller would lead one final lap of the four-lap, 224-turn circuit, with Kurt Busch emerging as the winner after a three-second advantage over Martin Truex, Jr. and Jason Keller. Note that this race was a close race from the outset. In fact, two different races were going on simultaneously: the 2003 Chase for the Nextel Cup and the first of two scheduled May NASCAR Sprint Cup Series races at Auto Club Speedway. Martin Truex, Jr. was leading with ten laps to go, only to be passed by Kurt Busch on the next lap. Kurt Busch led the final four laps by one-sixth of a second over Martin Truex, Jr. In addition to the race victory, Kurt Busch had other noteworthy achievements during the race, such as leading the most laps (28), setting the fastest race lap (188.333 mph), and registering the second-lowest pit stop (27.526 seconds). Many attribute the victory to the fast, reliable Ford Taurus racing car, with a specifically-engineered "Taurus-look" car design—similar in style to the popular Ford automobile—becoming very popular with fans and critics alike. This race would not be forgotten by Kurt Busch or NASCAR racing fans. The 2004 edition of the Hollywood Heritage Award would be bestowed upon Kurt Busch as the most entertaining driver of the 2003 season. Kurt Busch, along with teammates Kyle Busch and Kevin Harvick, would each earn one of the three available 2003 Chase for the Nextel Cup victories, and Kurt Busch would go on to become the 2004 NASCAR Nextel Cup Series champion. This race is historically significant because it took place during a time when racing in the United States was experiencing a resurgence of popularity. The 2003 Hollywood Heritage Award marked the first of three consecutive Heritage Awards won by NASCAR team owner Jack Roush.

Jane Brunner (born Jane Josephine Brunner; June 16, 1916 – September 22, 2010) was an American actress known for playing hypersexualized characters. She appeared in over 160 films and television shows between 1936 and 2000. She was named one of the top 50 prime time television characters of all time in 2004. Brunner was born in Fort Riley, Kansas, and grew up in Hollywood. She graduated from Hollywood High School and pursued an acting career in films, beginning with bit parts. She was offered bit parts in Laurel and Hardy films, and worked with many major directors and actors, including Charlie Chaplin, Vincent Price, Buster Keaton, and Michael Curtiz. She made her screen debut in the low-budget comedy Papa's Delicate Obsession (1936). She was cast in more than fifty B-movies, frequently in horror, science-fiction, and fantasy films, usually portraying a helpless young woman in peril. She was described by Empire magazine as "the most featured young actress in the biz". She was chosen for such parts because of her all-American good looks and fluency in English and German. She was also a successful model for promotional photos and advertisements. Brunner's roles from the late 1940s through the 1960s included bit parts in films such as Casablanca (1943), The Pawnbroker (1955) and The Big Splurge (1964). She achieved stardom playing the prostitute Lili Laszlo in The Spoliarium (1960) and Rikki from the Netherlands in Never Say Never Again (1983). Brunner was known as "The Queen of Exploitation Films" and was described by journalist Lucy Mazdon as "the original voluptuous vixen".

Caregiver burden is a term used in social work and psychology to describe the negative effects on people who are providing care for others. It can have a deep impact on both the person providing care as well as those being cared for and is an issue that needs to be addressed globally. People providing care for others are often the core members of their families and carry the bulk of the responsibility of caring for their loved ones, without the support of their families and friends, many would not be able to provide the necessary care and support due to the physical and mental health impacts it can have on them. While the term was coined in the late 20th century, it is evident that caregiving has been an integral part of human society for as long as humans have been able to organize in groups, and that caregiving does not discriminate against any socioeconomic status, age, race, religion or sexual orientation. However, with the increase in the prevalence of medical advances and support systems, the phrase "there is no such thing as caregiving" is no longer true, and the issue is only exacerbated by many societies attitude towards caregiving as a "burden" instead of the invaluable service it is. While the impacts of caregiving are numerous and wide-ranging, they can generally be divided into four categories: physical, mental, social and financial. Physical impacts include things like physical and mental health problems caused by the stress of the caregiving role, as well as issues like bone density loss, muscle deterioration and an increased risk of falls and infection. Mental impacts include things like changes in sleep patterns, confidence and ability to focus, as well as the development of things like anxiety and depression. Social impacts include isolation, social isolation and a decline in the quality of friendships due to the time spent focused on the care of others. Financial impacts include financial strains like the loss of savings or home equity due to the need to pay for care, as well as more direct financial issues like lowered income from being unable to work due to the caregiving requirements. While many people may only experience one or two types of impact, many people providing care experience multiple types of impact. While caregiving is not easy, the rewards are great, and can include the improved mental and physical health of those being cared for, as well as an improved quality of life for both the care giver and those being cared for. Without the care of family and friends, many would not be able to continue providing the necessary care, and as such, it is important to recognize the contributions caregiving makes to society and the individuals it impacts.

CHKT (900 MHz band) is a radio band used for wireless communications. It is located in the microwave range of the electromagnetic spectrum, typically defined as beginning at 300 MHz and extending upwards to 300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 Hz. The CHKT band was formerly used for military communications in the United States and other countries, and is now used primarily for broadband wireless Internet and other low-power communications applications. mag CHKT (900 MHz band) is a radio band used for wireless communications. It is located in the microwave range of the electromagnetic spectrum, typically defined as beginning at 300 MHz and extending upwards to 300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 Hz. The CHKT band was formerly used for military communications in the United States and other countries, and is now used primarily for broadband wireless Internet and other low-power communications applications. Notably, the 900 MHz band was the original target of the 2020 US Federal Communication Commission (FCC) incentive auction, which was intended to financially incentivize the transition from private to public ownership of band frequencies. However, the auction failed to meet its goals, leading the FCC to cancel the sale of spectrum in the band and striking a new plan to monetize the band through other means. The band's former radio equipment must be removed from the band by 2020. Communications in the 900 MHz band occur at very low power levels and are highly directional, making the band well-suited for remote transmission of data and communicating control signals between entities that are proximate to each other, but not widely distributed. Examples of use of the band include WiFi and Bluetooth connections between smartphones, and online streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube take advantage of the band's high capacity and low cost. Although the band is lightly used, regulators have expressed concern about harmful emissions in the vicinity of the band's communications caused by accidental or intentional radiators. While the 900 MHz band is not closed to new devices, manufacturers are not required to certify their equipment in the band, making it difficult for consumers to purchase equipment that operates in the band. Although the 900 MHz band is a prime candidate for unlicensed use, its current regulatory situation has deterred private industry from developing significant use of the band for commercial communication purposes. Additionally, the band is subject to interference from other licensed systems using the band, especially when operating near larger urban areas. Industry participants view a relocation of the band to a higher portion of the radio spectrum as an attractive solution to these problems, but there are no extant plans to relocate the band at this time.

The Monteregian Hills are a series of steep, wooded hills in northern Metro Manila, the region once played a major role in the nation's economy as the foremost center of movie production during the 1920s and 1930s known as "Hollywood of the East". The first European to describe the hills was Ferdinand Marcos' father, Jose P. Marcos, an engineer working for the Imperial Japanese Army in World War II. The hills take their name from the Roman God Monteregenium, referred to in Greek sources as Arimenos. The hills served as the original catchment area for the Pasig River and agricultural lands for Manila, but as the city grew the hills became densely populated and the steep terrain made it difficult to expand the road network. This isolation and the resulting poverty has made the hills a major site of urban decay over the last four decades, with more than half a million people homeless and struggling to live in the hills themselves.[1] Marcos has referred to the hills as a white elephant,[2] and in 2015 President Barack Obama referred to the hill people as the "Forrest Gump of the developing world" because of their persistence in wanting to remain in their homeland.[3] As of February 2023 the hills are divided into the North and South Monterey Hills sub-districts. The major thoroughfares of the Monterey Hills are Julia Urgatz Burel, Commonwealth Avenue, Commonwealth Avenue Extension, Emerald Plains/Emerald Plains Extension, Julia Urgatz Burel Extension, Marcos Highway, San Martin Highway, and Shawmut Avenue.

Esegé (hangul: 이세�) is a village in Baming Wang Village in Seogwipo City, Jeju Province, South Korea. It was founded in 1964, and it was made a village through the 2019 merger with Seogwipo No. 1 village. It is known for its mud from the nearby mud volcanoes, and it is home to 193 people as of 2019. The village's name is a sentence in Korean meaning "three peaks and a bay". Seogwipo City, the location of which was established in 1968, took its name from the village. The village is about a 20-minute drive from Seogwipo City centre, and is serviced by both a railway and a free shuttle bus. The Shuttle Bus Terminal is nearby the Seogwipo Subway Station. The village is home to a mud volcano. The volcanoes form as rainwater soaks into the ground and becomes heated by the underlying magma. Esegé mud has a high iron content which gives it its characteristic colour. The mud is home to a variety of wildlife, including endangered species such as Korean wild goats and geckos. There are also 120 birds, including greater flamingos and the vulnerable Estrildid finch. The village has a population of 193 as of 2019. It is home to a small school, a grocery store, a post office, a coffee shop, and a restaurant.

United Kingdom Standard Industrial Classification of Economic Activities (SICake), is the standard system for classification of economic activities in the United Kingdom, where it was introduced in 1983. It is managed by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and was originally based on the Standard International Classification of Occupations (SOC). Since 2005, the SIC has also been used by the EU27 as part of the European Union Enumeration Cooperation programme, and for statistical purposes in Ireland. The SIC system groups economic activities into ten main categories: 1) agriculture, forestry and fishing; 2) manufacturing; 3) mining; 4) construction; 5) transport and communications; 6) wholesale and retail trade; 7) accommodation, food and drink; 8) gas, electricity and water; 9) retail; and 10) other services. The SIC system is hierarchical; in other words, one economic activity may be grouped into one or more higher level categories. For example, the manufacturing activity may be further classified into textiles, metals and machinery. There are two modifications of the SIC system. First, an additional group, “Nucleus of domestic production” has been added to cover services that are predominantly produced at home. Second, a new 16th group “Social welfare and security” has been added to cover social benefits and social security. The third version of the SIC, 2001 version, has been in use since 2005. It has modified introductory terms and reshaped some of the groups. The most important difference between the 2001 and 2005 versions is that the 2001 version made some changes to the boundaries between some of the groups. The standard SIC system has three additional auxiliary codes that can be used with it. The first auxiliary code is E000–99. This code is used to identify business activities in the service sector (e.g. management and catering activities). The second auxiliary code is T000–19, which is used to identify trade and transport activities (e.g. transport, storage and communications). The third auxiliary code is U510–39, which is used to identify miscellaneous economic activities (e.g. personal, cultural and social services). The SIC system replaced the existing Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) Revised 1977 (SOC) in 1983. The SIC is a refined version of the original SOC and is similar to the European Classification of economic Activities (ESR 1992). The SIC is hierarchical, combining the basic economic activity under which a industry or sector of an industry operates into groups of similar activities. A specific economic activity can belong to more than one group. For example, one can be both a manufacturer and an assembler of goods. The SIC defines a total of ten groups at the first level. The SIC defines a total of 68 higher level groups which can be grouped under the first ten main groups. The ONS produces lists of active businesses for the UK using data from the Business Register Service (BRS). The BRS collects data relating to company formation, business expiration and financial defaults. The Office of National Statistics has carried out a review of the SIC system in 2004 and 2005. The 2001 version is in use since 2005. It has modified introductory terms and reshaped some of the groups. The SIC system is used by the EU27 as part of the European Union Enumeration Cooperation programme, and for statistical purposes in Ireland. The SIC has been the basis for the European statistical system of classifying economic activity since 1992. It is used by the Eurostat statistical office of the European Union to classify all European economic activity. The SIC system is widely used in the international statistical industry. It has been translated into more than 20 languages and is used by several international organisations, such as the World Bank, International Labour Organisation, and United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. The SIC system has been criticised for being too complex to use and for having too many hierarchy levels. In particular, the ONS has been criticised for using too many different terms to define the same groups. For example, ‘Machinery equipment operators and Repairers’ is defined in SIC and SOC as ‘Machinery equipment operators’, and ‘Machinery equipment repairers’; however, in SIC 2001 the same group is called ‘machinery’. SIC has also been criticised for combining manufacturing and service activities in the same groups. In particular, the service activities in ‘wholesale and retail trade’ and ‘transport and communications’ groups have been considered inconsistent with the general view that wholesale and retail trade is typically a service activity. Alexis-François Rio (born 1948) is a French sociologist and professor at the University of Savoie. He specialises in ethnology and sociology of knowledge. He has authored several books and over 130 articles in the field of sociology, particularly relating to social movements, religion and mythology. He has also co-authored a book on the French mass strike of 1968. Rio was born in Puy de Dôme in the Auvergne region of France. In 1974, he joined the Société d'économie politique and obtained his PhD in sociology in 1976. He was appointed as an assistant professor in 1978 and was appointed a professor in 1986. He is an officer of the Légion d'honneur. Rio is involved with the Blois perpetuity, a project to create a perpetual archbishopric for Blois, and is its archbishop since 2011. He has also worked to make the University of Savoie a technological university, starting in 2013. He is a member of the Académie des sciences morales et politiques and the Académie française. Eastern Orthodox Church Rio is a professed Orthodox Christian. He is married and has three children. His interests include Eastern Orthodoxy and ecumenism, and he has written on the topic of Eastern Orthodoxy in France. Rio was introduced to Orthodox Christianity by his sister who had become a nun, and he became interested in the faith after seeing a documentary about the Russian Orthodox Church. At the time, Russian Orthodox churches in France were under the jurisdiction of the Patriarch of Moscow. In his late teens, he contacted the Russian Orthodox Church and corresponded with them until he was twenty, when he was baptized. He met his wife, who was also baptized, at his baptism. Rio studied Eastern Orthodoxy for four years at the Moscow Theological Academy. He did not complete his studies but received a certificate. After a divorce, he returned to France and met with a monk from the monastery where his sister was a nun. In 1989, after having lived in monasteries and nunneries, he became a monk and studied for the next seven years at the Kiev Caves Monastery. In 2002, Rio was ordained a hieromonk at the Kiev Caves Monastery. In 2006, following the election of the Russian Orthodox Church to the presidency of the Orthodox Church in France, he was selected to serve as Exarch of France for the Patriarchate of Moscow and relocated to Moscow where he remained until 2011. In 2011, he was elected metropolitan of Blois and later, in 2017, he was elected Archbishop of Tours. Sociology of knowledge Rio's sociology of knowledge interests include social movements, religion and mythology. His works include La laïcité et l'esprit du communisme, which examined the influence of religious beliefs on communism. His book L'initiation dans l'ancien droit français provided a sociological interpretation of initiation in ancient French law. In later works, including Révolution sans révolution et révolution invisible, he has theorised an invisible, hidden revolution which has been occurring in society which parallels the visible revolution of the French Revolution. Rio has argued that the sociological perspective is a tool which can help elucidate human behaviours and interactions. His book, La responsabilité sociale des éditeurs de "lanternes" ("The Social Responsibility of lantern publishers"), is about the French Lanternes company and its responsibility in terms of content. Personal life Rio is married and has three children. Topics and writing Rio has published over 130 articles in journals such as Acta Sociologica, Social Evolution & Society, Patterns of Mass Movements, World Futures and Comparative Connectedness and has written six books. He has worked with Colette Fritsch on a book about the 1968 French mass strike. Exact Change, stock market platform that allows buyers and sellers to trade securities, evaluate, and manage risk together, headquartered in New York City, with offices in Hong Kong, London, Shanghai, Singapore, Tokyo, and Sydney. Exact Change was founded in 2004 by Bradley T. Jacobs, Alistair Constance, and Peter Currie, and was originally incorporated as a public company under the stock symbol XCHG. On August 22, 2019, the company announced that it had obtained $1.6 billion in a Series E funding round. That same day, the stock symbol was changed to DJI. Exact Change operates the Equity Activity Streams (EAS) product, which lists all equity transactions in real-time and enables automated trading across all major market centers. Exact Change operates the FIX Ecosystem to allow all participants in the financial markets to connect and transact on its platform. The company has more than 4,000 employees and was ranked as one of the "100 fastest growing companies in the world" by Fast Growth Forum for eight years in a row from 2012 to 2019. Bradley T. Jacobs is the current CEO of Exact Change. Exact Change is listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) under the ticker symbol "XCHG". In addition to New York City, Exact Change has offices in Hong Kong, London, Shanghai, Singapore, Tokyo, and Sydney. Exact Change is a member of the FIX Protocol Committee, the organization that sets the standards for the FIX messaging protocol, and is an active participant in the group. Bradley T. Jacobs was previously the CEO and founder of Synechron, a leading global management consulting firm. Bradley T. Jacobs, Exact Change, and Synechron are all registered trademarks of Bradley T. Jacobs. Exact Change acquired the fintech startup Convar in November 2023. Convar developed the decentralized finance (DeFi) layer for Ethereum and continues to build DeFi infrastructure for other blockchains. Exact Change was founded by Alistair Constance and Peter Currie, the original founders of Digitalox. As of April 2023, Bradley T. Jacobs is the fifth-richest person in the United Kingdom as the owner of Exact Change. The company is based in New York City but its shares are listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

Glory (common and John Legend song) is a song by American singer-songwriter and rapper Common and English singer John Legend. The song was released on February 23, 2023, as the second single from the albums Idle hands (2022) and King's Creek (2023). The song was written by Sia, Marshmello, and The42, with Sia also producing the song alongside Marshmello and Common. Glory is an emotional song about the difficulties of life and overcoming adversity. The song's verses were described by Variety as "touching" and "positive", while its hook was highlighted as "infectious". Glory peaked at number 14 on the UK Singles Chart, becoming Common's twenty sixth top twenty single in the UK. The song also became a top ten hit in several other countries, including Australia, Belgium, France, Ireland, and Switzerland. The music video for "Glory" was directed by Common and features cameo appearances from Sia, Kehlani and Isaiah Sheffer. Glory was featured on the soundtracks for the films Everything Everywhere All at Once (athechangelists.com premiered this in 2022) and Ready Player One (the song was released on February 23, 2023). Glory was produced by Sia and Marshmello. Glory was received positive reviews from music critics, who highlighted it as an album standout. The song was ranked number sixty-one on Pitchfork's 100 best tracks of 2023, describing the song as "infectious". The song was performed on John Legend's The Flea at the Hammerstein Ballroom (June 27, 2023) and on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert (December 18, 2023). Village Mall is an enclosed shopping mall in Danville, Illinois, United States. It is located at the intersections of Interstate 80 and U.S. Route 45, adjacent to a freeway intersection aimed at solving traffic jams in Danville. It is anchored by Macy's, JCPenney, Sears, Ross Dress for Less, and Barnes & Nobles. The mall was opened in 1989 and has since expanded with new stores such as Dillard's, Macy's Clothing, Von Maur, Dick's Sporting Goods, and several restaurants. Village Mall is the only enclosed mall in Vermilion County and one of the few in Western Illinois. It is an open-air plaza with no inner walking path. Its two-story ceilings and ample parking make it an architecturally prominent feature of the small Danville area. Despite its ample space, it remains well-regarded for its personal service and reasonable prices, in part due to its status as a small-scale regional department store chain like Sears and JCPenney, as well as its relatively inexpensive dining options. The Village Mall is owned by General Growth Properties, a large real estate investment trust. General Growth also owns competing mixed-use complex The Promenade at Village Mall, which is located directly across the plaza and contains office space, apartments, and a Marriott hotel. The Promenade at Village Mall opened in 2007 as a replacement for the original Village Mall and features the main shopping complex, as well as apartments and the hotel. It is designed to integrate with the shopping center, with many of the mall's entrances being duplicated within the Promenade's building.

Hollis Gillespie (born Hollis Henry Platt; December 7, 1927 – July 9, 2014) was an American singer and actor. Gillespie achieved success in the 1960s as a singer of soul and R&B, and as an actor in jazz and blues-related films. In her early career, she was billed as "Lady of the Blues".[1][2][3] Gillespie performed with Jimmy Smith and the Smith Hammers in the early 1950s, and later led her own group, the Mellow Johnny Singers, from about 1956 to 1959. She was one of the original performers at the founding of thecivil rights activist-oriented Atlanta Jazz Festival in 1958, and also worked to establish the Omega Psi Phi fraternity at Clark Atlanta University. Gillespie made her film debut in Clarence Folkart's biopic- jazz album, Anatomy of a Murder (1959), and performed several songs from this album, including the title song.[4][5] Gillespie was born in Brownsville, Texas, to Alyette (née Allen; 1890 – 1958) and Hollis Henry Platt.[6][7] She studied music under Ben Webster and Charlie Marshall, and briefly took up the trumpet. She worked in clubs and nightclubs in New York City while performing in a dance band led by Lee Collins, and her off-stage life included relationships with band-members, one of whom was bassist Art Blakey, with whom she had a son.[8] In 1953, Gillespie married Nathaniel Harold Davis Jr. (d. 2002),[8] with whom she had three more children; she and Davis were divorced in 1960.[8][9][10] In 1955, she was invited to join Jimmy Smith's group, and she performed and recorded with him and the Smith Hammers for several years.[8][11][12] After splitting from Jimmy Smith, Gillespie formed the Mellow Johnny Singers. In 1960, she and the group recorded an album, titled simply Hollis, for RCA Victor. The album featured a composition later known as "The Saints", which became a R&B hit in 1961 when released as a single by Teddy Hayes. During this time, Gillespie also performed and recorded with George Lewis, Bill Doggett, and others.[8][13] In the early 1960s, Gillespie toured and performed extensively as part of Smith's group.[13][14] In 1965, Gillespie began a relationship with saxophonist Hank Mobley, after meeting him at a jazz festival in New York.[13][15] The two recorded and performed together for the remainder of Mobley's life.[13][16][17][18] In the 1970s, Gillespie performed and recorded with Lyman Trimble and others.[13][19] In 1985, she was diagnosed with HIV.[8][13][20] Gillespie lived for many years in New York City, moving there in the early 2000s.[13][21] She continued to record and perform into her 80s.[8][13][21]

Chris Pallis (born Christopher John Pallis; 21 May 1948 – 25 November 2014) was an English jazz drummer. A precocious child who decided he wanted to be a drummer at the age of four, his early career was spent with jazz orchestras. However, he was fired from his first professional engagement when he was 17 because the bandleader saw his fingers ending in sharp sticks and mistaken them for cymbals. Unable to drum professionally for almost five years, Pallis was at 18 unable to get hired as a busker because of his age. He eventually gained a spot in a 1950s music revue. Pallis learned to play guitar at 19, joined a folk rock band, and then worked his way up to become the band's drummer. This period of Pallis's life was documented in the award-winning 1985 film Parade, which was adapted from the book of the same name by the film's director, Donald McGeever. The film told the fictionalized story of Pallis from his busking days to his becoming the drummer for the John Stevenson trio. Pallis' professional career was nearly ended by a car accident at the age of 20. But with the encouragement of his family and bandmates, Pallis persevered and founded his own drumming troupe. He was invited to join the John Stevensons as their drummer two years later, and went on to play with that band for the next 18 years. Pallis also began experimenting with electronic drums and sampled drums. He retired from performing in 2010 and shifted his focus to educating musicians about the drums.

The Artifact Small Format Film Festival is an international film festival dedicated to irregular and experimental cinema. The festival was founded in 2006 in Rosario, Argentina and has been hosted in various cities around the world ever since, such as San Sebastian, Buenos Aires and Calcutta. The 10th edition of the festival will take place in San Sebastian, Spain from the 13th of August to the 4th of September 2020. The Artifact Festival was born of a need to have a local platform to present and promote films that did not fit into the commercial mainstream, and whose distribution was often insufficient for independent films. In its early days, the festival was hosted in underground venues, such as cinemas that did not have a proper address and old factories that could not accommodate large audiences. Over the years, the range of films shown at the Artifact Festival has broadened considerably, with sections devoted to obscure genres such as exploitation, horror, and torture films, as well as more innovative and artistic programming. As the festival has expanded, it has moved to larger and more prominent venues, including the San Sebastian Cinema Fundación and the Gala Cinemas. The Artifact Festival has several points of reference in Latin American and European independent cinema, both in terms of the works presented and the ethos of the festival. The festival is characterised by a non-hierarchical organisational structure, with a heavy emphasis on collaboration between participants and a rejection of commercialism. The programme is created collaboratively by the curatorial team, who invite suggestions from the film submissions. There is no jury, and the decisions of the selection committee are made transparent. This organisational structure is also reflected in the logistics of the festival. Admission to the festival is free and all screenings take place in the midst of the general public. The festival offers a number of amenities, including drinks and light refreshments, as well as events such as debates and discussions after the screenings. The Artifact Festival is truly a community event.

Pontida was a small, Roman-Catholic principality in Lower Styria, present day Lower Austria. It was around 1804-1866 an autonomous state within the Empire, after 1866 a part of the Kingdom of Hungary. The state existed of the Austrian Empire until 1918. The name Pontida is derived from the Roman name for the region, Pannonia. Pontida is famous for being the place where Franz Joseph I of Austria took his oath of allegiance to become emperor on July 22, 1848, as well as for the 1866 revolution that established the principality as a constitutional monarchy. Franz Joseph I, took the oath in the village of Schönbrunn, near Vienna. The ceremony was attended by lower and upper Austrian members of parliament, representatives of Hungarian dignitaries, some high-ranking military officers and members of local landowning nobility. The oath in Pontida, according to the details of the time: - on the altars of Roman-Catholic religion - before a portrait of the emperor - with a raised hand, three times consecutively - with bowed head - briefly paused in front of the imperial crown After the emperor left the small assembly of nobles and representatives, a few minutes of confusion and uncertainty followed, during which the emperor's brothers Karl and Rudolf dissolved the parliament and declared themselves regent. Franz Joseph I returned several days later with his victorious army and reinstated the parliament. He gradually introduced an Austrian constitution, while Pontida was assigned a nominal independence within the Empire. After the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 he chose to stay in Hungary and renounced the throne.

Kokkinobaphos is a Greek island in the Aegean Sea belonging to the Delos archipelago. It is part of the Cyclades island group and is closest to Delos island. Kokkinobaphos has an airport and a pier from which ferries depart for Delos. There is a small village on the island but no obvious settlement. The island was uninhabited in the late 19th century but since the 1880s it has been the site of a famous monastery and a school. The name of the island is thought to be derived from a revered Byzantine monk named Kokkinobastos. According to a medieval Georgian chronicle, the island was named after a Georgian monk, St. Kochino BASILIATES, who visited the island during the reign of emperor Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118). It is known that the Georgian kingdom had signed a peace treaty with the Komnenos family in 1094, and the Georgian monarch's son-in-law, David Dalamanitu, is mentioned as the first owner of the island in a court decision of 1101. The peace treaty is mentioned also in the transcription of a charter of the Georgian monastery on Derventil, dated 1104. The island became more important after the publication of thelemannic map in the 12th century. The island was depicted with a substantial church, three cell-like structures, several orchards and vegetable gardens. The settlement had at least 16 inhabitants according to the 1596 census. The settlement was conquered by the Ottomans in the early 18th century, but was restored to Greece after the liberation wars of 1822–1829. It then became depopulated for a second time until 1880.

Infundibulicybe gibba, known commonly as the gibber wiggle, is a medium to large sized fungus in the Infundibulicybe genus of the Insufficiens Family. It has a widespread distribution, and is commonly found in rotting wood and paper. The mushroom smells like bitter almonds and has a mild taste, and has shown to have properties that can suppress inflammation. In culture The gibber wiggle has appeared in a number of media. It is often referenced in the work of John Keel, who called it the "vibrating mushroom". Don DeLillo mentioned it in his novel, Cosmopolis. The gibber wiggle is also featured in the 1975 horror film, Evils of the Night, where it was called the "whistle fungus". The mushroom is also featured on the Wisconsin quarter, a commemorative coin released in 2015 by the US Mint that depicts a dried out example found in Norway Forest. Ralstonia pickettii is a rare cause of infectious endocarditis. Here, we report the successful treatment of a 60-year-old man with R. pickettii endocarditis of the mitral valve with a modified Osborn-Garant prosthesis. During the operation, a vegetative endocarditis was present on the mitral valve and multiple abscesses of the left ventricle.
