Business casual is a dress code that is commonly followed in workplaces in many parts of the world. This dress code sits in between the formal dress code and the casual dress code. It is meant to provide a comfortable and relaxed dress code for employees without compromising the professional image of the company. Business casual dress code varies from office to office and from industry to industry. The components of business casual attire for men include dress slacks, khakis, polo shirts, button-down shirts, collared shirts, sweaters, blazers, loafers, and dress shoes. Men can mix, match and combine the outfits with different color combinations and patterns, but should aim to maintain a sophisticated and polished look. For women, business casual comprises skirts, dresses, blouses, slacks, trousers, sweaters, and dress shoes. It is essential to avoid any form of clothing that is too low-cut, tight-fitting, short, or revealing. Women can use accessories like scarfs, jewelry, and handbags to vary their outfit and personalize their look, as long as they remain professional. The term "business casual" is believed to have originated in the 1990s when employers and employees began looking for a more relaxed dress code. The dress code has since become widespread and has gained popularity in modern offices. Companies have adopted different policies and have defined their unique business casual requirements to suit their culture and brand. Business casual attire has several benefits, including boosting employee morale and wellbeing by allowing them to feel comfortable in their clothing, enhancing the team spirit in the organization, reducing the cost of buying expensive formal wear, and creating a relaxed environment that encourages creativity and productivity. In conclusion, business casual attire serves to provide a more relaxed dress code in a professional working environment. It ensures that employees remain comfortable while maintaining a professional appearance and contributing to the goals and objectives of the company.

Magyar Posse is a post-rock band formed in 2001 in Helsinki, Finland. The 1986 Philippine presidential election, also known as the Snap Election, was held on February 7, 1986. It was the first presidential election held under the new Constitution of the Philippines, which was ratified in 1983. The election was called by President Ferdinand Marcos, who sought to legitimize his more than twenty years of martial rule by winning a fresh mandate. The main opposition contender was Corazon Aquino, the widow of slain opposition leader Benigno Aquino Jr. Aquino ran under the banner of the United Nationalist Democratic Organization (UNIDO), which was composed of various opposition parties and groups, including the Lakas ng Bayan (People Power) movement. She was joined by former senator Salvador Laurel as her running mate. Marcos, on the other hand, ran under the Kilusang Bagong Lipunan (New Society Movement), the political arm of his regime. He was supported by various politicians, businessmen, and military officials. The election was marred by widespread allegations of fraud, violence, and intimidation. The Commission on Elections (Comelec) declared Marcos the winner with 10,807,197 votes, while Aquino garnered 9,291,700 votes. However, the opposition, led by the Catholic Church and various civil society groups, challenged the results and launched a campaign of mass protest and civil disobedience. The culmination of this movement was the People Power Revolution, a peaceful uprising that saw millions of Filipinos take to the streets in Manila and other cities. The military, which was previously loyal to Marcos, eventually shifted its allegiance to the opposition, and Marcos fled the country on February 25, 1986. Aquino was sworn in as the new President of the Philippines, marking a new era in Philippine politics. The 1986 Philippine presidential election remains a pivotal moment in Philippine history and democracy, as it led to the restoration of democratic institutions and the rule of law. It also inspired other movements for non-violent resistance and civil disobedience around the world.

Arthur Arz von Straußenburg was a notable Austro-Hungarian General who served during the First World War. He was born on October 22, 1857, in Straßburg am Vorberge, a market town in Upper Austria, now known as Strassberg. He began his military service as a cadet in 1875, rising through the ranks to become General in 1916. His accomplishments during the war are impressive: he was the commander of the Austro-Hungarian 7th Army during the successful Battle of Gorlice-Tarnow. Under his leadership, the army pushed the Russians back, securing the Galician oil fields and forcing the Russians to abandon their defenses in Poland. As a result of his contributions to the war effort, he was awarded the title of Count. However, his reputation was tarnished due to his participation in the military occupation of Serbia, which was known for its atrocities, including mass killings. After the war, Arz von Straußenburg served briefly as Chancellor of Austria in 1919, but was removed from the position after only one day due to his association with the failed Far Right coup attempt known as the Kapp Putsch in Germany. Despite his controversial past, Arz von Straußenburg was considered a talented military strategist, earning him a place in history as one of the foremost leaders of the Austro-Hungarian Empire during the First World War. Arthur Arz von Straußenburg died on 5 December 1935 in Vienna, Austria, at the age of 78. His legacy lives on as both a symbol of Austro-Hungarian military might during the First World War and a reminder of the dangers of militarism and far-right political ideology.

Hyo-sei is a Japanese term that refers to the principle of creating a harmonious and balanced design. Originally used in the field of traditional Japanese architecture, Hyo-sei is now widely applied in other fields such as fashion, graphic design, and landscape architecture, among others. The concept of Hyo-sei emphasizes a delicate balance between form and function, where aesthetics and utility are given equal importance. It also values simplicity, emphasizing on the use of natural materials and colors. In architecture, one can see the application of Hyo-sei in the use of open spaces, natural lighting, and the integration of the surrounding environment with the building. The goal is to create an outfit that is not only stylish but also comfortable and functional. In graphic design, the principle of Hyo-sei is seen in the use of negative space, minimalist design, and the use of natural elements such as water and trees. Hyo-sei is also applied in landscaping, where the principle of balance and harmony is used to create a serene and peaceful environment. This is achieved through the use of natural elements such as stones, water, and plants, and in the arrangement of these elements in a way that creates a sense of balance and tranquility. In summary, Hyo-sei is a principle that values balance, harmony, and simplicity in design. It emphasizes the importance of form and function, and the use of natural materials and colors. Hyo-sei is widely applied across various disciplines such as architecture, fashion, graphic design, and landscaping, among others.

Udo Hemmelgarn, born in 1952, is an acclaimed German political activist and environmentalist. Hemmelgarn was a leader of the German environmental movement being engaged in it since the 1970s. He was an active member of the German green party which was founded in 1980. He was one of the founding members of Greenpeace Germany which was established in 1980. Hemmelgarn worked with Greenpeace for nearly two decades from 1981 to 1999. During his tenure, he held various positions such as Director of the Toxic Waste Campaign and a member of the Board of Directors. He played an instrumental role in the organization’s efforts to bring attention to environmental issues and raise awareness about the dangers associated with nuclear energy, toxic waste, and whaling. In 1999, Hemmelgarn retired from Greenpeace and founded his own environmental organization, the Hemmelgarn Gesellschaft für Umwelt und soziale Gerechtigkeit (Hemmelgarn Association for Environment and Social Justice). His organization focused on finding solutions for various environmental issues such as sustainable consumption, climate protection, and preserving biodiversity. In addition to his environmental activism, Hemmelgarn was also politically active and served as a member of the German Bundestag from 1998 to 2002. He was a member of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) and focused on environmental and energy policy during his tenure. Udo Hemmelgarn was awarded the Federal Cross of Merit in 1998 for his services to environmental protection. He is highly regarded as one of the most influential environmentalists in Germany.

Sir Wilfrid Laurier Park is a popular riverside park, located in the city of Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. In conclusion, Sir Wilfrid Laurier Park is an oasis in the bustling city of Edmonton. Intercontinental Church of God (ICG) is a religious organization that was founded in 1978 by Garner Ted Armstrong. 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines The 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines is a battalion in the United States Marine Corps. The battalion is known as "The Walking Dead" and was formed during World War II. The battalion was first activated on June 1, 1942, at Camp Elliot, California. It took part in the battle of Guadalcanal, where it received its nickname "The Walking Dead" due to the high number of casualties it suffered during the campaign. In 2003, the 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines participated in Operation Iraqi Freedom, where it played a crucial role in the Battle of Nasiriyah. South Gare Lighthouse, also known as Teesmouth Lighthouse, is a historic lighthouse located at the end of South Gare, a man-made peninsula on the coast of Redcar and Cleveland borough in North Yorkshire, England. The lighthouse's primary purpose is to guide passing vessels through the Teesmouth, which is an important shipping lane. The original South Gare Lighthouse was constructed in 1884 and stood 37 feet tall. It was built of brick with an outer covering of stone, and a single revolving light could be seen from a distance of 13 nautical miles. In 1905, the lighthouse was dismantled and replaced with a larger structure made of reinforced concrete. The new lighthouse was designed by Henry Edmund Goodridge, a prominent lighthouse architect of the time. It stands 48 feet tall with a gallery and lantern room, and its light can be seen up to 20 nautical miles away. During its early years, the lighthouse was manned by a team of keepers who maintained the light and surrounding structures, including the fog signal, which was installed in 1907. After automated equipment was installed in the 1980s, the lighthouse was no longer staffed. However, the Coastguard continues to monitor the light and fog siren remotely. Today, the South Gare Lighthouse and its surrounding structures are listed buildings and protected by law. They are also popular tourist attractions, with visitors able to climb to the top of the lighthouse and enjoy stunning panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Overall, the South Gare Lighthouse is a significant engineering feat of the late 19th century and continues to serve the purpose for which it was built; to provide vital navigation aid to vessels passing through the Teesmouth.

Charles Cleveland Nutting (May 28, 1858 – February 18, 1927) was an American zoologist, biologist, naturalist, and educator who was known for his contributions to the study of marine biology and the theory of evolution. Born in Clearfield County, Pennsylvania, Nutting spent most of his early life in the Midwest. He received his undergraduate degree from Indiana University and then went on to earn a master's degree and a doctorate in zoology from the University of Michigan. After completing his studies, Nutting became a professor at the University of Iowa, where he remained for nearly 30 years. He also studied the evolution of various species and wrote several important papers on the subject. Nutting's research on coral reefs was particularly groundbreaking, as he was one of the first scientists to conduct extensive fieldwork on the subject. His studies helped to establish the importance of coral as a habitat for a wide variety of marine species. Nutting also made several important contributions to the theory of evolution, particularly in his research on the evolution of colonial organisms. In addition to his scientific work, Nutting was involved in many professional organizations, including the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Society of Naturalists, and the Iowa Academy of Science. Nutting's contributions to the field of marine biology continue to be recognized today, and many of his papers and publications remain important references for researchers in the field. Geoffrey I of Villehardouin (died 1218) was a French knight who became the first Prince of Achaea, a title he held from 1209 until his death. In 1205, he was appointed as one of the leaders of the Crusaders' conquest of the Peloponnese in southern Greece, where he played a prominent role in the Battle of the Olive Grove against the Byzantine Greeks in 1205. Upon the establishment of the Principality of Achaea in 1209, Geoffrey was appointed as its first Prince. He worked to establish the principality as a viable feudal state, constructing several fortifications and towns and encouraging the immigration of French settlers. Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson was a landmark case that was decided by the Supreme Court of the United States in 1996. The case resulted in a significant ruling that changed the way banks in the United States operate their businesses. In 1990, Carolyn Nelson, a loan officer at Barnett Bank in Marion County, Florida, filed a claim with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), alleging that she had been dismissed from her job because of her age and gender. Nelson was 47 years old at the time of her dismissal. After the EEOC was unable to resolve the matter, she filed a lawsuit against the bank in federal court. Barnett Bank of Marion County argued that it had dismissed Nelson for performance-related reasons. However, Nelson provided evidence that suggested otherwise. She claimed that her male colleagues, who had similar or even worse performance records, were not dismissed, and that the bank's management had made sexist and ageist comments about her. The case reached the Supreme Court, which ruled in favor of Nelson. The ruling established the "mixed-motive" framework, which means that if an employee can show that an employer had both legitimate and discriminatory reasons for taking an adverse action against them, the burden of proof shifts to the employer to prove that it would have taken the same action regardless of the discriminatory motive. This ruling made it easier for employees to file claims of discrimination, and it also put the burden of proof on employers to prove that they do not discriminate against their employees. The ruling sent a clear message to banks and other employers that they cannot dismiss employees on discriminatory grounds, and that they will have to provide clear evidence to justify their actions. Overall, Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson was a significant case that brought about positive change in the way banks and other employers operate in the United States, and it has continued to make an impact on the legal landscape of the country.

Holocytochrome-c synthase, also known as Hccs, is a protein found in mitochondria that is involved in the production of heme, a vital component of many enzymes including cytochrome c. Function Hccs is responsible for the final step of heme biosynthesis, which involves the insertion of a ferrous ion into protoporphyrin IX to form heme. Specifically, Hccs catalyzes the covalent attachment of a heme molecule to apocytochrome c to produce holocytochrome c. This process is essential for the proper functioning of the electron transport chain in mitochondria, which produces ATP, the primary energy source for cells. Structure Hccs is a multi-domain protein with a molecular weight of approximately 41 kilodaltons. It consists of a catalytic domain containing a heme-binding site and a membrane-spanning domain that anchors the protein in the mitochondrial inner membrane. Mutations Mutations in the Hccs gene have been linked to X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata, a rare genetic disorder characterized by abnormal bone and cartilage development, as well as cataracts and intellectual disability. These mutations may prevent proper heme synthesis and lead to the accumulation of toxic intermediates, contributing to the development of the disease. Inhibitors Several small molecules have been identified as potential inhibitors of Hccs, including triphenyltin and isoniazid. These inhibitors have shown promise as therapeutic agents for the treatment of cancer and tuberculosis, respectively. Conclusion Holocytochrome-c synthase plays a crucial role in heme biosynthesis and mitochondrial function. Mutations in the Hccs gene can lead to serious health problems, while inhibitors of the protein may hold therapeutic potential for a variety of diseases. Despite ongoing research in this field, further investigation is needed to fully understand the function and potential of this important enzyme.

Army Group Liguria was a German Army Group that operated during World War II. The Group was active from 1943 until 1945 and was primarily responsible for the defense of the Alpine region in northern Italy. Army Group Liguria was initially formed as a sub-group of Army Group C, which was responsible for the defense of the Italian peninsula. In June 1944, after the Allied invasion of Italy and the subsequent capture of Rome, Army Group C was split into two separate Army Groups: Army Group Liguria and Army Group South. As the Allies advanced northward through Italy, Army Group Liguria became responsible for the defense of the Ligurian coast and the northern Apennine Mountains. The Group was involved in several major battles, including the Battle of Monte Cassino and the Battle of Anzio. However, as the Allies advanced, Army Group Liguria was gradually pushed back towards the Alps. In April 1945, with the end of the war in sight, Army Group Liguria was disbanded and its remaining troops were absorbed into other German Army Groups. The Group's final commander, General Friedrich Schulz, was captured by Allied forces in May 1945 and was subsequently put on trial for war crimes. Today, the legacy of Army Group Liguria is still felt in the region. List of Neuroscience Databases Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system and the intricate network of neurons that allow us to perceive, interact, learn and adapt to the world around us. The field of neuroscience generates a massive amount of data every day, ranging from gene expression profiles to brain imaging data. To manage and share this data, a number of specialized databases have been developed by researchers and institutions around the world. This article provides a non-exhaustive list of some of the most widely used neuroscience databases. 1. Allen Brain Atlas The Allen Brain Atlas is a free, web-based collection of gene expression data that maps the entire mouse brain. It contains information on the expression patterns of over 20,000 genes relevant to neuroscience. The Atlas also offers a comprehensive brain mapping tool that allows users to visualize data from different brain regions and across different developmental stages. 2. Brain Image Library The Brain Image Library is a searchable database of neuroimaging data, including MRI, CT scans, and functional MRI (fMRI). It contains data from a range of neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. 3. BrainMap BrainMap is a database of functional neuroimaging experiments mapping the human brain. It contains information on the location, experimental design, and statistical significance of thousands of brain mapping studies. 4. Neuroscience Information Framework (NIF) NIF is a collaborative initiative to provide researchers with unified access to neuroscience data and tools. It includes databases on genes, brain structures, neuroinformatics tools, and research literature. 5. NeuroMorpho.org NeuroMorpho.org is a database of 3D digital reconstructions of neurons. It provides a wealth of data on the morphology and structural properties of different types of neurons in the brain. 6. Synapse Web Synapse Web is a database of synapses, the connections between neurons in the brain. It contains information on the types, properties, and distribution of synapses in different brain regions. 7. Brain Connectivity Toolbox The Brain Connectivity Toolbox is a MATLAB-based software package that provides tools for evaluating and analyzing networks of neurons in the brain. It includes functions for graph theory, connectivity analysis, and network visualization. In conclusion, these databases are invaluable resources for the neuroscience research community, providing access to a vast array of data and tools. With the continued growth of the field, we can expect more databases to emerge, playing a critical role in advancing our understanding of the complex workings of the nervous system.

The album's artwork, created by artist John Baizley, features a dark, foreboding image of a wolf in the snow, perfectly capturing the album's sinister sound and mood. SMS Deutschland was a large German merchant ship that was commissioned into service during World War I in 1914. The ship was built in 1900 by the German shipbuilder Bremer Vulkan in Vegesack, Bremen, and was originally named Reval. SMS Deutschland was the first German armed merchant raider of World War I. The ship was used for commerce raiding in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. SMS Deutschland was initially designed as a fast passenger and cargo ship for the Hamburg America Line. However, during the outbreak of World War I, the ship was requisitioned by the Imperial German Navy as an auxiliary cruiser. The ship was equipped with several 4.1-inch guns, as well as six torpedo tubes and a wireless telegraph. The SMS Deutschland spent most of the war patrolling the Atlantic Ocean, where it captured several Allied vessels. The ship became famous for its tactics, which included disguising itself as neutral vessels such as Norwegian or American ships. It also avoided detection by disabling its wireless communications and sailing at night. The most significant achievement of the SMS Deutschland was its capture of the British steamer Indian Prince. This capture was significant because the Indian Prince was carrying a large amount of war supplies for the British Army in East Africa. The goods captured included several railway guns, which the Germans later used to great effect against the British Army. The SMS Deutschland was eventually cornered by the British in the Mediterranean in November 1914. The ship was severely damaged in a battle with the British cruiser HMS Highflyer, and its crew was captured. The ship was later sunk by a British submarine in 1916. The SMS Deutschland was a significant addition to the German Navy's commerce raiding capabilities during World War I. Its successes and tactics were studied by navies in several countries. The ship's legacy lives on in its place in history as a standout example of the effectiveness of commerce raiding during a major war.

The division was also instrumental in the Battle of Kursk, where it played a key role in the Soviet Union's counteroffensive against the German army. After the war, the 88th Rifle Division was disbanded, but its legacy lives on. The division was awarded the title of "Guards" in recognition of its heroic efforts during the war. Today, the history of the 88th Rifle Division is celebrated by military historians and enthusiasts alike, as it represents the courage, sacrifice, and determination of the Soviet Union soldiers who fought and died on the battlefields of World War II.

Hequ horse, also known as the "Yellow Horse", is a breed of horse found in China's Hequ County region. This horse is believed to have originated from the ancient Aqihai grasslands of Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and is known for its hardiness and endurance. The Hequ horse is considered as one of the four famous horse breeds in China. Physical characteristics of the Hequ horse include a compact body, a short, broad head with a slightly convex profile, and a strong jaw. The coat color is usually yellow, chestnut, or bay. The breed has a high set neck, sloping shoulders, muscular legs, and robust hooves, which enable it to maneuver over rough terrain at high speeds. These features make Hequ horses particularly suited for long distance travel and endurance events. Hequ horses have strong and agile bodies that have been used for various purposes over the centuries, such as transportation, agriculture, and war. During the Chinese civil war, the Hequ horse was used as a cavalry horse and was admired for its stamina, courage, and loyalty. They proved to be an important asset for transport and communication in China's mountainous and rugged terrains. The Hequ horse has been bred selectively for over 2,000 years, and the breed is known for its exceptional adaptability to harsh environments. These horses have been produced mostly in the autonomous regions of Qinghai and Gansu, and received recognition as a breed in 1983. The Hequ Horse has been listed as a National indigenous breed of China, and efforts are underway to expand the breed's gene pool and strengthen its population numbers. Today, the breed is still considered one of the most suitable breeds for long distance travel and has been used in the production of recreational and sports horses. The Hequ horse continues to be admired for its strength, endurance, and adaptability, making it an essential part of Chinese equine heritage.

The Wayward Cloud is a 2005 Taiwanese romantic-comedy film, directed by Tsai Ming-liang. The film stars Lee Kang-sheng and Chen Shiang-chyi. Matthew 8 is the eighth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew in the New Testament of the Christian Bible. Overall, Matthew 8 is an important chapter in the Gospel of Matthew, illustrating Jesus' compassion, power, and role as a healer and Savior to all who seek him.

GG Tauri is a multiple-star system located in the Taurus constellation, approximately 450 light-years away from Earth. It gained significant attention from astronomers and scientists due to its young age and the presence of a disk of gas and dust that surrounds it, which is believed to be in the process of forming planets. The GG Tauri system consists of six stars grouped into three pairs, which are separated by different distances. The primary star, GG Tauri A, is a binary star system comprised of two stars that orbit each other at a distance of about 6 astronomical units. The other pairs of stars, GG Tauri B and C, and GG Tauri D and E, are separated by 200 and 1000 astronomical units, respectively. The disk around GG Tauri A is estimated to have a diameter of about 450 astronomical units, which is equivalent to the distance from the sun to Saturn. The disk's presence is inferred from observations of the central star, which shows evidence of excess infrared radiation due to the dust in the disk absorbing the star's UV radiation and re-emitting it as heat. The disk's properties, such as its size and mass, have been studied extensively using instruments like the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA). The GG Tauri system's young age, estimated to be around 1-2 million years old, indicates that it is in the process of forming planets. Observations of the disk around GG Tauri A have shown gaps and asymmetries that may be caused by the gravitational influence of developing planets. One such gap, named the "greater arc" because of its shape, was discovered in 2017 and is believed to be a sign of a young planet orbiting the star. In summary, GG Tauri is a young multiple-star system with a disk of gas and dust around its primary star that is undergoing planetary formation. Its proximity to Earth and unique properties make it an object of interest for astronomers and scientists studying the origins of our solar system.

Gender Equality and Family Development Select Committee The Gender Equality and Family Development Select Committee is a committee within the Parliament of the United Kingdom that is responsible for the examination of issues related to gender equality and family development. The Chaesang typically consists of a large rectangular or square desk made from high-quality wood, such as oak or birch. In addition to the main desk surface, the Chaesang often features additional drawers or storage compartments that are used to store ink stones, brushes, and other writing supplies. These drawers would have been especially important to scholars who needed easy access to their materials while studying or writing. Because of its historic and cultural significance, the Chaesang has become an object of great interest and value to collectors and enthusiasts of Korean art and antiques. Many fine examples of Chaesang can be found in museums and private collections both inside and outside Korea. Overall, the Chaesang represents a unique aspect of Korean culture and history. Its design and function reflect the importance placed on scholarship and learning in Korean society, and the craftsmanship and materials used to create these desks make them an enduring testament to the skills and dedication of Korean artisans.

Edward Ruthazer is a renowned scientist in the field of neurology, best known for his contributions in understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying learning and memory. Ruthazer earned his Ph.D. in Neurobiology from Harvard University in 1995 where he worked under the supervision of Dr. Carla Shatz. After completing his Ph.D., he moved to the Montreal Neurological Institute at McGill University where he became a faculty member in 2001 and is currently a tenured professor. Ruthazer's research focuses on understanding the molecular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie experience-dependent plasticity, which is the ability of the brain to change in response to experience. His research group mainly focuses on studying the neural circuits that underlie visual system development and function, using the zebrafish as a model organism. Ruthazer has published over 70 papers in well-established scientific journals such as Neuron, Nature Neuroscience, and Journal of Neuroscience. He has also been the recipient of several awards, including the Sloan Foundation Fellowship and the EJLB-CIHR Michael Smith Chair in Neurosciences and Mental Health. In addition to his research, Ruthazer is actively involved in mentoring students and postdoctoral researchers in his lab. Many of his former trainees have gone on to successful careers in academia and industry. In summary, Edward Ruthazer is a neuroscientist who has made significant contributions to our understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying experience-dependent plasticity in the visual system. His research has yielded insights into how neural circuits form and function, and how they can be modulated by experience. His work has been recognized with numerous awards and his mentorship has helped to train the next generation of scientists in his field.

Overall, Morpeth is a charming and historic town that offers a unique blend of natural beauty, cultural heritage, and modern amenities.

The Southampton Blitz was a series of bombings that took place during World War II, specifically between 30th November 1940 and 6th June 1942. The bombings were carried out by the German Luftwaffe and were aimed at Southampton, a port city located on the south coast of England. The bombings began on 30th November 1940, in what became known as the "Baby Blitz." The initial attack saw 50 people killed, with hundreds more injured and 2000 homes destroyed. The attacks continued throughout the following months with a significant increase in attacks during May 1941. During this period, the city was hit by bombs almost every night, with the most significant attack taking place on 30th May 1941, when the city was hit by 60 high-explosive bombs in just 30 minutes. The attacks caused significant damage to the city's infrastructure, with many homes and buildings destroyed or damaged beyond repair. A total of 631 people were killed and over 1,500 injured during the Southampton Blitz. The city's port was also hit, which significantly impacted the country's war efforts. However, despite the damage, the port continued to function, and Southampton played a crucial role in the Normandy landings, which began on 6th June 1944. After the Southampton Blitz, the city was rebuilt, and many new homes and buildings were constructed to replace those that had been destroyed. Today, the city remembers the events of the war through a range of memorials, including the Memorial to the Civilian Dead, which is located in Watts Park. The Southampton Blitz serves as a reminder of the significant impact that war can have on civilian populations, and the need to work towards peace and stability, both locally and internationally.

USS Koka (AT-31) was a Navajo-class fleet tugboat that served in the United States Navy from 1943-1974. It was named after the Koka tribe, a Native American tribe in Arizona. The ship was built at the Gulfport Boiler and Welding Works in Port Arthur, Texas, and was launched on January 23, 1943. The Koka was approximately 143 feet long, 33 feet wide, and had a draft of 13.5 feet. The tugboat had a displacement of 840 tons and was powered by two diesel-electric engines, giving it a top speed of 13 knots. During World War II, the Koka served in the Pacific theater, providing support to fleet units and engaging in rescue and salvage operations. In 1944, the Koka was one of the first ships to arrive at the scene of the USS Tang (SS-306) sinking, and it assisted in the search for survivors. After the war, the Koka continued to serve in the Pacific, providing support for military operations in Korea and Vietnam. In 1964, the Koka was involved in Operation Dominic, a series of nuclear tests in the Pacific. The tugboat was responsible for helping with the testing of underwater sensors and monitoring the surrounding area for safety. The Koka was decommissioned in 1974 and sold for scrap in 1975. Throughout its service, the Koka was awarded numerous commendations and campaign medals. In recognition of its contributions, the Koka was donated to the Maritime Museum of San Diego in California, where it remains on display today. The USS Koka (AT-31) was a vital part of the United States Navy's fleet and played a significant role in many important events throughout its long service history. Its legacy lives on not only through its own story but also through the Museum exhibit that immortalizes its memory.

Expenditure Management Commission (EMC) is a committee established by the government of Canada to examine and improve the efficiency of public spending. It was created in 1994 as part of the government's efforts to reduce the federal deficit and improve management of public expenses. The purpose of the EMC is to review all government spending, identify ways to reduce wasteful spending, and recommend measures to improve the value for money of public expenditures. The Commission's work is mainly focused on examining the largest areas of public expenditure, such as healthcare, defense, and infrastructure development. The EMC is responsible for developing and implementing expenditure management policies and guidelines throughout the Canadian federal government. These policies aim to ensure that public resources are used effectively and efficiently, and that government operations are carried out with maximum efficiency. The Commission also works closely with other government departments and agencies to review their budgets and identify areas where savings can be made. The EMC has been very successful in its efforts to reduce government spending and reform public finance management in Canada. Its policies and recommendations have resulted in significant savings for taxpayers and have helped improve the quality of public services. The Commission's work has also encouraged other countries to adopt similar reforms in their own public expenditure management. Overall, the Expenditure Management Commission serves as an important instrument for ensuring that public resources are used effectively and are allocated in a responsible and efficient manner. Its work has contributed significantly to the improvement of public finance management in Canada and serves as a model for other countries to follow.

William Guy was a Scottish physician and epidemiologist who made significant contributions to public health during the 19th century. He eventually became interested in the study of public health and epidemiology, and began conducting research on various diseases, including cholera and typhus. In 1847, Guy was appointed as the first medical officer of health for the city of London. He was a strong advocate for improving sanitation and hygiene, and his efforts led to significant improvements in the health of Londoners. Guy also played a key role in the development of the field of epidemiology. He wrote several influential works on the subject, including "Lectures on the Theory and Practice of Medical Police" and "Principles of Forensic Medicine". These works helped to establish epidemiology as a distinct field of study, and laid the groundwork for future advances in public health. In addition to his work as a physician and epidemiologist, Guy was also a prominent social reformer. He was a member of the Society of Friends, and was actively involved in many campaigns for social justice, including the abolition of slavery and the improvement of working conditions for laborers. Guy passed away in 1885, but his contributions to public health and epidemiology continue to be recognized and celebrated today. He is remembered as a pioneering figure in the field of public health, and his work continues to inspire researchers and practitioners around the world.

Ephippiger terrestris, commonly referred to as the mole cricket, is a species of insect that belongs to the family of Gryllotalpidae. Found primarily in the Mediterranean region, the mole cricket has a distinct physical appearance and distinctive way of life. Appearance: The mole cricket has a unique appearance that allows it to blend in with its surroundings. Its wings are reduced to small pads, which it uses for balance while burrowing. It has large, spade-like front legs with shovels on the ends that are used for digging. Its body is brown in color and covered in tiny hairs. Habitat and Life cycle: The mole cricket lives in a variety of soil types, but it prefers sandy soil where it can easily dig and burrow. John Calvin's view of Scripture John Calvin's view of the Bible is derived from his belief that God is the author of all of creation, including the words of the Bible, and that as a result the Bible is a collection of God's revealed knowledge. Calvin wrote, "All the content of our religion, however, consists in the knowledge of God and of ourselves, and in the comprehension of the reciprocal relation between us."[1] For Calvin, this knowledge of God and of ourselves is revealed in the Bible. In his view, the Bible contains the divinely inspired words of God, but the words do not necessarily correspond to specific divine meanings. Rather, they are words which God has chosen to use in order to reveal himself to humanity and to teach humanity about himself and about how to live righteously in a fallen world. Thus, the words of the Bible are "the very words of God," but their meaning is not always straightforward and can be difficult to determine.[2] Calvin recognized the difficulties involved in determining the meaning of the Bible. In response to these difficulties, Calvin proposed that the Bible be interpreted according to the "analogy of faith." This analogy of faith is based on the idea that the Bible is a product of God's revelation, and that as a result, it has a internal logic to it which can be discovered by the reader.[3] In other words, the meaning of the Bible is not arbitrary, but is rather a coherent whole which can be discovered through careful reading and consideration of the text. The key to understanding Calvin's view of the Bible is the idea that the Bible is a book which is both divine and human. That is to say, the Bible is a book which is inspired by God and which also contains the words and thoughts of human beings. As a result, the Bible is a unique book which is greater than the sum of its parts, and which has a internal logic which is both divine and human in origin.[4]

Euseby Cleaver (fl. 15th–16th century) was an English compiler of medieval manuscripts. Cleaver was a Catholic who lived in the reigns of Henry VII and Henry VIII. He was associated with the church of St. Margaret in Lynn, Norfolk, and may have been a priest. He is known only from a single manuscript, now in the British Library (MS Harley 674). This manuscript is a collection of historical texts, mostly concerning the medieval kings of England. The first part of the manuscript is a copy of the contemporary De regis Angliae genealogia of John de Fordun, which was written in the early 14th century. The manuscript also contains the works of earlier medieval historians, such as William of Malmesbury, Historia Regum, and Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum. The manuscript is notable for containing the only known copy of the 15th century illuminated romance, The King and the Quene, which is related to the story of How Bold Sir Guy bore the banner. The manuscript is preserved at the British Library. A typescript facsimile of the Harley MS 674 was made by the Historical Manuscripts Commission in the early 20th century, and is available in some libraries.

Arredondo, Florida Arredondo is a census-designated place (CDP) in St. Johns County, Florida, United States, located on the northern side of State Road 210 between I-295 and US 1. The population was 1,523 at the 2010 census. Arredondo is located in the Jacksonville metropolitan area. The name "Arredondo" is a corruption of the Spanish name "Aredondo", which means "along the river". This area was first settled by the Spanish in the early 18th century. A redoubt was constructed south of the mouth of the Arredondo River (renamed the St. Johns River in the 19th century) in 1736 to protect the river approach to St. Augustine, the capital of Spanish Florida. The redoubt was named Fort Arredondo after Don Arredondo, the Spanish governor of Florida from 1734 to 1737. The fort was attacked by British forces led by General Oglethorpe in the Battle of Fort Arredondo, a victory for the British. The fort was destroyed by British forces in 1739 during their retreat from the area after the Battle of St. Augustine. The area was resettled by the Spanish in the late 18th century, and a community was established at the site of the former fort. A small village was located at the intersection of the Arredondo River and the St. Johns River, near the present-day San Marco neighborhood in Jacksonville. The area was purchased by the Florida East Coast Railway in the early 20th century for the construction of the railroad. The community of Arredondo was located near the present-day Arredondo Railroad Overpass. The railroad was constructed south of the St. Johns River in the early 1920s, and the community of Arredondo was gradually abandoned. The railroad was acquired by the Florida East Coast Railway in 1961. The population of Arredondo was 1,995 at the 2000 census. The median age was 32 years. Hridayakumari was born in Ernakulam district of Kerala state, in a family of poets, as the daughter of K. T. Mohammed, a poet and writer, and his wife Zuhra, a housewife. She accompanied him to Delhi, where she spent six years, and returned to Kerala in 1967, after the death of her father, to look after the family. Hridayakumari started writing poetry at the age of thirteen, and her first published work was a translation of a story by Jack London, which was published in the Sunday edition of the Mathrubhumi newspaper. Her first book of poetry, Chila Kathanar, was published in 1955, when she was twenty, and she followed it up with a novel, Avalude Chithram, in 1961. Her other works include Akkithamathil Asanthiyunnu, a collection of poems published in 1979, and a translation of the play The Proposal by Anton Chekhov, which was published in 2001. She has also written a play, Prathidhwani, which was performed at the Cochin Festival in 1999. Her works have been translated into English, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Hindi, and Bengali. Hridayakumari has received several awards and honours for her literary work, including the Kerala Sahitya Academy Award in 1985, the Sahitya Academy Award in 1990, the C.B. Kumar Award in 1997, the O. N. V. Literary Award in 2001, the Basheer Puraskaram in 2002, the FOKANA Award in 2002, and the 2004 Indian Literary Academy Award. She has also received the K.A. Stovall (January 21, 1923 – October 13, 2017) was an American politician and educator who served as a member of the Louisiana House of Representatives for the Orleans Parish-based District 80 from 1976 to 1980 and again from 1992 to 1996. Stovall was born in Loreauville in Iberia Parish in 1923. He attended Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge and the University of New Orleans. In 1976, Stovall was elected to the Louisiana House of Representatives for District 80, which encompasses the Treme neighborhood in New Orleans. He was a member of the House from 1976 to 1980 and again from 1992 to 1996. He was the first African American to represent District 80. In the early 1990s, Stovall was instrumental in bringing together federal, state, and local government officials, along with private-sector leaders, to develop a plan to revitalize the Treme neighborhood, which had suffered from years of economic decline and neglect. The plan, known as the Treme Initiative, included the development of affordable housing, the restoration of historic buildings, and the creation of new businesses and job opportunities. Stovall was a member of the Treme Sidewalk Museum Board of Directors and the New Orleans Jazz National Park Board of Directors. In 2013, Stovall was honored with a lifetime achievement award by the Treme Sidewalk Museum. He died in New Orleans on October 13, 2017, at the age of 94.

James Cullingham (born October 18, 1945) is a Canadian journalist, author, and documentary filmmaker, who has written extensively on the history and culture of British Columbia. His other books include The Medicine Trail: The Search for a Cure for Cancer (1983), The Fire Garden: A Profile of Burning Man (1990), and The Road to Gold: A History of the Alaska Highway (1995). In the early 1980s, Cullingham worked with the Canadian director Norman Cowie on the documentary film, The Fire Ship, which was released in 1983. Bidens hyperborea is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to northern North America. It is an herbaceous perennial plant that can reach 100 cm (39 in) in height. Bidens hyperborea is widely distributed throughout Canada, the United States, and Greenland. It occurs in coastal areas, open moist meadows, and along streams. Bidens hyperborea is a traditional medicinal plant used by the indigenous peoples of the Americas. The leaves are used as a poultice for wounds and as a tea for colds, while the roots are used for the same purposes, as well as for stomach and intestinal ailments. The seeds have been used as a coffee substitute. The species was first described by Linnaeus in 1753 as Bidens hyperborea.
