The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, also known as the Brunhes–Matuyama transition, was a planetary-scale reversal of the Earth's magnetic field that occurred relatively recently in the Earth's history, approximately 774,000 years ago. The event has been dated to the abrupt onset of the Matuyama period, an interval of reversed polarity in the Earth's magnetic field, which has lasted until the present day. The Earth's magnetic field is a vector quantity, characterized by both strength and direction, and is a result of the convection currents in the Earth's liquid core. The Earth's core has an internal magnetic field that is approximately equal in strength to the field observed on the Earth's surface. However, the direction of the internal magnetic field is opposite to that of the surface field: the north magnetic pole is located in the Earth's south, and vice versa. The Earth's field is the result of the interaction of the internal field with the surface field, and is characterized by a number of different components. The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is the most recent magnetic reversal of the Earth's surface field. The previous reversal, the Olduvai event, occurred approximately 1.5 million years ago. There have been at least 100 reversals in the last 70 million years. The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal was first identified in 1906 by the French geophysicist Bernard Brunhes. Brunhes discovered the event by studying the magnetic properties of samples of volcanic rocks from the Pacific coast of Japan, which had been collected during a Japanese expedition to the Bonin Islands in 1895. The samples were of the right age to be associated with the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, and the reversal was eventually confirmed by the measurement of the magnetic properties of other rocks and sediments. The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is of particular interest because it corresponds to a period of dramatic climate change, including a number of rapid and intense glacial episodes. The reversal also corresponds to a period of increased volcanic activity, and a number of large volcanic eruptions have been dated to the Brunhes–Matuyama period. The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is thought to have been caused by a process of secular variation, in which the Earth's magnetic field slowly changes in strength and direction over time. The secular variation is thought to be driven by the convection currents in the Earth's core, which are in turn driven by the heat from the Earth's interior. The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal was a particularly intense episode of secular variation, and the sudden change in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field had a number of dramatic effects on the Earth's climate and environment.

Multiprotocol Encapsulation MPLS is often used to encapsulate other protocols. A common usage is to provide multiprotocol functionality to an Ethernet network. In this scenario, the MPLS network is connected to the Ethernet network at the edge. The Ethernet frames are then encapsulated with an MPLS header and transmitted across the network. At the other edge, the MPLS header is removed and the original Ethernet frame is transmitted to the destination. This is called multiprotocol encapsulation because the MPLS network can also handle other protocols such as ATM, Frame Relay, and High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC). Another usage of multiprotocol encapsulation is to provide an MPLS network with the ability to carry IP packets over an ATM network. In this scenario, the ATM network is connected to the MPLS network at the edge. The IP packets are then encapsulated with an ATM header and transmitted across the network. At the other edge, the ATM header is removed and the original IP packet is transmitted to the destination. This method of encapsulation can also be used to provide an MPLS network with the ability to carry IP packets over a Frame Relay network. In this scenario, the Frame Relay network is connected to the MPLS network at the edge. The IP packets are then encapsulated with a Frame Relay header and transmitted across the network. At the other edge, the Frame Relay header is removed and the original IP packet is transmitted to the destination. In all of these scenarios, the MPLS network is providing a layer 2 connection between two or more sites. The MPLS network is transparent to the layer 2 protocol that is being encapsulated.

Amal Tamimi (born 1985) is a Palestinian-American journalist and author. She is the author of A Country in a State of Emergency: The medical and human cost of the Israeli invasion of Gaza ( Pluto Press, 2009) and the editor of Life on a Cross: A Palestinian diary of survival, written by her mother, Dr Izzeldin Abuelaish, and published by Quartet Books in 2011. Tamimi was born in Chicago, Illinois, to a Palestinian father and an American mother. She spent her childhood in the United States and the West Bank, and attended the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where she studied biology. In 2005, she became the first Arab woman to be named a Truman Scholar. She received her M.A. in journalism from New York University in 2007. Tamimi has worked as a reporter for the New York Daily News, and as a researcher and producer for ABC News and Channel 4. She has written for The Nation, The Jerusalem Fund, and The Electronic Intifada, and has been a contributor to the BBC World Service, Al Jazeera English, and The Nation. In 2008, Tamimi was the recipient of a Project Censored award for her article "The Gaza Olympics", which was published in The Nation. In 2009, she was named one of "25 Women to Watch" by the Muslim Women's Network. In 2013, Tamimi was the host of a television show called Palestine: A journey to Freedom, which aired on Al Jazeera.

Priestfield railway station serves Priestfield, a district of the town of Rochester in the English county of Kent. The station and all trains serving it are operated by Southeastern, and it is on the Chatham Main Line, between Rochester and Chatham. The station was opened by the South Eastern Railway in 1858 as one of three intermediate stations on the new line they built from Rochester to Chatham, the others being Borstal and Rochester West Gate. The line had been planned by the London, Chatham & Dover Railway, who had obtained permission to build it in 1853, but had been taken over by the South Eastern Railway before it was built. The station has two platforms, one on each of the two tracks that make up the Chatham Main Line, and a small ticket office on the "up" (towards London) side. The platforms are connected by a subway, with steps on both sides. The station is at the point where the Chatham Main Line passes under the A2 road. To the west of the station, the A2 crosses the railway on a bridge, while to the east the railway passes beneath the road in a tunnel.

Montezuma is a census-designated place (CDP) in San Benito County, California, United States. The population was 6,320 at the 2010 census. It is located 3 miles (5 km) west of the city of Hollister. The area was first settled by the Chumash and then by the Spanish. The settlement was named for Moctezuma II (c. 1466–1520), the last Tlatoani (ruler) of the Aztec Empire before the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. The community includes the San Juan Bautista mission and the surrounding lands. After the Spanish established the mission in 1721, they forced the local Chumash to construct the mission and its lands. The area was part of the Rancho San Justo, given to Don Miguel Pacheco by the Spanish governor in 1834. Pacheco's daughter, Ysabel, was married to the Mexican military captain, Mariano Goni. The couple's daughter, Mercedes, was the mother of Ygnacio del Valle, who was born in Montezuma in 1843. Montezuma is located in the San Juan Valley. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. The main industries in the area are agriculture and dairy farming. Crops include artichokes, brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, celery, peas, beans, sugar beets, and potatoes.

Regular complex polygon A regular complex polygon is a polygon in the complex plane with all sides equal and all angles equal. If the polygon has an even number of sides, it is called regular and equilateral. If it has an odd number of sides, it is called regular but not equilateral. For a polygon to be regular, the following conditions must apply. 1. All sides must be equal. 2. All angles must be equal. 3. The polygon must be closed. The equilateral regular polygon is the special case of a regular polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal to 60 degrees. The regular complex polygon is the complex polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal. It is a polygon with vertices on the complex plane and with sides that are complex numbers. The regular complex polygon is a generalization of the regular polygon to the complex plane. It is used in many areas of geometry, including the theory of algebraic curves, the theory of surfaces, and the theory of partial differential equations. In particular, it is used to define the boundary of a domain in the complex plane. The regular complex polygon can be thought of as the boundary of a disk with spikes at the vertices. The spikes are the lines that connect the center of the disk to the vertices. The interior of the polygon is the open region inside the border of the polygon, and the exterior is the outside region. The regular complex polygon is a special case of a generalization of the regular polygon to higher dimensions. In three dimensions, this generalization is called a regular polyhedron, and in n dimensions, it is called a regular n-polytope.

St David's Church, Barmouth St David's Church, Barmouth is an Anglican church in the village of Barmouth, on the west coast of Wales. The church is built on a prominent position on the edge of the village, overlooking the beach and the sea. The church is dedicated to Saint David, the patron saint of Wales, and is part of the Parish of Dyffryn Ardudwy. It is a grade II* listed building and has a ceiling with Jacobean-style barrel-vaulting. It also has a prominent position on the Barmouth seafront, and is built on a site that has been used for Christian worship since the 6th century. The present building dates from the early 18th century, with a porch added in the 19th century, and the whole church was restored in 1892. The church is built of local stone, with a roof of slate. It has a rectangular plan, with a porch on the south side. The porch has a pointed arch, above which is a sundial. The church has a barrel-vaulted ceiling, and a plain, square-plan font. The pulpit and the pews date from the 19th century. The church was restored in 1892 by the Chester architect John Douglas, who added a vestry and a organ-chamber. The church's original box pews were replaced by the present pews, and the font was moved to its present position. The church's stained glass includes a window on the south side, dedicated to the memory of Prince William Henry, Duke of Clarence, who died in 1421. The window, which was donated by the Lord Mostyn, was made by W. G. Taylor of London, and shows the Duke of Clarence with his coat of arms. The church also has a number of other windows, dating from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, which were made by a variety of different companies, including Burlison and Grylls, and C. E. Kempe.

Baddiel and Skinner Unplanned is a British television programme that was produced by Graham Stuart for BBC Choice and BBC One. It was presented by David Baddiel and his friend and flatmate Frank Skinner, both of whom were at the time best known for their work on the BBC's top-rated alternative comedy show, Fantasy Football League. The show was filmed in a similar documentary style to the earlier show, and was originally broadcast on BBC Choice, the BBC's then-new digital television channel, in 1998. It was shown on BBC One the following year. Unplanned was recorded in a similar fashion to the earlier show, with Baddiel and Skinner ad-libbing in front of a live studio audience, with some material written beforehand. Many of the sketches were based on contemporary news stories. The show also featured some of the pair's excursions, such as a trip to Las Vegas, and a journey across the Sahara Desert. The series ran for two series, with the second series featuring a live episode, and an episode where each of the pair was sent to a different country (Baddiel in South Africa, and Skinner in Israel). The show has never been repeated, although some clips have been shown on other shows.

Adult/child This article is about the adult/child relationship. For the film, see Adult/Child (film). The adult/child relationship is a complex and multilayered relationship. As children, we are totally dependent on adults for our survival and well-being, and most of us are brought up by adults who are related to us. As we grow up, we gradually gain more independence and freedom, and the balance of power in the relationship shifts. The adult/child relationship is one of the most important relationships in our lives. It is the basis for our development and well-being, and it shapes who we are and how we relate to the world around us. As children, we rely on our parents and other adults to provide us with the love, support, and guidance we need to grow up healthy and happy. As adults, we continue to rely on our relationships with children to give us a sense of purpose and fulfillment. The adult/child relationship is also a complex and dynamic relationship. It is constantly evolving and changing as we grow and develop. As children, we may be completely dependent on our parents or caregivers, but as we grow up, we gradually gain more independence and freedom. The balance of power in the relationship shifts, and we may begin to see our parents or caregivers more as equals or even as authority figures. The adult/child relationship is a special relationship that is full of love, laughter, and learning. It is a relationship that is based on mutual trust and respect, and it is a relationship that can bring us great joy and fulfillment. Whether we are a child or an adult, we can all benefit from a strong adult/child relationship.

Lund v Boissoin, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 613 is a leading case of the Supreme Court of Canada which deals with the issue of prohibition of sexual discrimination in the workplace. Lund involved a restauranteur who was charged with sexual discrimination for refusing to hire women as hostesses. The restaurant had a policy of hiring only male hostesses, and the court held that the policy was in violation of the Ontario Human Rights Code. The restauranteur appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada. The issue before the court was whether the restaurant's policy of only hiring male hostesses was a form of sexual discrimination prohibited by the Ontario Human Rights Code. The court held that it was, reasoning that the policy was "characterized by the gender of the employees and not by the nature of the work." The court found that the policy was "based on the belief that women are less suited than men for the employment in question and that the employment of women in that capacity would tend to lower the general standard of efficiency." The court rejected the restaurant's argument that the policy was not discriminatory because the work was of the same value and quality, regardless of the gender of the employee. The court held that the Ontario Human Rights Code was intended to prevent such discrimination and that the policy was in violation of the Code. The Lund decision was the first time that the Supreme Court of Canada had considered the issue of sexual discrimination in the workplace. The decision was widely seen as a landmark decision in the area of human rights law in Canada. The decision was also notable for its broad interpretation of the Ontario Human Rights Code, and its finding that sexual discrimination could be found even in the absence of an explicit policy prohibiting the hiring of women. The decision has been frequently cited in subsequent cases dealing with sexual discrimination in the workplace.

Beata Maria Kitsikis Panagopoulos (born January 15, 1966) is a Greek journalist and television personality. Beata Kitsikis was born in Athens, Greece, to a Greek father, Dimitrios Kitsikis, and a Swedish mother, Monica, both journalists. She studied journalism at the London School of Journalism. Kitsikis began her journalism career in London in 1985, working for the cable television channel Music Box. She then worked for Sky News and Sky Sports from 1987 to 1989, before returning to Greece to work for ANT1 TV. In 1991, she joined Mega Channel, where she worked as a newsreader and presenter, before becoming a commentator for the channel's sports section in 1994. In 1996, Kitsikis joined Alpha TV, where she hosted the morning show Good Morning, the afternoon show Beata Live, and the weekly show Beautiful. She also presented the daily news show News Update. In 2000, she joined the newly launched ANT1+ channel as a newsreader and presenter. Kitsikis has also worked as a freelance journalist, writing for the newspapers Ta Nea and Eleftherotypia, and the magazines Status and Women's Health. Kitsikis has been married to Greek politician and former journalist Nikos Panagopoulos since 1996. The couple has two daughters, Eleni (born 1996) and Kirsi (born 1998).

Overland Trail The Overland Trail was a route across the Great Plains of the United States that was used by settlers, traders, soldiers, and explorers during the 19th century. It was also known as the Oregon Trail, the California Trail, and the Old Military Trail. The trail began in Missouri and followed the Missouri River west to Fort Kearney, Nebraska. From there, it crossed the Great Plains to South Pass, Wyoming. The trail then split into two branches: the Oregon Trail followed the Columbia River to the Pacific Northwest, and the California Trail followed the Sierra Nevada Mountains to California. The Overland Trail was first used by traders and explorers in the early 19th century. It was later used by settlers who were migrating to the West in search of land, gold, and other opportunities. The trail was also used by the military to transport troops and supplies to the West. The Overland Trail was an important route for the settlement and development of the West. It helped to open up the region to trade and commerce, and it facilitated the spread of settlements and the extension of the United States' political and economic influence. The trail was also a key route for the military, which used it to defend the West and to suppress Native American resistance to westward expansion. The Overland Trail was an arduous and dangerous journey. Many pioneers died from disease, exhaustion, or attacks by Native Americans. The trail was also subject to dangerous weather conditions, such as blizzards and floods. Despite these risks, the Overland Trail was an essential part of the West's history and development.

South Croydon railway station is in the London Borough of Croydon in south London. It is 9 miles (14.5 km) south-east of London Bridge and is on the Brighton Main Line between East Croydon and Purley. It is in a cutting on the south side of South Croydon, a suburban area, and the A23 road. The station was opened as part of the railway line to Epsom which was built by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway (LB&SCR) in the mid-1860s. The station, which was originally named South Croydon Road, opened on 1 April 1868. The line through the station was suburbanised in the early 1930s, and a number of stations on the line had their names changed to reflect this. The station was renamed South Croydon on 4 July 1937. The station has four platforms. Platform 1 is for services to London and is situated on the fastest, and most direct, route to the capital. Platform 2 is for services to East Croydon and is also used for services to London which do not stop at all stations along the route. Platform 3 is for services to Purley and Carshalton. Platform 4 is for services to Epsom. The station has a ticket office and a waiting room on platform 1. There is also a waiting room on platform 4.

The Starfish and the Spider is a business book by Ralph Kimball and Joe Leppitt, published in 1998, discussing the management of data in a data warehouse. The authors compare the management of data in a data warehouse to a starfish, and the management of data in an operational system to a spider. The book discusses the differences between data in a data warehouse and data in an operational system. Data in a data warehouse is static, in that it is not expected to change, while data in an operational system is dynamic, in that it is expected to change frequently. Data in a data warehouse is aggregated, in that it is often summarized, while data in an operational system is detailed, in that it is not summarized. The book also discusses the different ways in which data can be stored in a data warehouse. Data can be stored in a normalized format, in which data is stored in a set of related tables. Data can also be stored in a denormalized format, in which data is stored in a single table. The authors argue that a denormalized format is often better for data warehouses, because it can be more efficient to retrieve data from a single table than from multiple tables.

Fat Man and Little Boy "Fat Man and Little Boy" is the twenty-first and twenty-second episode of the fifth season and the 101st and 102nd episode overall from the American animated show The Simpsons. It originally aired on the Fox network in the United States on April 30, 1994. In this two-part episode, a nuclear bomb goes off in Springfield, and the residents of the city must deal with the aftermath. The episode is a satire of the way American society reacted to the detonation of the first atomic bomb, "Little Boy", on the city of Hiroshima, as well as the popular 1950s film, The Day After. The episode begins with a lighthearted musical number, introducing the main characters and setting the tone for what is to come. As the episode progresses, more and more Springfield residents are introduced, and each one has a unique and hilarious reaction to the disaster. In the end, Homer Simpson, who has been frozen in a state of confusion, is the only person who can answer a ringing payphone, which connects him to the President of the United States. In the second part, "Little Boy", the Simpsons visit the ruins of their former hometown, and discover that the radiation has caused Springfield to be populated by a new race of mutant animals. The episode was written by John Swartzwelder, and directed by Mike Polcino. Swartzwelder came up with the idea after reading a book about the making of The Day After. The episode featured the first appearance of the Blue Haired Lawyer, who was designed by Steve Parchuk, although he was voiced by Harry Shearer. The character was originally supposed to be a one-time appearance, but he proved to be popular and has since appeared in several other episodes. "Fat Man and Little Boy" is one of the most popular episodes of The Simpsons. In 2007, it was voted the best episode of the series by Entertainment Weekly.

Monteregian Hills The Monteregian Hills (or Monteregian mounts) are a group of low, isolated, steep-sided hills and mountains in the Quebec region of the Canadian province of Quebec. They are geologically related to the Monteregian Plain, a vast area of relatively flat and low-lying land to the north and west of Montreal. The hills and the plain are formed from the same strata of volcanic rock, mainly the basalts and the andesites, which are part of the Canadian Shield. The Monteregian Hills are a chain of six mountains, each of which has a distinct personality. The two most prominent, and the ones that are most often referred to as the Monteregian Hills, are located in the Montreal area. They are Mount Royal, the site of Montreal's Mount Royal Park, and Mont Saint-Hilaire, located south of the city in the Deux-Montagnes region. A third prominent mountain, Quebec's second-highest peak, is located to the north of Montreal. This is Mount Logan, which is part of the Laurentian Mountains and therefore not a Monteregian hill. South of Montreal, the next two mountains in the chain are usually considered to be the Monteregian Hills. However, they are in the Eastern Townships, which many consider to be a distinct region from the Monteregian Hills. The first of these is Mount Glen, located in the city of Granby. The last mountain in the chain is Mount Pinnacle, located in the city of Sherbrooke. The name "Monteregian" comes from the Latin words monte ("hill") and regio ("region"). It was first used by geologists to describe the region in 1899.

2008 United States House of Representatives elections in Arkansas The 2008 United States House of Representatives elections in Arkansas were held on November 4, 2008, to elect the state's 4 representatives to the United States House of Representatives. All four incumbents were re-elected, although one incumbent, Vic Snyder, was defeated in the primary. Primary elections were held on March 4, 2008. The Republican and Democratic Party held open primaries, in which all voters could participate. The Green Party of Arkansas held a closed primary, in which only party members could participate. The Green Party nominated David Koon as its candidate for the 2nd district. Koon was the party's nominee for the same district in 2006, when he received 5.9% of the vote. In the 2nd district, incumbent Democratic Representative Vic Snyder was defeated in the primary by former Representative John Boozman, who had represented the district from 2001 to 2007. Boozman was one of the few incumbent representatives to be defeated in a primary election in 2008. In the 3rd district, incumbent Republican Representative Tim Griffin was opposed by Green Party candidate Christopher Hayes, who received 2.8% of the vote. In the 4th district, incumbent Democratic Representative Robert Marion was opposed by Constitution Party candidate Bill Raper, who received 4.5% of the vote. In the 6th district, incumbent Republican Representative Mike Ross was opposed by Green Party candidate Jim Lendall, who received 2.0% of the vote. General elections were held on November 4, 2008. All four incumbents were re-elected without serious opposition.

The King of the Street Cleaners is a 2005 novel by the Scottish writer James Kelman. The novel is set in and around a Glasgow housing estate, and follows a group of neighbours as they try to cope with the death of one of their number. The title comes from the name given by the children of the estate to a local street sweeper, Frank, who is something of a local celebrity. The story is told through the eyes of a local teenager, Danny, who is trying to come to terms with the recent death of his mother. His father, a drunk, is struggling to cope both with his wife's death and his inability to provide for his son. The death of Danny's mother is the latest in a string of similar deaths, and the community is attempting to come to terms with this loss. The King of the Street Cleaners was published in 2005 by Jonathan Cape. It was shortlisted for the 2005 Booker Prize, the 2006 Scottish Book of the Year Award, and the 2006 Saltire Society First Book of the Year Award. It won the 2006 Scottish First Book of the Year Award. The novel was well received by critics. The Guardian described it as "a powerfully convincing story of loss, love and survival". The Telegraph called it "an astonishing, devastating book". The King of the Street Cleaners was adapted for television by the BBC, and aired in January 2009. The adaptation was written by Neil Cross, and stars John Gordon Sinclair as Frank.

Nitration Nitration is the process of adding nitro groups to a molecule. The most common method is to treat a nucleophilic organic compound, such as aniline or cyclohexane, with nitric acid (HNO3). The attack of the nucleophile on the nitronium ion results in the addition of a nitro group to the organic molecule. Nitration can also be accomplished using other nitronium sources, such as nitromethane, nitroethane, and nitrous oxide. Because the nitronium ion is relatively weakly basic, its concentration in these mixtures is very low. The low concentration and the presence of other functional groups that may react with the nitronium ion makes the use of these nitronium sources difficult for nitration of complex organic molecules. The mechanism of nitration is based on the formation of a nitronium ion from nitric acid. The nitronium ion is a good leaving group and is able to replace the leaving group in the organic molecule. In the case of a nucleophilic organic compound, the leaving group is often a halide, such as chloride or bromide. The replacement of the leaving group by the nitronium ion results in the addition of the nitro group to the organic molecule. In the case of an electrophilic organic compound, the leaving group is often a carboxylate, such as acetate or propionate. The replacement of the leaving group by the nitronium ion results in the addition of the nitro group to the organic molecule. The addition of the nitro group to an organic molecule often results in a change in the properties of the molecule. In many cases, the nitro group increases the acidity of the molecule. This is because the nitro group is a strong acidic group. In addition, the nitro group can also change the reactivity of the molecule. In many cases, the nitro group can increase the electrophilic character of the molecule. This can make the molecule more reactive to electrophilic reagents, such as acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride. The nitration of organic molecules is a common reaction in organic chemistry. It is used to make a variety of different organic molecules, including amino acids, explosives, and dyes.

Frank Budd (born August 20, 1945) is an American former professional football player who was a running back in the National Football League (NFL) for four seasons, from 1968 to 1971. A native of Detroit, Michigan, Budd attended Eastern High School and played college football at the University of Washington in Seattle. He was the leading rusher on the Huskies' 1967 team that won the Pacific-8 Conference championship and played in the 1968 Rose Bowl. In three seasons at Washington, Budd gained 2,008 yards and scored 18 touchdowns, including a 96-yard run in 1967 that remains the longest touchdown run in school history. Budd was selected in the first round of the 1968 NFL Draft by the Los Angeles Rams, the 11th overall pick. He was the second running back selected, behind Mel Renfro of the University of Oregon. In four seasons with the Rams, Budd gained 1,325 yards and scored 48 touchdowns, including 13 in 1970. His best season was in 1969, when he led the team with 773 yards and scored 11 touchdowns. He also led the NFL that year in yards per carry with 5.2. In 1970, he was the Rams' offensive captain and a Pro Bowl selection. Budd was traded to the San Diego Chargers in 1972, but did not appear in any games for them due to a knee injury. He retired from football after sitting out the 1973 season. In his four seasons in the NFL, Budd appeared in 59 games and gained 1,325 yards on 337 carries with 48 touchdowns. He also caught 37 passes for 368 yards and two touchdowns. After his retirement from football, Budd became a broadcaster. He was the color commentator for the Rams' radio broadcasts from 1972 to 1974 and the San Diego Chargers' radio broadcasts from 1975 to 1977. He also was a sports anchor for San Diego television station KGTV-10. Budd is the uncle of former NFL safety and punter Terrence Johnson, who played for the Seattle Seahawks and Kansas City Chiefs.

Marvin Powell (born September 30, 1944) is an American politician who served as a member of the New York State Assembly from 1983 to 2000 and was the first African American to serve as Speaker of the New York State Assembly. Born in Baltimore, Maryland, Powell attended public school in Baltimore and graduated from the University of Baltimore with a B.A. in 1969. He served in the United States Army from 1969 to 1971 and was a stockbroker in New York City from 1973 to 1983. In 1982, he was elected to the New York State Assembly, where he represented the 35th Assembly District, which included the Brooklyn neighborhoods of Brownsville, East New York, and Starrett City. He served as assistant majority leader from 1987 to 1988, and as majority leader from 1988 to 1996. In 1996, he was elected Speaker, the first African American to hold the post. He served as speaker from 1996 to 2000. Powell was the author of New York's "Son of Sam" law, which put a lifetime ban on parole for anyone convicted of a felony murder. The law was later extended to include murder committed during the commission of another serious felony. In 1997, Powell supported the death penalty for the Noida automailleurs, who were convicted of killing a New York City police officer. In 1998, Powell supported the re-election of Governor George Pataki, and was a featured speaker at Pataki's first inauguration. Powell was an early supporter of Mayor of New York City Michael Bloomberg, and served as Bloomberg's campaign chairman when he first ran for mayor in 2001. Powell is a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People (NAACP) and the Urban League. He is a former member of the New York State Board of Regents, having been appointed by Governor David Paterson in 2008, and he was re-appointed by Governor Andrew Cuomo in 2012. He is the author of The Education of an American: A Memoir of a Negro from the South ( scales).

Stuart Townend (born 1963) is an English Christian musician, singer, and songwriter. He has written several well-known worship songs, including "In Christ Alone" and "How Deep the Father's Love for Us", the latter of which was written with his brother, Keith. Stuart Townend was born in Manchester, England, to a Christian family. He attended Elim Bible College in squidgy London, England. He learned to play the guitar and began writing his own songs. In the early 1980s, he became involved with the UK-based Christian rock band Quasar, who released an album, Life, in 1983. In 1984, Townend became a part of the Bible-based, Christian rock band Delirious? (then known as The Cutting Edge Band). He was the band's guitarist, and he also contributed to the band's lyrics and songwriting. He stayed with Delirious? for six years, performing on their first three albums, Cutting Edge (1984), Storm the Gates of Hell (1986), and King of Fools (1988). He left the band in 1990. In 1996, Townend released his first solo album, I Will Be Here, on which he was the primary vocalist. The album was not commercially successful. A re-recorded version of the album was released in 1998, and it included a new song, "In Christ Alone", which became the album's most popular track. The song has been recorded by several other artists, including Michael W. Smith, the Newsboys, and Jami Smith. In 2001, Townend released a second solo album, God Is in the House. In 2002, he recorded a live album, Sing for the Saviour, which was released on CD and DVD. His other albums include New Day (2004), The Best of Stuart Townend (2005), Heal Our Land (2009), and In Christ Alone: The Songs of Stuart Townend (2011). Townend has also written a number of books, including In Christ Alone (2005), The Life of Worship (2008), and The Ultimate Collection of Christian Hymns (2011).

Screen direction The direction of movement of the camera or the observer is called the screen direction. Most films are shot with a single screen direction, but some, such as Citizen Kane, are shot with multiple screen directions. Screen direction is one of the basic elements of film style and is used to create a sense of space and movement. The screen direction is determined by the placement of the camera in relation to the subject. If the camera is placed to the left of the subject, the screen direction is said to be left-to-right. If the camera is placed to the right of the subject, the screen direction is said to be right-to-left. If the camera is placed behind the subject, the screen direction is said to be rear-to-front. If the camera is placed in front of the subject, the screen direction is said to be front-to-rear. There are several ways to change the screen direction. One way is to move the camera to a new position. Another way is to use a different lens, such as a wide-angle lens, to change the field of view. A third way is to use a process called "warping," in which the image is distorted to change the screen direction. In some cases, the screen direction is intentionally changed to create a specific effect. For example, in the film Citizen Kane, the screen direction is changed several times to create a sense of disorientation and confusion. In other cases, the screen direction is changed to accommodate a specific shot or scene. For example, if a shot requires the camera to be placed in a certain position, the screen direction may have to be changed to make the shot work. Screen direction is an important element of film style and is used to create a sense of space and movement. It can be used to create a specific mood or atmosphere, and it can be used to direct the audience's attention to a particular area of the screen. Screen direction is often used to create a sense of depth and space, and it can be used to make a shot more dynamic and interesting.

Heauton Timorumenos Heauton Timorumenos (Greek: Χεαυτον Τιμωρηνως, Self-condemned) is a novel by the Greek writer and poet Constantine P. Cavafis. It was first published in two parts, in 1911 and 1912, and then in a single volume in 1915. The book is Cavafis's longest work and is notable for its unusual style, mixing poetry and prose. The work is set in a prison, where the narrator, or perhaps the writer, is serving a sentence for murder. The story is structured as a first-person account of the narrator's life, and the circumstances that led to his imprisonment. The narrator's life is divided into three distinct "life stories", each one marked by a specific, significant event. The first life story is the narrator's childhood and youth, and ends with his first murder; the second is the story of the narrator's young adulthood, and ends with his second murder; and the third and final life story is the narrator's old age, and the story ends with the old man's death in prison. The most significant event in the narrator's life is his love for his cousin's wife, and the murder that is committed out of passion. The story is a tragic one, since the narrator is fated to live the rest of his life in prison, and is also a "self-condemned" man, because he believes that he is unworthy of happiness.

Frank McDonough (born 1 June 1946) is an English actor, writer, and director. He is known for his work with the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre, and for his numerous appearances on British television. McDonough was born in London. His father, Peter, was a doctor, and his mother, Sheila, was a housewife. He was educated at St. Paul's School, London, and at the University of East Anglia, where he read English and American literature. In 1978, McDonough joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he was a member of the regular company for five years. He appeared in numerous productions, including The Comedy of Errors, As You Like It, Love's Labour's Lost, Othello, King Lear, and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead. In 1982, McDonough joined the National Theatre, where he appeared in a number of productions, including The Merry Wives of Windsor, Much Ado About Nothing, The Merchant of Venice, and Troilus and Cressida. He also appeared in the National Theatre's production of The Lord of the Rings as Sam Gamgee. In addition to his stage work, McDonough has appeared in many British television series, including Blackadder, Red Dwarf, The Young Ones, The Office, Spooks, and Doctor Who. He also played the role of Mr. Charity in the BBC's The Little and Large Show. McDonough has also written and directed a number of plays, including A Slight Case of Death, which was nominated for an Olivier Award for Best New Comedy.

Del Webb Explosion The Del Webb Explosion was a nuclear weapons test conducted on July 1, 1957, as part of Operation Plumbbob, at the Nevada Test Site. The test was a joint project of the Atomic Energy Commission and the Defense Department, with the objective of developing a "supersonic missile-deliverable nuclear warhead". The first of several " Priscilla " tests, Del Webb was the first of the Plumbbob series to be conducted jointly with the United States Air Force. Del Webb was the second test of a nuclear device with a yield over 25 megatons, after the US's first thermonuclear test, Ivy Mike, in 1952. The device had a yield of 43 megatons, and was the first nuclear device to be fired at the Nevada Test Site. The device was also the first to be tested with an atomic artillery shell, fired from a specialized cannon toward a target tank. Following the test, the Atomic Energy Commission held a press conference, where they stated that the test "appears to have been successful". However, an investigation by the AEC's "Project Caesar" committee later found that the warhead had been destroyed in the explosion, and that the test had been a failure. The committee determined that the cause of the failure was a design flaw, which resulted in the warhead's destruction after only 2.5 inches (6.4 cm) of its movement into the missile. In the test, the device was fired from a Jupiter-C rocket, a modified Redstone missile. The missile was fired from the Green River, Utah, missile complex, and traveled 2,500 miles (4,000 km) to the test site. The warhead was a three-stage device, with a yield of 43 megatons in the first two stages, and a third stage designed to produce a yield of only 1.5 kilotons. The test was the first of a series of three tests, the others being the Blue Jay and the Kingfisher tests.

The album was Adams' first since the North American release of the 1993 compilation, So Far So Good, to be released outside of North America. "The Best of Me" was released as a single, and reached No. 1 in Canada and No. 16 in the United States. In 2001, a special edition of The Best of Me was released, containing a bonus disc with eight additional tracks, including two more new songs, "Here I Go Again" and "We're All Here," the latter of which was to be used as the theme song for the television series Smallville. The Best of Me is Adams' only album to be certified diamond by the RIAA, and it is his biggest-selling album to date, with sales of over 6 million copies worldwide. Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome (PTSS) is a controversial diagnosis that refers to the mental and emotional injuries that African Americans have suffered as a result of slavery and racism. PTSS is not an official diagnosis listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, but the symptoms of the disorder are similar to those of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The main difference between the two disorders is that PTSD is experienced by individuals who have suffered a traumatic event, while PTSS is experienced by individuals who have suffered repeated exposure to traumatic events. The symptoms of PTSS include depression, anxiety, nightmares, flashbacks, and hypervigilance. These symptoms can be triggered by events that remind the individual of their trauma, such as seeing a police officer or hearing a racial slur. PTSS is believed to be highly underdiagnosed, as many African Americans who suffer from the disorder may not seek help due to fear of discrimination, racism, or lack of access to mental health resources. However, it is estimated that up to 40% of African Americans may be affected by PTSS. Treatment for PTSS typically involves psychotherapy and medication. Psychotherapy can help individuals with PTSS process their trauma and learn how to cope with their symptoms. Medication can be used to treat any co-occurring mental health disorders, such as depression or anxiety, and to help manage PTSS symptoms. PTSS is a complex and deeply rooted disorder, and recovery can be a long and difficult process. However, with proper treatment and support, individuals with PTSS can improve their symptoms and lead healthy and fulfilling lives.

Cruciate ligament, also called the cruciate tendon, is a ligament that crosses from one side of a joint to the other, in front of the other ligaments, and in front of the joint cavity. The ACL is located in the front part of the knee and the PCL is located in the back part of the knee. The ACL and PCL are both attached at the top to the thigh bone (femur) and at the bottom to the lower leg bone (tibia). The ACL and PCL work together to stabilize the knee and prevent the thigh bone and the lower leg bone from moving in opposite directions. This is important for the normal functioning of the knee. The cruciate ligaments are the most commonly injured ligaments in the knee. The ACL is most often injured when the knee is twisted or bent in a traumatic way. The PCL is most often injured when the knee is bent too far backward. When the cruciate ligaments are injured, the knee can become unstable and prone to further injury. In many cases, surgery is needed to reconstruct the cruciate ligaments and restore stability to the knee.

In 1920, Naba Kishore Ray was a student at the Scottish Church College of the University of Calcutta, and a member of the radical Students' Federation. He was influenced by the revolutionary ideals of the Indian independence movement, and became a member of the Jugantar group of revolutionaries, working under the direction of its leader, Bhupendranath Datta. In 1928, Naba Kishore Ray was arrested and charged with the murder of a police officer. He was convicted and sentenced to death, but the sentence was later commuted to life in prison. Naba Kishore Ray spent more than 15 years in various prisons across India, and was released in 1945. After his release from prison, Naba Kishore Ray joined the Communist Party of India (CPI), and worked as a full-time activist for the party. He was a member of the CPI's West Bengal State Committee, and served as the editor of the party's newspaper, "The People's Paper". In the early 1970s, Naba Kishore Ray was diagnosed with cancer, and died on 4 February 1974, at the age of 76.

Erith Dockyard was a dockyard on the south bank of the River Thames in England, at Erith in the London Borough of Bexley. It was owned and operated by the London and India Docks Company, a subsidiary of the East India Company, from 1899 to 1909, and was then acquired by the Port of London Authority in 1909. It covered 25 acres (10 ha) and had three dry docks and one wet dock. The dockyard opened in 1899 and was built on a plot of land previously used for malaria research by the Royal Navy. The main dry dock was 365 feet (111 m) long by 67 feet (20 m) wide. The two eastern dry docks were smaller: No. 3 dock was 180 feet (55 m) long by 36 feet (11 m) wide and No. 4 dock was 151 feet (46 m) long by 33 feet (10 m) wide. The wet dock was 125 feet (38 m) long by 33 feet (10 m) wide. The dry docks were equipped with six steam cranes, each with a capacity of 20 tons, and one electric crane with a capacity of 5 tons. The London and India Docks Company went into voluntary liquidation in 1909, and the dockyard was taken over by the Port of London Authority. In 1913, it was proposed that the dockyard should be converted into a yacht harbour, but this idea was not implemented. In 1916, the PLA built a large shed, the "Derrick shed", on the site. In 1917 the Royal Flying Corps (later the Royal Air Force) took over the dockyard and used it as a base for the No. 1 (Erith) Wing of the Royal Flying Corps, which included No. 13 and No. 41 Squadrons. The Royal Flying Corps' engineering unit was also based at Erith. In 1919, the dockyard was returned to the Port of London Authority, and it was used as a base for the British & Irish Steam Packet Company (B&I Line). The B&I Line used the dockyard until 1924, when it moved its base to Liverpool. The Port of London Authority then sold the dockyard to the Lindsey Oil and Wax Company, which used it as a base for its marine operations. In 1926, the Port of London Authority constructed a new pier, the "Woolwich-Erith Pier", to link the dockyard to the Woolwich foot tunnel. In 1928, the dockyard was acquired by the L. Ross & Company, a group of shipbrokers and ship owners. It was used as a base for the Blue Funnel Line, the British & Irish Steam Packet Company, and the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. In 1949, L. Ross & Company sold the dockyard to the Port of London Authority, which used it as a repair facility. The PLA also used it as a base for the London and North Eastern Railway's paddle steamers, the London, Tilbury and Santos Steamers, and the British Transport Commission's coasters. In 1968, the Port of London Authority sold the dockyard to a property company, which demolished most of the site to make way for a housing development. The housing development was not built, and the site was used as a storage yard until about 1990, when it was redeveloped as the Erith Westernised Marina.

Robert Peter Gale (born November 5, 1945) is an American physician, researcher, and academic. He is best known for his work with HIV/AIDS, including his role as a main researcher in the first case of the disease in the United States, his development of the "Gale-Melarsoprol" treatment for patients with advanced HIV disease, and his advocacy for the use of zidovudine (AZT) to treat HIV infection in the 1980s. He is also known for his contributions to the field of transfusion medicine, including his work on the development of blood donation policies. Gale is a graduate of Harvard Medical School and the Harvard School of Public Health. He completed his residency in internal medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, and a fellowship in infectious diseases at the National Institutes of Health. He is a professor of medicine at the University of Washington School of Medicine and an adjunct professor of health policy and management at the Harvard School of Public Health. In 1981, Gale was one of the first physicians to diagnose and report the disease that would come to be known as HIV/AIDS, after a young gay man in his practice was diagnosed with Kaposi's Sarcoma, a rare cancer that was later found to be associated with HIV infection. In the early years of the epidemic, Gale was one of the leading researchers in the field, and he played a major role in the development of the first effective treatments for HIV/AIDS. In the late 1980s, he was a pioneer in the use of zidovudine (AZT) to treat HIV infection, and he played a key role in the development of the "Gale-Melarsoprol" treatment for patients with advanced HIV disease. In addition to his work with HIV/AIDS, Gale has also made significant contributions to the field of transfusion medicine, including his work on the development of blood donation policies. He has also conducted research on the transmission of viruses through blood and blood products, and he has been a leading advocate for the use of nucleic acid testing to screen blood donations. Gale has received numerous awards and honors for his work, including the Arthur L. Carter Award for Excellence in HIV/AIDS Research, the William D. Carey Award for Excellence in Health Policy, and the Distinguished Investigator Award from the Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy. He is a member of the National Academy of Medicine and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and he is a fellow of the American College of Physicians, the American Academy of Microbiology, and the Royal College of Physicians.

Izumi Muto (budō: イズミムト, real name: Mutō Izumi, born July 13, 1948) is a Japanese actress who is best known for her role as Mayumi Kanda in the 1970s television series The Water Margin. Muto was born in the western Japanese city of Osaka. In 1969, she won the "Miss Doshisha" beauty pageant while attending Doshisha Women's College, a Christian women's school in Kyoto. After graduating in 1970, she worked for a time at a department store in Osaka before moving to Tokyo in 1971. She was discovered by a talent scout while walking through the streets of the city's fashionable Harajuku district. After making her television debut in a 1972 episode of the series Hanzawa Naoki, Muto was cast as Mayumi Kanda, the wife of the character Goemon Ishikawa, in the new series The Water Margin which premiered the following year. The series was an instant hit and made Muto a household name. She also made a number of guest appearances on the variety show Japan Countdown. In 1974, she starred in the television series The Barrier, which was shot in Australia. In 1975, Muto married Japanese actor Tomokazu Miura (best known for his role as Captain Japan in the television series Space Sheriff Gavan) and retired from acting. The couple had two daughters and later divorced in 2003.

Clara Louise Burnham (March 11, 1901 – September 25, 1996) was an American author and screenwriter, best known for her children's books. She also wrote under the pseudonym Mary Jean. She was born in Effingham, Illinois, the daughter of Joseph William Burnham, a station agent for the Illinois Central Railroad, and his wife Clara (Hoffman) Burnham. She attended the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where she received a bachelor's degree in English in 1921. Burnham began her career as a journalist, working as a reporter for the Urbana Courier for three years. From 1924 to 1925 she was the editor of the Illinois Alumni Magazine. In 1925 she became a publicity director for the Illinois Central Railroad, a position she held for five years. In 1930 she married Fred E. Bailey, a fellow employee of the Illinois Central. The couple had two children. In 1933, she began to write fiction, and her first book, The Lady and the Panda, was published in 1935. She and her husband both worked for the Illinois Central until 1942, when they moved to Los Angeles, California. In 1951, she divorced Bailey and married film and television writer George Lefferts. Burnham's works for children included picture books, juvenile novels, and a series of short stories. Her best-known books were the Little Fat Policeman series, which featured a overweight police officer who was a friend to children. The series, which included four books, was illustrated by Lynne Avadenka and won the IRA Children's Choice Award in 1986. Burnham died at the age of 95 in Los Angeles.

Dr Benjamin Twist is a fictional character from the British soap opera Doctors, portrayed by Harry Visinoni. The character first appeared on 9 March 2015 as a love interest for Alia Hanif (Neelam Gill). Benjamin is a doctor at the fictional St Mark's Hospital in Letherbridge and is in his third year of foundation training. He begins a relationship with Alia, despite their age difference and the fact that he is engaged to another woman, and continues seeing her behind his fiancée's back. When his fiancée, Jessica, discovers the relationship, she forgives him, but he chooses to end the relationship with Alia and resume his engagement to Jessica. In 2016, Benjamin returns to Letherbridge and tells Alia that he has ended his engagement to Jessica. They later get back together and begin a relationship, which is complicated by their age difference and the fact that she is a medical student and he is a doctor. In 2018, Benjamin asks Alia to move in with him, and she accepts. However, after finding out that he had previously slept with her friend, Zara, she decides to move out. Later in the year, Benjamin begins a relationship with another medical student, Emma Reid (Daisy Wood-Davis), and they move in together. In early 2019, Emma dumped Benjamin after he confessed to having cheated on her. Later in the year, Benjamin begins a relationship with Heston Carter (Jem Wall), a foundation doctor.

Mnesia is an open-source distributed database management system for keeping data in memory and on disk. It can be used in a variety of applications, such as a database, a distributed cache, a messaging queue, and a shared disk. The Mnesia database is used in the Erlang programming language, and is part of the Open Telecom Platform (OTP) suite. The Mnesia database is designed to be scalable, fault-tolerant, and flexible. It can be used as a distributed database, with multiple nodes (computers) running Mnesia and sharing data. The database can also be used as a local database, with data stored on a single node. The Mnesia database is transactional, which means that all changes to the database are made as part of a single transaction. This ensures that the database remains consistent, even if there is a power failure or other problem. The database is also recoverable, which means that if there is a problem, it can be restored to a previous state. The Mnesia database is used in a variety of applications, such as distributed caching, distributed messaging, and distributed databases. It is also used as a local database, for example, as a database for a single process.

Beckham in Peckham The area of Peckham in South London is renowned for its association with football. In the early 20th century, three of the dominant teams in the area were based in Peckham, with two of them, Nunhead and Peckham Town, both playing in the Southern League. The most successful team based in Peckham, and the only one to have progressed to the highest level of English football, was Crystal Palace, who played at the now-demolished Crystal Palace Stadium from 1917 until their relocation to Selhurst Park in South Norwood in 1924. Manager Alf Ramsey, and players Jimmy Greaves, Ron Springett, George Eastham, Ron Springett, Ron Greenwood, Norman Hunter, Terry Paine, Ron Springett, and Alan Ball all lived in the area. Charles William Dyson Perrins (9 June 1864 – 14 June 1951) was an English businessman, philanthropist, and patron of the arts, who gave his name to the C W Dyson Perrins Museum in Worcester, England. Dyson was born in Worcester, the son of William Henry Perrins, a partner in the family firm of chemists, and his wife, Annie. He was educated at Eton College and then at New College, Oxford, where he gained a first class degree in chemistry in 1887. He joined the family business as a partner in 1895, and with his brother, Edgar, took it over on the death of their father in 1908. The firm became the largest manufacturer of cough medicines in the country, with a £1 million turnover by the time of Charles's death in 1951. Dyson was also a generous patron of the arts, particularly in Worcester, where he funded the construction of the C W Dyson Perrins Museum (what is now the Museum of Worcester), and a gallery at the Worcester Art Museum. He was also a considerable donor to the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. Dyson was a member of the county councils for Worcestershire and Herefordshire, and a member of the city council for Worcester. He was also a member of the Royal Commission on the Historical Monuments of England, and a trustee of the British Museum. Dyson was made a knight bachelor in the 1902 Coronation Honours list, and was knighted in the same year. He was awarded the Order of Merit in 1948. Dyson married Grace Tindal in 1891. They had two sons, Gerald (born 1895) and Henry (1897–1916), and a daughter, Mary (1893–1983). Grace died in 1898. In 1901, Dyson married Grace's cousin, May Tindal, and they had two sons, William (1903–1994) and John (1905–1994). May died in 1941. Dyson died at his home in Worcester on 14 June 1951, aged 87.

Cursor grass mouse The cursor grass mouse (Megonomys cursor) is a species of rodent in the family Muridae. It is found in Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, South Africa, South Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zimbabwe. Its natural habitats are dry savanna, moist savanna, and arable land. It is a very common species and the status of the species is Least Concern. The cursor grass mouse has a short, dark brown to black tail. The upperparts are dark to yellowish brown with a patch of darker brown behind the ears. The underparts are white to pale yellow. The fur on the upperparts is short and notched above the shoulders. The ears are small and placed high on the head. The whiskers are short and sparse. The tail is 2.5 to 3.5 cm (1.0 to 1.6 in) long. The cursor grass mouse is a terrestrial species that occurs in a variety of habitats including moist savanna, dry savanna, and arable land. It is found from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to South Africa and south to the Cape. It is a very common species and lives below 3000 m (9842 ft) in elevation. It is a solitary species and lives with others of its species only during the breeding season. It feeds on seeds on the ground and sometimes climbs grass stems to reach the seeds. It also eats small insects. The cursor grass mouse is a social species. It lives in family groups with one dominant male. The male is territorial and marks his territory with scent. He will defend his territory and the females in it from other males. The breeding season is during the rainy season. The gestation period is 22 to 24 days. The litter size is two to four young. The young are born with their eyes closed and with a thin covering of fur. They are able to follow their mother at around 21 days old. They are fully weaned at around 28 days old.

Dominion Timber and Minerals Railway The Dominion Timber and Minerals Railway was a gauge railway line in British Columbia, Canada. It ran from the Canada–United States border at Sumas, Washington, to a point near Prince George, British Columbia. The line was constructed in the early 1930s to serve the forest products industry in the region, and was abandoned in 1958. The railway was built by the Canadian National Railway (CNR) in the early 1930s. Construction began in 1931, and the first section of the railway, from Sumas to Creston, was opened in 1932. The remainder of the railway was opened in 1933. The railway was built to serve the forest products industry in the region, and was designed to allow the transportation of logs and other forest products from the interior of British Columbia to the coast at Vancouver. The railway ran for approximately 100 miles (160 km), and had three branch lines, two of which connected to the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR). The main line ran from Sumas to a point near Prince George, British Columbia, and the two branch lines connected to the CPR at Prince George and Quesnel. The third branch line ran from a point near Prince George to a point near Quesnel. The railway was abandoned in 1958, and the tracks were removed in 1959. The line was primarily used for the transportation of logs and other forest products, and the decline of the forest products industry in the region led to the closure of the railway. The tracks were removed in 1959, and the right-of-way is now used for the Trans-Canada Highway.

Geopolitik (German: Geopolitik [ˈɡeːɐ̯pɔlitɪk]) is a field of study concerned with the impact of geography upon politics. The word geopolitik is a German loanword that was first used in 1880. The term was coined by German geographer and political scientist Friedrich Ratzel in 1901 to describe the relationship between geography and politics. Geopolitik has been defined as "the attempt to understand politics, war, and international relations in terms of the geographical basis for the development of human society, the spatial structures that influence political events, and the geographical consequences of political events." The term has been used in a wide range of contexts, with many authors defining it differently. For example, Barry Buzan has defined geopolitik as "the art of tracing, mapping and explaining political power." The approach of geopolitik is to study the influence of physical, social, and economic geography, along with the distribution of resources and population, on politics and international relations. For example, a key concept in geopolitik is that of the power center, which is a political or military center of power that is valuable to a country for its resources and access to markets. Geopolitik also considers the impact of geography on the formation of political boundaries, such as the division of East and West Germany and the Soviet Union, and the location of cities. In the early 20th century, geopolitik was widely used in Germany, and it became popular in the United States after World War II. However, the field of geopolitik has been criticized for being deterministic, or for claiming that geography determines political events. Additionally, the term geopolitik is sometimes used to refer to a political agenda, rather than to a scientific discipline.

Laventille is a neighborhood in Trinidad and Tobago. It is located in the central portion of the island of Trinidad, just off the Churchill-Roosevelt Highway and is immediately east of the town of Arima. It is also located about 2 km south of the town of Morvant. The Laventille River flows through the community. The Laventille area was settled by French colonists, after the capture of the island by the British in 1797, as a result of the French Revolution. The village of Laventille was established in the early 19th century after a large estate was broken up. With the expansion of the Arima oil refinery and the growth of other heavy industries in the area, Laventille became a working-class community. The area has been the subject of many criminal reports, particularly murders and armed robberies, since the 1990s. The population of Laventille is 16,000. The main religion is Christianity. Laventille is also the birthplace of the steelpan. The first steelpan was created in Laventille in the early 1930s, when the inhabitants, who were mostly from the Caribbean islands of Trinidad and Tobago, started to create music using steel drums. The steelpan is the national instrument of Trinidad and Tobago. Every year, thousands of people flock to the streets of Laventille to participate in the annual Pan competition.

Hequ horse The Hequ horse (鹤嘬马, Pinyin: Hèqūmǎ) is an indigenous breed of the Hequ region in Guilin, Guangxi, China. The Hequ horse is well-known for its hardiness and adaptability to mountain life. The neck is of medium length and is set low on the shoulders. The body is compact and well-muscled. The legs are short and sturdy, with broad, flat knees and hocks. The mane and tail are short. The Hequ horse is a good jumper, and is known for its sure-footedness and ability to negotiate steep, rocky terrain. It is also known for its endurance and can be used for long-distance riding and driving. The Hequ horse is used for many activities, including agriculture, transport, and sport. It is used to pull carts and wagons, and to carry packs. It is also used for racing, riding, and driving. The Hequ horse is an important part of the culture and history of the Hequ region. It is featured in many traditional festivals and events, and is a symbol of the region's heritage and pride. The Hequ horse is a rare breed, and is listed as "endangered" by the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture. There are fewer than 1,000 Hequ horses in existence, with the majority living in the Hequ region. The Hequ horse is a versatile breed, used for a variety of purposes, from agriculture and transport to sport and leisure. 3850 Peltier The 3850 Peltier is a Peltier cooler designed and sold by Thermo Cool. It is thermoelectric device that uses the Peltier effect to create a heat pump over a semiconductor junction. The thermoelectric cooler has four terminals, two on each side. The top has a DC+ and a DC-, while the bottom has the same with the addition of a TEM< and a TEC>. The TEM and TEC are used to monitor the temperature of the hot and cold side respectively. The 3850 Peltier cooler can produce a maximum temperature difference of approximately 64 K (uppermost limit of its specifications) when the DC current is 2.5 A, and the hot and cold side temperatures are at 20 and -30 °C respectively. The maximum current that the thermoelectric cooler can withstand is 5 A. The cooling capacity of the 3850 Peltier cooler is 100 W when the temperature difference over the thermoelectric device is 50 K. The maximum cooling capacity is 200 W when the temperature difference is 25 K. The device can be used for both cooling and heating. As a heater it can generate up to 150 W when the temperature difference is 25 K and the current is 3 A. The thermal resistance of the 3850 Peltier cooler is 0.9 K/W with a 25 K temperature difference and a current of 2.5 A. The 3850 Peltier cooler can be stacked with other similar devices to produce a greater temperature difference, or to cool a larger heat source. The limit to the number of Peltier coolers that can be stacked is the maximum temperature difference that the stack can withstand. This means that the hot side of the Peltier cooler will be at a higher temperature.

Alfred Robin (fl. 1120–1170) was an English medieval musician. Alfred Robin (or Robert) was born in England, possibly in London, and was a contemporary of the medieval composer and music theorist, Léonin. Robin was one of the early composers of organum, and his style is characterized by the use of drones and a certain amount of chromaticism. He may have been the teacher of the noted English composer, Thomas of England. Two of his works survive in the Old Hall Manuscript (British Library, Add. MS 5000), a collection of English music from the mid-12th century: a Magnus liber organi (Great book of organum) and a Nova organum experimentum (New book of organum). The Nova organum experimentum is in the form of a gradual, and the underlay of the parchment on which the music is written shows that it was originally part of a book of hours. The music of both works is in two-part organum. The styles of the two works are quite different, which has led scholars to suggest that they may have been written by different people. The composer of the Magnus liber organi is anonymous, but it has been suggested that this may be the work of Robin, as the style is similar to that of the Nova organum experimentum. Both works are edited and published in theCorpus Mensurabilis Musicae, vol. 72, by the Institute for Musicology of the Austrian Academy of Sciences.

James Hodge Codding (September 6, 1927 – August 25, 2022) was an American electrical engineer and computer scientist, who, with his wife, Barbara, invented the concept of a "linked list", a data structure used in nearly every modern computer application. Codding was born in Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1927. He received a B.S. in electrical engineering from the University of Nebraska in 1949, and an M.S. in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1950. In 1952, he joined the Information Control Division of the Stanford Research Institute, where he remained for the rest of his career. In 1981, he became the head of the division, which was later renamed the Computer Science Laboratory. In 1990, he became the institute's associate director for computing, and in 1992, he became the director of the Center for Integrated Systems, a position he held until his retirement in 1996. In 1956, Codding and his wife, Barbara, invented the concept of a linked list, a data structure used in nearly every modern computer application. The Coddings published their invention in a paper in the December 1957 issue of the Proceedings of the IEEE. The paper, entitled "A Method for Impressing Information on a Persisting Memory", described a method for organizing data in a memory so that the information can be updated efficiently. The paper has been cited more than 2,000 times, making it one of the most cited papers in computer science. Codding was a fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, the American Association for Artificial Intelligence, and the Association for Computing Machinery. He was also a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 1994, he received the IEEE Computer Society's Charles Babbage Award, and in 1996, he received the ACM's Turing Award, along with his wife, Barbara, and Robert Tarjan, for their work on linked lists. In 1998, the three received the AAAS' Prize for the Application of Science. Codding died in 2022 at the age of 94 from complications related to COVID-19.

Edward Tyrrel Channing (13 September 1790 – 31 December 1856) was an English classical scholar, theologian, and author. He was born in London, the son of William Channing the younger and his wife Mary, and was educated at Charterhouse School, London, and at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. In 1812 he was elected to a fellowship at Caius, and in 1814 he took holy orders. He was assistant tutor at the college from 1816 to 1819, and tutor from 1820 to 1824. In the latter year he was appointed Blundell's Professor of Music in the university, an office which he resigned in 1840. In 1825 he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society. Besides numerous contributions to the Quarterly Review, the Edinburgh Review, and other periodicals, he published, separately, An Oration, delivered before the University of Cambridge, on the Benefits of the Study of History, in 1820, The Life of William Pitt, Earl of Chatham, in 1825, and The History of England, from the Peace of Paris, in 1815, to the Accession of George IV, in 1830, in 4 volumes. In the latter work he sought to combine the political history of England with a narrative of its social and economic development. The same plan was followed by his History of the United States, from their Settlement as Colonies, in 1776, to the Close of the Mexican War, in 1848, in 4 volumes, the first volume of which was published in 1855, shortly before his death, the second in 1857, and the third and fourth in 1860 and 1864, respectively. The fourth volume was completed by his son, William Leonard Channing. In addition to these works he published a series of volumes of sermons, lectures, and addresses, and a number of articles on classical and other subjects in the Quarterly Review, the Edinburgh Review, the Westminster Review, the Edinburgh Review, and other periodicals. He died in London on 31 December 1856.

It Can't Happen Here (original title in Spanish: No puede ser) is a novel by the Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, published in 1985. The narrative focuses on a writer (presumably Goytisolo himself) who, while traveling in Spain in the early 1930s, becomes convinced that the country is about to be overthrown by a Soviet-style revolution, and that the change will be brought about by the wealthy, the clergy, and the military, in league with the Nazis. The book was written in the early 1980s, at the height of the Cold War, and published in 1985, four years before the Revolutions of 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall. The title is taken from the book It Can't Happen Here, a 1935 novel by Sinclair Lewis which was adapted into a film of the same name in 1936. It Can't Happen Here is structured as a first-person account, in the form of a diary, by a writer in the months leading up to the hypothetical revolution. The narrator is Goytisolo himself, in his late thirties, living in Paris, and traveling frequently to Barcelona, where he has a part-time job in a publishing house. The narrator's mother, who lives in Barcelona, is a staunch supporter of the Right, and a friend of the editor of the newspaper El Sol. The narrator's father, a doctor, is more moderate, and is sympathetic to the Left, which he sees as "the least bad of the existing options". The narrator's sister, who is married to a Frenchman and lives in Paris, is a convinced Communist. In the course of his travels through Spain, the narrator meets various characters who reinforce his belief in the coming revolution, including a Madrid friend who works for the newspaper El Sol, a priest, a group of students, and a wealthy friend of his mother's, Doña Lucrecia, who is planning to sell her property in Spain and move to Argentina. The narrator's travels also introduce him to the poverty and social unrest that he believes will soon erupt in revolution. He spends time in Barcelona with a friend who is active in the underground, and who tells him about the various working-class organizations and their revolutionary plans. The narrator also visits a mining town, where he sees first-hand the miserable living conditions of the workers and the squalid housing provided for them by the company. The narrator's belief in the coming revolution is further strengthened by his observations of the behavior of the wealthy, the clergy, and the military, all of whom he sees as collaborators in the coming coup. He notes that the wealthy are increasingly fearful of the workers and the poor, and are therefore planning to leave the country. He also observes that the Catholic Church is preparing for the revolution by creating an underground network of churches and religious schools, where the young will be indoctrinated with conservative ideology. Finally, he notes that the military is increasing its spending and recruitment efforts, and that the officers are making plans to seize power when the time comes. In the end, the narrator's belief in the coming revolution is not borne out, and he is left disappointed and confused. However, he is able to find a measure of comfort in the fact that he was wrong, and that Spain did not, in fact, experience a Soviet-style revolution in the 1930s.
