Auxvasse Creek is a creek in northern Missouri. The creek is 45 miles (72 km) long and is a tributary of the Missouri River. The creek's name comes from the French word auxvasse, meaning "reeds" or "willows." The area along the creek was settled by French trappers and traders in the early 1700s. The French established a trading post at the mouth of the creek in the early 1800s. The trading post was later occupied by the Spanish and, in 1804, by the Lewis and Clark Expedition. The creek begins in northern Pettis County, Missouri, just south of the city of Sedalia. It flows west-southwest through northern Pettis and southern Boone counties, past the communities of Spickard, Auxvasse, and the western outskirts of Columbia. It joins the Missouri River in northern Cooper County, Missouri, about 4 miles (6.4 km) west of Boonville. The creek is a small, shallow stream, with a flow of about 65 cubic feet per second (1.7 m3/s). It is formed by the confluence of its East and West Forks, which are both about 25 miles (40 km) long. The East Fork begins in northern Pettis County, just south of the city of Sedalia, and flows south-southwest. The West Fork begins in western Pettis County, about 5 miles (8.0 km) west of the East Fork, and flows northwest. The two forks join near the community of Spickard. The creek's most significant tributary is Indian Creek, which flows into it from the east, just south of the city of Auxvasse. Indian Creek is about 15 miles (24 km) long and joins the creek in northern Boone County. The Missouri Department of Conservation owns and operates a conservation area along the creek, consisting of 1,200 acres (49 ha) of forest, meadows, and savanna. The area is known as the Auxvasse Creek Bottoms Conservation Area. It is located in northern Pettis and southern Boone counties, about 4 miles (6.4 km) west of the community of Sedalia. The conservation area was established in 1952 and includes a 4-mile (6.4 km) stretch of the creek. The area surrounding the creek is prone to flooding, and the creek has been the subject of a number of flood studies. A 2007 study by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) found that the 100-year floodplain for the creek was about 4,000 acres (1,600 ha) in size, and that the 25-year floodplain was about 2,000 acres (810 ha) in size. The FEMA study estimated that the 100-year flood had a peak flow rate of about 20000 cubic feet per second (5.5 m3/s), and that the 25-year flood had a peak flow rate of about 13000 cubic feet per second (3.7 m3/s).

State Highway 24 (SH 24) is a state highway in the western North Island of New Zealand. It runs for approximately 55 kilometres (34 mi) from the intersection with SH 1 and SH 3 in New Plymouth, via the town of Waitara, to SH 3 and SH 4 at Te Awamutu. The road was built in the 1930s and was one of the first roads in the North Island to be sealed with Bitumen. The New Plymouth Urban Area is the major population centre served by SH 24. In the 2013 Census, the population of the New Plymouth Urban Area was 44,630, making it the 10th largest urban area in New Zealand. SH 24 is a two-lane highway in rural areas, with short four-lane sections in the New Plymouth and Waitara urban areas. The highway passes through mostly rural areas, with some residential and commercial areas along the route. The road is generally straight, with some sweeping bends. There are few passing lanes, with the only long passing lane, a 3-kilometre passing lane between Mimi and Waitara, being the longest in the North Island. Most of the highway is less than 100 metres above sea level, with the highest point being the Whakamarama Summit, at 128 metres (420 ft) above sea level. The current route via Mimi was established in 1962, and was sealed in the 1980s. Prior to this, the highway ran via the settlement of Okato, to the south. The old route is still visible on maps, and is referred to as the "Old Waitara Road" on road signage in Okato. SH 24 is the main highway between New Plymouth and Te Awamutu, and is the only road between the two towns that does not pass through Hamilton. The highway is a key route to the port of New Plymouth, and carries traffic from the city to the port, as well as being a key freight route between New Plymouth and the Waikato. The highway is also a key tourist route, linking the towns of New Plymouth, Waitara, and Te Awamutu.

The route heads north as a two-lane road through the village, intersecting NY 48 (James Street) and NY 31 (Baldwinsville Road) before leaving the village. North of Baldwinsville, CR 41 passes through an area of farmland as it heads toward the village of Brewerton. The route passes under Interstate 481 (I-481) with no access and enters the village of Brewerton. In the village, CR 41 turns east onto Oneida Street, then north onto Madison Street, running concurrent with NY 37. North of NY 37, CR 41 leaves Brewerton and heads northwest through an area of farms as it enters the town of Lysander. The route ends at an intersection with NY 5 (Brant Street) just south of the village of Lysander. CR 41 was assigned in the early 1930s to a series of roads connecting NY 91 in Baldwinsville to NY 5 in Lysander. The route has not been changed since that time.

Shipp discovered the cause of scurvy, a disease which had been an annoying and sometimes fatal problem for sailors and others since ancient times. They discovered that the disease could be cured by the administration of lemon or orange juice. This was the first demonstration of the importance of vitamin C in preventing scurvy. For this discovery, Guy was awarded the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 1942, Guy became director of the Institute of Medical and Veterinary Research in Melbourne, Australia. He retired in 1952 and died in Melbourne in 1968.

The Tntnet project is composed of two main parts: the Tnt protocol, which is the peer-to-peer protocol used to interconnect nodes, and the Tnt services, which are the various services provided by the network. The Tnt protocol is designed to be efficient, simple, secure, and robust, and to provide a high level of decentralization. The Tnt services are designed to be easy to use, and to provide a high level of functionality. The Tntnet project is currently in the development phase, and the first version of the Tnt protocol has not yet been released. Air Force of the Independent State of Croatia The Air Force of the Independent State of Croatia (Croatian: Hrvatsko Ratno Zrakoplovstvo) was the aviation branch of the Croatian Armed Forces during the existence of the Independent State of Croatia, a puppet state of Nazi Germany which was established on 10 April 1941, and which ceased to exist on 8 May 1945. The Air Force was established by the Hrvatsko Narodnooslobodilačka Vojska (Croatian National Defense War Army), which was formed on the basis of the Croatian Air Force which, in turn, was formed on the basis of the Zrakoplovstvo Nejedržava Hrvatska (Croatian Private Air Force), which had been formed in the spring of 1940. The Air Force was organized into three groups, which in turn were divided into squadrons and flights. It consisted of around 20,000 members, of whom around 5,000 were officers and NCOs, and 15,000 were airmen. The Air Force used the Zrakoplovni Vojnik (Air Force Pilot) military service branch. Roth (German: Rotte) is an Ortsgemeinde – a municipality belonging to a Verbandsgemeinde, a kind of collective municipality – in the Bernkastel-Wittlich district in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany. Roth is a state-recognized health resort (Erholungsort) and is hence also called Roth-Siedel. The municipality lies in the western Hunsrück, near the border with the Saarland. It belongs to the Verbandsgemeinde of Thalfang am Erbeskopf. ## History Roth lies in a dale between the low Erbeskopf (a mountain) and the high Hunsrück. This area was already settled in prehistoric times. In 1985, a stone ax was found in Roth, and in the nearby village of Niedersayn a stone hatchet. Both finds are from the Neolithic period. Roth's municipal area is rich in prehistoric and early historic finds. Some of them have been gathered together and are on display at the municipal museum. Roth's oldest parts are the so-called Römerberg (German for "Roman mountain") and the old village (alte Dorf). The Römerberg is a hill whose eastern slopes, toward the Dierbach valley, have been terraced. On the higher of these two terraces, some of the stone remnants of a Roman country estate (villa rustica) have been preserved. It is believed that the villa had two building phases, the first in the 1st century and the second in the 3rd century. In the lower, western part of the municipal area, towards the Binger Scharlachberg (a hill), have been found several graves from the New Stone Age, the Iron Age, and the Roman period. One of these graves, from the 1st century, yielded the first evidence of a Celtic settlement in the area. Roth had its first documentary mention in 1263. At that time, it was called Rutha. The local saying "as old as Roth" (German: alt wie Roth) refers to this. In the 14th century, Roth was pledged to the County of Sponheim. Later it was ruled by the Margraves of Baden and the Counts of Veldenz. After the Veldenz line died out, Roth, in 1556, passed to the Margraviate of Baden. The Margraves of Baden introduced the Reformation into their territories early on. The subjects of the Römerberg farmstead, however, remained Catholic. In the 17th century, the Römerberg was the seat of a noble family, the "Römer" (German for "Roman"). The last of this line, Anna Regina, died in 1757. She had outlived her two sons, and so the Römer part of the farmstead was inherited by the Protestant branch of the von Gymnich family. After the Thirty Years' War, the Römerberg, which had belonged to the Catholic branch of the family, was sold to the Protestant branch. Since 1707, Roth has been in the Kingdom of Prussia, later the German Empire, and since 1949 in the Federal Republic of Germany. In 1757, the Römerberg was acquired by the counts of Metternich. It remained in their ownership until the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) took over the so-called "Römerturm" ("Roman tower"), which was part of the Römerberg, in 1979. After German reunification, the tower was returned to the municipality of Roth, and it is now in private ownership. In the 19th century, the Römerberg was the home of the so-called Römerkind (German for "Roman child"), a girl who was allegedly raised by the "Römer" (the last owner of the Römerberg, who had no children of his own). In 1974, Roth became the seat of the Verbandsgemeinde of Thalfang am Erbeskopf, which was newly formed by the merger of the former municipalities of Thalfang, Kaperich, and Roth. ## Politics ### Municipal council The council is made up of 16 council members, who were elected by majority vote at the municipal election held on 7 June 2009, and the honorary mayor as chairman. ### Mayor Roth's mayor is Klaus Schoneweg (FDP). ### Coat of arms The municipality's arms might be described thus: Azure a Wheel of Fortune argent. ## Culture and sightseeing ### Buildings The following are listed buildings or sites in Rhineland-Palatinate's Directory of Cultural Monuments: * Saint Nicholas's Catholic Church (Kirche St. Nikolai),

Holocytochrome-c synthase is an integral membrane protein found in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of the cell. The dimethoxybenzoquinol is attached to the cytochrome c by a thioether bond to a conserved cysteine residue in the protein. The assembled holocytochrome c is then transported to the mitochondrial inner membrane, where it is involved in the electron transport chain. The holocytochrome c synthase is expressed in all tissues and is found in all eukaryotes, including plants, animals, and fungi. In humans, the gene encoding the synthase is located on chromosome 19, and mutations in the gene can lead to the development of anemia. The synthase is also a drug target for the treatment of malaria, as it is involved in the production of the heme cofactor for the malaria parasite. Continental collision A continental collision, also known as a continent-continent collision or Thrusting, is a tectonic event in which two or more continents collide. While this term is used mainly for describing the collision of two continents, it can also describe the collision of a continent and a subcontinent, and even the collision of two subcontinents. The most significant continental collisions are associated with the formation of mountains and the development of basins. The most important mountain belts are formed along the collisions of the following: - the Caledonian and Scando-gnemy ranges between the Baltica and the Anglo-Scandinavian shields; - the Appalachian and the Caledonian-Appalachian ranges between the Laurentia and the Anglo-Scandinavian shields; - the Hercynian and the Midlandian ranges between the Laurussia and the Western Australian Shield; - the Thompson and the Appalachian- Oraasian ranges between the Eurasiatic and North American cratons; - the Rocky and the Cordilleran ranges between the Laurentia and the Pacific craton; - the Taurus and the Zagros ranges between the Arabia and the Iranian craton; - the Alpine-Himalayan and the Hindukush-Karakoram ranges between the Indian and the Tibetan Plateau; - the Golden Gate and the Kaapvaal ranges between the South America and the African craton. The term "continental collision" was first used by the geophysicist Paul S. Taff at the California Institute of Technology in 1978 to describe the collision of the Australian and Asian continents. Taff used the term to explain the formation of the folding and thrusting that had created the mountain ranges of southeast Asia and the islands of the western Pacific. The term is now used more generally to describe any continent-continent collision. The process of a continent-continent collision is similar to the process of an ocean-continent collision, which is also known as an orogenic event. The main difference between the two processes is that an ocean-continent collision occurs along a convergent ocean boundary, while a continent-continent collision occurs along a convergent continent boundary. The same process of subduction and overthrusting occurs in both cases. Continent-continent collisions are more energetic and create higher mountains than ocean-continent collisions. This is because the continents are much more rigid and thick than the oceans, so the process of subduction and overthrusting is more intense. Also, the continents are more wide and the convergence is along a longer boundary, so the forces are more equally distributed along the boundary. The boundary between two colliding continents is known as a suture. The suture zone is the area where the two continents meet, and it is usually defined by the location of the main mountain ranges. The suture zone is also the location of most of the mineral deposits and economic resources of the region. The collision of two continents is a slow process that can take millions of years. The first stage of the collision is the formation of a collisional belt, which is a zone of folding and thrusting that is parallel to the boundary between the two continents. The collisional belt is the location of most of the deformation and the development of the mountain ranges. After the formation of the collisional belt, the two continents begin to overlap each other, and the boundary between the two continents becomes more complex. The next stage of the collision is the formation of a sinuous zone, which is a zone of irregular folding and thrusting that is perpendicular to the boundary between the two continents. The sinuous zone is the location of most of the strike-slip deformation and the development of the basins. Finally, the two continents are completely fused together, and the boundary between the two continents is no longer visible. The last stage of the collision is the formation of a stable craton, which is a large, stable block of the Earth's crust that is made up of two or more formerly separate continents. The stable craton is the location of most of the old, stable mountain ranges. The collision of two continents is a major event in the history of the Earth, and it has had a major impact on the development of the planet's geography. The collision of the two continents creates large mountain ranges and deep basins, and it changes the climate and the biology of the region. The collision of two continents is also a major cause of earthquakes and volcanic activity.

The eggs are incubated by the female for fourteen days, with the chicks being fed by both parents. The young birds leave the nest after fifteen days. The Australasian treecreeper is insectivorous, with ants making up a large part of the diet. It is sometimes known to take small fruits and seeds.

Fishbein convention The Fishbein convention is a bidding convention in the game of bridge, used to force a reply by the partner of the player who has opened the bidding. It is used when the player to the left of the opener has already bid, and the opener's partner wishes to force the opener to bid again. It is named after its inventor, Milton Fishbein. After the opponent of the opener has made a bid, the partner of the opener may make a bid, known as a Fishbein bid, of two notrump, two clubs or two diamonds. This bid forces the opener to rebid, but does not necessarily force the opponent to bid again. The partner's bid may be higher than two notrump, two clubs or two diamonds, but it then becomes a conventional bid and the opener is not forced to rebid. The Fishbein convention is used only in Acol bridge, where it is an extension of the weak notrump convention. In other systems it is not used, as the opener's partner can instead make a pre-emptive bid of three notrump, three clubs or three diamonds, which are natural but not as powerful as the Fishbein bids. The advantage of using the Fishbein convention is that the opener's partner can make a powerful bid that is not normally available. For example, after 1 - 2NT - 3NT, a bid of 4 is a Fishbein bid, and forces the opener to rebid, providing information to the partner. Without the Fishbein convention, the partner would have to bid 4 , which is not a pre-emptive bid and does not force a reply.

Hammana is a village in the Bint Jbeil District in southern Lebanon. It is located 42 kilometers (26 mi) south of Beirut. Hammana has an elevation of 1,210 meters (3,990 ft) above sea level and a total land area of 3,200 hectares (7,500 acres). The village is located in the south of the Beqaa Valley, between the Western and the Eastern Beqaa, and it is the highest village in the district. The name of the village is derived from the Aramaic word "Hamman" which means "bath" or "spa", referring to the many hot springs in the area. In the early 20th century, the German scholar Alois Musil described Hammana as a "place of delightful, clean air". During the 2006 Lebanon War, Hammana and the surrounding area were heavily damaged by Israeli airstrikes. The inhabitants of Hammana are Druze, with a small Christian minority. The village has one school, which had an enrollment of 130 students in the academic year 2008–2009. The villagers work in agriculture, including the growing of olives, grapes, almonds, and other fruits and vegetables. The village has a population of 2,500, the majority of them being elderly.

Frederick John Turner (3 October 1876 – 2 May 1948) was an English professional footballer who played in the Football League for Port Vale, in the Southern League for Southampton, and in the Scottish League for Partick Thistle. Born in Birmingham, Turner played for the Small Heath and Birmingham & District Friday afternoon leagues before moving to Scotland to play for Partick Thistle in the Scottish First Division. He was a "tough-tackling" centre-half and was part of the Thistle team that won the Scottish Cup in 1901, defeating Rangers 2–1 in the final. In the summer of 1901, Turner returned to England to play for Burslem Port Vale of the Second Division. He made his debut in a 3–1 win over West Bromwich Albion on 9 September and scored his first goal in a 4–1 victory over Barnsley on 7 October. He became a key member of the Vale defence, and his "un blossom-like" style earned him the nickname "Dumpy". He also played in all but one of the club's 46 matches in the 1902–03 season, as the team finished second in the Second Division, missing out on promotion by just one point. In the summer of 1903, Turner moved to the south coast to join Southern League champions, Southampton. He was a replacement for the club's former captain, Harry Wood, and went on to become a "standard-bearer" at The Dell. A "fine athlete", he was known for his "speed, tricky footwork and dribbling" and his "accurate and powerful" shooting. Turner also became a regular penalty taker and was "renowned for his ability to score from any angle". He was the only player to appear in all three games of the 1910–11 South Hams District Challenge Cup final, as the Saints won the trophy for the first time. In 1911, the Saints finished second in the Southern League, and in the following season Turner helped the team to win the championship. He remained with the club throughout World War I, although he spent part of the 1914–15 season with Plymouth Argyle, and also made guest appearances for Portsmouth and Bristol Rovers during the conflict. He retired from football in 1920, having made 312 appearances in all competitions for Southampton, and took up smoking pipes and cigars. In 1927, at the age of 51, he returned to the pitch to play for the combined Hampshire and Southampton Police team. Turner died in Itchen, Hampshire, on 2 May 1948, aged 71.

British silent horror films refers to British films with a horror theme made during the silent era from the turn of the twentieth century to the introduction of sound in cinema. British silent horror films were a significant part of the British film industry's output during the period, and although less well-known than the German expressionist horror films or the American horror films, they are notable for their influence on later British horror films, particularly the Hammer Horror films which became prominent in the 1950s and were a major influence on the evolution of the horror genre. During the early decades of the twentieth century, the British film industry was one of the largest in the world, alongside the American and German film industries, and British films were distributed across the globe. The First World War had a devastating effect on the British film industry, and although it recovered by the early 1920s, it was a relatively small industry in comparison to the American and German film industries, and a large proportion of its output consisted of comedies and melodramas. In the early 1920s, the German expressionist horror film Nosferatu (1922) was a major critical and commercial success, and in the same year, the British film industry began producing its own horror films, beginning with The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1919), a British adaptation of the German film. The 1920s saw a number of important British silent horror films, including The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, The Asphyx, and The Cat and the Canary. The influence of German expressionism was particularly strong, and many British silent horror films featured dark shadows, twisted sets, and other expressionistic elements. In addition, many British silent horror films featured supernatural elements, such as ghosts, monsters, and mummies. The British silent horror films of the 1920s were a major influence on the later Hammer Horror films, which became prominent in the 1950s and were a major influence on the evolution of the horror genre. The Hammer Horror films were notable for their use of dark shadows, twisted sets, and other expressionistic elements, as well as their use of supernatural elements, such as ghosts, monsters, and mummies. In addition, the Hammer Horror films often featured medieval settings, and were influenced by the Gothic novel and the works of authors such as Edgar Allan Poe. In the early 1930s, the British film industry began to produce a number of sound horror films, including The Ghoul, The Invisible Man, and The Terror. These films were notable for their use of sound effects and music to create a mood of fear and suspense, and were a major influence on the later development of the horror genre.

Gunnar Karlson (25 April 1898 – 10 October 1952) was a Swedish astronomer and mathematician who worked at the Swedish Optical Institute and the University of Uppsala. He was known for his contributions to the field of spectroscopy, such as the Karlson-Rittner method, and for his work on the theory of the astroschematic. Gunnar Karlson was born in Töreboda, Sweden in 1898. He received his bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1921 and his master's degree in mathematics and astronomy in 1923, both from the University of Uppsala. He worked as an assistant at the Swedish Optical Institute from 1923 to 1925 and as a lecturer in mathematics at the University of Uppsala from 1925 to 1928. He then returned to the Swedish Optical Institute as a senior astronomer and worked there until his death. Karlson's research focused on the fields of spectroscopy and the theory of the astroschematic. He was known for his contributions to the field of spectroscopy, such as the Karlson-Rittner method, and for his work on the theory of the astroschematic. He was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and the Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences.

Zoltán Demeter (March 3, 1916 – October 3, 2013) was a Hungarian-born American jazz bassist, who appeared on more than 100 recordings in the course of a career spanning more than six decades, including with some of the most prominent names in the history of the genre. Demeter was born in Budapest, Hungary in 1916. He began his musical studies when he was six, playing the violin. He also played the tuba in the school orchestra. He was introduced to the double bass at the age of 16, and played his first professional gig at 18. In 1939, he moved to Prague to play with the Jimmy Kálmán orchestra. In 1946, Demeter emigrated to the United States to play with the Charles Spivik band, with whom he stayed for three years. He then worked with Boyd Raeburn for two years, and recorded with Raeburn's orchestra in 1949. In 1950, he became the bassist with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, a position he held for 33 years. In the 1950s, Demeter also performed with the likes of John Serry Sr., Tony Mottola, and Al Hirt. He became a U.S. citizen in 1955. In the 1960s, he played with the New York City Ballet, the Metropolitan Opera, and the New York Philharmonic. He also played with the Paul Lavalle Orchestra during this period. In the 1970s, Demeter played with the National Symphony Orchestra, and in 1979 he retired from the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra after serving for more than a quarter of a century. In 1980, he moved to Florida, where he played with the Florida Symphony Orchestra, and also performed with the Paul Lavalle Orchestra, the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra, and the Harry James Orchestra. Demeter died in 2013, at the age of 97.

Upper Saxony (German: Oberlausitz) is a federal state (Land) in northern Germany, bordering on the states of Saxony-Anhalt to the north, Thuringia to the east, Bavaria to the south, and Lower Saxony to the west. Its capital is Dresden, and it is the second-largest state in Germany by area, second-largest by population, and the eighth-largest by population density. It is located in the historic heart of Germany, along the River Elbe, which rises in the Saxon Switzerland, a mountainous national park in the southeast of the state. The Elbe Valley of Dresden is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as is the town of Bautzen. The state has a long history as the former stomping grounds of Dresden's ruling families, the House of Wettin, and the Ascanian margraves and prince-electors of Brandenburg, who for centuries furnished the region with brilliant art and architecture. In the 20th century, Upper Saxony was the scene of fierce fighting during the final stages of World War II, and it was the area most affected by the Soviet-installed communist regime in the former German Democratic Republic. The state has a diversified economy, with strong manufacturing and high-tech industries. In 2009, it had an economic output of €72,100 per capita and a GDP of €87,300 per capita, the highest in the new states of Germany. In the 21st century, Upper Saxony has an unemployment rate lower than the German average. The state has a population of 4.3 million people (as of 31 December 2018), making it the second-most populous state of Germany after Lower Saxony. In 2006, the state had an immigration rate of 11.2%, the third highest in Germany, and a birth/death rate of +4.3%, the second highest in Germany. The state is one of the four new states (German: Neues Deutschland) that were created in 1990 by the reunification of Germany. It was formerly the arts and cultural hub of the German Democratic Republic, and the administrative and economic centre of the Saxon state, which included the historic provinces of Saxony and Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. The state of Saxony, which included the territory of present-day Saxony-Anhalt, was one of the six states of the German Empire. Upper Saxony has a long history as part of the German-speaking world. It has been the site of a major German language event, the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, and the area of the medieval German Hanseatic League. The state has a rich cultural history, with numerous artists, scientists, and composers, and a significant architectural history, with numerous styles and sub-styles. The state is a parliamentary republic of sixteen states, called Landkreise in German, and one urban district, called kreisfreie Stadt in German. Three cities have more than 100,000 inhabitants: Dresden, Leipzig, and Chemnitz.

Irving Lowens (May 7, 1914 – June 2, 1996) was an American musicologist, conductor, composer, and violist, primarily known for his work in the field of opera. Lowens was born in Bialystok, Poland in 1914, and his family moved to the United States in 1922. He studied music at the Juilliard School under Max Persin and Walter Damrosch, and conducting with Herbert von Karajan in Berlin. He joined the faculty of Juilliard in 1946, and later served as a professor of music at New York University (NYU) from 1956 to 1982. In 1981 he was appointed professor emeritus at NYU. Lowens was a music critic for The New Yorker magazine from 1948 to 1950, and also wrote for The Musical Quarterly. He was the editor of The Opera Quarterly from 1973 to 1985, and was a regular contributor to that journal as well. He was the author of two books, The Opera Library (a catalog of recordings) and Opera: A History (with Michael Korska). Lowens was also a violist, and was a member of the New York Philharmonic for 25 years, from 1950 to 1975. He also played with the Juilliard String Quartet. He was a founding member of the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, and was a longtime member of the faculty at the Marlboro Music Festival.

Vagad Vagad (IAST: Vāgad), is a village in the Indian state of Gujarat. It is located in the Ahmedabad district, on the banks of the Sabarmati River. The people of Vagad celebrate the festival of Navrati, during which the village is decorated with lights. Kites are flown from the rooftops. Ptolemais in Phoenicia Ptolemais in Phoenicia (also known as Ptolemais ad Libanum; Greek: Πτολεμαΐς ἐπὶ τῆς Φoenίτιδος, Latin: Ptolemais in Phoenicia) was an ancient city in the Seleucid Empire, located in what is now Syria. The city was founded in the 3rd or 2nd century BC and was named in honor of the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt. The city was located in the northern Beqaa Valley, between the cities of Antioch and Damascus, on the border between the Seleucid Empire and the Ptolemaic Kingdom. The city was mentioned by several ancient writers, including Pliny the Elder, Appian, and Strabo. Although the city was founded in the 2nd or 3rd century BC, the site had been inhabited since at least the Neolithic period. In the 3rd century BC, the region was occupied by the kingdom of Syria, which was subsequently conquered by the Egyptians under Ptolemy I Soter. The city was captured by the Seleucids in the 2nd century BC, and became the seat of a governor. The city also had a temple dedicated to the gods of the underworld, which was used for the burial of the city's elite. The city was destroyed in the 1st century BC, and its site remained abandoned until it was reoccupied in the 6th century AD. The city was mentioned by the historian Procopius, who described it as a flourishing city. The city was eventually abandoned again, and its site was forgotten until it was discovered and excavated in the 20th century. The site of Ptolemais in Phoenicia was identified in the 20th century AD, and excavation of the site began in the 1970s. The city was located on a hill in the northern Beqaa Valley, between the modern cities of Damascus and Homs. The city was surrounded by a wall, and had a theater, a temple, and a number of houses and streets. The city's ruins are located in a modern-day Syrian military base.

St. Matthew's Church, Dunedin St. Matthew's Church is an Anglican church in the city of Dunedin, New Zealand. It is one of the city's most prominent landmarks, and is commonly referred to as "the Cathedral of the South". The church was designed by the English architect R. A. Lawson, and is one of the largest Gothic-style churches in the southern hemisphere. It has a distinctive grey colour, which was originally chosen to make the building more visible amongst the area's plentiful fog. The church can accommodate 1,100 people, and has three organs. The church was built between 1863 and 1866, and was consecrated in 1873. It has been rebuilt twice, in 1904 and in 1959. It is constructed of Oamaru stone, with some additional marble and other stonework in the sanctuary. St. Matthew's Church is the mother church of the Anglican Diocese of Dunedin, and as such is the seat of the Bishop of Dunedin. It is one of only two churches in New Zealand that has (or has had) the status of pro-cathedral (the other being St. John's in Napier). It is also one of only four churches in the world that has the status of "Aided Church" (the others being St. John's in Wellington, St. Peter's in Hamilton, and St. Stephen's in Auckland). The church is located in the heart of Dunedin, on the corner of George Street and State Highway 1 (known as Great King Street). It is adjacent to the University of Otago campus, and is a short distance from the Dunedin Railway Station. The church is an iconic building in the city, and is one of the city's most distinctive landmarks. It is also a popular tourist attraction, and is one of the most visited buildings in the city.

Newham Collegiate Sixth Form Centre (NCSC) is a co-educational sixth form college in East London, England. It was established in 2002 and is part of the Newham Sixth Form College Federation. The college is located on the border of East Ham and Beckton, close to the boundary with Barking and Dagenham. It is a specialist sixth form, offering A-Levels, BTECs and the International Baccalaureate. The college has been consistently one of the top performing sixth form colleges in the country, and in 2013 was named the best sixth form college in the country by The Times. The college offers a range of both A-Level and BTEC courses. It has a mixed intake, with students from a variety of schools around east London, and from a variety of ethnic and socio-economic backgrounds. The college is divided into four "colleges" which are named after four notable alumni: Sir John Cass, Lord Birkett, Sir Frank Whittle and Lord Bernard Levin. Each "college" has its own principal, who is a member of the college's Senior Leadership Team. The college's overall principal is Ian Rampling. In 2013, the college was named the best in the country for its A-Level results, achieving a 99.3% pass rate with over three-quarters of students achieving A* and A grades. The college was also named the top state-funded school in the country for the third year in a row. The college was featured in the BBC's documentary series Britain's Best School.

Water supply and sanitation in Azerbaijan Water supply The water supply system in Azerbaijan provides mostly drinking and irrigation water to agricultural lands. Water supply is provided through a network of underground and surface water reservoirs, rivers and lakes, as well as through wells and water pumps. The area of the country is 86,600 square kilometers (33,400 sq mi). The total water supply in the country is 3.3 billion cubic meters (1,274 billion cubic feet) with 1,220 million cubic meters (46.3 billion cubic feet) from the surface water resources (including 694 million cubic meters (24.3 billion cubic feet) from the lakes) and 2,100 million cubic meters (74.3 billion cubic feet) from the underground water resources. The total water supply per capita is 3,210 cubic meters (106,600 cu ft) a year. There are 6,350 wells and water pumps, as well as 1,200 water supply networks in the country. Most of the wells are located in the low-lying coastal areas and in the central part of the country. The water from the wells is used for irrigation, as well as for drinking water supply to the settlements. The water from the surface water resources is used mainly for irrigation, as well as for the water supply to the settlements in the Absheron Peninsula and in the low-lying coastal areas. There are two main sources of water supply to the capital of the country, Baku: the Bolshoy (Big) and Maly (Small) Araz Rivers. The water from these two rivers is collected in a reservoir near the city, and then distributed through the city water supply system. The city water supply system is also fed from the water sources in the Absheron Peninsula and from the bottomless lake Lokbatan. Sanitation Azerbaijan's sanitation systems are generally in poor condition, with much untreated wastewater and limited opportunities for the use of modern sanitary facilities. In most rural areas, sanitation facilities are limited to open sewage pits. In the 1990s, the government began a program to construct individual household septic tanks and to organize the use of water treatment plants. The program has had only limited success, primarily in the Baku area, because of the lack of financial resources for the maintenance of the facilities. In the 2000s, the government began a new program to improve sanitation in the country. The program includes the construction of new water treatment plants and the rehabilitation of the old ones, as well as the improvement of the sewage collection and transportation system. The program is being implemented with the help of international donors, such as the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank and the European Union.

Tonia Buxton (born 25 September 1973) is an English actress, television presenter, and food writer, best known for her work on the BBC Two television series Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two. Buxton was born in London. She trained as a dancer at the Arts Educational School, London, and then at the Rambert School of Ballet and Contemporary Dance, before becoming a professional dancer. She danced with the English National Ballet for four years, and then with Northern Ballet Theatre, before an injury ended her dancing career. While still a dancer, Buxton began to work as a television presenter. She has presented for the BBC, ITV, Channel 4, and Sky. László Szőgyény-Marich Sr. (szögyény-marich means "sun-ray-blessed" in Hungarian) (February 8, 1889 – August 31, 1959) was a Hungarian track and field athlete and a prominent lawyer and politician in the 1920s and 1930s. He was born in Kecskemét, Hungary. He was Jewish. He competed for Hungary at the 1912 Summer Olympics in Stockholm, Sweden, and won a silver medal in the 4x400 metres relay, and a bronze medal in the 110 metres hurdles. After the Olympics, he went to study law at the University of Budapest, and later became a lawyer. He worked for theTax Office of Budapest for a short time, then became a lawyer in his father's office. He was an excellent lawyer and very successful. In the early 1920s, he was one of the founders of the Hungarian Olympic Committee, and also one of the organizers of the first Hungarian Olympic Games. He was a member of the Hungarian National Olympic Committee for more than 20 years. In the 1930s, he became a member of the Hungarian Parliament for a short time, and also served as the Minister of Public Welfare for a short time. He was the father of László Szőgyény-Marich Jr., a famous Hungarian athlete, who won a bronze medal in the 100 metres at the 1928 Summer Olympics in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.

List of Mobile Suit Gundam ZZ episodes The episodes of Mobile Suit Gundam ZZ were broadcast on TV Tokyo from October 1989 to December 1989, and the rest of the series was broadcast from January 1990 to January 1991 on the same station. The episodes were also broadcast on ATX in Korea. The series is set in the Universal Century year "UC 0093", with the battle of the One Year War still in recent memory. The series is a direct continuation of Mobile Suit Gundam Z, taking place a few months after that story. The story centers on the new mobile suits, the ZZ, and their pilots, the Civillian Special Forces (CSF), who are fighting against the Zeon remnant forces. The show is a much lighter and more comical take on the Gundam franchise; the fighting is much less serious and much more intense, with a much greater emphasis on the comedy. Lightweighting is the process of reducing the weight of a structural component through a combination of material removal and material replacement. It is closely related to the concept of "lightweight structures", which are structures that have a lower weight than would be achieved through the use of conventional materials and section shapes. Lightweighting is often achieved by replacing some or all of the conventional materials (e.g., steel, aluminum, titanium, magnesium, and ceramics) with lightweight materials (e.g., fiber reinforced polymers, polymer matrix composites, metals, and ceramics). Lightweighting can also be achieved by removing material from sections of the structure through the use of holes, cut-outs, and notches. Lightweighting is an important consideration in many industries, such as aerospace, automotive, and consumer products. In the aerospace industry, lightweighting is used to improve the fuel efficiency of aircraft and spacecraft. Lightweighting is also used to improve the performance and range of missiles and spacecraft. In the automotive industry, lightweighting is used to improve the fuel efficiency and handling of automobiles and motorcycles. In the consumer products industry, lightweighting is used to reduce the weight and improve the portability of electronic devices, such as laptops, mobile phones, and personal digital assistants. There are several methods for achieving lightweighting. One method is to use lightweight materials to replace heavier materials. For example, fiber reinforced polymers can be used to replace steel and aluminum. Another method is to use a lightweight material to replace a heavier material in a specific area of the structure. For example, a carbon fiber-reinforced polymer can be used to replace steel in the cockpit of an aircraft. A third method is to remove material from sections of the structure to reduce its weight. For example, holes can be drilled in a steel beam to reduce its weight.

The fraternity's historical national headquarters was in Baltimore, Maryland. The chapter designation "Alpha" indicates a chapter that was established by the fraternity's founding members. The "Gamma" series of chapters were the first ones established after the fraternity became nationally incorporated in the early 1930s. He was also the athletic director at Texas State from 1965 to 1968. In 1969, Madore was hired as the general manager of the Houston Oilers of the American Football League (AFL), a position he held for three years. He was an assistant coach with the Washington Redskins in 1970, and was the interim head coach for the last three games of the season after the firing of Vince Lombardi. He later became a scout for the Redskins. Madore died in 2015 at the age of 90. ## Early years Madore was born in 1924 in Portland, Oregon. He attended Lincoln High School in Portland. ## College career Madore played college football at the University of Washington in Seattle from 1942 to 1944. He was a halfback for the Huskies and was co-captain of the 1943 team. In three years at Washington, Madore gained 3,502 yards (5.7 yards per attempt), scored 282 points, punted 171 times for 6,317 yards (36.5 yards per punt) and returned 67 kickoffs for 1,685 yards (25.3 yards per return). In 2005, Madore was selected by Washington's student body as the most outstanding undergraduate athlete in the history of the university. ## Professional career Madore was selected by the Chicago Bears in the seventh round, 63rd overall, of the 1945 NFL Draft. Omaha, Arkansas Omaha is a town in Arkansas County in the U.S. state of Arkansas. The population was 1,620 at the 2010 census. It is the county seat of Arkansas County. Omaha was incorporated in 1889. The community had been platted in 1871 after the railroad was built through the area. A post office has been in operation in Omaha since 1873. Omaha is located in east-central Arkansas County at 33°44′56″N 91°39′11″W (33.745527, -91.649905). According to the United States Census Bureau, the town has a total area of 2.5 square miles (6.5 km2), of which 2.5 square miles (6.5 km2) is land and 0.24 square miles (0.62 km2) is water. The climate in this area is characterized by hot, humid summers and generally mild to cool winters. According to the Köppen climate classification system, Omaha has a humid subtropical climate, Cfa on the climate map. As of the census of 2000, there were 1,8848,131 in the town. The population density was 765.1 people per square mile (295.3/km²). There were 1,063 housing units at an average density of 418.6 per square mile (161.3/km²). The racial makeup of the town was 67.56% White, 29.06% Black or African American, 0.84% Native American, 0.54% Asian, 0.05% Pacific Islander, 0.92% from other races, and 1.51% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 2.06% of the population. There were 1,063 households out of which 30.7% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 45.3% were married couples living together, 14.6% had a female householder with no husband present, and 36.3% were non-families. 32.6% of all households were made up of individuals and 13.1% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.19 and the average family size was 2.84. In the town, the population was spread out with 21.6% under the age of 18, 8.8% from 18 to 24, 29.4% from 25 to 44, 20.4% from 45 to 64, and 20.7% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 39 years. For every 100 females, there were 102.1 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 103.1 males. As of 2000 the median income for a household in the town was $21,458, and the median income for a family was $29,118. Men had a median income of $22,426 versus $16,250 for women. The per capita income for the town was $12,041. About 10.9% of families and 16.4% of the population were below the poverty line, including 20.1% of those under age 18 and 17.2% of those age 65 or over. The town is served by the Omaha School District, which includes the Omaha High School. The school's teams are known as the "Omaha Eagles".

Ruth Cardoso (born July 10, 1930) is a Brazilian writer, anthropologist, and educator. She is the widow of the former Brazilian president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, and was First Lady of Brazil from 1995 to 2002. Cardoso was born in 1930 in Rio de Janeiro, the daughter of a businessman and a teacher. She studied anthropology at the National Museum of Brazil and the University of Brazil. In addition to her academic work, Cardoso has published several books on anthropology and sociology, including The House of the Devil: The Life and Times of a Brazilian Slave Family (1994), which was a finalist for the National Book Award. She has also written for The New York Times, The Washington Post, and other publications. Cardoso was married to Fernando Henrique Cardoso from 1961 until his death in 2008. She is the mother of the writer and diplomat Sérgio CCD (born 1962), the photographer Pedro Baby (born 1965), and the economist paths (born 1966). She is the daughter of pt:Mário Soeiro da Silva (1898–1977), a businessman and pt:Dra. Nenê de Souza Ferraz (1898–1994), a teacher.

Richard Vesey Hamilton (30 November 1767 – 18 February771) was an Irish politician, soldier, and diplomat. He was the son of Sir John Hamilton, 1st Baronet, of Woodbrook, County Roscommon, by his second wife, Anne, daughter of William Vesey, 1st Baron Vestey. He was born at his father's residence in London, but spent much of his childhood in Ireland, where his father had extensive lands. He was educated at Eton College, and later at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich. He was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Royal Irish Artillery in 1786, and promoted to first lieutenant in 1791. In 1793, Hamilton was elected to the Irish House of Commons for Tulsk, and was returned for that constituency at every election until the Acts of Union 1800 dissolved the Irish Parliament. He was a supporter of the government, and his most significant achievement in the Irish House was to steer the Registry of Deeds Act through the House in 1796. The Act was designed to improve the security of land ownership in Ireland, and was a major part of the Irish government's efforts to tackle the problem of Irish land tenure. In 1800, Hamilton was appointed as a member of the Irish delegation to the British Parliament, where he was an active supporter of the government. He was also a member of the Dublin Society, and served as a governor of the Irish Hospital for the Insane. In 1807, Hamilton was appointed as the British Minister to the Swiss Confederation. He died in office in Berne in 1808.

Mr Brownlow is the guardian of Oliver Twist in the novel Oliver Twist by Charles Dickens. The character of Mr. Brownlow is a foil to that of Fagin, the leader of a gang of pickpockets and the man who takes in Oliver after his escape from the workhouse. While Fagin is a corrupt and evil man who uses people, Mr. Brownlow is a morally upstanding, kind man who is an example of what all people should strive to be. He is depicted as a "benefactor" and "fatherly friend" who takes Oliver in and cares for him as if he were his own son. Mr. Brownlow is a wealthy and well-respected member of society, and he uses his position to help those less fortunate than himself. He is a strong supporter of the system of philanthropy, and he believes that it is the duty of those who are fortunate to help those who are not. He is also a strong supporter of the idea that education is the key to improving the lives of the poor, and he works to provide education to those who would otherwise not have access to it. Mr. Brownlow is a complex character, and he is not without his faults. He is a man of strong emotions, and he can be quick to anger. He is also a man of great pride, and he can be stubborn and inflexible. However, these faults are counterbalanced by his strong sense of justice and his desire to help those less fortunate than himself.

The rhinoceros auklet (Cerorhinca monocerata) is a species of seabird in the family Alcidae, the auk family. It is one of three species of auklets in the genus Cerorhinca, and one of 21 species in the Alcidae family. The rhinoceros auklet is found from the Aleutian Islands in Alaska to the Sea of Okhotsk in Russia. It occurs as a breeder in Russia, North Korea, South Korea, China, and Japan; and as a winter migrant to the North Pacific coast of North America from Alaska to Baja California. It has also been recorded from Taiwan. The rhinoceros auklet is named for its distinctive horn-like bill. It is 20–23 cm (7.9–9.1 in) in length and weighs 100–400 g (3.5–14 oz). It has a dark greyish-brown head, pale greyish-brown upperparts, and white underparts. The feet and legs are pale grey. The male and female are similar in appearance. The rhinoceros auklet feeds at night on small crustaceans and marine worms. It nests in colonies on islands and coastal headlands in Russia and North America. It winters in the open ocean and in protected coastal waters. The rhinoceros auklet is the subject of a conservation effort by BirdLife International. Although the species' population is currently stable, there is a lack of information on its population size, and it is believed to be at risk of becoming endangered.

Murder of Jermaine Goupall Jermaine Goupall (born 10 October 1996) was a 14-year-old boy who was stabbed to death in South London in August 2015. He was stabbed four times in the chest by a 16-year-old boy, who was later convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison. Goupall was born on 10 October 1996 in Lambeth, South London, to mother Brenda and father Stanley. He had two older brothers, one of whom was Andile, and two older sisters. He attended St. Matthew's Church of England Primary School in Lambeth and then Archbishop Tenison's Church of England Secondary School in Croydon. Goupall was stabbed four times in the chest on 8 August 2015 by a 16-year-old boy, named by the media as Danozolamide (Dano) Moore. After the attack, Goupall managed to walk back to his home in Ferndene Road, Lambeth, where he collapsed and was found by his mother. He was taken to a hospital in South London, where he was pronounced dead. Goupall's murder was the 17th teenage homicide in London in 2015, and the 30th teenage homicide in England and Wales in 2015. In the four weeks before his death, four other boys, aged 15 to 16, were stabbed to death in London. Goupall's murder prompted a call for a zero-tolerance approach to knife crime by the Mayor of London, Boris Johnson. On 21 December 2015, the Metropolitan Police charged Moore with Goupall's murder. On 21 February 2016, Moore pleaded not guilty to murder; he was then tried at the Old Bailey the following month. On 7 April 2016, Moore was found guilty of murder and sentenced to life in prison, with a minimum term of 15 years. In memory of Goupall, a campaign called "Don't Start, Don't Carry, Don't Hide" was launched in South London by the Metropolitan Police and the council in Lambeth.

Albert Scardino (born October 30, 1947) is an American journalist and businessman who was the editor and publisher of the Houston Chronicle from 1997 to 2013. Scardino was born in Dallas, Texas, and graduated from St. Mark's School of Texas in 1965. He received a bachelor's degree in journalism from the University of Texas at Austin in 1969 and a master's degree in English literature from the University of Bristol in England in 1970. Scardino began his journalism career at the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, where he was a reporter from 1971 to 1975. He then worked for 12 years at the Dallas Morning News, where he was a reporter, feature writer, and editor. From 1987 to 1997, he was editor and publisher of the El Paso Times. In 1997, Scardino became editor and publisher of the Houston Chronicle, a position he held until 2013. During his tenure as publisher, the Chronicle won three Pulitzer Prizes, including two for its coverage of Hurricane Katrina and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. In 2009, the Chronicle was named the best large newspaper in the United States by the National Newspaper Association. Scardino has served on the board of directors of the Associated Press, the Texas Democracy Foundation, and the Journalistic Education Foundation of Texas. He is a member of the American Society of Newspaper Editors and the Texas Press Association. In 2013, Scardino was inducted into the Texas Newspaper Hall of Fame.

On February 6, 2014, an earthquake struck the Lao People's Democratic Republic. The magnitude 6.1 earthquake occurred in the province of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, near the town of Yagdeng, at a depth of 55.0 km (34.1 mi). The tremor caused strong shaking in the capital city of Vientiane and nearby provinces, causing extensive damage to the city's infrastructure, and killed at least one person and injured over 100 others. The earthquake was felt as far as Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The tremor caused extensive damage to Vientiane's infrastructure, with many buildings suffering severe damage. The city's electricity and water supply were knocked out, and many roads were blocked by fallen trees and power lines. The Lao government launched an emergency response to the earthquake, with the military being deployed to help the injured and displaced. The government also appealed for international assistance, and several countries, including China, Thailand, and Vietnam, offered assistance. The earthquake was the second major disaster to strike Laos in less than a year, following the deadly 2012 Savannakhet bus crash. The country's disaster management authorities have been criticized for their response to both disasters.

Julius Fromm (6 June 1888 – 17 April 1980) was a German businessman, art collector, and patron of the arts. Fromm was born in Berlin, the son of a Jewish grain dealer. He initially worked for his father's business, but the family was expropriated after the Nazis came to power in 1933 and their business was Aryanized. He then worked as a broker on the Berlin Stock Exchange, before emigrating to Switzerland in 1937. After a brief period in the Netherlands, he settled in France, where he worked in business and became a collector of art. Fromm became a patron of the arts and collected works by German artists, including approximately 100 works by the painter Max Beckmann, whose work he is credited with having saved from obscurity after the Nazi rise to power; he also acquired works by the German expressionists, including paintings by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, and Emil Nolde, as well as the Austrian Expressionist Oskar Kokoschka. Fromm was also a collector of the work of French artists, including paintings by Picasso, Matisse, and Braque, as well as the surrealists, including works by Max Ernst, Salvador Dalí, and René Magritte. In the late 1960s, Fromm sold a number of his French works, and in 1978 he sold a large part of his German collection to the German art dealer Georg Karg, who in turn sold it to the German government. The remainder of Fromm's collection was inherited by his daughter, Susanne, and after her death in 1986, it was acquired by the Jewish Museum in New York.

1814 In the War of 1812, the United States takes control of the Canadian city of Fort York (modern-day Toronto). After the United States invades Canada in the previous year, British forces launch a counterattack with the objective of capturing the American capital of Washington, D.C. In the Chesapeake Bay, the British Navy surprises the American Navy in a battle that ends in a U.S. victory. On August 24, in the Battle of Plattsburgh on Lake Champlain in New York, the British Navy suffers a defeat after being ambushed by the American Navy. On September 11, the British burn Washington, D.C. The British army, under the command of General Robert Ross, had intentions of capturing the capital. After an intense battle, the British overwhelmed the American forces and set fire to the Capitol building, the White House, the Library of Congress, and other government buildings. On September 13, at the Battle of Plattsburgh on Lake Champlain in New York, the British Navy is defeated again by the American Navy. The British are defeated at the Battle of Baltimore on September 13–14. The Star-Spangled Banner, the U.S. national anthem, is composed by lawyer and amateur poet Francis Scott Key on September 13, after he witnessed the British attack on Fort McHenry in Baltimore Harbor the morning of September 13. On October 5, the British are defeated at the Battle of New Orleans. The British, under the command of General Edward Pakenham, made a plan to capture the American city of New Orleans, which was a vital port for the American South. The British were delayed by the Americans for several days and were eventually defeated by a Louisiana Militia under the command of General Andrew Jackson. This battle is known as the Battle of New Orleans and is considered the greatest American victory of the War of 1812. On October 25, in the Gulf of Mexico, British forces destroy the USS Carolina, the USS Enterprise, and the USS Syren. On November 5, the British destroy the USS Wasp in the North Atlantic. The War of 1812 ends on February 17, 1815, with the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent. The United States does not gain any territory, but it does prevent the British from taking over the American Northwest Territory. The British also agree to stop helping the Indians attack American settlements in the Northwest Territory.

Thrice Woven Thrice Woven is an American doom metal band from Minneapolis, Minnesota, formed in 2012. The band's name was inspired by a passage in the Norse mythology tale Volundar Saga. The band's current lineup includes guitarist/vocalist Josh Graham (ex-Novembers Doom), guitarist Matt Kokaly (ex-Bury Your Dead), bassist/vocalist Kyle Stevenson (ex-Wretched Spawn), and drummer Ben Hutcherson (Throes of Ataraxia). Thrice Woven's music is characterized by dramatic song structures, majestic vocal lines, and complex guitar work. The band's style is influenced by traditional doom metal bands such as Candlemass, Trouble, and Witchfinder General, as well as by the classic rock bands Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. Thrice Woven has released three studio albums, two EPs, and one live album. The band's latest album, The Fringes of Psychosis, was released in 2021. Thrice Woven performs live regularly and has shared the stage with many well-known doom metal bands, including Black Sabbath, Sleepytime Gorilla Museum, Cathedral, Saint Vitus, and The Obsessed.

Wazir Ali was a Pakistani film actor and producer. He was born inirties, in Jalandhar, British India now India. After the partition of India in 1947, his family moved to Pakistan and settled in Lahore. Wazir Ali was a famous actor of the silver screen in the 1960s and 1970s. He worked with many famous actors and actresses like Meena Kumari, Madhubala, Naghma, Babra Sharif, and Neelo. He was a producer and actor in the film industry and played a significant role in the progress of the film industry in Pakistan. He produced many films in the 1960s and 1970s in both Pakistan and India. Some of his films were Taxiwala, Bank Robbery, pyar kiya to darna kya, Chalo ek baar phoolon se khoj, pasand naein zindagi. He was also a film director and worked with famous Indian actress Meena Kumari in the film Meenai Meenai Panj Dori (1960). He also worked with Meena Kumari in the film Baghi (1956). Wazir Ali's real name was Abdul Hafeez. He was a very tall man, standing 6 feet 4 inches. He married the famous Pakistani actress Zoya in 1966 and had a son, Shahzad, and a daughter, Samina. Wazir Ali retired from the film industry in the late 1970s and the couple moved to Los Angeles, California, U.S.A. in the 1990s. Zoya died in Los Angeles in 2000, and Wazir Ali died there in 2008.

Helen Foster (November 24, 1917 – January 3, 2002) was an American actress. Foster was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. She was the daughter of Helen V. (née Hanley), a singer, and John F. Foster, a lawyer, banker, and businessman. Her family moved to Detroit, Michigan, when she was age three, and then to Los Angeles, California, four years later. She attended St. Mary's Dominican School in Detroit and the Dominican Convent School in San Rafael, California. She studied singing and dramatics at the Detroit Institute of Music and the Arts and at the University of Michigan. In 1936, Foster acted in a production of George Bernard Shaw's You Never Can Tell, which was seen by producer Max Gordon, who was in the audience. Gordon was impressed and offered her a role in the Marx Brothers' film A Night at the Opera (1937). She played the role of Margaret Dumont's daughter in the film. Her other film roles include the college friend in Test Pilot (1938) and the bridesmaid in Topper (1937). Her last role was as Mrs. North in the television series The George Burns and Gracie Allen Show. Foster married actor George Montgomery in 1943. After their divorce, she married again, to actor Don Taylor in 1949. They had three children together and divorced in 1956. Her third marriage was to actor George Nader in 1957. They had one daughter together and were divorced in 1961. Foster died at age 84 from complications of a stroke at the Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital in Los Angeles.

NGC 3175 is a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Antlia. It was discovered in 1886 by German astronomer Hermann Struve. NGC 3175 lies in the zone of avoidance, so it is not easily visible from the Earth's surface, but it can be observed using the Hubble Space Telescope. NGC 3175 is approximately 70 million light-years away from Earth. Like many galaxies, NGC 3175 is moving away from the Earth. Yukio Iketani (池谷 幸雄, born July 31, 1960 in Niigata, Japan) is a Japanese professional wrestler and the first Asian to become a WWE Champion. Iketani was also one of the first inductees into the WWE Hall of Fame. Iketani began his professional wrestling career in Japan in the early 1970s, working for Japan Pro Wrestling Alliance (JWA), the promotion run by his father, Rikidozan. He adopted his father's ring name upon his debut and became known as "Rikki" Iketani (often misspelled as "Ike" or "Ikeki" in the West). Like his father, Iketani was a massive crowd favorite, in part due to his imposing height and build, and came to be known as "The Superboy of Japan". In 1981, Iketani, along with his mother, father, and younger brother, Tomo, relocated to the United States to work for the World Wide Wrestling Federation (WWWF), which would later be renamed WWE. The following year, he defeated WWE Champion Bob Backlund to win the title, becoming the first Asian to hold the championship. He would go on to successfully defend the title against the likes of Backlund, John "Hacksaw" striped, and "Macho Man" Randy Savage, before losing the title to Savage in 1985. After his initial title reign, Iketani returned to Japan to compete for New Japan Pro-Wrestling (NJPW), where he became a one-time IWGP Tag Team Champion and a one-time IWGP Junior Heavyweight Tag Team Champion. In 1989, he returned to WWE for a brief period, competing in the 1989 Royal Rumble and going to a draw in a match for the WWE Championship against "Hacksaw" Jim Duggan before leaving the promotion later that year. Iketani has made occasional appearances for WWE since, including at the 25th Anniversary of WrestleMania in 2009, and was one of the first inductees into the WWE Hall of Fame, in 2013.

57th Utah State Legislature The 57th Utah State Legislature was elected Tuesday, November 4, 2008, and will convene on January 26, 2009, at the Utah State Capitol in Salt Lake City. The Utah State Senate will have 24 Republicans, 8 Democrats and 1 vacancy. The Utah State House of Representatives will have 40 Republicans, 19 Democrats and 1 vacancy. The new makeup of the State Legislature was decided by the 2008 elections, in which incumbents Senator Kevin Van Tassell (R-8) and Representative Meriam Nelson (R-58) were defeated in their bids for re-election. The 2009 Utah State Legislature will be the first to serve under the state's new Governor, Gary Herbert. The new Legislature will be sworn in during an organizational session on January 26, 2009, in the Utah State Capitol in Salt Lake City. 2009 is the 60th year that the Utah State Legislature has met. The first Utah State Legislature met in 1851, but was known as the "General Assembly" until the state constitution was amended in 1896 to change the name to the "Legislature." The Republican Party has controlled both houses of the Utah State Legislature since the 1970s.

Dongas road protest group The Dongas road protest group was a South African opposition political movement that existed from 1984 to 1989, notable for its radical opposition to, and successful resistance against, the apartheid government's Programme of Action. The name "Dongas" was a playful spoonerism on the word "dงos", meaning "idiots" in Portuguese, and was first used as the name of an anti-apartheid street committee in the Western Cape. The first dongas protest march took place on 30 March 1984 in Athlone, Cape Town. The organisation was launched in August 1984 at an underground conference attended by over 30 delegates from various anti-apartheid groups. The conference was held in a flat in Johannesburg, and was organised by the Vaal Civic Association. At the conference, the constitution of the organisation was drafted. The constitution called for the organisation to have a "non-racial and non-sexist" membership, and to work towards the creation of a "non-racial and non-sexist society". The Dongas movement was heavily influenced by the ideas of the Africanists, a group of African National Congress (ANC) members who had broken away from the ANC in the early 1970s, and who believed that the ANC should focus on the liberation of black Africans, rather than all people of colour. The Dongas movement therefore drew many members from the ANC, and from organisations that had been formed by the ANC's internal opponents, such as the Black People's Convention (BPC), the South African Students' Organization (SASO), and the Black Workers' Project (BWP). The Dongas movement was also influenced by the ideas of the PAC's Amandla Cultural Group, which had been formed by PAC members who were critical of the PAC's leadership. The Dongas movement was opposed to the idea of a negotiated settlement with the apartheid government, and instead called for a revolutionary struggle, in which the black working class would lead the way. The Dongas movement was also critical of the ANC's policy of non-racialism, and called for a revolutionary movement that was exclusively black. The movement's constitution stated that "the national democratic revolution can only succeed if it is a revolution of the majority, the black working class, and not a revolution of all the people of South Africa". The Dongas movement was active in a number of anti-apartheid campaigns, including the Black Wednesday campaign, in which the apartheid government's introduction of the Tricameral Parliament was opposed, and the "Gatvol" campaign, in which the government's attempt to force coloured people to carry Passes was opposed. The Dongas movement also participated in a number of protest marches, including the 1984 march in Athlone, the 1985 march in Soweto, and the 1989 march in Cape Town. The Dongas movement was active in the Vaal Triangle, Johannesburg, and the Western Cape, and had a number of prominent members, including Steve Biko, the leader of the South African Students' Organization (SASO), and the PAC's Amandla Cultural Group. The movement also had a number of prominent white members, including the PAC's Amandla Cultural Group, and the Black Workers' Project (BWP). The Dongas movement was banned in 1989, and a number of its members were arrested. The movement's leaders, however, continued to operate underground, and the movement was able to maintain a presence in the Vaal Triangle, Johannesburg, and the Western Cape. The Dongas movement was one of the most influential anti-apartheid movements in South Africa, and its radical opposition to the apartheid government's Programme of Action, and its successful resistance against the programme, helped to bring about the end of apartheid.

Institute for East European Studies The Institute for East European Studies (German: Institut für Osteuropäische Geschichte) is a research institute at the Faculty of Philosophy of the Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg in Halle, Germany. It was founded in 1964 as the Institute for Soviet and East European Studies. The institute's director is Heribert Adam. The Institute for East European Studies specializes in the history and cultures of the countries of Eastern Europe, with a particular focus on the Russian Federation, Ukraine, and Belarus. The institute is home to the Germany-Russia Forum, which is supported by the German Foreign Office. The institute's research library has more than 240,000 volumes and is one of the largest libraries of its kind in Germany. The institute also has a large collection of films and documentaries about Russia and Eastern Europe. In addition to offering courses in Russian and East European history at the undergraduate and graduate levels, the Institute for East European Studies offers a number of courses in Russian and East European culture, society, and politics. The institute also offers a number of courses in Russian and East European languages. The Institute for East European Studies is a member of the Association for Slavic, East European, and Eurasian Studies, and the European Association for Russian and East European Studies. The institute has been home to a number of notable scholars, including Alexander von Plato, Peter Grieder, and Martin Mittenzwei. The institute's current faculty includes Heribert Adam, Werner Bachmann, Thomas Berec, Michael Driesen, Birgit Embrechting, Hendrick Hasenec, Panayiotis Kounnas, and Vasiliy Fedotov.

Buckrose Buckrose is a village and civil parish in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England. It is situated on the A163 road, and lies approximately 3 kilometres (2 mi) west of the market town of Pocklington. According to the 2011 UK Census, Buckrose parish had a population of 3,068, an increase on the 2001 UK Census figure of 2,818. The village is home to a primary school, a secondary school and a village hall. The name "Buckrose" is derived from the Old English "Bucgros" meaning "a farmstead where bucks or does (deer) are reared". The civil parish of Buckrose includes the village of Barmby on the Marsh. The parish also includes the deserted medieval village (DMV) of Gircy. Gircy, or Gyrcy, is listed in the Domesday Book as a settlement of three households, and in the 12th and 13th centuries it had a small medieval village, of which no trace remains. There are several medieval period earthworks in the area, and a moated site, suggesting the possible location of the medieval village. The moated site is a protected Scheduled Ancient Monument, and is designated as a Grade II listed building. Buckrose was formerly a civil parish in the district ofHumberside. In 1974 it was transferred from the county of Humberside to the new county of North Yorkshire. In 1996 it was transferred from the district of North Yorkshire to the East Riding of Yorkshire. In 2005 it became part of the new East Riding of Yorkshire Council unitary authority.

John Wallace Scott (June 15, 1932 – September 13, 2014) was an American politician and businessman who served as the 52nd governor of the state of South Dakota from 1987 to 1991. Scott was born in Shanghai, Republic of China, to American parents, John Junior and Florence (Wallace) Scott. His family moved to the United States in 1941, and he grew up in Maryland and graduated from Baltimore's City College high school in 1950. He attended college at the University of Maryland, College Park, and graduated in 1954 with a degree in business. He served in the United States Army from 1954 to 1957, reaching the rank of captain. After his time in the Army, Scott returned to Maryland and entered the insurance business, eventually becoming a partner in the firm of Grant, Traditional, & Scott, Inc. In 1970, he married the former Barbara Jean Verkys of Baltimore, and the couple had three sons. In 1978, Scott and his family moved to Rapid City, South Dakota, and he began a successful campaign for the Republican nomination for governor in 1986, defeating attorney General Larry Long in the primary and businessman Harlan Jones in the general election. Scott was sworn in as governor on January 1, 1987, and during his four years as governor, the state's economy grew, with an increase in the number of jobs and a decrease in the unemployment rate. However, the state's population continued to decline, and the state's agriculture and mining industries struggled. Scott's term as governor was not without controversy. In 1988, the state's tourism director, Al Ybarra, was fired for allegedly making a sexually explicit remark to a female employee. Ybarra later sued the state, claiming wrongful termination, and the case was eventually settled out of court. In addition, Scott's relationship with the state's Native American population was strained. In 1989, the state's official song, "Hail, South Dakota!" was criticized for its lyrics, which included the phrase "when we hit the trail to the West/The Indians gave us hell". Scott initially resisted calls to change the song, but eventually agreed to do so, and the state legislature approved a new version of the song in 1990. In 1990, Scott was defeated in his bid for re-election by Democratic state senator George S. Mickelson. After his term as governor ended in 1991, Scott returned to his insurance business and also became involved in several business and charitable organizations. Scott died in 2014 at a hospital in Rapid City, South Dakota, at the age of 82.

Fred Alan Wolf (born November 14, 1934) is an American theoretical physicist, writer, and lecturer, best known for his popularization of quantum mechanics, and his books on the subject, including the 1984 book Taking the Quantum Leap. He is a retired senior scientist at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Wolf received his B.S. in physics from the University of Michigan in 1956, and his Ph.D. in theoretical solid state physics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1961. He worked in the research and development division of General Electric from 1961 to 1964, and then as a faculty member at the University of California, San Diego from 1964 to 1970. In 1970, he joined the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory as a staff scientist, and became a senior scientist in the Materials Science Division in 1990. He retired in 2000, but continues to lecture on the subject of quantum mechanics. Wolf has written numerous popular books on quantum mechanics, including The Quantum World (1975), Space-Time and Beyond (1982), Taking the Quantum Leap (1984), and The New Quark and Lepton (2011). He has also written a number of books on the relationship between science and society, including The Soul of Science: A New Look at the Place of Science in the Soul (2000), and The Physics of Social Interactions (2009).
