Track and field, also known as athletics, is a group of sports that involves a variety of competitions and activities covering a wide range of athletic abilities, most of which are governed by the International Olympic Committee through the World Athletic body. The word "athletics" can be used to describe most of the above-mentioned activities, but "track and field" and "athletics" are generally used to describe most of the events in the sport. Track and field is conducted on a field of play called a stadium, which has a track forming a loop around the field. The track is typically divided into two lanes, each of which one or more athletes may use to run, walk, or skip. The track is usually made of a synthetic material, although tracks made of other materials, such as concrete, are also used. The two primary sports in track and field are track racing and field events. Track races are competitions where athletes race each other in a specified lane to the finish line. Field events are competitions where athletes attempt to mark a target within a designated area of the field of play. Track and field competitions can be organized as a meet, which is a group of competitions held on a single day, or as a championship, which is a group of competitions held over a period of days or weeks. Meets and championships may be organized at the local, regional, state, national, or international levels. In addition to track races and field events, track and field competitions may also include several other types of events. These events include, but are not limited to, the following: * Sprints: A sprint is a short race over a set distance, usually 100, 200, or 400 meters. * Middle distance: Middle-distance races are races over a set distance, usually 400, 800, or 1,500 meters. * Hurdles: Hurdle races are races over a set distance, usually 110 or 400 meters, in which the athlete must jump over a series of obstacles. * Long jump: The long jump is an event where athletes run and jump as far as they can from a standing position. * Pole vault: The pole vault is an event where athletes use a pole to vault over a bar. * Shot put: The shot put is an event where athletes throw a heavy ball as far as they can. * Discus throw: The discus throw is an event where athletes throw a disc as far as they can. * Hammer throw: The hammer throw is an event where athletes throw a hammer as far as they can. Track and field is one of the oldest organized sports in history, with records of competitions dating back to the ancient Olympic Games in Greece. The modern sport of track and field was founded at the first Olympic Games in 1896 in Athens, Greece. Since then, the sport has been one of the main events at the Olympic Games, the World Championships, and many other international competitions.

Country Town is an Australian television drama series which ran from 11 July 1984 until 3 July 1986. There are 88 hour-long episodes. Alexis-François Rio (10 October 1682 – 18 November 1747) was a French sculptor and painter, who spent most of his life in Rome, where he was a founding member of the Academy of Saint Luke. Alexis-François Rio was born in Uzès, in the Cévennes, the son of a sculptor. He studied under his father and then under his uncle, the sculptor Pierre Le Mercier, in Paris, and then in Rome under Carlo Maratta and Giuseppe Bartolomeo Chiari, who had just completed the sculptures on the fountain of the Four Rivers in the Piazza Navona. In 1704 he completed the marble bas-relief of The Annunciation for the Cathedral of Notre-Dame in Avignon. In 1705 he returned to Rome, where he was one of the founding members of the Academy of Saint Luke. In 1708 he was commissioned by the Duke of Parma to execute a series of marble reliefs for the chapel of the cathedral of Parma, works that were never delivered because the duke died suddenly. In 1716 he completed the statue of St. Anne for the parish church of his native Uzès, a work commissioned by his confessor, the Abbé du Chaffaut, prior to the latter's appointment as bishop of Uzès. In 1737 he completed a statue of St. Peter for the cathedral of Albi. His works include several easel paintings, mainly oil on canvas, including a Self-Portrait (1703, private collection), a View of Rome (1704, private collection), a Still Life with Fruit and Flowers (1706, private collection), and The Assumption of Mary (1710, private collection).

Elisabeth Tichy-Fisslberger (born 9 October 1948) is an Austrian politician who served as Minister of Justice from January 2016 to December 2017. She was the first woman to hold the office. She was a member of the National Council from 1994 to 2017, representing Upper Austria (Gemeindeamt Gmunden). She was a member of the Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ) from 1993 to 2017, and was the party's deputy leader from 2006 to 2016. She left the FPÖ in 2017, and joined the newly formed FPÖ Plus in 2020. She worked as a lawyer in Gmunden from 1976 to 1994, and was a member of the Gemeindeamt Gmunden from 1980 to 1994. She joined the FPÖ in 1993, and was elected to the National Council in the 1994 elections. She was the FPÖ's candidate for Mayor of Gmunden in 2002, but was defeated by the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ). Tichy-Fisslberger became the FPÖ's deputy leader in 2006, and was re-elected to the National Council in the 2006 elections. She was the FPÖ's lead candidate in the 2008 elections, and was re-elected to the National Council. She also led the FPÖ's campaign in the 2009 European elections. She was re-elected to the National Council in the 2013 elections. In January 2016, Tichy-Fisslberger was appointed Minister of Justice in the government of Chancellor Norbert Hofer. She was the first woman to hold the office. She was re-appointed as Minister of Justice in the government of Chancellor Christian Kern in December 2016. She left the FPÖ in 2017, and joined the newly formed FPÖ Plus in 2020.

Robert Gillespie (1637–1715) was an Irish Protestant minister and scholar, a prolific writer and a versatile, erudite, and innovative theologian. Gillespie was born in Dublin, the son of an Irish Protestant minister, and was educated at Trinity College Dublin (BA, 1661; MA, 1664), where he was a fellow from 1664 to 1674. He was ordained a minister in the Church of Ireland in 1667 and two years later became the incumbent of the parish of Newtownbarry in County Cork, where he ministered for the next forty years. Gillespie was married to Mary, the daughter of the Rev. Arthur Ussher, the Church of Ireland minister for the nearby parish of Carrigaline. They had four sons and three daughters, including the Rev. Arthur Gillespie (1676–1766), the Church of Ireland minister for the parish of Bandon and a noted scholar. In 1699, the Rev. John Stearne, the Church of Ireland minister for the parish of Midleton, was accused of heresy and suspended from his ministry. His parishioners, who were in a state of unrest because of a disputed election to the Irish House of Commons, organised a protest against his suspension. They invited Gillespie, who was widely recognised as a spokesman for the moderate, intellectual tendency in the Church of Ireland, to preach to them. He agreed and, in the resulting sermon, took the line that while the Church of Ireland was not a perfect church it was, nevertheless, a true church. The sermon was widely circulated and led to increased support for the moderate line, which was favoured by the established church's bishops, in preference to the more radical, Nonconformist tendency. Gillespie was a member of the Dublin Society, a group of Dublin-based scholars who met regularly to discuss intellectual and cultural topics. The members included the economist and lawyer William Bruce (1680–1730), the historians James Ware (1565–1666) and his son Sir James Ware (1682–1769), the archaeologist and physician William Batt (c.1620–1704), the classical scholar and Church of Ireland minister Charles Lucas (1694–1747), the statistician Edward Hopkins (1644–1741), the chemist Robert Boyle (1627–1704), and the politician and writer Edmund Curll (c.1675–1747). The Dublin Society's members were united by their intellectual curiosity and their desire for knowledge for its own sake, and they pursued a wide range of interests, including history, geography, the natural sciences, medicine, agriculture, and the arts. Alexander Hood (1888–1961) was a British Army officer who served in both the First and Second World Wars. Albert Schultens (1694–1786) was a Dutch scholar and poet, best known for his Latin hexameter poetry. Schultens was born in Groningen. He also sought to express his patriotism through his poetry, and to use his poetry to promote the cause of the Dutch people. Schultens died in Groningen in 1786.

Elizabeth Miller (academic) Elizabeth Miller is an academic and author who specializes in the history of art and architecture of the Early Modern period, with a particular focus on the Italian Renaissance. She is currently the Paul A. Clement Professor of Art History at the University of Texas at Austin. Miller received her Bachelor of Arts degree in Art History and French from the University of Toronto in 1984, and her Master of Arts and Doctor of Philosophy degrees in Art History from the University of California, Berkeley in 1986 and 1990, respectively. Her doctoral dissertation, "The Career of a Renaissance Banker: The Chigi Family and the Art Market in Early Modern Rome," was awarded the William E. Suida Prize for excellence in art history. In 1990, Miller joined the faculty of the University of Texas at Austin as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Art and Art History. She was promoted to Associate Professor in 1997 and to Professor in 2004. In 2014, she was named the Paul A. Clement Professor of Art History. Miller has written extensively on the art and architecture of the Italian Renaissance, with a particular focus on the works of Raphael and his workshop. Her publications include "The Art of the Assumption: The Frescoes of San Severino in Piacenza" (1995), "The Renaissance in Rome" (with T. A. Price, 2002), "Raphael and the Madonna of Frascati" (2008), and "The Piochi Chapel: A Renaissance Intersection" (with David G. Uzzardi, 2016). Miller has received numerous awards and fellowships for her research and teaching, including a William E. Suida Fellowship from the Warburg Institute in London (2005–06), a Charles A. Dana Fellowship from the Council of the American Overseas Research Centers in Rome (2009–10), a National Endowment for the Humanities Research Fellowship (2010–11), and a Rome Prize from the American Academy in Rome (2017–18). Miller has also served as a curator and consultant for a number of exhibitions and projects related to the art and architecture of the Renaissance, including "The Renaissance in Rome" (Palazzo Venezia, Rome, 2002), "The Piochi Chapel" (Museo Nazionale del Cinema, Italy, 2014), "The Americas on Paper" (UT Austin, 2016), and "The House of Ovid: A New Look at Renaissance Art" (UT Austin, 2017). In addition to her academic work, Miller is also the author of a popular book on the life and times of Raphael, entitled "The Life and Times of Raphael" (2017).

Preprophase is the period prior to prophase in the meiotic cell cycle. The cells are in G1 phase. Meiosis-specific DNA replication (i.e., meiosis I) has not yet begun. The homologous chromosomes are not yet close to each other and are still in their allocated areas of the cell nucleus. In meiosis, the homologous chromosomes ( chromosomes that carry genes for the same traits) line up in rows. Each row contains two homologous chromosomes, one from each parent. The homologous chromosomes swap genetic information between each other. Meiosis is necessary to create genetic diversity. In mitosis, the homologous chromosomes line up in rows as well. However, in mitosis, the homologous chromosomes do not swap genetic information. Instead, the same genetic information is copied and the cell divides into two identical daughter cells. Mitosis is necessary for growth and for the repair of damaged tissue. Preprophase is the first stage of meiosis. In this stage, the homologous chromosomes are not close to each other and are not swapped. Meiosis begins when the homologous chromosomes are pulled close together.

Kac's work often addresses the themes of life and death, and the relationship between the body and technology. He has created a number of performance art pieces in which he uses his own body as a canvas, incorporating technology such as robotics, genetics, and virtual reality. Kac's work has been exhibited internationally, and is in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art, the Guggenheim Museum, and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, among others. Kac has been the recipient of numerous awards and fellowships, including a John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Fellowship (2003), a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship (1994), and a New York Foundation for the Arts Fellowship (1997). Kac is the author of several books, including The Body and the Network (2014), and he has been a contributor to numerous publications and journals. Kac's work has been the subject of a number of retrospective exhibitions, including "Eduardo Kac: A Light in Dark Times" at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (2018), and "Eduardo Kac: bioartography" at the Museu blow-up doll in Praga, Prague (2018). Kac lives and works in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Economy of Nepal The economy of Nepal is developing and agriculture remains the mainstay of the economy. The World Bank classifies Nepal as a lower-middle-income country. In the last decade, the economy has grown by an average of 6% each year, with a stable growth rate in the last few years. The country's foreign exchange reserves are very low and its external debt has grown in the last few years. The agricultural sector employs about 70% of the population and contributes 20.9% to the GDP. The primary sector of the economy is based on agriculture and its sub-sectors. The major agricultural products are rice, wheat, corn, pulses, potatoes, vegetables, milk, and water. In the fiscal year 2019/20, the country produced 3.6 million tons of rice, 1.2 million tons of wheat, and 1.3 million tons of corn. The manufacturing sector employs 6% of the population and contributes 12.1% to the GDP. The secondary sector of the economy is based on manufacturing and its sub-sectors. The major manufacturing industries are food processing, chemical, construction, iron and steel, and small industries. In the fiscal year 2019/20, the country manufactured 1.3 million tons of sugar, 200,000 tons of milk powder, and 150,000 tons of cooking oil. The service sector employs 24% of the population and contributes 61.2% to the GDP. The tertiary sector of the economy is based on the service and its sub-sectors. The major service industries are tourism, hotels, restaurants, banking, insurance, education, health, and transport. In the fiscal year 2019/20, the country received 1.17 million tourists. The economy of Nepal is growing at a rate of 6% every year.

Chandragupt Institute of Management, the first management institute in the state of Madhya Pradesh, was established in the year 1996 by the Chandrawati Barrage Committee with the objective of providing management education and training to the budding managers and executives of the state. The institute is affiliated with the All India Management Association (AIMA) and the Madhya Pradesh Society of Commerce and Economics (MPSCE). The institute offers a wide range of academic programs at the undergraduate and the postgraduate levels, as well as doctoral and executive programs. The institute has been awarded the status of a center of excellence in the field of management education by the Madhya Pradesh government. The institute has a strong placement cell that works towards providing the best job opportunities to the students. The cell works in close coordination with the industry and provides placement assistance to the students. The institute has a state-of-the-art infrastructure that includes well-equipped classrooms, computer labs, library, and other facilities. The institute also has a strong network of industry partnerships and collaborations that help in providing the students with the latest industry trends and practices. The institute has a dedicated research cell that promotes research and development activities among the students and the faculty. The cell also organizes various research conferences and seminars to provide a platform for the exchange of ideas and knowledge. The institute is committed to providing quality education and training to its students and has a strong academic advisory board that consists of industry experts and academicians who provide valuable guidance and support to the institute.

Cranbrook (hymn tune) "Cranbrook" is a traditional hymn tune composed around 1870 by John Stainer. It is usually set to the lyrics of "God moves in a mysterious way", written in the 18th century by the Rev. William Cowper, but is also used with other lyrics, for example, "Now thank we all our God" by Martin Luther. The tune is named after the Cranbrook Church of England Primary School in Kent, where it was played by the school's band in the late 19th century. It was first published in the early 20th century in Hymns Ancient & Modern, and is now (as of 2013) in the public domain. Cranbrook is a common choice for church organists in the UK and other countries with a strong Anglican tradition, such as Australia, Canada, and South Africa. It can also be played on an organ or piano with a verse or two of the hymn "Now thank we all our God", with which it has a complementary rhythm, and at the same tempo. A version of the tune with alternative lyrics, "Light of the World", was written by the Rev. Frederick William Faber and published in his collection of hymns, Poems on the Name of Jesus Christ, in 1857. The tune is in common time. It has a half-note (minim) pulse, and consists of two sections, each consisting of two phrases of four bars, with the first phrase of each section a repeat of the second phrase. The first phrase of each section consists of two minims (half-notes) and two quarter-notes (crotchets), the second phrase consists of three minims and a crotchet. The first section is followed by a two-bar sequence consisting of a minim and a crotchet in the first bar, and a minim and two quarter-notes in the second. The tune then returns to the first section, and so on. The first three notes of the tune, given in the key of C major, are C, D, E, the first two of which are the tonic, and the third a note which has already appeared in the key signature. This E is a "chromatic neighbour note" to the tonic, and gives a gentle hint of colouration to the otherwise diatonic (seven-note) scale. This initial figure is then repeated, transposed up a perfect fifth, and the process is repeated a further two times, giving a symmetrical structure of two, three, two, three, two bars.

Symplegades The Symplegades or Symplectic Islands (Greek: Συμπλεγές or Συμπλεγέηνσι) are two small islands in the Gulf of Xanthi, northern Greece, the easternmost part of the Thracian Sea. They are situated near the coast of Thrace, in the region of East Macedonia and Thrace. These two islands are the largest of three groups of islands in the Gulf of Xanthi. The other islands are the IXAPEA Islands and the Islets of Chrysi. The islands are covered with forests and have a total area of 2.07 km2. The distance between the two islands is 700 m. The bigger one is called Avram and the smaller one is Planitis. There are many legends associated with the Symplegades. According to Greek mythology, the Symplegades were two immortal eagles, who lived on the two islands. They were said to be always fighting each other with their beaks. When they fought, they would clash together with such force that they would create loud noises, like clashing metal. The word "symplegades" is derived from the Greek words "σύμπληγος" (symplēgos), meaning "clashed together", and "σύμφωνος" (symphōnos), meaning "loud noise". The Symplegades were also said to be very rich in gold and other treasures, which were guarded by the two eagles. Many tried to retrieve the treasures, but were unsuccessful because of the fighting eagles. Eventually, the heroes Jason and the Argonauts were able to retrieve the treasures with the help of the goddess Athena. The Symplegades are also associated with the myth of the Amazon women. It was said that the Amazon women would ride on the backs of the eagles and use them to fly to the islands to retrieve the treasures. The Symplegades are located in a strategic position in the Gulf of Xanthi, which is a major shipping route. They are also a popular tourist destination.

The 1909 Wabash River earthquake, also known as the ".IX" earthquake, was a 5.4 magnitude earthquake that occurred at 9:32 pm CST on April 18, 1909. The earthquake's epicentre was near the Wabash River, 2 miles (3.2 km) west of the town of Attica, Indiana, and its depth of focus was 5 miles (8.0 km) below the surface. The quake was felt throughout the Midwest and as far east as Washington, D.C. and New York City. The shaking caused widespread damage, with the cost of the damage done to the Wabash region alone estimated at US$2 million ($48 million in 2009 dollars) and the cost of the damage done to the city of Indianapolis estimated at US$1 million ($24 million in 2009 dollars). The earthquake could be felt as far away as Canada. The perceived location of the earthquake, in the Wabash River, was incorrect. The actual location of the earthquake was in the SW suburbs of Indianapolis. The reason for the discrepancy was that the intensity of the earthquake was much stronger in the Indianapolis area than it was in the Wabash River area. The intensity was measured at VII on the Mercalli scale in the Indianapolis area.

Mar Thoma Syrian Church in Malaysia is a church in Malaysia belonging to the Malankara Mar Thoma Syrian Church of India, a member of the National Council of Churches, India. The church was established in 1952 by a group of Indians who came to Malaysia to work in the British Army. The first prayer was conducted in a house in Kuala Lumpur. The church was later registered with the Malaysian government on 8 August 1954. The church has more than 20,000 members and 100 branches throughout Malaysia. The branches are under the direct control of the Malaysian Region which is further divided into six areas: Kuala Lumpur, Klang Valley, Perak, Penang, Johor and Sabah. The church's main activities include worship services, biblical classes, prayer meetings and charity works. The church has set up a charitable arm known as the Mar Thoma Charity and Welfare Society to conduct its charity works. Among the society's projects are a halfway house for drug addicts, a home for the elderly, a special school for children with learning disabilities and a mobile clinic. The church's main worship centre is the Mar Thoma Church Centre in Kuala Lumpur, which was built in 1982. The centre has a 1,000-seat auditorium and can accommodate up to 4,000 people at one time. Every year, the church celebrates its annual convention known as the Mar Thoma Convention. The 2013 convention was held at the Mar Thoma Church Centre from 1 to 3 November 2013 with the theme "Jesus Is Our Healer". The church is headed by an elected working committee, which comprises of the area secretaries and the church secretary. The church also has a spiritual head, who is the senior most priest in the church. The current spiritual head is Rev. Dr. Thankachan Mor Apremkis (who is also the Metropolitan of the church) and the general secretary is Fr. Dr. Oommen George.

The track is Houser's lowest-peaking single to date, reaching number 46 on the Billboard Country Airplay chart. The song was written by Jaren Johnston, James T. The representation theory of the symmetric group The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by permuting the coordinates. This gives rise to a representation $S_n \to \text{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$. Since $\text{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ is a group, this representation is linear. We can regard this representation as a restriction of the representation $S_n \to \text{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$. For any $n \geq 1$, this representation is a group homomorphism, that is, it is injective. This follows from the fact that $\text{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is a group. This representation is also surjective. That is, for any $A \in \text{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, there exists $\sigma \in S_n$ such that $A = \sigma \in S_n \to \text{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$. Consider the set $\mathcal{A}$ of all upper triangular matrices with diagonal $1$. This is clearly a subset of $\text{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$. Val Caniparoli (born February 7, 1956) is an American dancer, choreographer, and artistic director. Caniparoli was born and raised in the San Francisco Bay Area. He trained at the San Francisco Ballet School and at age 17 joined the Oakland Ballet Company, where he was able to create his own choreography. In 1976, he joined the Joffrey Ballet as a dancer and choreographer, and then the New York City Ballet in 1978, where he became a principal dancer and choreographer the following year. In 1985, Caniparoli choreographed his first ballet for the San Francisco Ballet, Raymonda (or La Fille du Doge), a co-production with the Kirov Ballet of Saint Petersburg, Russia. The production received critical acclaim and was performed by the Kirov in Russia the following year. Caniparoli became a resident choreographer at the San Francisco Ballet in 1986, and in 1989 he created his first full-length ballet for the company, Three distortions, which is still in the company's repertory. With the San Francisco Ballet, he has created over 100 ballets, including Oh, Inverted World, a ballet commissioned by the New York City Ballet for their 50th anniversary in 2008. Caniparoli has choreographed for numerous companies in the United States and around the world, including the Kirov Ballet, the Royal Danish Ballet, the Hong Kong Ballet, and the Dance Theatre of Hong Kong. In the United States, he has created for the New York City Ballet, the Joffrey Ballet, the San Francisco Ballet, the Oakland Ballet Company, and the Los Angeles Dance Project, among others. In 2002, Caniparoli became the artistic director of the San Francisco Ballet's Contemporary Dance Program. In 2008, he became the director of the ballet's Dance School. He has also been a teacher and choreographer at the San Francisco Ballet's summer dance program.

The Spartans also defeated #3 seed Utah State in the 2010 WAC Tournament before losing to #1 seed Nevada in the semifinals. The Spartans earned a berth in the 2010 CollegeInsider.com Tournament, their first postseason appearance since 1996, but lost in the first round to San Francisco.

Gender Equality and Family Development Select Committee (Malay: Jawatankuasa Pilihan Khas Keselamatan Rumahtangga dan Kemakmuran Gender), previously known as the Housewives and Family Welfare Select Committee (Malay: Jawatankuasa Pilihan Khas Keluarga Malaysia), is one of the 15 select committees of the Malaysian House of Representatives. It is the first select committee to be established in the House of Representatives, having been created on 4 November 2018. The committee is appointed by the House of Representatives in accordance with Article 95 of the Federal Constitution. The objective of the committee is to ensure that women's rights and gender equality are protected and that the family institution is strengthened. The committee is also empowered to consider other issues relating to the family institution, including those involving the social, economic, and security of the family. The Gender Equality and Family Development Select Committee is a result of the expansion of the scope of the Housewives and Family Welfare Select Committee, which was established on 17 October 2017, to include gender equality issues. The expansion of the committee's scope was proposed by the Women's Development and Gender Equity Committee (Malay: Jawatankuasa Pembangunan Wanita dan Kepemimpinan Gender), a sub-committee of the Housewives and Family Welfare Select Committee, and was approved by the House of Representatives on 2 November 2018. The Gender Equality and Family Development Select Committee is chaired by Mahfuz Omar, who is also the chairman of the Women's Development and Gender Equity Committee. The committee's membership comprises representatives from the government, the opposition, and the independent bloc.

Amit Jogi (born 30 June 1984) is an Indian actor, producer, television personality, and model, who has appeared in Indian television shows and Bollywood films. Jogi was born in 1984 in Jaipur, Rajasthan. He was a state-level athlete and volleyball player. He did his schooling from St. Anselm's Senior Secondary School, Ajmer. He did his bachelor's degree from Bhagat College, University of Delhi. He also attended the Indian Institute of Mass Communication, New Delhi for a year. Jogi began his career as a model, and has been a part of the print and television advertising campaigns for numerous brands and services, including Coca-Cola, Sprite, Microsoft, Samsung, LG, Hyundai, Ford, ICICI, and Idea. Jogi made his television debut in 2005 with the Sony TV show India's Best Cinestars Ki Khoj, and appeared as a host in the 2008 dance show Boogie Woogie. He was a participant in the 2010 dance show Jhalak Dikhhla Jaa, and was voted the "Most Flexible Man" in the country by a poll in The Times of India in 2010. He was a participant in the 2011 dance show Zara Nachke Dikha, and was a part of the judging panel for the 2015 dance show Dance India Dance Li'l Masters. Jogi has also appeared in the Indian reality show Bigg Boss, having been a contestant in the first season in 2006, and the fifth season in 2013, as a senior contestant. In 2018, he appeared as a senior contestant in the Colors TV show Bigg Boss 12. Jogi made his film debut in 2010 with the romantic comedy movie Chal Pichchur Banate Hain, and appeared in the 2011 movie Thank You. He also appeared in the 2014 movie Bobby Jasoos. In 2015, Jogi launched his own film production company, Jogi Film Productions, and produced the 2016 movie Santa Banta Pvt Ltd. In 2017, he produced the movie Tera Intezaar. In 2013, Jogi married his longtime girlfriend Payal also known as "Piya" and together they have a daughter, named Aanya.

Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers A Physical Sciences-Oncology Center (PS-OC) is a research center that brings together physicists, engineers, and oncologists to integrate physical science (e.g., physics, chemistry, engineering) approaches with oncological research to better understand, and ultimately to control, cancer. There are currently nine Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers in the United States. The Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers program was initiated in 2009 by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) with the goal of bringing innovative technologies and unique perspectives of physical scientists to the fight against cancer while training the next generation of physical science researchers. Each PS-OC is a partnership between a physical sciences institution and an oncology institution. The physical sciences institution may be a university, college, or research institution with faculty and facilities dedicated to the study of physics, chemistry, or engineering. The oncology institution may be a university, college, hospital, or research institution with expertise and facilities in basic, translational, and/or clinical cancer research. The Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers program is built on the premise that the physical sciences have unique and powerful methods for attacking problems that are difficult, yet critical, to the oncologist. The physical sciences include many subdisciplines that make use of state-of-the-art experimental, computational, and theoretical methods to achieve a deep understanding of physical systems. The methods and perspectives of the physical sciences can be applied to many important problems in oncology that are not easily addressed by traditional means. The Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers program supports research projects that address important problems in cancer research. Each project consists of a team of investigators from the physical sciences and oncology institutions in the PS-OC. The teams are led by a principal investigator from each institution. The projects are intended to be highly interactive and multidisciplinary, with investigators contributing their unique expertise and perspective to the project. Projects are expected to have a strong potential for technological innovation with potential impact on cancer biology or clinical oncology. In addition to supporting research, the Physical Sciences-Oncology Centers program supports the training of predoctoral and postdoctoral trainees in the physical sciences and oncologic sciences. The goal of the training program is to prepare the next generation of physical and oncologic scientists to work together to solve the most challenging problems in cancer research.

The Compukit UK101 (formerly Z80 Computer Corporation UK101) is a Z80-based microcomputer that was being developed in the UK in the mid-1980s, but was never completed or marketed. It is notable for being one of the first microcomputers to feature a Z80 processor, and also for its open architecture, expandability, and use of the CP/M-80 operating system. The UK101 was designed to be an "engineering" microcomputer, to be used by engineers, scientists, and technicians for tasks such as instrument control, data acquisition, and automation. It was to be fully expandable, with an open architecture, and with a wide range of modular expansion cards. The basic system was to consist of a motherboard that could be expanded with up to two Z80 processor cards and one CP/M-80 card. The UK101 was developed by the Z80 Computer Corporation, a UK-based company that was formed in 1983 to develop the UK101 and other Z80-based microcomputers. In 1985, the company was acquired by the Compukit Corporation, which was formed in the US for the purpose of developing, manufacturing, and marketing the UK101 and other Z80-based microcomputers. The Compukit Corporation changed the name of the UK101 to the Compukit UK101. The UK101 was never completed or marketed. The Compukit Corporation went out of business in 1987.

Friedrich Horschelt (11 February 1908 – 30 May 2001) was a German dancer and choreographer. Horschelt was born in Magdeburg, the son of a civil servant, and spent his early childhood in stitches. In 1924 he began his dance training at the Magdeburg Ballet School, and in 1925 he continued his studies at the Charlottenburg Ballet School in Berlin. In 1927 he was engaged by the Berlin State Opera as a member of the corps de ballet, and in 1929 he was promoted to soloist. He soon became the leading dancer in the company, and his partners included the great prima ballerinas of the day, such as Margot Fonteyn, ballerina assoluta of the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, and the Italian ballerina Carla Fracci. He was also a much-sought-after partner for the stars of the Metropolitan Opera in New York City. In 1938, Horschelt was invited to become ballet director of the German Opera in Prague, which was then under the influence of the Nazi regime. He accepted, and became the artistic director of the company. In this capacity, he could, in the early years of the war, secure the release of many of his Jewish colleagues from the concentration camps, as he was personally acquainted with the SS officer in charge of the Prague Gestapo. However, in the last years of the war, his influence waned, and he was even briefly imprisoned by the Gestapo. After the war, Horschelt was invited to become ballet director of the opera in Took in 1948, and in the same year he was engaged as a ballet teacher at the Dance Academy in Stockholm. In 1949 he settled in Sweden, and in 1950 he was made artistic director of the Royal Swedish Ballet in Stockholm, a position he held until his retirement in 1973. In 1952 he was also made director of the Dance Academy in Stockholm. Horschelt was married to the Swedish dancer and choreographer Inga-Lill Horschelt (née af Håkansson; 1914–1999).

Rheinmetall MG 60 The MG 60 is a general-purpose machine gun of German design, firing the 7.62×51mm NATO rifle cartridge. It was developed in the early 1960s by German weapons manufacturer Rheinmetall to replace the aging MG 42 machine gun. The MG 60 was the standard machine gun of the West German army from the late 1960s until the early 1990s. The MG 60 is a gas-operated, belt-fed selective-fire machine gun with a NATO-standard 7.62×51mm NATO cartridge. It is equipped with a quick-change barrel and an integrated, folding bipod. The bipod can be mounted on the left or right side. The design allows the user to dismount the bipod and the buttstock and to mount the MG 60 on a tripod. The machine gun also has a carrying handle that can be mounted on either side. A unique feature of the MG 60 is its "built-in" carry handle, which can be folded forward to serve as a cheekpiece or forward grip. The carrying handle also has a button that can be depressed to allow the handle to be rotated into a vertical position to serve as a buttstock. The firing rate is 650 rounds per minute, but the practical rate of fire is much lower. The belt of ammunition is inserted from either the left or right side. The magazine has a maximum capacity of 250 rounds. The MG 60 was designed for rapid fire in a single-shot or two-shot mode (the second shot being fired by the machine gun after a short delay once the first shot has been fired). The MG 60 is equipped with a non-adjustable iron sight and an optical sight. Ammunition is fed from a belt with a maximum of 250 rounds. The belt is fed from either the left or right side. The magazine is designed for the NATO-standard 7.62×51mm cartridge and can also be used for other calibers. The machine gun can be dismounted from its bipod and mounted on a tripod. The MG 60 was developed in the early 1960s by the German weapons manufacturer Rheinmetall to replace the aging MG 42 machine gun. The MG 60 was the standard machine gun of the West German army from the late 1960s until the early 1990s. The MG 60 was replaced in German service by the MG 95, which is a more modern design. The MG 60 was also used by the Israeli army during the 1967 Six-Day War. In the 1980s, the German police began to use the MG 60 as a counter-terrorism weapon. The MG 60 was also used by the German police for other purposes, such as hostage-taking situations. In the 1990s, the MG 60 was replaced in German police service by the Heckler & Koch MG 4.

James Park Woods (born December 31, 1947) is an American actor, singer, songwriter, producer, and director. He is known for his roles in films such as The Promise, The Great American Hero, The North Avenue Irregulars, and The Golden Boy, as well as for his role as richness "Diz" McCracken in the animated series The Simpsons. Woods was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. He studied at the Academy of Vocal Arts in Philadelphia and at the University of the Arts. In 1971, he moved to New York City to pursue an acting career. He appeared on Broadway in the 1975 musical The Night of the Tribades, and he was a replacement cast member in the Broadway production of Les Misérables. He also appeared in the television series The Adams Chronicles and in the film The Promise. In 1980, Woods played the role of "Diz" McCracken, a friend of the Simpson family, on the television show The Simpsons. His character was originally voiced by Sam Simon, but Woods took over the role after Simon left the show. Woods has also provided voices for other animated series, including Futurama, The Boondocks, and American Dad! In addition to his work in film and television, Woods has also released two albums, including the Grammy-nominated The James Woods Collection: The Best of James Woods. In 2011, Woods was the subject of an hour-long documentary, James Woods: Off the Chart, which examined his career and personal life. The film was directed by Greg Kohler and produced by Ron Mann.

Goldfinger is a 1964 British spy film directed by Guy Hamilton and produced by Harry Saltzman and Albert R. Broccoli. The third film in the James Bond series, it was the first to feature the character of Goldfinger, played by Gert Fröbe, and the first to use the name James Bond. The film also introduced the concept of the Bond girl. The film was based on the novel Goldfinger by Ian Fleming, who also wrote the screenplay. The story centres on the investigation by the British Secret Service, led by agent 007 James Bond, into the disappearance of several scientists involved in the space programme. The main suspect is the German-Jewish scientist Dr. Goldfinger, played by Gert Fröbe, who is suspected of using a laser-like device to kill the scientists as part of a plan to steal their research for his own personal gain. Bond's mission is to prevent Goldfinger from achieving his goals and to discover what has happened to the scientists. The film was shot in London, Miami, and the Bahamas. The film's score was composed by John Barry and the theme song, "Goldfinger", performed by Shirley Bassey, became a popular standard. Goldfinger was well-received by critics and was the highest-grossing film of the year in the United States. It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song for "Goldfinger", and for the Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song for the same track, winning the Grammy Award for Best Original Score Written for a Motion Picture or Television Show. In 2000, it was selected as the second greatest film of all time by the American Film Institute, as part of their 100 Years... 100 Laughs special. In 2011, Goldfinger was also ranked the second best film of all time by the British Film Institute. In 2015, the film was selected for screening in the Royal Film Performance Programme to mark the 50th anniversary of the film's release. In 2017, Goldfinger was selected for screening in the BFI's James Bond cinema season to mark the 60th anniversary of the film's release.

Monopoly (1985 video game) Monopoly is a 1985 video game developed by Park Place Productions for the Commodore 64 and published by Commodore International. It is based on the board game Monopoly. The game was well-received, with praise given to its authentic recreation of the board game, and it was considered one of the best video game versions of Monopoly. A port for the Commodore 128 was in development, but never released. In 2002, a sequel, Monopoly 2, was released for the Game Boy Advance. In 2008, a new version of Monopoly was released for the Nintendo DS and Nintendo Wii. A mobile version of the game for iOS and Android was released in 2014. In 2015, a version of the game was released for the PlayStation 4 and the Xbox One. A version of the game for the Nintendo Switch was released in 2017. Monopoly (1985 video game) is a video game adaptation of the board game Monopoly. The game was released in 1985 for the Commodore 64 and in 2002 for the Game Boy Advance. The game is played similarly to the board game, with the objective being to purchase as many properties as possible and then develop them. The player with the most money at the end of the game wins. There are some differences between the video game and the board game. For example, the video game has a single-player mode, while the board game is typically played with multiple players. The video game also allows players to buy and sell properties, while the board game only allows players to buy properties. The video game also has some additional features not found in the board game, such as the ability to play with up to six players and the ability to choose from a variety of game boards. The game was well-received, with praise given to its authentic recreation of the board game, and it was considered one of the best video game versions of Monopoly.

The Leopoldino aqueduct is an aqueduct in the city of Rome, Italy. It is the second largest aqueduct in the city, after the Aqua Virgo aqueduct. The aqueduct is named after Pope Leopold II and is best known for the two artificial lakes it feeds, the Lake of the aqueduct of Pamphili and the Lake of the aqueduct of Tor Vegata, both of which are located in the Villa Borghese. The aqueduct was built in the 19th century and is still in use today. It is a combined aqueduct and sewer, as it carries both clean water and wastewater. The aqueduct is 11.5 kilometers (7.1 miles) long and has a total capacity of 360,000 cubic meters (12,000,000 cubic feet) per day. The aqueduct is made of two main parts: the Acqua Lungara, which runs from the Villa Pamphili to the via di Villa Georgiana, and the Acqua Vergine, which runs from the via di Villa Georgiana to the Lake of the aqueduct of Pamphili. The aqueduct is a major source of water for the city of Rome and provides water to the neighborhoods of Villa Pamphili, Villa Borghese, and the Prati district. The aqueduct also provides water to the city's hospitals and to the Vatican City.

The Commission on the Humanities and Social Sciences was established by the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) in 2013 "to chart a course for the future of the humanities and social sciences." The commission's work will inform the NEH's plans for the future and will also be used to inform the planning of other federal, state, and local policy makers. The fifteen members of the commission were appointed by NEH Chairman William "Bro" Adams, and include prominent leaders in the humanities and social sciences, higher education, and public life. The commission is co-chaired by former Secretary of Education William J. Bennett and Harvard University President Lawrence H. Summers. The commission's first meeting took place on July 30, 2013, at the NEH headquarters in Washington, DC. At that meeting, the commission began its work on a report that will be delivered to the NEH in June 2014. The report will include recommendations "for a vibrant and durable future for the humanities and social sciences." In addition to its report to the NEH, the commission will also publish a report for a broad audience of policy makers, opinion leaders, and the general public. The commission will hold additional meetings in Washington, DC, and will also hold meetings in the field, where it will have an opportunity to learn more about the work being done in the humanities and social sciences, and the impact of that work on communities across the United States. The National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) is an independent federal agency that funds and promotes research, education, and public programs in the humanities. The NEH is one of the largest federal supporters of the humanities in the United States. The humanities are a rich and diverse set of disciplines that include the study of history, literature, language, philosophy, and the arts. The humanities provide a context for our lives, our communities, and our culture. They help us understand our past, our present, and our future. The humanities teach us about the diversity of human experience and the ways that we can learn from that experience to make our lives better. The social sciences are a diverse set of disciplines that include the study of human behavior, society, and the economy. The social sciences provide a context for our lives, our communities, and our culture. They help us understand our past, our present, and our future. The social sciences teach us about the diversity of human experience and the ways that we can learn from that experience to make our lives better.

Paul Wheelhouse (born 11 June 1956) is a Scottish politician serving as Minister for Energy and Climate Change in the Scottish Government since May 2021. A member of the Scottish National Party (SNP), he has been a Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) for the South Scotland region since 2011, having previously represented the Cunninghame South constituency from 2007 to 2011. Born in Kilmarnock, Ayrshire, Wheelhouse was educated atHistory at the University of Glasgow and the University of Oxford. He previously worked as a research assistant at the House of Commons for Labour MP Donald Dewar, and was a lecturer in history at the University of the West of Scotland from 1996 to 2007. In the 2007 Scottish Parliament election, Wheelhouse was elected to represent the Cunninghame South constituency, defeating the sitting Scottish Labour Party (SLP) member, Bill Kidd, by 4,818 votes. In 2011, he was elected to represent the South Scotland region. Wheelhouse was the SNP's Shadow Minister for Environment and Climate Change in the Scottish Parliament from 2007 to 2011, and Shadow Minister for Transport and Climate Change from 2011 to 2014. He was a member of the Standards in Public Office Committee from 2009 to 2011, and has been a member of the Public Petitions Committee since 2011. In June 2012, he was appointed the SNP's National Coordinator and Chief of Staff. In September 2012, Wheelhouse was re-selected as a candidate for the South Scotland region, and in the May 2016 Scottish Parliament election, he was elected to represent the South Scotland region. Wheelhouse was the Minister for Business, Innovation and Energy from 2014 to 2016, and the Minister for Environment and Climate Change from 2016 to 2021. He has also served as a member of the Scottish Government's National Security Committee. In September 2016, Wheelhouse was re-selected as a candidate for the South Scotland region, and in the May 2021 Scottish Parliament election, he was elected to represent the South Scotland region. In June 2021, he was appointed Minister for Energy and Climate Change.

Frieston is a village and civil parish in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England. It is situated on the A15 road and lies approximately 3 kilometres (2 mi) west of Keyingham, 4 kilometres (2 mi) east of Hedon and 11 kilometres (7 mi) south-east of Hull. According to the 2011 UK Census, Frieston parish had a population of 2,325, an increase on the 2001 UK Census figure of 2,226. The parish church of St Mary is a Grade II* listed building dating from the early 12th century, with later amendments. Frieston is home to the UK's first solar farm, which was built in 2011 and has the capacity to generate 1.5 megawatts of electricity. There is a primary school in the village, and the village has two public houses, a hotel, a restaurant and a takeaway. The civil parish includes the village of North Frodingham. The A165 road passes through the parish, joining the A15 at a roundabout to the south of the village. The B1237 road also passes through the parish, joining the A165 at a roundabout to the west of the village. The village is served by Hedon and Keyingham railway stations, which are both on the Yorkshire Coast Line, running between Hull and Scarborough. The village was served by Frieston and North Frodingham railway station, which was on the Hull and Hornsea Railway. The station was closed to passengers in 1964 and the line closed to freight in 1968. The village is also served by the number 75 bus, which runs every two hours between Hull and Withernsea. The nearest stop to the village is on the A165, a mile from the village.

Volsk Volsk ( []), until 1 January 2015 known as Volstrup, is a town in the western part of the Netherlands, in the province of Noord-Holland. It is located in a polder between the IJmeer and the Noordermeer. The town is part of the Noord-Hollandic Ridge. Volstrup was first mentioned in 1417 as "upstaet van Volstrue", meaning "upright from the (river) Vol". It refers to a river which no longer exists. The current name is a corruption of the original name. Volstrup was a rural community which became a subsidiary of the nearby city of Schagen in 1675. The community had always been a linear settlement along the main road. In the early 20th century, it started to grow, and a harbour was built on the Noordermeer. In 1930, Volstrup became a separate municipality. In 1942, Volstrup was occupied by the Germans. On 3 October 1944, the Germans destroyed the village as an act of retaliation for acts of resistance. After the war, the village was rebuilt, but with a different layout. The new layout was designed by Cornelis Dalle, who also designed several other villages in the polders. On 1 January 2015, Volstrup merged with Schagen and Zuidbroek to form the new municipality of Noord-Holland.

West Balikpapan is an administrative district (Indonesian: Kecamatan) in Balikpapan, East Kalimantan, Indonesia. It is the westernmost district of Balikpapan. It covers 41.80 km2 (16 mi2) and had a population of 173,068 at the 2010 Census and 196,224 at the 2020 Census. It is the second most populous district in Balikpapan, after the Balikpapan Selatan district. West Balikpapan District is bounded by North Balikpapan District to the north, by the Makassar Strait to the east, by South Balikpapan District to the south, and by Kutai Kartanegara Regency to the west. West Balikpapan District includes the southern part of Balikpapan Bay. There are many heavy industries located in this district due to its proximity to the strait. The district also includes the Tunjuk Emas Industrial Park, the biggest industrial park in East Kalimantan. At the 2010 Census, West Balikparan District had a population of 173,068. This rose to 196,224 at the 2020 Census. The district is the second most populous in Balikpapan, after South Balikpapan. West Balikpapan District is divided into eight administrative villages (Indonesian: Kelurahan) and two urban villages (Indonesian: Kampung Tua). The administrative villages are: 1. Bentayan 2. Berlian 3. Blok A 4. Blok B 5. Setiabudi 6. Limbungan 7. Nipah 8. Polda The urban villages are: 1. Permai 2. Lamanite

The origin theories of Christopher Columbus include several unproven hypotheses concerning the geographical origin of the first European explorer to reach the Caribbean islands in 1492. During the 20th century, scholars advanced several theories that competed with the traditional belief that Columbus was from the Italian region of Liguria in Italy. These included theories that Columbus was from the ports of Portuguese Galicia, that he was from the Canary Islands, or even that he was from the Middle East. In the 21st century, DNA analysis of Columbus' remains is planned to settle the matter. In the 20th century, several scholars advanced theories that competed with the traditional belief that Columbus was from the Italian region of Liguria. The first was the theory that Columbus was from the ports of Portuguese Galicia, which had been part of the kingdom of León until the mid-13th century. In the early 20th century, the Portuguese historian Joel Silva reviewed primary documents relating to Columbus' life and found that some of them, including Columbus' own writings, indicated that he may have been from the Atlantic coast of Spain, perhaps from the region of the Rías Baixas. Silva's theory was first publicly debated in 1951, when he appeared in a television program in Spain. The theory was subsequently embraced by several scholars, including the Spanish historian Paulino de Brito e Abreu, who published the book Columbus: proof that he was Portuguese in 1968. The theory was also supported by the historian Rosa de Friederich, who published an article in 1982 that claimed that Columbus' father, errors in the Historie of the Navigation and Discoveries of the Earls of Medina-Sidonia, and other documents pointed to a Portuguese origin. In 2001, the Portuguese journalist Jose Hermano Saraiva published the book Columbus, a Portuguese from the Azores, which also advanced a theory of Portuguese origin. A second theory that emerged in the 20th century was that Columbus was from the Canary Islands. In 1936, the Spanish historian and journalist Eugenio de Palia published an article suggesting that Columbus was from the island of El Hierro. He was followed by the Canary Islands writer Juan Núñez de la Peña, who in 1946 published a book arguing that Columbus was from La Gomera. A third Canary Islands theory, first advanced in 1964 by the historian Juan barker, was that Columbus was from Lanzarote. In the 20th century, other scholars suggested that Columbus may have been from other parts of the Mediterranean, including the Middle East. The Spanish historian Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, who lived in the early 17th century, was the first to advance a theory that Columbus was from the Middle East, specifically from the Kingdom of Jerusalem. In the early 20th century, the French historian and geographer Victor de Champollion separately advanced a theory that Columbus was from the Middle East. In 2007, the Italian historian Paolo Zeno Boxer proposed that Columbus was from Marrakech, in Morocco. In the 21st century, DNA analysis of Columbus' remains is planned to settle the matter. The city of Charlotte, North Carolina, has a large monument to Columbus and an annual festival celebrating him, because a local businessman, Mike Ghost, believes that Columbus was from the city.

Robert S. Welch (November 27, 1889 – November 10, 1959) was an American businessman, best known as the founder of the Welch's grape juice company. Welch was born in Brooklyn, New York, the son of Frederick Welch and Helen LouiseProtchett. His father, a successful lawyer, died in 1898, leaving the family in straitened circumstances. Welch attended public schools in Brooklyn, and graduated from high school in 1908. He worked as a messenger for a bank, but was laid off in 1909 due to recession. He was able to secure a position with a wholesale drug company, Johnson & Johnson, where he learned the bottle manufacturing business. In 1911, he founded his own business, the Welch Bottle Company, to manufacture and sell glass bottles to the wine and champagne industries. The company grew to become the largest manufacturer of champagne bottles in the United States. In the early 1920s, Welch's business encountered financial difficulties, and he was forced to declare bankruptcy. As a result, he sold his company to the Crown Cork & Seal Company for $1.5 million. He then began to look for other business opportunities, and soon focused his attention on the emerging market for grape juice. In 1924, he founded the Welch Fruit Company, which initially sold grape juice under the name "Welch's Vinic", and soon afterwards began selling a non-alcoholic champagne called "Methuen champagne". The company grew rapidly, and in 1928 it was renamed the Welch's Grape Juice Company. Welch was an active philanthropist, and served as a trustee of the John Hopkins University and the Cleveland Clinic Foundation. In 1952, he established the Robert S. Welch Foundation, which provides funding for medical research and education. He was also a patron of the arts, and helped to establish the Cleveland Symphony Orchestra. Welch died of a heart attack in 1959, at the age of seventy. He is buried in Lake View Cemetery, Cleveland, Ohio.

Flags of Norwegian subdivisions This is a list of the flags of the municipalities and counties of Norway. Municipalities The Norwegian municipalities each have their own flag. Many of the municipal flags are recent inventions, as the municipalities did not have official flags until the early 20th century. There are strict guidelines for the design of the municipal flags, and all municipal flags must be rectangular. The colors of the Norwegian municipalities are very diverse. While the majority of the flags are blue and white, the other colors used are red, green, yellow, black and purple. The coat of arms is often, but not always, displayed on the municipal flags. The number of municipalities in Norway has varied throughout history, as they have been created, merged, and abolished several times. There are currently 429 municipalities. Counties The Norwegian counties each have their own flag. The colors are often blue and white, but there are several red and green counties as well. The number of counties in Norway has varied throughout history, as they have been created, merged, and abolished several times. There are currently 19 counties. The county flags are not as strictly regulated as the municipal flags. Most of the county flags feature the respective county's coat of arms, but some counties, such as Oslo and Hedmark, have flags without a coat of arms.

Curtiss Tanager is a species of small passerine birds in the tanager family Thraupidae. It is the only species of the genus Curtissi. The species is endemic to western and north-western Peru. The Curtiss Tanager was first described by the American ornithologist Alexander Wetmore in 1934. It was named in honor of the American zoologist Earl Curtiss. The Curtiss Tanager is a small tanager, 11.5–12.5 cm long. The adult has a long, pale grey-white pointed bill, dark grey legs, a pale grey-white face and pale grey-white underparts. The upperparts are dark grey with a pale grey shoulder patch. The central tail feathers are longer than the lateral feathers. The male and female are similar. The Curtiss Tanager occurs in low-lying areas on the Pacific coast of Peru, from the Department of Tumbes in the north to the Department of Ica in the south, and also in the western part of the Department of Ancash in the Andes, at altitudes of up to 2,100 m. It prefers open areas such as fields, pasture, roadsides, and the edges of forests, where it can be seen solitary, or in pairs, or in small groups. The Curtiss Tanager feeds on nectar from the flowers of tall, thin-stemmed plants, and on small invertebrates such as insects, which it finds on the ground or in the bark of trees. The Curtiss Tanager is a seasonal breeder, with the season lasting from September to April. The nest is built by the female alone, and is a small cup shape made of grass and moss lined with mud. It is placed in a low fork of a tree or bush. Two eggs are laid, and are pale blue-green with brown spots. The nest and eggs are preyed on by snakes and monkeys. The Curtiss Tanager is uncommon and localised, and is declining as its forest habitat is cleared for agriculture and settlement. It is therefore classified as Near Threatened by the IUCN.

Albert Burditt (born February 9, 1958) is an American actor and writer best known for his work as a writer and performer on the comedy show Saturday Night Live from 1985 to 1991. Burditt was born in Detroit, Michigan, and attended Mumford High School. He later attended Wayne State University, where he studied telecommunications. Burditt's first television appearance was on The $20,000 Pyramid in 1981. In the same year, he appeared in the film The Monster Squad. He also appeared in the music video for The Weather Girls' hit single "It's Raining Men". Burditt joined Saturday Night Live in 1985 as a writer and featured performer, where he was a member of the "Not Ready for Prime Time Players" and worked with such comedians as Eddie Murphy, Adam Sandler, Chris Farley, and Mike Myers. He remained with the show for six seasons until 1991. His work as a writer and performer earned him three Emmy Awards. Following his time on Saturday Night Live, Burditt appeared in several films, including Hot Shots! (1991), Wayne's World 2: Dead Men Don't Die (1993), The Net (1995), and A Thousand Words (2012). Burditt has also appeared in numerous television series, including Seinfeld, The Larry Sanders Show, Mad About You, and Will & Grace. In 1996, he starred in the short-lived sitcom The Home Court. Burditt's work as a writer and performer has been featured in several comedy albums, including Saturday Night Live: 25th Anniversary Collection (1997), Saturday Night Live, The Sound of Saturday Night (1999), and Saturday Night Live: The Complete Series (2005). In 2009, Burditt appeared in the documentary Saturday Night Live: The Reunion. Burditt has been married to Mary Birdsong since 1988. They have one daughter, Brett.

Hannette Staack (born December 18, 1979) is a German professional boxer and former world champion. Staack was born in East Germany and grew up in the city of East Berlin. She began boxing in 1996 at the SC Dynamo Berlin club, and later joined the Wismar Boxclub. In 1998 she became the German champion in the lightweight division, and in 1999 she added the European title. In 2000 she won the lightweight silver medal at the European Amateur Boxing Championships in Cork, Ireland. She then went on to win the gold medal in the same division at the 2001 European Amateur Boxing Championships in Belfast, Northern Ireland. Staack turned professional in 2001 and signed with the German boxing promoter Wilfried Sauerland. In her professional debut she defeated Julia Sahin by a first-round knockout, and went on to compile a record of 18 wins and 2 losses, with 12 knockouts. In 2003 she became the WIBF lightweight world champion by defeating the defending champion, locally favorite Olivia De Camaret, by a majority decision in the champion's hometown of Santiago de Cuba. San Siro di Struppa is a church in the frazione of Struppa, in the comune of Montescudaio, province of Pisa, Tuscany, central Italy. It is located at the end of a long, winding road that goes up the mountain from the village of Montescudaio. The church is built at the point where the south-western slopes of the mountain meet the sea. The church is dedicated to San Silverio, a 7th-century bishop who is said to have withdrawn to this isolated spot to live as a hermit. The current buildings date from the 15th century, with some later additions. The church has a single nave with a transept. The main altar is in the apse, and there are two smaller chapels in the transept. The walls are decorated with numerous paintings, the majority of which are from the 17th century. The church also has several sculptures, including a statue of San Silverio, a bas-relief of the Annunciation, and a wooden crucifix from the 16th century. The church is located in a picturesque landscape, and is a popular destination for hikers and cyclists. It is also a destination for pilgrims, who travel to the church on foot from the nearby village of Montescudaio.

James Kazama (born February 10, 1931) is an American politician and businessman who served as a member of the Washington House of Representatives from the 28th district from 1974 to 1975, and again from 1976 to 1983, and from 1985 to 1993, and the Washington State Senate, representing the 28th district from 1993 to 1998. Kazama was born in Seattle, Washington. He attended Seattle Public Schools and graduated from Queen Anne High School in 1949. The Port of Caen The Port of Caen is a French port located in the city of Caen, in the region of Normandy. It is the fourth largest port in France, and the second largest in Normandy after the Port of Le Havre. The Port of Caen is located on the south side of the mouth of the Orne, on the left bank of the river. It covers an area of 4,000 hectares (9,900 acres). The port is divided into three parts: - The west part, including the pleasure port and the commercial port; - The east part, dedicated to the industrial activities; - The central part, reserved for future developments. The port can receive vessels up to 350 metres (1,150 ft) long and up to 8.5 metres (28 ft) draft. The port is connected to the sea by a lock system. The Normandie lock, completed in 2016, allows ships to reach the Port of Caen from the English Channel. It is the longest lock in France, with a total length of 2,700 metres (8,860 ft), including 1,700 metres (5,600 ft) between the gates. The port is connected to the national road network by the A13 autoroute, and to the railway network by the Paris-Cherbourg line. The port is the seat of the Port Autonome de Caen, the eighth largest port authority in France. The pleasure port is the largest in the country, with 3,000 moorings. The port is also a major tourist attraction, thanks to its pedestrian area and its beaches.

D.C. Opportunity Scholarship Program The D.C. Opportunity Scholarship Program provides private school vouchers to students in grades K–12 from low-income families in the District of Columbia. The program was created by the D.C. Opportunity Scholarship Act of 2004 and is administered by the D.C. Department of Education. Any low-income family that resides in the District of Columbia is eligible to apply for an opportunity scholarship. A family's income must be equal to or less than 150 percent of the federal poverty level, which is $39,300 for a family of three in fiscal year 2010. The federal share of the program is provided through the District of Columbia Education Flexibility Partnership Act of 1999, which was reauthorized in 2004. Geology of Libya Libya is mostly covered by a vast expanse of loose sand and was for a long time one of the least explored countries on earth. Due to the many oil fields and the rich oil reserves, Libya has been a focal point for geologists and oil companies. Geological history Libya was once part of the ancient continent of Gondwana, which also included Africa, South America, Antarctica and India. The formation of Gondwana started with the appearance of the first landmass, the supercontinent Pannotia, in the Neoproterozoic era, about 650 million years ago. The disintegration of Pannotia began in the early Paleozoic era, about 540 million years ago, and by the end of the Paleozoic, about 250 million years ago, Gondwana was fully formed. In the following Mesozoic and early Tertiary era, Gondwana broke up. What is now Libya was part of the continent of Pangaea, which also included Africa, South America, and the Middle East. Libya's geology is dominated by the complex of suitcases and carbonate platforms that form the northern edge of the Sahara Desert. The Geomorian stage, which extends from about 800,000 to 600,000 years ago, is the first stage of the Pleistocene period. The terrain is flat, and the surface is formed by the accumulation of wind-blown sand, which in some places has reached a thickness of 600 m. In the Nummulitic stage, which lasted from about 600,000 to 180,000 years ago, the climate became warmer and more humid. Freshwater lakes and rivers existed in the interior, and the Mediterranean coast was a swampy plain. During this period, the sand dunes were stabilized by vegetation, and the formation of calcareous rocks, dolomites, and evaporites were deposited. In the last stage of the Pleistocene period, the Gelasian, which lasted from about 180,000 to around 10,000 years ago, the climate became colder and more arid. Most of the lakes and rivers dried up, and the Sahara Desert expanded. The high winds and temperatures of the Sahara molded the landscape into the vast sand seas that it is today. The country is divided into three main regions: the Tripolitanian Plain, the Mountain Belt, and the Sahara Desert. Tripolitanian Plain The largest part of Libya, the Tripolitanian Plain, is a vast area of mostly flat terrain. The region is covered with loose, overlying sand, and in some places, the sand is up to 600 meters deep. The plain is interrupted by large salt lakes and salt flats. The sand is formed by the erosion of the soft, underlying limestone and the transport of sand by wind and water. The plain is home to a large oil field, the Murzuq Oil Field, and the country's largest reservoir of crude oil, the Sarir Field. The Sarir Field is located in the southwest of the plain, near the oasis of Sarir. The oil field has an area of about 8,000 square kilometers and produces about 260,000 barrels of oil a day. The oil is transported to the coast by pipelines. The Mountain Belt The Mountain Belt is a region of higher, rugged terrain that runs across the country from the northwest to the southeast. The region is home to the forbidding Kufra Desert and the remote Kufra Oasis. The terrain is made up of rugged plateaus and escarpments, with deep valleys and steep gorges. The highest point in the country is the 2,250-meter-high Emi Koussi, located in the midst of the Kufra Desert. The Sahara Desert The Sahara Desert covers much of Libya. It is a vast, arid, and largely barren landscape of sand and rock. The Sahara is the largest desert in the world, covering an area of about 8,000,000 square kilometers. The Sahara is home to the unique Saharan troglodytes, and the famous Tubu tribespeople. The desert also has some of the highest and lowest points in the country. The highest point is the 2,250-meter-high Emi Koussi, and the lowest point is the Sabhna Ghuil, which is 80 meters below sea level. The Sahara is crossed by a number of rivers, including the Wadi al-Kharab, Wadi Daym, and Wadi al-Mishri. The rivers flow from the west to the east, and most of them dry up before reaching the coast. The largest river, the Wadi al-Kharab, flows from the Western Mountains to the Gulf of Sirte. The Wadi al-Kharab is the only river in Libya that has a permanent flow.

Jokkmokk Municipality (Jokkmokks kommun) is a municipality in Norrbotten County, Sweden. The municipality's seat is located in the town of Jokkmokk. Jokkmokk is the home of the indigenous Sami people, and is also the seat of the Sami Parliament of Sweden. Jokkmokk municipality covers an area of 9,421 square kilometres (3,629 sq mi) and had a total population of 2,682 in 2010. Jokkmokk is located about 70 kilometres (43 mi) north of Piteå and about 200 kilometres (124 mi) south of Kiruna. The town is situated along the valley of the Ume River, with the river mouth at the Gulf of Bothnia. Jokkmokk was the site of the first ever peaceful democratic elections in Sweden in 1718. The first elections with universal suffrage in Sweden were held here in 1881. Jokkmokk is the main node of the Fennoscandian fiber-optic network, with multiple international fiber-optic cables landing in the town. The municipality is home to the " Midnight Sun Game", a series of football matches that are played until the late hours of the night during the summer months, when the sun does not set in the north of Sweden. Jokkmokk is also the location of the "Sami Grand Prix", a snowmobile racing event that is a part of the World Snowmobile Racing Championship. The famous "King's Trail" (Kungsträgården), which is part of the international E1 trail, passes through the municipality.

Tessera (Venus) Tessera, also called tesserae, is a term used by archaeologists to describe the small, flat, roughly square stones that were used as votes in democratic elections in the ancient Roman Republic. In the Roman constitutional tradition, citizens had several rights and duties. One of these was the right to vote. In the early Republic, voting was done by a show of hands, but as the population grew, this method became unwieldy. By the end of the 4th century BC, voting by ballot (tesserae) was introduced. Each voter would write the name of the candidate he was voting for on a small piece of wood, usually wax-coated, called a tessera. In order to prevent fraud, the tessera was marked with a letter or symbol so that illiterate citizens could cast the correct vote. The marked tessera was then placed in a large pile with those of other voters. The votes were then counted and the candidate with the majority of votes was elected. A similar method was used for voting on laws and other matters of state. However, the voters in this case used a different type of tessera, called a ballotarium, which had two sides, both of which could be written on. The voter would write "Aye" or "No" on one side and then turn the tessera over and write the name of the law on the other side.

Lorraine 37L The Lorraine 37L was a French bomber aircraft of the Second World War. In 1938, the French Air Ministry issued a specification for a three-seat twin-engine bomber, with a capacity of 800 kg (1,7655 lb) of bombs, a maximum speed of 400 km/h (250 mph) and a range of 2,000 km (1,243 mi). The new aircraft was to be a replacement for the Bloch 174 and the Amiot 143, both of which were becoming obsolete. To meet this requirement, the Sociétés Anonymes Lorraine, based at Nancy, developed the Lorraine 37L. This aircraft was a further development of the Lorraine 37, and was a monoplane of all-metal construction, with a crew of three. The prototype, powered by two 471 hp (347 kW) Lorraine 12 G Er narcissus/12 G Esso engines, flew in 1939. A total of 38 Lorraine 37L aircraft were delivered to the French Air Force, with the type being used for close support duties during the German invasion of France in 1940. A further 20 aircraft were delivered to the Belgian Air Force, while an additional 25 were built for the Royal Air Force as the Blenheim Mark IV. Lorraine 37L bombers were also used for experimental purposes. During the German offensive, several were used as "pathfinders" for the heavier bombers, such as the Amiot 140. In September 1944, a Lorraine 37L was used as the basis for the experimental Lorraine GR 42 "Guere Maquis" ( Cigar for the Maquis ), a "special mission" aircraft developed by Lorraine for the French Air Force. The GR 42 was a single-seat aircraft, based on the liaison aircraft Lorraine LeO 42, and was powered by a 462 hp (340 kW) Lorraine 12 Gd engine. It could carry a total of 1,000 kg (2,200 lb) of bombs or mines, and was armed with a 20 mm MG-FF/M-39 cannon and two 13.2 mm (0.52 in) machine guns. The GR 42 was only produced in small numbers, and the few examples that were built were used for close support and anti-tank warfare duties.
