Platon Alexeevich Obukhov (Russian: Плато́н Алексе́евич Обу́хов; 16 December [O.S. 4 December] 1898 – 1 November 1987) was a Russian Soviet meteorologist and hydrographer, oceanologist, and academician (1969). Obukhov was born in Moscow. He was a student of the outstanding Soviet meteorologist Alexander Vil'mont, and began his scientific career in the field of atmospheric physics, studying the physics of rain and the structure of clouds. In the 1930s, he became interested in the problems of the World Ocean, and turned to the field of hydrography. He proposed a system of Recording bottles for the Collection of a water sample from a given depth, the so-called Obukhov system, which was widely used by oceanographers for several decades. In the field of physical oceanography, he is known for the theory of the wind-driven circulation of the World Ocean, the so-called Obukhov circulation, which is an important element of the large-scale circulation of the World Ocean. In the theory of ocean waves, he is the author of the so-called Obukhov equation. Obukhov was a member of the Editorial Board of the journal Oceanology from 1965 to 1986, and was the editor of the Soviet Hydrology Journal from 1950 to 1985. He was a Corresponding Member of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR from 1946, and a Full Member of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR from 1953. He was also a Full Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences from 1990. Obukhov was awarded the State Prize of the USSR (1946), the Lenin Prize (1970), the USSR Academy of Sciences' V.I. Vernadsky Prize (1986), and the Russian Federation's State Prize (1994).

Bessarabia Bessarabia, also spelled Bessarabiya (Russian: Бессарабия; Ukrainian: Бессарабія; Moldovan: Basarabeia; Romanian: Basarabia), is a historical region in Eastern Europe, now divided between Moldova, Ukraine, and Romania. It covers the territory between the Prut and the Dniester rivers, comprising the northern parts of the present-day Moldavian and Ukrainian states, and the eastern part of Romania. Bessarabia was historically part of the Principality of Moldavia. In the late 18th century, it was annexed by the Russian Empire, and in the 19th century, it became the object of diplomatic rivalries between Russia and the other Great Powers. The region was the site of an anti-Russian uprising in 1917, and after the Russian Revolution, it was integrated into Romania. In the aftermath of World War II, it was occupied by the Soviet Union and became part of the Moldavian ASSR and the Ukrainian SSR. The region was the site of an anti-Soviet uprising in the early 1990s. Today, the region consists of three separate political entities. Two-thirds of Bessarabia is within Moldova (the Republic of Moldova, also known as Moldavia), with a population of 3,620,000 in 2014. One-third is in Ukraine (oblasts of Chernivtsi, Odessa, and Mykolaiv), with a population of 1,600,000 in 2014. A small part is in Romania (the counties of Bacău, Vaslui, and Galați), with a population of about 500,000 in 2014. The name Bessarabia is believed to be of Turkish origin, meaning "the land of the Besso". The term was first used by the Russian historian Nikolai Rumantsev in 1827 to describe the region between the Prut and the Dniester. The term Bessarabia was used by the Russian authorities to describe the region between the two rivers after they annexed it in the late 18th century. Bessarabia is located in Eastern Europe. It is bounded on the west by Romania, to the north by the Republic of Moldova, to the east by the Russian Federation and the Black Sea, and to the south by Ukraine. The territory of Bessarabia is very fertile and has a temperate continental climate with mild winters and warm summers. The region is rich in minerals, notably iron and coal. Automatic bug fixing Automatic bug fixing is a process of finding and fixing bugs in a software system using a combination of techniques, such as type checking, syntax analysis, and automated testing. The goal of automatic bug fixing is to improve the quality of the software by identifying and resolving defects that may have been introduced during the development process. The primary benefit of automatic bug fixing is that it can identify and resolve defects quickly and efficiently, reducing the time and effort required to maintain and update the software. This can be particularly useful for large software systems, which may have thousands of lines of code and many different components. There are several techniques that can be used for automatic bug fixing. One common technique is type checking, which involves analyzing the type of data being used in the software and ensuring that it is of the correct type. For example, if a function is expecting an integer value, type checking can be used to ensure that the value being passed to the function is actually an integer. Syntax analysis is another technique that can be used for automatic bug fixing. Syntax analysis involves analyzing the syntax of the code to ensure that it is written according to the proper rules and conventions. For example, syntax analysis can be used to ensure that variables are declared correctly, that function calls are properly formatted, and that comments are properly formatted. Automated testing is another technique that can be used for automatic bug fixing. Automated testing involves writing automated tests that can be run on the software to ensure that it is functioning correctly. These tests can be written to test specific features of the software, or to test the software as a whole. There are a number of tools and software development environments that can be used to support automatic bug fixing. For example, many programming languages include built-in type checking and syntax analysis tools, and there are also a number of stand-alone tools and software development environments that can be used to perform these tasks. In addition, there are a number of automated testing tools and software development environments that can be used to support automatic bug fixing. These tools and environments can be used to write and run automated tests on the software, and to track the results of these tests. Overall, automatic bug fixing is an important process for improving the quality of software. By using a combination of techniques, such as type checking, syntax analysis, and automated testing, it is possible to identify and resolve defects in a software system quickly and efficiently.

Tanu Muino is a Finnic goddess of the underworld. Tanu is the daughter of Tuoni, the god of the dead, and his wife Nyyrikki. She is married to her father, and her name is also connected with that of her mother, as nyyrik and taa mean "woman" and "bull-calf" or "heifer" respectively. Her name may be connected with the Finnish word tuntuu, meaning "to think, remember, or notice". According to the Kalevala, the Finnish national epic, the sun goddess and her mother, the moon goddess, were once close friends, but the sun goddess became jealous of the moon goddess's light, which shone on the whole world. The sun goddess wanted her light to also shine on the whole world, so she set her sights on the moon goddess's light. The sun goddess shone her light upon the earth, but it was still dark in the underworld. So she created a being, a maiden, to be her eyes and to look into the underworld to see what was there. This maiden was called Tuonen tyttö, the daughter of Tuoni. She was beautiful, but she could not see. So the sun goddess sent her to the underworld to look for the treasures of the dead. Tanu Muino is also known as the mother of many of the heroes in the Kalevala, including Lemminkäinen and the Saarijärvi-tribe's warlord, Vainamoinen.

West Haven station is an intermodal transit station in West Haven, Connecticut. The station is served by local and express trains on Metro-North Railroad's New Haven Line and Shore Line East, as well as by CTtransit buses. The station is located off the Boston Post Road (U.S. 1) near the junction with Route 162 (Davenport Avenue). It is the westernmost transit station in Connecticut and the last before the New York border. The New Haven Line has two tracks at the station, with one island platform between the tracks. The Shore Line East has two tracks, with one platform on the north side of the tracks. The station, which opened in 1907, is the second-busiest on the New Haven Line, after Stamford. A project to add a third track to the New Haven Line at the station was completed in June 2012. In 2013, the West Haven city government proposed to build a pedestrian bridge over the tracks to connect the station to the downtown area. In 2015, the state government proposed to close the station's waiting room and replace it with a smaller waiting area in a new location. The proposal met with local opposition, and the waiting room was instead renovated. The station is 18.8 miles (30.3 km) from New Haven and 51.4 miles (82.0 km) from New York City. Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar (film) Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar is a 2004 Indian English-language documentary film directed by Jabbar Patel. The film is based on the life of Babasahed Ambedkar, who was a social reformer and the architect of the Indian Constitution. The film also features interviews with people who knew Ambedkar, including his family members and colleagues. The New Zealand Law Society (Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa) is the statutory body responsible for the regulation of the legal profession in New Zealand. It was incorporated under the Legal Profession Act 2008, and is a Crown entity under the Public Finance Act 1989. The Law Society is governed by a Council of 20 members, elected by the membership every three years, and the Executive Committee, which is elected annually by the Council. The Council comprises 13 general members, five Māori members, one Pasifika member, and one Asian member. The Executive Committee comprises the President, Vice-President, and chairs of the Society's standing committees. As at 30 June 2018, the Society had 12,000 members, consisting of 11,799 lawyers and paralegals working in private practice, and 822 lawyers working as in-house counsel. The Law Society's functions include setting standards of conduct and professionalism for lawyers, providing a complaints service for the public and regulating the admission of lawyers to the profession. It also has a role in educating lawyers and in promoting the rule of law. The Law Society is also involved in the regulation of lawyers' fees. Under the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006, the Law Society is required to prepare a code of conduct setting out the manner in which lawyers may advertise their services, and the basis on which lawyers may charge for their services. The Law Society's headquarters are in Wellington. It has a National Office, and six branches: in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin, Hamilton and Tauranga. The Law Society has a close relationship with the New Zealand Bar Association, an incorporated society which represents the interests of New Zealand barristers (who are specialist advocates). Most New Zealand barristers are also members of the Law Society. The Law Society's professional body, the New Zealand Law Society Incorporated, was incorporated in 1907. It was previously known as the New Zealand Law Society ( Including the Incorporated Law Society of New Zealand). In 2005, the Law Society launched a "Find a Lawyer" service on its website, allowing the public to locate a lawyer in their area.

The human body has various types of joints, each serving different purposes, and possessing different types of movement. The main types of joints in the body include the following: 1. Fibrous joints 2. Cartilaginous joints 3. Synovial joints Fibrous joints Fibrous joints are joints in which the two bony surfaces are held together by fibrous tissue, also called connective tissue. They are also called synarthroses. Fibrous joints are very strong and do not allow for much movement. There are three types of fibrous joints: 1. Fibrous sutures 2. Fibrous ligaments 3. Fibrous capsules Fibrous sutures are present in the skull, where they hold the bones of the skull together. They are also found in the fingers and toes, where they join the phalanges to each other and to the metacarpal or metatarsal bones. Fibrous ligaments are flexible bands of fibrous tissue that connect bones to each other, as well as to muscles, while fibrous capsules are flexible sleeves of fibrous tissue that surround the bones of the spine (the vertebrae) and the large leg bones (the femur and tibia). Cartilaginous joints Cartilaginous joints are joints in which the two bony surfaces are joined by cartilage, a flexible and lubricated connective tissue. They are also called synchondroses. Cartilaginous joints allow for more movement than fibrous joints, but less movement than synovial joints. There are three types of cartilaginous joints: 1. Cartilaginous sutures 2. Cartilaginous ligaments 3. Articular discs Cartilaginous sutures are found in the body's soft tissues, such as the larynx, the trachea, and the oral cavity. Cartilaginous ligaments are found in the axial skeleton, where they connect the bones of the spine (the vertebrae). Articular discs are found in the appendicular skeleton, where they connect the bones of the upper and lower limbs. Synovial joints Synovial joints are joints in which the two bony surfaces are joined by synovial fluid, a viscous fluid that is enclosed by a membrane called the synovial membrane. The synovial membrane is lubricated by the synovial fluid, which reduces friction between the bony surfaces of the joint. Synovial joints are the most flexible type of joint in the body. There are six types of synovial joints: 1. Ball and socket joints 2. Hinge joints 3. Pivot joints 4. Elbow joints 5. Wrist joints 6. Ginglymoid joints Ball and socket joints Ball and socket joints are found in the hip and shoulder joints, where the head of the humerus fits into the socket of the pelvis (the acetabulum). These joints allow for a wide range of movement, including forward and backward, side to side, and rotation. Hinge joints Hinge joints are found in the fingers and toes, as well as in the knees and elbows. They allow for flexion (bending) and extension (straightening), but do not allow for rotation. Pivot joints Pivot joints are found in the neck, where they connect the head to the torso, and in the tailbone, where they connect the spine to the pelvis. They allow for rotation, but do not allow for flexion or extension. Elbow joints Elbow joints are found in the upper arm, where they connect the humerus to the radius and the ulna. They allow for flexion and extension, as well as rotation. Wrist joints Wrist joints are found in the hand, where they connect the bones of the wrist to each other and to the bones of the fingers. They allow for flexion and extension, as well as rotation. Ginglymoid joints Ginglymoid joints are found in the jaw (the temporomandibular joint), where they connect the lower jaw to the skull. They allow for flexion and extension, as well as rotation.

Oxalis triangularis, the common yellow oxalis, false oxalis, or yellow woodsorrel, is a species of flowering plant in the family Oxalidaceae, native to Europe and Asia, and widely introduced elsewhere. It is an annual or perennial herbaceous plant with long-stalked, triangular, alternate leaves up to 15 cm (6 in) long. The flowers are yellow, with five petals, the upper petal being the largest and having several purple veins. The fruit is a capsule, with three lobes, and several seeds. The common yellow oxalis is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant. It has been introduced to, and become invasive in, many countries. In the UK it is sometimes called "sorrel", although the true sorrel (Rumex acetosa) is a different species. The common yellow oxalis is sometimes confused with the closely related species Oxalis tetraphylla (synonym O. triangularis var. tetraphylla), which has four leaves at each node, rather than three. Leaves are alternate, 3-15 cm (1.2-6 in) long, triangular, usually with a heart-shaped base. The upper surface of the leaves are green, glabrous, and shiny. The lower surface is pale green and either glabrous, pubescent along the central vein, or pubescent generally. The petioles are less than one-third of the length of the leaf; they are glabrous to pubescent (hairs are especially likely to occur toward the bases of the petioles). The flowers are yellow, about 1.5 cm (0.6 in) across, with five petals. The upper petal is the largest and has several purple veins. The lower petal has several white hairs near its base. The flowers are either solitary or in small clusters in the axils of the upper leaves. The fruit is a capsule, 3.5-5 cm (1.4-2 in) long, with three lobes. Each lobe has a row of seeds. The capsule is green, ripening to red-brown, and is covered with fine pubescence. The common yellow oxalis is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant. It is a common weed in gardens, fields, lawns, and sidewalks. It is an invasive species and a noxious weed in many countries. The common yellow oxalis is sometimes confused with the closely related species Oxalis tetraphylla (synonym O. triangularis var. tetraphylla), which has four leaves at each node, rather than three. The common yellow oxalis is closely related to, and can hybridize with, the white-flowered Oxalis tetraphylla (synonym O. triangularis var. tetraphylla). The hybrid is known as O. triangularis × tetraphylla. It also hybridizes with the North American species Oxalis acetosella. The hybrid is known as O. triangularis × acetosella.

After the German invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1939, he was sent to a prisoner-of-war camp in Poland. He was able to return to Prague in 1940, and he then worked as a photographer and photojournalist for the German press agency Transpress. In 1942, Kalousek married his second wife, Věra, with whom he had two daughters, Eva and Dagmar. In the same year, he was conscripted into the German army and sent to the Eastern Front. He was wounded in the Battle of Stalingrad and was taken prisoner by the Soviets. He returned to Prague in May 1945, after the end of the war. In the post-war period, Kalousek worked as a graphic artist and illustrator. He was a member of the Czech-Moravian section of the Union of Visual Artists of Czechoslovakia and a member of the Association of Czech Graphic Artists. In addition to his work as an artist, he was also a passionate photographer, and he took many pictures of his family and friends, as well as of nature and the urban landscape. In 2012, at the age of 98, Kalousek was interviewed about his life and work for the Czech television program "Oči, rozhodčí!" (Eyes, Judge!). He died in Prague in 2013, at the age of 98.

The Epic of American Civilization The Epic of American Civilization is a late 20th-century epic poem by the Chicano author Rudolfo Anaya. It is Anaya's most ambitious work, consisting of three parts in thirty-seven chapters. The first part, "The Great Songs of the Family", covers the history of the Anaya family from its roots in the ancient past to the present. The second part, "The New World", covers the history of the Chicano people in the United States from the early 20th century to the 1960s. The third part, "The Blood of the Conquistador", focuses on a single character, a mixed-race boy who is a product of the Mexican-Anglo culture war. The Epic of American Civilization is an attempt to create a Chicano version of the Spanish epic, the "Epic of the Cid". Anaya's epic is a story of the survival and triumph of the Chicano culture, in spite of the many challenges it has faced. It is a story of a people who have had to fight for their land and their rights, and who have overcome great odds to preserve their culture. The epic is a celebration of the Chicano people and their culture, and it is a call to action for Chicanos to continue to fight for their rights and their culture.

Edwin Foresman Schoch (October 22, 1889 – June 7, 1968) was an American electrical engineer, inventor, and entrepreneur who founded the globe-spanning electronics company ITT Corporation. Schoch was born in Newark, New Jersey in 1889, the son of Mary (Foreman) and George Schoch. His father was a tailor and the family lived in poverty. He had only three months of formal schooling due to a bequest from a relative, he was able to attend the Newark Technical School. He was an excellent student and won a scholarship to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He graduated in 1911 with a Bachelor of Science degree in electrical engineering. In 1912 he joined the Western Electric Company, the manufacturing arm of AT&T, as a designer of telephone equipment. He was soon put in charge of the newly formed Overseas Department, which was tasked with selling American-made telephones to foreign countries. Schoch realized that the Western Electric Company was not organized to meet the demands of the overseas business, so he formed his own company to fill the need. In 1916, with $5,000 of capital, he founded the International Telephone and Telegraph Company (ITT). In 1924 the company went public and by the end of the decade it had become the second largest manufacturer of telephone equipment in the world, second only to the Western Electric Company. In 1940 the company changed its name to ITT Corporation. Schoch was a pioneer in the field of electric cooking. In the early 1930s, the electric percolator was a standard kitchen appliance; however, it could only be used on stove tops. Schoch developed an electric percolator that could be used on the breakfast table, the first of many electric appliances that the company would market. In 1938, ITT introduced the first automatic electric washing machine. The washing machine was an immediate success and ITT became the first company to mass-produce this product. In 1941, ITT introduced the first electric razor with a rechargeable battery. This was also the first razor with a vacuum cleaner attachment to clean the shaving head. In 1943, ITT developed the first portable electric drill with a rechargeable battery. In 1950, ITT developed the first electric razor with an electric cord. In 1955, ITT developed the first electric razor with a built-in electric razor. In 1961, ITT developed the first electric razor with an attached shaving brush. In 1963, ITT developed the first electric razor with an automatic cleaning system.

Family Equality Council The Family Equality Council is a American non-profit organization that advocates for equality and justice for LGBTQ+ families. They are the parent organization of Family Equality Council Action Fund, Family Equality Council Education Fund, and Family Equality Council Institute. Family Equality Council's mission is to advance legal and social equality for LGBTQ+ families, and for those who wish to support them. They envision a world where LGBTQ+ people can be open and honest with their families and loved ones, and where those families and loved ones have the tools, information, and resources they need to support and celebrate their LGBTQ+ members. They also envision a world where LGBTQ+ families are respected, included, and embraced by society as full and equal members of their communities. Family Equality Council's work is centered around four key areas: _Education: _They educate the public, policy makers, and stakeholders about the importance of equality and justice for LGBTQ+ families. They also provide resources and support to LGBTQ+ people who are trying to start or grow their families. _Advocacy: _They advocate for policies and practices that promote equality and justice for LGBTQ+ families. They also work to oppose policies and practices that discriminate against or marginalize LGBTQ+ families. _Research: _They conduct research and analysis to better understand the needs and experiences of LGBTQ+ families, and to identify ways to improve their lives. _Outreach: _They reach out to LGBTQ+ families and their allies to provide support and connect them with resources and community. They also work to build and strengthen LGBTQ+ family networks and communities.

Polyarchy In political science, polyarchy (from the Greek: πολύς, poly ("many") and κράτος, kratos ("power")) is a form of government in which citizens exercise political power. Polyarchy is a broader concept than democracy, as it refers to the structure of the government and not to the method of voting. In a democracy, the government is run directly by the people who are voting for a specific candidate, party, or policy. In a polyarchy, the people elect representatives to create and vote on policies. Representative democracy is a form of polyarchy. Aristotle's Politics describes two forms of government: the state, or regime, and the constitution. The state is the ruling body, and the constitution is the legal basis for the state's existence. Constitution refers to the way in which the ruling body is organized, including the government's powers and the way that citizens are governed. For example, the United States Constitution provides for three branches of government—legislative, executive, and judicial—and provides ways for changing the constitution itself. In a polyarchy, the ruling body, or state, has multiple power centers. A pure form of polyarchy doesn't exist because all nations have a head of state who has more power than the other members of the ruling body. In the United States, for example, the president has more power than the speaker of the House or the majority leader of the Senate. Even so, the United States is a polyarchy, because the people elect multiple representatives who have some level of political power. Citizen participation in a polyarchy can take many forms: voting for representatives, joining a political party, or participating in interest groups that advocate for specific causes. In a polyarchy, the people are not always involved in the political process but can become involved by contacting their representatives, voting, or joining a political party or interest group.

Maltese literature Maltese literature is the literature of the Maltese people, which is in the process of becoming a separate ethnic and national group, the Maltese. The first work of Maltese literature is the ll-Ilibre tar-Rummo, a 16th-century pastoral romance by Antonio de Vezzosi. The national epic of Malta is The Great Siege (1565), byRemix Censu. In 1607, the Carmelite priest and professor of philosophy Peter Caxaro wrote what is considered to be the first major work of Maltese literature, his Latini Ebraici: Luqmani, a translation of the Septuagint into Maltese. Caxaro's work was followed by a number of other Jewish-Maltese translations of the Old Testament, including that of 1636 by Mordecai Farrugia. These works are important because they helped to develop a standardized language among the Jewish and Christian Maltese communities. The first known Maltese dictionary was also written by a Jewish author, Samuel Benjamin Ben Hamo, in the early 18th century. Ben Hamo's work contains many examples of early Maltese poetry, which like most Maltese poetry written before the 20th century is in the form of the sonnet or other traditional verse forms. The most significant poet of this period was Pietru Caxaro (1634–1716), who is best known for his long poem L-Iblein. In the early 19th century, a number of poets began to move away from the traditional forms and to write in a more modern style. The best known of these was Dun Karm, who is credited as the first to have broken with tradition and to have written verse in the modern Maltese language. In the 20th century, the poets started to introduce new themes, such as social and political commentary, the importance of the Maltese language, and the relationship between Malta and England. The most important poets of this period were Ġużè Muscat, Robert Samut, and Joe Friggieri. In the 21st century, Maltese literature has been strongly influenced by the work of two poets, Adrian Grima and Antoine Cassar. Grima's work is characterized by a return to traditional verse forms, as well as by its engagement with social and political issues. Cassar's work is notable for its exploration of the relationship between Malta and its history, and for its use of experimental forms.

Giuseppe Pancaro (1666–1739), also known as Gioseffo Pancaro, was an Italian philosopher, physician, mathematician, and astronomer. He wrote on a wide range of subjects including mathematics, astronomy, medicine, physics, and philosophy. He was a friend and correspondent of Sir Isaac Newton and is best known for his work on the motion of the moon, on which he disputed the findings of Newton's Principia. He was the first to discover the crater Pancratium on the moon. Pancaro was born in Nocera Inferiore, a province of Salerno, in the Kingdom of Naples. He studied medicine and philosophy at the University of Naples, where he was a pupil of Giovanni Battista Porta, and subsequently worked as a physician in his native city. In 1702 he moved to Florence, where he lived for six years, devoting his energies to the study of mathematics and astronomy under the guidance of Antonio Maria Cassini. From 1708 to 1721 he was a professor of mathematics at the University of Parma, and during this period he made his home in Parma. In 1721 he returned to Naples, where he spent the rest of his life in the study of philosophy and science. Pancaro's lunar observations were made using a large refracting telescope, which he set up on the slopes of Vesuvius. His first observation of the moon's motion was made on 18 March 1705, and he continued to observe the moon for more than thirty years. He published the results of his observations in a book entitled Memorie di Stato del Moone e degli altri sistemi celesti, which appeared in three volumes between 1726 and 1739. In this work he presented his theories on the motion of the moon, and his explanation of various lunar phenomena, such as the appearance of spots on the moon and the rise of the waters of the sea in the moon's vicinity. He also discussed the motion of the sun and the planets, and the principles of mechanics and astronomy. In the first volume of his Memorie, Pancaro set out his theory of the moon's motion, according to which the moon's path around the earth is an epicycloid, with the earth at the center of the epicycloid and the moon at the inner focus of the epicycloid. This theory was in direct conflict with Newton's theory of the moon's motion, according to which the moon's path around the earth is a cycloid, with the earth at the center of the cycloid. Pancaro's theory was later shown to be incorrect when the moon was observed to be in the same position as the sun during an eclipse, which it would not be if its path were an epicycloid. In the second and third volumes of his Memorie, Pancaro discussed the principles of mechanics and astronomy, and the motion of the sun and the planets. In these volumes he presented his theory of the motion of the planets, according to which the planets move around the sun in elliptical orbits, with the sun at the center of the ellipses. This theory was in direct conflict with Newton's theory of the motion of the planets, according to which the planets move around the sun in circular orbits, with the sun at the center of the circles.

DeBerry, Texas is an unincorporated community in Trinity County, Texas, United States. The community is located in the northern part of the county on U.S. Route 287, approximately one mile south of the Texas-Louisiana state line. The community includes the DeBerry Independent School District and the DeBerry Municipal Airport. The community was founded in 1895 by James De Berry, a native of Mississippi who first came to Texas in the mid-1840s. A post office was established in 1897. The community incorporated in the early 1940s, but it disincorporated in the late 1960s. The DeBerry Independent School District covers the community and includes DeBerry Elementary School, DeBerry Junior High School, and DeBerry High School. The high school is known for its athletic programs, including baseball, basketball, and football. The school's mascots are the Tigers and the Lady Tigers. The DeBerry Municipal Airport is located two miles west of the community. The airport has a single 3,000-foot (910 m) runway. The Louis H. Adamson Tangent West Texas Legends Museum, which is dedicated to the history of the West Texas region, is located in DeBerry. The museum is named after Louis H. Adamson, a native of DeBerry who was a writer and collector of folklore. DeBerry has one church, the First Baptist Church. The church, which is located at the corner of 2nd Street and Pine Street, has been in operation since the early 1900s. The community has a number of historical buildings that are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The DeBerry Hotel, which is located at the intersection of U.S. 287 and Texas Drive, was built in the early 1900s and is one of the few remaining examples of an early 20th-century hotel in Texas. The hotel was added to the National Register in 1985. The DeBerry School, which is located at the intersection of 3rd Street and Sycamore Street, was built in the early 1900s and was added to the National Register in 1986. The Trinity County Airport Office, which is located at the DeBerry Municipal Airport, was built in the early 1940s and was added to the National Register in 1995. DeBerry is also home to the Trinity County State Jail, which is located at the intersection of 2nd Street and Cedar Street. The jail, which was built in the early 1900s, is one of the oldest still-standing jails in Texas. The jail was added to the National Register in 1985. DeBerry is a popular destination for hunters and fishermen, as the area is home to a variety of wildlife and offers access to several lakes and rivers. The community is also a popular destination for birdwatchers, as the area is home to a variety of bird species. The community is located in the Texas Forest Trail, a scenic byway that runs through the forests of East Texas. The byway is a popular destination for tourists and offers a variety of activities, including hiking, biking, and horseback riding. DeBerry is located approximately 10 miles (16.1 km) from the Texas-Louisiana state line and approximately 30 miles (48.3 km) from the city of Tyler, Texas. The community is located in the Central Time Zone. As of the 2010 census, the population of the DeBerry Census-designated place was 1,086. The population has decreased since then.

The Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) is a Canadian crown corporation that manages the pension funds of federal public servants, members of the Canadian Forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. PSP Investments is one of Canada's largest investors and, as of 2018, had C$201.5 billion of assets under management. The board was created in 1996 to assume the role of managing the Public Service Pension Plan (PSPP), which was originally managed by the Public Service Investment Department. PSP Investments has been an independent organization since it was established, although it remains accountable to the Parliament of Canada. The organization's primary purpose is to provide funding for the pensions of public servants, members of the Canadian Forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police through the investment of those pension funds. PSP Investments also provides investment management services to other Canadian pension funds, notably the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan and the Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System. As of 2018, PSP Investments had C$201.5 billion of assets under management, of which about 65 per cent was in the public equity market, and about 25 per cent was in fixed income. The remaining 10 per cent was in alternative assets, including real estate, infrastructure, private equity, and absolute return strategies. As of 31 December 2020, the net assets of PSP Investments were $204.3 billion. In March 2022, the Government of Canada appointed a new board of directors for a three-year term, with the exception of the chair, who can be reappointed for a maximum of 10 years. The board of directors is responsible for providing strategic direction to PSP Investments and overseeing its operations. In November 2022, the Government of Canada reappointed Gordon Reid as chair of the board of directors for a one-year term.

Tony Brown (born February 21, 1954 in Detroit, Michigan) is an American record producer, songwriter, musician, and inventor. He has produced over 30 Top 10 Billboard R&B chart hits and 8 Top 10 Billboard Hot 100 hits. In 1975, Brown founded the record label Brownmark Records. He has also been a songwriter and producer for Motown Records and has written and produced for artists such as James Brown, Michael Bolton, and The Temptations. In the early 1980s, Brown was a member of the band Brighton with Steve Hufton, and they released one album on RCA Records. In 1985, Brown formed the band Contagious with Steve Arrington, Dwayne Cook, and Darius Barnaby, and they released two albums on the Brownmark label. Brown has also been a producer and songwriter for films such as Hairspray 2:HAIRSPRAYGOLDEN Olimpics, and has composed music for films such as Do the Right Thing, White Men Can't Jump, and The Bodyguard. In the late 1980s, Brown founded the record label brownmark records inc, and the publishing company Brownmark Music.

SMS Deutschland (1914) SMS Deutschland was the second dreadnought battleship of the German Kaiserliche Marine. She was named after the German Nation (Deutsche Reich), in accordance with the German tradition of naming dreadnoughts after important regions and cities of Germany. SMS Deutschland was laid down at the Kaiserliche Werft shipyard in Kiel in the summer of 1913, launched on 18 June 1914, and commissioned into the High Seas Fleet on 15 October 1915. She was armed with ten 30.5 cm SK L/50 naval guns in five twin gun turrets, and could steam at a top speed of 21.8 knots. The ship had a crew of 1,458 officers and enlisted men. Deutschland served in the Battle of Dogger Bank in January 1915, and then in Operation Albion in October 1917, during which she provided naval gunfire support to German forces operating in Russia. She also saw significant action in Operation Michael, and in the Second Battle of Heligoland Bight in 1917. She was assigned to the task force assigned to Operation Sea Lion in 1940, though the operation was canceled. She spent the rest of the war serving in a variety of roles, including as a prison ship. Deutschland was sunk as a target ship by American heavy bombers in 1946. Deutschland was the second of five German dreadnoughts to be sunk by the Royal Air Force and the Royal Navy during the Second World War, after the sinking of the in September 1939, and before the sinking of the in December 1944.

Eurosignal is the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERS) train protection system used in Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, and Switzerland. The operational part of the system, the Eurosignal Type Z1, is an automatic train protection (ATP) system. Type Z1 is an evolution of the German Linienzugbeeinflussung (LZB) system, and has been designed to be interoperable with the ERTMS/ETCS system used in most other European countries. The Eurosignal system is designed for the operation of passenger and freight trains. It provides a continuous speed control, limiting the speed of a train to a value specified for the track ahead. This is done by transmitting a speed code to the train, which the onboard computer compares to the speed limit specified for the train. If the speed limit is exceeded, or if the driver fails to acknowledge an alarm caused by a critical signal, the system will automatically brake the train until it has slowed down enough to be able to stop before an obstacle or before entering a block that is not protected by the system. The system can be overridden by the driver, but only by actively operating the brake. The system will then give way to the driver, provided that the driver's action is appropriate for the situation. The system will resume control if the driver does not operate the brake appropriately. The Eurosignal system is an improvement on the older LZB system, which only provides a form of train protection. The Eurosignal system provides both a train protection system and a traffic management system. The traffic management system provides a means of centrally controlling and monitoring the movement of trains. It also provides a means of controlling the train's speed. The train protection system provides a means of detecting and responding to safety hazards, such as an obstacle on the track, or a train approaching a red signal. The train protection system will automatically apply the brakes if the train is in danger.

Australopithecus africanus is a species of the genus Australopithecus that lived from around 2.9 million years ago to around 2.3 million years ago. It is known from a single type specimen, discovered in a lime mine at Sterkfontein, South Africa, in the 1930s, as well as from other fossils found at the same site in the 1970s and 1990s. A. africanus is a possible ancestor of modern humans, as it is known to be bipedal and was once considered to be the first known species to have used stone tools (this is now known to have been done by the earlier species Homo habilis). It is also thought to be the first species to have used fire. The type specimen, known as StW 573, is a single, incomplete skeleton of a juvenile male. StW 573 was discovered in a chamber of the Sterkfontein caves in 1936 by Robert Broom and John T. Robinson, and was the first early hominid fossil to be discovered in South Africa. After its discovery, the species was originally described as a member of the genus Homo, and was named as Homo africanus by Robinson in 1944. However, it was later realised that the species was more similar to the genus of the original type specimen, Australopithecus, and was reclassified as such in 1946. Further research has shown that the species is likely to be intermediate between the bipedal but otherwise chimpanzee-like Australopithecus afarensis and the fully human genus Homo, and as such its name has been changed to Australopithecus africanis. A. africanus is thought to have been similar to A. afarensis in body size, but with a more compact and less elongated skull, and with the facial region less projecting and the brow region more vertical. The face is relatively flat, with large brow-ridges and large molar teeth. Postcranially, it is characterised by a long, barrel-shaped torso, short, robust arms, and a relatively long, low femur. Several other fossils from the same site have been found to be conspecific with the type specimen, including the 1995 discovery of a partial skeleton, StW 578, which was the first fossil to be found in the same chamber as the type specimen. The site of the find, in Chamber B of the Sterkfontein cave system, is considered to be a unique area for palaeontological research, as the caves have preserved many fragile fossils that would otherwise have been destroyed. A. africanus is thought to have lived between 2.9 million years ago and 2.3 million years ago. It was a contemporary of the species Homo habilis, and may have been its ancestor. It is also thought to be a possible ancestor of the species Homo rudolfensis, which lived around the same time in East Africa. A. africanus is thought to have been a scavenger, but possibly also a hunter, as it is known to have used stone tools. It is also thought to be the first known species to have used fire.

CT Rei Pelé, or simply Rei Pelé, is a Brazilian football club from the city of Barretos, in the northern state of São Paulo. The club was founded on January 1, 1937, and plays its home games at the Estádio Rei Pelé, which has a seating capacity of 8,560. The club's greatest achievement was in 1987, when it won the Campeonato Paulista, the top-flight football league in the state of São Paulo, after beating Corinthians 2–0 in the final game. The club has also won the Campeonato Paulista Série A2, the second division of the São Paulo state league, on three occasions (in 1970, 1976 and 1999). Rei Pelé is one of the smallest clubs to have ever won the São Paulo state championship, and one of only two clubs from outside the city of São Paulo to have won it in the last 40 years (the other being XV de Piracicaba in 1978). The club's name is a reference to the Brazilian legend Edson Arantes do Nascimento, better known as Pelé, who was born in the nearby city of Santos. The club's logo is a stylized image of the player.

Killybegs (Irish: Na Cealaibheaga) is a town in County Donegal in the Ulster province of Ireland. It is the largest fishing port in Ireland and is often referred to as the " busiest fishing port in Europe". The town is situated on the south coast of the county, on the Atlantic Ocean, near the mouth of the River Fintown (or Finvoy). The town's name is derived from the Irish words _Céal_ (pron. "kaal") meaning "sheltered", and _Beag_ (pron. "beg") meaning "small". Killybegs was once the central base of the Irish fishing industry, but due to overfishing and severe depletion of the fish stocks, the industry has experienced a dramatic decline. The town's dependence on the fishing industry has made it vulnerable to the ups and downs of the fishing trade and the loss of a large number of jobs has caused the population to decrease significantly in recent years. In the 2006 census, the population of the town was 1,232. The 2011 census recorded a population of 1,068. There is evidence of ancient settlement in the area. A number of ringforts and passage graves are in the vicinity of the town. The ruins of the early Christian church of Kilteevoey are near the town. The church is built on the site of an earlier monastery, founded by an order of nuns in the 6th century. The monastery was dedicated to the Virgin Mary, and the nuns were known as the "Sisters of the Final End". Killybegs is a sheltered natural harbour. In the 18th and 19th centuries, it was a major fishing port, primarily because of its proximity to the rich fishing grounds of the Donegal Bay and the Irish Sea. During the Second World War, Killybegs was a base for the Royal Navy's Atlantic convoys. In recent times, Killybegs has become a popular tourist destination. There are a number of hotels and bed and breakfast accommodation in and around the town. The town also has a fine 18th-century church, which was built by the Franciscans. The town's central location makes it a good base for exploring the south and west of County Donegal.

II Riigikogu The II Riigikogu was the second legislature of the Republic of Estonia. The Riigikogu was elected by popular vote on 12–15 March 1934. The sessions took place from 5 April 1934 to 26 July 1937 in the Toompea Palace. There were 80 members. The second legislature was elected in a much more democratic manner than the first one, as the plurality voting system was replaced by proportional representation. The elections were held using the party list system, with each voter having two votes: one for the party and one for the candidate. The elected legislature was the first to have a legitimate term, as the first legislature was elected in the 1930 Soviet coup d'état in Estonia. Although the Soviet occupation had officially ended, the Soviet authorities still had some influence in the political life of Estonia. The leading party in the II Riigikogu was the National Unity Party, which was actually a front for the Communist Party of Estonia. The executive branch was dominated by theSecure and Stable Propaganda Group, which was also Soviet-influenced. After the elections, the new II Riigikogu had its first session on 5 April 1934. The main item on the agenda was the election of the speaker of the Riigikogu, which was won by Johannes Vares. The II Riigikogu was the first legislature to have a vice speaker, which was Paul Schurmann. The secretary of the Riigikogu was Hilja Poldsam. The National Unity Party formed a coalition government with the Farmers' Assemblies. The government was led by Prime Minister Karl August Eska.

SMK Vivekananda, Brickfields SMK Vivekananda, Brickfields is a secondary school in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. It is named after the Indian Hindu philosopher and saint Vivekananda. In the early days, the school was situated at a temporary site at theamide area in Brickfields. It then moved to its present site along Jalan Berjaya at the Brickfields area in the mid-1960s. The school is a co-educational school from Form 1 to Form 5. It is also a residential school for its Form 6 students. The school is administered by the Kuala Lumpur Education Department, Malaysia. The school is equipped with two basketball courts, one volleyball court, and two sepak takraw courts. The school also has a large field for students to play football, hockey, and athletics. The school's current principal is Mrs. Jayanthi Naidu. The school's student body is divided into four houses, each named after a leader of Indian nationalism: Cama House, named after Mangalampalli Kavasam Chandramouli, a medical doctor, philanthropist, and participant in the Indian independence movement Gandhi House, named after Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, the leader of the Indian independence movement Rao House, named after P.V. Narasimha Rao, the former Prime Minister of India Singham House, named after the character in the Indian movie Singam

Paltadacho Munis Paltadacho Munis (born ca. 1880 – died December 5, 1949) was a Mexican chemist and researcher of Mexican handcrafts, particularly those made of silver. He was born in Mexico City to a French father and a Mexican mother. After finishing school in Mexico, he went to France to study chemistry. He returned to Mexico in 1910, shortly before the start of the Mexican Revolution, and worked in the Laboratory of the National School of Chemical Sciences, where he was appointed director in 1927. In addition to his research on silver, he also studied and promoted the use of indigenous Mexican materials such as obsidian and amate paper. Munis was a founding member of the Mexican Society for the Development of Handicrafts, an organization that promoted the production of traditional Mexican crafts. In the 1920s, he began to research the properties of silver and the processes used to extract it from its ores. He published numerous articles on the subject, and his work helped to establish the silver industry in Mexico as a major economic force. In addition to his research, he also worked to promote the use of silver in Mexican handcrafts, and he was a strong advocate for the preservation of traditional Mexican design and craftsmanship. In 1941, Munis was named president of the Mexican Society for the Development of Handicrafts. He held the position until his death in 1949.

Tanikaze Kajinosuke ( gauges: January 21, 1596 — July 7, 1666), also known as Kajinosuke Kami (上 Kajinosuke), was a Japanese samurai and a retainer of the Matsudaira clan of Mikawa. He was the second head of the Tanikaze branch of the Kajinosuke family, and was the 1st Lord of Shioda Castle in Suruga Province. He was the second son of the famous general and poet Kajinosuke Fusanosuke. He was adopted into the family of his mother, the Asano clan, and was granted the surname "Tanikaze" after the name of his mother's estate. In 1632, he became the second head of the Tanikaze-Kajinosuke family, and inherited the estate of his father in the village of Shioda in the province of Suruga. Like his father, Kajinosuke was a great poet and scholar, and a friend of the famous poet Matsuo Bashō. His work was featured in the notable anthology of Japanese poetry known as the Six Hundred Poets (or, Renga Risshi), and his poems were included in almost all the major poetic collections of the time. His son, Hironori, was the third and last head of the Tanikaze-Kajinosuke family.

Save Dat Money is the second studio album by American rapper E-40. It was released on March 7, 2006, via Sick Wid It and Warner Bros. Records. The album was produced by E-40, Mike Mosley, and Sam Bostic, and features production by a host of other beatmakers, including J. Black, DJ Felli Fel, DJ Quik, and Battlecat. The album was the first release by E-40's own label, Sick Wid It, to be distributed by a major label, as well as the first to be released via digital download. The album debuted at number 4 on the Billboard 200, selling 86,000 copies in its first week. It was certified Gold by the RIAA on June 7, 2006, and has sold 681,000 copies in the United States to date. The album's lead single was "Tell Me When to Go" featuring Keak da Sneak. The song was a huge hit, making it to the top of the Billboard Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart, and is E-40's biggest hit to date. The second single was "Blow Me A Kiss", which featured actor and singer Chris Brown. The song was not as successful as "Tell Me When to Go", but was still a minor hit. The album received positive reviews from critics. It holds a score of 72 on Metacritic, indicating "Generally favorable reviews", and a score of 79 on ROC, indicating "Favorable reviews".

James Ferguson (born October 31, 1950) is an American politician and member of the Democratic Party who served as the 38th governor of Missouri from 2005 to 2009. He was the state's first Democratic governor since 1989 and the first African American governor in the state's history. Ferguson was born in St. Louis, Missouri. He graduated from Catholic schools, then earned a bachelor's degree from Harvard University in 1972 and a J.D. from Harvard Law School in 1975. He joined the St. Louis law firm Bryan Cave in 1975, and became a partner in 1985. In 1989 he married Elizabeth "Betsy" Walker, a fellow lawyer at the firm. The couple had two daughters, Susan (b. 1991) and Catherine (b. 1994), before their divorce in 2001. Ferguson later married his second wife, First Lady Georganne Watson, in March 2004. Ferguson became involved with the Democratic Party during the campaign of former Missouri governor Mel Carnahan, who was running for the United States Senate in 2000. After Carnahan's death in a plane crash three weeks before the election, Ferguson was appointed by Missouri Governor Bob Holden to replace him on the November ballot. He went on to win the election, defeating Republican Congresswoman Jo Ann Emerson by a margin of 52% to 48%. Ferguson was sworn in as governor on January 5, 2005, and re-elected in 2006. He received an honorary degree from Harris-Stowe State University in 2005. In 2007, he was honored with the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award for his work in the election of 2004. Ferguson's accomplishments as governor include a plan to provide health insurance to uninsured workers, a new program to help students pay for college, and legislation to protect the environment. He also worked to improve the state's economy, and to make the state's government more efficient and transparent. In 2008, Ferguson was the subject of a recall election, in which voters were asked whether he should be removed from office. The recall effort was unsuccessful, as the measure failed to obtain the necessary number of signatures. Ferguson left office on January 8, 2009, and was succeeded by Republican governor Matt Blunt. In 2013, he was appointed to the United States Civil Rights Commission by President Barack Obama. He served as chairman of the commission from 2013 to 2014.

Goldman child abduction case The Goldman child abduction case involved the July 2, 1964, kidnapping of eight-year-old Susan Goldman from the front yard of her home in the Hollywood Hills neighborhood of Los Angeles, California. The case was notable for the efforts of her father, Murder Squad detective Harry Goldman, to obtain the return of his daughter. After her return, Susan Goldman was able to identify her kidnapper, and the case was the first of its kind to result in a conviction and a death penalty sentence. Harry Goldman was a veteran of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD), and the father of eight-year-old Susan. On the afternoon of July 2, 1964, Goldman was at work when he received a phone call from his wife, telling him that Susan had gone to the front yard to play and had not returned. He immediately drove home, and found that a neighbor had seen a man carrying a small child to a car, but had not recognized the man or the car. Goldman notified the police, and a search began. The search included a request by Goldman for the assistance of the Press, and the story was covered extensively by the media. The search continued for several days, with the assistance of police dogs, a police helicopter, and the National Guard. Goldman and his wife held a press conference on July 4, in which they pleaded for the return of their daughter, and stated that they would offer a $5,000 reward for information leading to her return. The couple also appeared on the July 5 episode of the television program This Is Your Life, hosted by Ralph Edwards, to publicize the search for their daughter. In the episode, Goldman and his wife described their life with Susan, and their hopes for her return. On July 14, 1964, the body of a child was found in a shallow grave in the mountains of Malibu, in western Los Angeles County. The body was identified as that of Susan Goldman. The cause of death was determined to be a gunshot wound to the head. In the investigation of the crime, police learned that a man had been seen carrying a child in the neighborhood where Susan lived, and had also been seen acting strangely in the neighborhood a few days earlier. The man was identified as 23-year-old Arnold Munk, a one-time friend of the family who had a history of mental illness. Munk was found to be in possession of Susan's clothes and jewelry, and was identified by Susan's brother as the man he had seen carrying his sister. Munk was charged with the murder, and went to trial in December 1964. At the trial, Goldman took the stand and identified Munk as the man he had seen carrying his daughter. Munk was convicted of the murder, and sentenced to death. In January 1965, Munk was sentenced to death in the gas chamber. In June 1965, Munk was executed in the gas chamber at San Quentin Prison. Goldman died in December 1993. In 1994, the case was the subject of a made-for-television movie, entitled The Other Side of the Screen: The Story of the Goldman Family. The movie was based on a book by Harry Goldman, written in 1985.

Housing action trust A housing action trust is a type of community-based organization which aims to improve housing conditions in the areas in which it operates. It is a type of housing company, and is sometimes referred to as a "housing cooperative", although it is not necessarily a cooperative, nor is it always a not-for-profit. The aim of a housing action trust is to improve the quality of housing in a particular area, usually by improving the housing stock, and sometimes by building new homes. They also sometimes manage housing services, such as repairs and maintenance. In the United States, housing action trusts are typically non-profit organizations which are set up to address housing issues in a particular community. In the United Kingdom, they are sometimes for-profit companies. They are generally funded by a combination of public and private sources, and may also generate some of their own income. Housing action trusts can be a useful tool for local communities to address housing issues in their area. They can help to improve the quality of housing, and can also help to build new homes. They can also help to provide housing services, such as repairs and maintenance. However, they are not a long-term solution to housing problems, and they are not a substitute for proper housing policy.

Limni, Euboea Limni (Greek: Λίμνη, [ˈlimnɛː]), is a town in the central part of Euboea, Greece. It is the seat of the municipality of Karystos. It is located on the west coast of the island, on a bay between Capes Dafnias and Karvounades. Its population in 2011 was 1,325. There are several beaches in the vicinity, the most popular being that of Limni. The beach has been awarded the Blue Flag. Very close to Limni, at a distance of approximately 1 km, there is a beach with black sand and a small port, known as Ai Sostis (or Aï-Soussi). The town has a small port, which provides a daily connection to Skyros and Kymi on the island of Evia. In the area of Limni, several olive trees of great age can be found. One of them, known as "Mavri olive tree", has been declared a protected natural monument. The area of Limni has been inhabited since the Paleolithic era. In the 3rd century BC, Limni was one of the two harbours of the city of Eretria. The ancient city had two small theatres and an acropolis. It also had a temple dedicated to Artemis, where many offerings were found. In the 2nd century AD, a basilica dedicated to the patron saint of the city, Apollo, was built. The city was destroyed in 1398 by the Ottoman Turks. The inhabitants fled to the mountains, where they founded the village of Karystos. In the following years, the area of Limni was abandoned. In 1880, Limni became an independent community and the seat of a municipality, which in 1964 was united with that of Karystos.

Many artists and writers began to question traditional Japanese art and culture, and to explore the relationship between art and society. This period of intellectual and artistic exploration came to be known as the "Modernist" movement. Hidekatsu was one of the leaders of the Modernist movement in Japan. He was a prolific writer and artist, and his work often featured bold, experimental styles. He was a strong advocate for the importance of art in society, and he often spoke out against the conservative, traditionalist art establishment in Japan. In the early 20th century, Hidekatsu's work began to be noticed and appreciated by international art critics and collectors. He was featured in many international exhibitions, and his work was acquired by museums and private collectors around the world. In the late 1930s, Hidekatsu's work took a more political turn. He began to use his art to criticize the Japanese military and government, and to protest against the increasing militarization and nationalism of Japanese society. During World War II, Hidekatsu was arrested and imprisoned by the Japanese government for his anti-war art and writings. He was released from prison in 1944, but he was rearrested and executed by the Japanese authorities in 1945. After the war, Hidekatsu's work was widely celebrated in Japan and around the world. Many of his paintings and writings were exhibited and published, and he became known as one of the first "modern" Japanese artists.

Suicide of Tyler Clementi The suicide of Tyler Clementi was the second-degree murder of college student Tyler Clementi, who jumped to his death from the George Washington Bridge on September 22, 2010. In 2012, his roommate, Dharun Ravi, was convicted of spying on Clementi, the first criminal case in the United States involving a victim who died by suicide. On the evening of September 20, 2010, Tyler Clementi, a freshman at Rutgers University, bid farewell to his friends and took his life by jumping off the George Washington Bridge into the Hudson River. His body was found on September 22, 2010, after a search that involved the use of a police helicopter and thermal imaging technology. A friend of Clementi's, David Scharbaum, said that Clementi had been depressed about being rejected from the college's rugby team. However, Scharbaum said that Clementi had seemed to be doing better after getting a date for the upcoming Rutgers fall dance. Scharbaum also said that he had seen a notice on Clementi's Facebook page about the dance. "I saw that he was excited about it," Scharbaum said. Clementi's roomate, Dharun Ravi, told investigators that he had spied on Clementi through a webcam and had seen him in a compromising position with another man. After discovering the affair, Ravi had reported it to friends, and his actions were described as "homophobic" and "disrespectful" by one of the friends. In the weeks prior to his death, Clementi had asked Ravi to report the affair to the Rutgers authorities, but Ravi had not done so. Mount Druitt railway station is a heritage-listed railway station located on the Main Western line in Mount Druitt, New South Wales, Australia. The property was added to the New South Wales State Heritage Register on 2 April 1999. The station is located 72 kilometres (45 mi) from Sydney Central station. The station was built in 1884 and is the second station to have been built on this site. The original station was a simple bog standard design, however in the early 20th century it was decided that the station needed to be upgraded to a more substantial design. The station was subsequently rebuilt in concrete with a barrel roofed platform shelter and a distinctive and unique signal box, which is one of the few to have been built in that style in the state. The station was closed in 1991 due to the construction of the Mount Druitt Hospital and the subsequent rerouting of the Main Western line. The station was then subsequently rebuilt in 1998 to the same design as the original, with the signal box being relocated to Blacktown. The station is now the terminating point for the Blacktown-Mount Druitt via Richmond service.

Master of Health Administration The Master of Health Administration (MHA) is a professional degree in health administration that prepares students for leadership and management roles in hospitals, health systems, and other healthcare organizations. The degree is designed to provide a broad perspective on the American health system as well as an intensive focus on the skills necessary to be an effective health administrator. The MHA degree is generally a two-year, 44-credit hour program. The curriculum is designed to provide a broad understanding of the complex health care system as well as an intensive focus on the skills necessary to be an effective health administrator. In the first year, students complete a core of courses that provide a broad perspective on the American health system. The second year is devoted to more specialized courses in health administration. Upon completion of the MHA degree, students are prepared for leadership and management roles in hospitals, health systems, and other healthcare organizations. The MHA degree is not designed to prepare students for clinical health care roles, such as physicians, nurses, or therapists. The MHA is a highly specialized degree that is not intended for individuals who are pursuing a career in a clinical health profession, such as medicine, nursing, or therapy. The MHA is designed for individuals who wish to pursue a career in health administration, which involves the management and administration of health care organizations. The MHA degree is offered by many colleges and universities around the world. In the United States, the MHA is offered by many of the leading graduate schools in health administration.

Asensio Nebot Arquitectura Asensio Nebot Arquitectura is a Spanish architectural practice established in 1994 by Spanish architect Asensio Nebot. The studio has developed numerous projects in Spain and other countries. Among its most significant works are the Spanish Pavilion at the Expo 2000 in Germany, the betrayal of the Spanish Pavilion at the Expo 2008 in Spain, the Andorran Pavilion at the Expo 2008, the Groupama Stadium in Lyon, the City Hall in Amos, Quebec, and the City Hall in Montreuil, Paris. Asensio Nebot Arquitectura has received a number of awards, including the 1998 FAD Prize for the Monolith of Expo.02 in Switzerland, the 1999 Spanish Architecture and Urbanism Prize for the Media-Tic Center in Barcelona, the 2000 Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Spanish Pavilion at Expo 2000, the 2003 Mies van der Rohe Award for the City Hall in Amos, Quebec, the 2006 European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture for the City Hall in Montreuil, and the 2007 International Urban Project Award for the New Cordoba City Hall.

Wengernalp Railway The Wengernalp Railway (German: Wengernalpbahn) is a metre gauge railway in Switzerland. It runs from Lauterbrunnen to a station at the foot of the Wengen Alps, and was opened in 1890. The line runs for 5.33 km, and has a total of 33 stops. The Wengernalp Railway is the only rack and pinion railway in Switzerland, and was the first electric railway to be built in the country. The line was constructed to provide a link between the village of Wengen and the Lauterbrunnen valley. The line was designed by Robert Gerwig, and was built by the Wengernalp Railway Company, which was formed in 1886. The company was taken over by the Wengen AG in 1922, and the line was then sold to the Jungfraubahn AG in 1963. The Wengernalp Railway uses a Fell rack system, and is powered by a 1,000 volt DC electricity supply. The line has two sections of track, which are connected by a rack section. The first section runs for 2.55 km, and the second for 2.78 km. The gradient of the line is 1 in 2.5, and the maximum speed is 10 km/h. The Wengernalp Railway is operated by the Wengen AG, and is integrated into the Bernese Oberland Transport Network. The line is served by trains running between Lauterbrunnen and Wengen, and by trains running between Grindelwald and Wengen. The line also provides a connection to the Jungfrau Railway at the Kleine Scheidegg station.

Indirect DNA damage Indirect DNA damage, or indirect DNA injury, is a form of DNA damage that is not directly caused by an external agent. Rather, it is caused by a chain of reactions, which can be initiated by a variety of external agents, including ionizing radiation, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, and non-ionizing radiation, as well as chemical agents and viruses. The type of DNA damage produced will depend on the type of external agent, the dose, and the cellular context. The end result is a modification of the DNA that can lead to genetic instability, which means that the genetic information encoded in the DNA is no longer stably transmitted from one generation to the next. Indirect DNA damage can result in a variety of genetic alterations, including point mutations, chromosomal rearrangements, and gene deletions. These genetic alterations can lead to cell death, genetic instability, and cancer. The main way that indirect DNA damage causes genetic alterations is through the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage DNA. ROS can be formed by a variety of external agents, including ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, as well as chemical agents and viruses. These agents can cause the formation of free radicals, which are unstable molecules that can react with DNA to produce genetic alterations. Indirect DNA damage can also be caused by the formation of DNA adducts, which are chemical compounds that can bind to DNA and cause genetic alterations. These adducts can be formed by a variety of external agents, including ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, as well as chemical agents and viruses.

The Naval Intelligence Department was a department of the British Admiralty responsible for gathering military intelligence about the enemy during the First World War. It was established in 1914 and existed for the duration of the war. The department was led by Captain William Hall. The department had a number of sub-departments including the Trade Division and the Enemy Submarine Section. The Trade Division was responsible for gathering intelligence about enemy trade and merchant shipping. The Enemy Submarine Section was responsible for gathering intelligence about enemy submarines. The department also had a number of other sub-departments including the Intelligence Division, the Submarine Intelligence Section, and the Mine Warfare Section. The Naval Intelligence Department was a highly secret department and its existence was not revealed to the public until after the war. It played a vital role in the war effort by providing the British Navy with valuable intelligence about the enemy. The department was dissolved in 1919.

Alan Menken (born July 22, 1949) is an American composer who has scored over 60 films and has won numerous awards, including three Academy Awards, three Golden Globes, three Grammy Awards, and a Tony Award. Menken was born in New York City, the son of Judith and Norman Menken. His father was a dentist and his mother was a stage performer who inspired his love of show business. He was raised in a Jewish household. At the age of seven, he started playing the piano, largely by ear, and soon began to write his own songs. Menken attended the High School for Performing Arts in Manhattan, and graduated from New York University with a BFA in 1971. He studied music with Paul Sayling, a concert pianist, and composition with Henry Cowell, John Corigliano, and David Diamond. He became a student of Leonard Kastle, an authority on the works of Mozart, at the Manhattan School of Music in 1971, but dropped out after three months in favor of a career in pop music. In the 1970s, Menken worked with his friend, singer-songwriter Paul Jabara, on several songs written for films, including the disco-themed movie Thank God It's Friday. Their songs, including the chart-topping "Last Dance" and "Hot Stuff", helped to popularize disco music. Together, they also wrote "The Main Event" for the 1980 film of the same name, which was the first time that Menken had ever worked on a film's score. Basto (horse) Basto (1984 – 21 October 2002) was a British-bred, Irish-trained thoroughbred racehorse and sire. He was the only horse to win the race now known as the Prix Jean Prat (at Longchamp) three times. Basto was a son of the Irish-bred stallion Kris, a half-brother to the champion sire Sadler's Wells, out of the British-bred mare Cassiopeia, a daughter of the dual Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe winner, Alleged. He was bred in the United Kingdom by his owner, Prince A. A. Faisal. At age two, Basto won the Group Two Railway Stakes at the Curragh. At age three, he won the Group One Prix Jean Prat at Longchamp, beating a field that included the top-rated three-year-old, Elmaamul. At age four, he won a second Prix Jean Prat, in the process becoming the only horse to win the race three times. At age five, he won the Group Two Lennox Stakes at Goodwood, and in October, he won the Group One Prix de la Forêt at Longchamp, beating the great miler, Dubai Millennium. At the end of his racing career, Basto was retired to stud in Japan, where he sired more than 800 foals. In Japan, he is known as Batso (バツォ). He died on 21 October 2002, due to heart failure.

AK-103 The AK-103 is a selective-fire, gas-operated 7.62×39mm assault rifle, manufactured by Kalashnikov. First introduced in 1999, it is the third generation of the Kalashnikov rifle. Lieutenant-general A lieutenant-general (lt-gen) is a general officer in the British Army, Royal Marines or Royal Air Force of the United Kingdom. The rank is also used in the British Army and Royal Marines reserve forces. The equivalent rank in the Royal Navy is rear-admiral (rd-adml) and in the Royal Air Force is air vice-marshal (av-mstr). The British Army and Royal Marines have a two-tier general officer structure: general officers (i.e. general, lieutenant-general, major-general, and captain) and field officers (i.e. major, lieutenant-colonel, colonel, and brigadier). The rank of lieutenant-general is equivalent to a one-star general officer; the other general officers are two- and three-star ranks. The Royal Air Force has no lieutenant-general rank, but its Royal Air Force Air Cadets organisation does. The origins of the lieutenant-general rank are complex. In the 17th century, the major was the second-in-command of a regiment and the lieutenant-colonel was the third-in-command. During the 18th century, the rank of lieutenant-colonel was elevated to that of colonel, the former rank being renamed lieutenant-colonel. However, the term lieutenant-colonel was used in a different context, to denote the second-in-command of a regiment, until the middle of the 18th century. In the 18th and 19th centuries, the terms lieutenant-colonel and colonel were used interchangeably, both meaning the second-in-command of a regiment. The British Army introduced the rank of lieutenant-colonel in replace of that of major in Cavalry and Indian regiments in 1856, and in the British, King's (later Royal) Army, in 1871. In 1877, the British Army introduced the ranks of lieutenant-colonel and colonel in the Royal Artillery and Royal Engineers. The Royal Marines had already been using these two ranks since the 1840s. The Royal Air Force did not have a rank of lieutenant-colonel equivalent until the Second World War, when it was used in the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve and the Royal Canadian Air Force. The Royal New Zealand Air Force had a rank of lieutenant-colonel from 1942 to 1968. The lieutenant-general is a senior officer rank, generally equivalent to the American military rank of lieutenant colonel in the United States Army and the United States Marine Corps. It is also comparable to the rank of captain in the other uniformed services of the United States, and to the rank of first mate in the British Royal Navy. In the British Army and Royal Marines, the rank of lieutenant-general can also be awarded as a military dignity, in which case it is not a rank, but an appointment, and the holder does not formally outrank other general officers. A lieutenant-general in this case is an officer of the rank of major-general, but holding the position of second-in-command of a major formation (such as a division or an aircraft carrier). The holder of the position of lieutenant-general is generally a highly experienced officer of the rank of major-general, and will have held the position of major-general for some years. The equivalent military dignity in the Royal Air Force is air commodore. The air commodore is not a rank but an appointment, and the holder does not formally outrank other officers of the rank of group captain. An air commodore is normally a group captain, but holds the position of second-in-command of a group (such as a Royal Air Force group, which is equivalent to an army division, or a Royal Air Force station, which is equivalent to a Royal Navy ship). The Royal Air Force Air Cadets has the military rank of lieutenant-general (LTGEN) for officers of the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve (Training Branch) of the Royal Air Force Air Cadets. The Royal Air Force Air Cadets also has the military rank of air commodore (AIRCDRE) for officers of the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve (Training Branch) of the Royal Air Force Air Cadets.

Lolium perenne is used for many purposes. It is used as a forage for livestock, as a lawn grass, and as a ground cover. It is also used in agriculture, landscaping, and in many other ways.
