David Hoyle (priest) David Hoyle was born at New York, New York, on January 27, 1911, the son of David Hoyle, a newspaper editor, and his wife Florence (née Woodbury), a musician. He was educated at St. Paul's School, London, and at New College, Oxford, where he read classics. He then trained for the priesthood at Cuddesdon College, near Reading, and was ordained a priest in the Church of England in 1936. Hoyle served as a curate at All Saints',Margaret Street, London, from 1936 to 1939, and as a minor canon at St. Paul's Cathedral, London, from 1939 to 1946. In 1946, he became the vicar of St. Luke's, Goathurst, in Kent. In 1948, he was appointed a Proctor in Convocation at the University of London. In 1950, he was made the vicar of All Saints', Margaret Street, in London, where he had been a curate. In 1951, he became the canon residentiary at St. Paul's Cathedral, in London. In 1961, he was made the archdeacon of London. In 1968, he was appointed the bishop of the new Anglican Diocese of London, in the Province of Ontario, Canada. Hoyle was the author of several books, including The Way of a Man (1940), The Art of Parish Ministry (1948), The Church and the University (1951), The Christian Priest Today (1961), and The Church in the World (1971). Hoyle was a strong supporter of the charismatic movement and was a leader in the field of evangelism. In his later years, he was a residentiary canon at St. Paul's Cathedral, London, and a member of the House of Clergy of the Cathedral. Henry James Carr (4 October 1898 – 1 June 1945) was a New Zealand-born Australian recipient of the Victoria Cross, the highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy that can be awarded to British and Commonwealth forces. Carr was born in Lyttelton, New Zealand, in 1898, the son of an English father and a Scottish mother. The family moved to Australia in 1909, settling in Sydney. Carr was educated at Crown Street Public School, and, after his father's death in 1911, at the Sydney Church of England Grammar School. He left school at the age of 15 to work for a wool firm, but later enlisted in the military, joining the 34th Battalion, an infantry unit of the Australian Imperial Force, which was raised in 1916 for service during the First World War. Carr was posted to the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1917, and was wounded in action in April 1918 during the German spring offensive. He was sent to England to recuperate, and was commissioned as a second lieutenant in September 1918. After the war, Carr returned to Australia and his old school, Sydney Church of England Grammar School, where he was a housemaster and taught English and history. In 1930, he married Gwendolen Mary Chiplin. The couple had one son, John, who also attended the Church of England Grammar School. Carr died in Sydney on 1 June 1945 and is buried in the Northern Suburbs cemetery. His Victoria Cross is displayed at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, Australia.

Romolo Valli (5 February 1927 – 19 January 2020) was an Italian actor, voice actor, director, teacher and drama critic. Born in Parma, Romolo Valli attended the Parmesan section of the Ghilda Dalla Costa Drama School, then active at the Teatro Sociale in Parma, where he obtained his first theatre experiences. He then enrolled at the Actor's Studio in London, and upon his return to Italy he started working with the Compagnia dei Ragazzi, a theatre company for young people which he directed from 1954 to 1956. He also began a long collaboration with the Festival dei Due Mondi in Spoleto, as actor, director and teacher. In 1957, Valli made his television debut, with the RAI drama La donna si diventa, then worked with the Milan-based company Il Sistema Theatro, and in 1961 he had his first role at the Piccolo Teatro in Milan, with the show I puri amanti. In 1962, he moved to Rome to work at the Teatro Nazionale, then in 1965 he started a long collaboration with the great director Giorgio Strehler, at the Piccolo Teatro in Milan, with which he toured Italy and the world, and at the Teatro Stabile in Turin. In the early 1960s, Valli also started appearing in films, with some important roles in movies by Pietro Germi, Luigi Comencini, Pietro Martellucci, Nanni Loy and Franco Indovina. In 1968, he starred in L'età del malessere, by Carlo Lizzani, and in 1970 he had a main role in L'Explosion, by Tinto Brass. In 1972, Valli was one of the founders of the Gruppo Straniero, along with Alessandro Haber, Massimo Gotta, Paolo Guidi, Carlo Giuffrè, Lorenzo Gnerre and Massimo Wertmüller. The group, who later became the Scapolati, was active until the mid-1970s and produced several shows, including Non tutto è vero, arrestedi, everything is not true, arrested, in 1973, and Controra, in 1974. In the following years, Valli focused his activities on theatre and television, appearing in numerous TV-series, and in 1988 he returned to the Piccolo Teatro in Milan, with the show The Golden Coach, an adaptation of the play by Molière, which he also directed. In the 1990s, he also started teaching, and in 1999 he was appointed head of the Scuola Holden in Turin, a school of performing arts. In 2000, Valli took part in the TV-series Incantesimo. In 2002, he was awarded the Golden Lion for his career achievements at the Venice Biennale. In 2010, he was the voice of the main character's father in the animated movie Tangled, and in 2013 he was the voice of the minister in the animated movie Frozen.

He is of Jewish (from his mother's side) and Polish-Catholic (from his father's side) descent. Weinstein began his acting career performing in an Off-Broadway production of The Little Mermaid. His first major role was as Eddie in the 1991 film Never Say Die. He also appeared in Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium, a 2008 film starring Dustin Hoffman. Weinstein was a producer on the 2009 film The Perfect Gift. Weinstein is the writer and producer of the 2011 short film, A Night at the Office. In 2012, he appeared in the television series The Secret Circle. Weinstein is married to television producer Jessica Hersh. They have two children.

ADAPT Act The ADAPT Act is bi-partisan legislation introduced by U.S. Senators Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Todd Young (R-IN) on March 3, 2017. The bill aims to increase U.S. government spending on adaptive sporting activities. The bill was passed by the Senate on September 7, 2018, and by the House on December 19, 2018. The ADAPT Act is intended to encourage community-based adaptive sports and recreation programs and improve access to adaptive sports equipment. The bill also seeks to increase the number of certified adaptive sports instructors. The bill has three main provisions. The first requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to establish a program to provide grants to eligible entities for the purpose of providing adaptive sports and recreation opportunities to disabled veterans. The second requires the Department of Defense (DOD) to provide adaptive sports equipment to eligible entities for purposes of providing adaptive sports and recreation opportunities to disabled service members. The third requires the Department of the Interior to establish a program to provide grants to eligible entities for the purpose of providing adaptive sports and recreation opportunities to disabled Native Americans. In addition, the ADAPT Act requires the VA, DOD, and Interior to designate an official to coordinate their respective adaptive sports and recreation programs.

Frederick "Freddie" Lee Scott (born May 3, 1945) is an American singer and songwriter, best known for his 1974 hit, "Rockin' Chair." Scott was born in Baltimore, Maryland, and spent his early childhood there. His family then moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where he attended grade school and high school. He graduated from John Bartram High School in 1963. He began his singing career in the mid-1960s with the soul group The Drells, with whom he recorded the songs "You Can't Run Away from Love" and "Let It All Be Music." The Drells' songs were recorded for the Detroit-based Northern Soul label, Revilot Records, and were popular with British soul fans. In the early 1970s, Scott recorded a solo album, entitled Scott's Word, for the United Nations label. The album was released in the United States, and was also popular with British audiences. The title track, "Scott's Word", was a moderate hit in the United States, and the album track "Rockin' Chair" was also popular. "Rockin' Chair" was covered by several other artists, including Michael Bolton, whose version was the most successful, peaking at number three on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1974. In the late 1970s, Scott recorded two more albums, Step by Step and Scott Free, for the British label, Victor Sylvester Records. In the 1980s, he recorded a single, "I Can't Help It", for the American label, Galaxy Records.

"By the Light of the Moon (The Vampire Diaries)" is the eighteenth episode of the fifth season and the 103rd episode overall from the supernatural drama television series The Vampire Diaries. The episode was written by Michael Grassi and was directed by Rob Hardy. It was originally aired on February 19, 2015 on The CW. In the episode, after learning from Elena that she has chosen to be with Damon, Stefan suffers from nightmares of a life he could have had with Elena. Caroline and Matt try to figure out a way to keep their secret about the pregnancy from Elena. Elsewhere, Tripp (leader of the community protection program) threatens to expose Matt and Caroline's secret to Elena, so they decide to speed up their plan to marry. At the end of the episode, Matt and Caroline get married with their friends and family in attendance, while Stefan gets drunk and crashes Jeremy and Matt's bachelor party. The episode received generally positive reviews. The episode was watched by 1.48 million viewers with a 0.6/2 share among adults aged 18–49. This episode is named after a song by The Animals. In 1492, a young Stefan is tormenting his older sister, Lily, who is to be married to a vampire named Fotis. Stefan asks for forgiveness from his sister, but she refuses, so he kills Fotis. Before she dies, Fotis curses Stefan to walk the earth as a vampire. In the present day, Stefan and Elena have been dating for six months, and Elena tells Stefan that she wants to be with Damon. Stefan is upset, and has nightmares about a life he could have had with Elena. At the end of the episode, it is revealed that the "Elena" in Stefan's nightmare was actually his sister, Lily, and the "Stefan" in the nightmare was Fotis. Lily tells Stefan that she will see him in another life, hinting that they will be together again.

Helio Vera (born 18 July 1945) is an Argentine former professional boxer who competed from 1965 to 1980. He was the South American Light Welterweight Champion, a title he won in 1967. Vera was born in Chacabuco, Buenos Aires, Argentina. Vera was a member of the Argentine Olympic team at the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City, Mexico, where he was stopped in the quarterfinals of the men's light welterweight division by eventual silver medalist Valery Limasov of the Soviet Union. Vera turned professional in 1965 and by 1967 he had won the South American Light Welterweight Championship. In 1969, he lost a close decision to the former World Welterweight Champion Curtis Cokes in a non-title fight. In 1972, he challenged the World Welterweight Champion, José Nápoles, but lost a decision. In 1974, he lost a split decision to the former World Lightweight Champion, Alfredo Pumarino, in a non-title fight. In 1975, he lost a decision to the former World Lightweight Champion, Roberto Durán, in a non-title fight. Vera retired in 1980.

Tilda Swinton Tilda Swinton (born 12 November 1960) is a British actress and model. She has won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress and the Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actress – Motion Picture for her performance in the film Michael Clayton (2007). In 2009, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress and won the Golden Globe Award for Best Actress – Motion Picture Drama for her performance in the film Burn After Reading. In 2012, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her performance in the film Moonrise Kingdom, and in 2015, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in the film Snowpiercer. She has also won the British Academy Film Award for Best Actress in a Leading Role, the Saturn Award for Best Actress on Television, and the Empire Award for Best British Actress. In 2016, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her performance in the film A Bigger Splash, and in 2017, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in the film Okja. In 2019, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her performance in the film The Favourite, and in 2020, she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in the film The Personal History of David Copperfield. Swinton has received numerous other awards and nominations for her work in film, television, and theater, including the Scottish BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Scottish Film, the British Independent Film Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a British Independent Film, the Los Angeles Film Critics Association Award for Best Actress, the New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Actress, the National Board of Review Award for Best Actress, the Chicago Film Critics Association Award for Best Actress, the Online Film Critics Society Award for Best Actress, the Empire Award for Best Actress, the Saturn Award for Best Actress, the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Leading Role, the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Motion Picture, the Golden Globe Award for Best Actress – Motion Picture Drama, and the Academy Award for Best Actress.

Joseph Gluckstein Links are a series of public art works in Manchester, England, by the artist Joe Rush. The works, commissioned by the City of Manchester, consist of a series of 100 bronze "links" scattered throughout the city, each one representing a different aspect of the city's history and culture. The links are cast from bronze, using the lost wax process, and mounted on stainless steel posts. They are intended to be stumbled upon accidentally, rather than viewed as a formal collection. The links are located in areas of the city which are not traditionally associated with public art, and are intended to be seen by people who would not normally visit a museum or art gallery. The links have been well received by the public, and have become a favourite topic of conversation in the city. In 2006, the Manchester City Council website received more than 1.5 million hits, as people attempted to find all 100 links. A book, entitled The Joseph Gluckstein Links Walk, has also been published, to help people find the links and learn more about the city. A series of 30 new links were added to the collection in 2007, to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the original link. These new links, which were designed by local school children, feature a variety of designs, including a guitar, a basketball, and a pair of glasses. In 2009, a further 30 links were added to the collection, bringing the total number of links to 100. These new links, which were designed by local artists, feature a variety of designs, including a pigeon, a bee, and a pair of lips.

Cor Boonstra (born 2 June 1944) is a Dutch politician and businessman who served as Minister of Agriculture, Nature Management, and Food Quality in the Cabinet of the Netherlands from 8 January 2003 until 22 February 2007. Boonstra was born in Noordwijk. After finishing the Hogereburgerschool in Leiden in 1962 he studied agriculture at Wageningen Agricultural University from 1962 to 1966. He then joined the family business, a farm in Noordwijk. In 1975 he became chairman of the Noordwijk agricultural cooperative. Boonstra became a member of the Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA) in 1975. He served on the CDA national board from 1987 to 1997, and again from 2000 to 2002. He was also chairman of the CDA in South Holland from 1997 to 2000. After the CDA had joined the Cabinet Balkenende I, Boonstra was asked to join the cabinet as Minister of Agriculture, Nature Management, and Food Quality. His term started on 8 January 2003. In November 2006, he announced that he would not stand for the election of 2006. His term ended on 22 February 2007.

Elliott Roosevelt (born Hamilton James Elliott; May 30, 1916 – August 13, 2001) was an American author, soldier, public servant, and a younger brother of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Born in Manhattan, New York City, New York, Elliott was the fourth and youngest son of James Roosevelt I and Sara Delano Roosevelt. His father was a prominent New York banker and his mother was a member of the Delano family, which had served as ancestors to U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Along with his brothers James, Franklin, and John, Elliott grew up in a high-profile New York family and attended private schools. After attending the Groton School, where he was captain of the soccer and hockey teams, Elliott went on to Harvard University, where he joined the ROTC and graduated with the class of 1938. In 1940, he married his first wife, Betty Donner, and had two daughters with her. After the United States entered World War II, he joined the Army and was commissioned as a second lieutenant. He served in the cavalry and the Air Corps, attaining the rank of captain before the war's end. In 1946, he joined the staff of Congressman Jonathan Bingham and served as an assistant director of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs. In 1948, he was elected to the New York State Assembly, where he served three terms. In 1950, he was elected to the New York State Senate, where he served as assistant majority leader. In 1954, Elliott married his second wife, Mary Livingston Walles, with whom he had two sons. After his retirement from politics in 1964, he devoted his time to writing, and published a number of books on his life growing up with Franklin Roosevelt, including an autobiography, As He Saw It (1946), and a collection of correspondence with his mother, Mother R: The Life and Times of Eleanor Roosevelt (1983). He also wrote a book about his war experiences, FDR: An Intimate History (1995), and was a frequent contributor to the Nation and other magazines. Elliott was a member of the New York Society of the Sons of the American Revolution and served as its president from 1998 to 1999. He was also a trustee of the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum, in Hyde Park, New York, and an honorary trustee of the Roosevelt Institute, in New York City. He was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the United States, by President Bill Clinton in 1998. In his later years, Elliott's health began to deteriorate. He died in his sleep at his home in Manhattan on August 13, 2001, at the age of 85. His wife Mary died in 2004.

The M1934 helmet (Spain) was a military helmet used by the Spanish Army from the 1930s until the 1970s. The M1934 was a Spanish-made copy of the German World War II M35 helmet, but with a slightly different shape. It was made in Spain by the ''Ejército del Aire'' (Spanish Air Force), and was used by the Spanish Army and some police forces. It was a standard Spanish military helmet for over 40 years, and many were also sold to other countries. The M1934 was made in two versions: with a short, straight neck, and with a longer, curved neck. The short-neck version was used by the Spanish Air Force, and the long-neck version was used by the Spanish Army. Both versions had a similar design, with a steel shell and a leather lining. The shell was made of 1.2 mm thick steel, and the lining was made of 3 mm thick leather. The M1934 was designed to provide protection from small arms fire and shrapnel. The M1934 was widely used by the Spanish Army during the Spanish Civil War, and many were captured by the Republicans. It was also used by the Francoist regime during the 1940s and 1950s, and by the Spanish Army during the 1960s and 1970s. The M1934 was gradually replaced by the M76 helmet, which was a Spanish-made copy of the French M51. However, the M76 was not widely used by the Spanish Army until the 1980s, so the M1934 was still in use during the 1970s.

Fitzroy Talbot (15 December 1851 – 14 April 1928) was a British Liberal politician and a member of the Talbot family. He was the son of Henry Talbot, a builder, and his wife Mary, and was educated at the Royal Indian Engineering College at Cooper's Hill, near Windsor. He then served an apprenticeship with a firm of engineers and attended classes at the South-Eastern School of Art. In 1874 he joined the family firm of J. W. Talbot & Co. at their works at Saltford, near Bristol, and then at Guo di Volo, near Milan, Italy, where he was placed in charge of the drawing office. In 1885 he was elected to the House of Commons as the Member of Parliament (MP) for Westbury in Wiltshire, winning the seat from the Conservatives by 607 votes to 564. He was re-elected in 1886, when he won the seat by 68 votes to 61, but in 1892 he lost the seat to the Conservatives by 681 votes to 674. He did not stand for Parliament again, but devoted his time to the family business, which was then run by his brother, Sidney. In 1898 the firm was converted into a limited company, with Fitzroy Talbot as chairman. The company was taken over by Messrs. Hill & Smith in 1927. Talbot married firstly, in 1876, Mary Georgina, daughter of George coupling, of Bristol, and secondly, in 1905, Helen, daughter of Thomas Curbishley, of Bristol. He died in April 1928, aged 76, when his home address was given as 36, Great George's Street, Bristol.

In the early 1970s, the middle class in the United States began to feel squeezed by the rising cost of living and by taxes. At the same time, the middle class was also upset about the decline in the quality of education and the increase in crime. In response to these concerns, a movement of middle-class Americans began to organize politically. The movement, which became known as the Middle Class Revolt, began to press for lower taxes, higher quality education, and lower crime. In the 1980s, the Middle Class Revolt began to gain traction. In 1980, the Republican Party nominated Ronald Reagan for president. Reagan, who was a strong supporter of the Middle Class Revolt, won the election. Reagan's victory helped to popularize the Middle Class Revolt. In the 1990s, the Middle Class Revolt began to falter. In the early 1990s, the economy began to improve, and the middle class began to feel less squeezed. At the same time, the quality of education began to improve, and crime began to decline. As a result, the Middle Class Revolt began to lose momentum. Today, the Middle Class Revolt is still alive, but it is no longer a major force in American politics. However, the ideas and concerns that drove the Middle Class Revolt are still important to many Americans.

1102 in Ireland The High Cross at Monasterboice While much of the Irish population was still adherence to Celtic Christianity, the process of replacing this tradition with one that was Romanesque in its entirety had begun in the late 10th century and was largely completed by the end of the 12th. The process was gradual and it has been estimated that at any one time half the population was Celtic and half Romanesque. Ireland was a bilingual and bicultural state for several centuries, and it is not until the late 12th or early 13th century that the use of the Gaelic language was restricted to the Irishry. In the 11th and 12th centuries, the Viking influence on Ireland faded as the Vikings withdrew from Ireland, and the Irish state collapsed into the hands of local chieftains and petty kings. The east of Ireland was dominated by the Dál gCais and their Cianachta allies, the south by the Eóghanacht, and the west by the Uí Conchobhair. The north was divided into numerous small kingdoms, including the Cruthin, the Dál Fiatach, and the Dál nAraidi. The east was the most powerful, and in the early 12th century, the Dál gCais and their Cianachta allies merged to form the kingdom of Thomond, c. 1150 under the O'Brien dynasty. The kingdom of Dublin was also powerful, and in the 1160s, the Dublin king Diarmait Mac Murchada (d. 1166) conquered much of the south and established the kingdom of Leinster. In the 1130s, the Anglo-Norman barons invaded Ireland and by 1171 they had occupied the east and south of Ireland. In the 1180s, the Irish revolted and for a time defeated the Anglo-Normans. The Irish had grown powerful at this time and the Anglo-Normans were in turn defeated. In the early 14th century, the Gaelic lords were again defeated by the Anglo-Normans and forced to pay tribute to the English crown. Over the next century, the Picts and Scots from Scotland invaded the north of Ireland and the Welsh from Wales invaded the south. These invaders were in turn defeated and the Irish state was reunified for a brief period before being conquered by the English in the 15th century.

Fred Perrett (27 March 1927 – 14 June 2018) was an English professional footballer who played as a centre half in the Football League for Tranmere Rovers, Portsmouth and Southport, and in the Scottish Football League for Morton. Perrett was born in Liverpool in 1927. He began his career as a centre half with his local club, Liverpool Stanley, before joining Tranmere Rovers in 1949. He made his debut in the Football League the following year, and went on to make 128 appearances for the club, scoring eight goals. In 1955, he joined Portsmouth, where he won the Football League Third Division South championship in 1956–57. He played for the club in the Football League Second Division for a further three seasons, making 123 appearances and scoring five goals, before joining Southport in 1961. He stayed with the club for three seasons, making 72 appearances, and then joined Scottish club Morton in 1964. He returned to England to play for non-league Worcester City in 1966, and then became a coach at the club. Perrett also managed the club for a short period in the early 1970s.

The town was very distant from Rome, and the exiled poet was able to secure a permit from the Emperor to return to Rome for a visit. He stayed in the city for two years, before returning to Tomis. In the following year, 12, Ovid composed the Tristia (Sorrows), a series of five books in which he expressed his discontent at being banished to the edge of the empire, so far from the center of culture and learning in Rome. In the Tristia, Ovid poured out his complaints to his friends and pleaded for their help in securing his recall to Rome. He also published the Epistulae (Letters), a collection of letters to his friends and patrons in Rome, in which he sought their assistance in his hour of need. In the end, Ovid's efforts were successful. The Emperor Augustus, who had been impressed by the poet's abilities, relented and allowed Ovid to return to Rome in 17. After his recall, Ovid composed the Fasti, a six-volume work on the religious festivals of the Roman year. The Fasti is unique among Ovid's works in that it was not written in verse, but in prose. The work provides a valuable record of the religious practices of the Roman world. After the Fasti was published, Ovid died in 17, at the age of 60.

Pembroke, Kentucky, is an unincorporated community and census-designated place in Christian County, Kentucky, United States. As of the 2010 census, it had a population of 1,451. It is located on Kentucky Route 101 (the Pennyrile Parkway) between Hopkinsville and Madisonville. The community was named for the Pembroke Hill neighborhood in Kansas City, Missouri, the home of a railroad official. Pembroke is located at 36°49′46″N 87°52′59″W (36.831694, -87.863472). According to the United States Census Bureau, the CDP has a total area of 2.9 square miles (7.4 km2), all land. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 2.31% of the population. There were 562 households out of which 36.6% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 59.3% were married couples living together, 10.6% had a female householder with no husband present, and 26.4% were non-families. 21.5% of all households were made up of individuals and 9.2% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.54 and the average family size was 2.93. In the CDP, the population was spread out with 23.5% under the age of 18, 7.9% from 18 to 24, 28.2% from 25 to 44, 25.4% from 45 to 64, and 13.2% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 37 years. For every 100 females, there were 99.3 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 100.6 males. As of the 2000 census, the median income for a household in the CDP was $35,417, and the median income for a family was $40,417. Men had a median income of $29,444 versus $20,417 for women. The per capita income for the CDP was $16,325. About 4.8% of families and 9.5% of the population were below the poverty line, including 11.4% of those under age 18 and 15.8% of those age 65 or over. The first post office in Pembroke opened in 1884. The ZIP Code for the community is 42268.

An air-start system (also called an auxiliary power unit (APU), air turbine starter (ATS), or the like) is an aircraft engine starting system that uses compressed air to power an engine. The air-start system is part of the aircraft's auxiliary power unit (APU). The APU is a small gas turbine engine, typically mounted in the aircraft's tail section. The APU provides power to start the main engines, as well as auxiliary power to the aircraft's electrical and pneumatic systems during flight. The APU can also provide emergency power to the aircraft's electrical and pneumatic systems during flight if the main engines fail. The air-start system is used to rotate the aircraft's main engines before they are ignited. The air-start system uses a small turbine, which is driven by compressed air from the APU, to turn the main engine's crankshaft. The APU is typically started by an electric starter motor, which is powered by the aircraft's auxiliary power unit battery. Once the APU is running, the air-start system is used to start the main engines. The air-start system is typically controlled by the aircraft's main engine control computer. The air-start system is designed to provide a specific amount of compressed air to the main engine's starter turbine. The starter turbine is designed to provide a specific amount of torque to the main engine's crankshaft. When the main engines are started, the air-start system must provide enough compressed air to the starter turbine to turn the crankshaft at a specific speed. The speed is typically between 60 and 70 rotations per second (rpm). The air-start system will continue to provide compressed air to the starter turbine until the main engine's ignition system is activated. After the main engines are started, the air-start system is shut down and the APU is typically shut down. The APU can be shut down by the aircraft's main engine control computer, or by the aircraft's APU control system. Once the APU is shut down, the air-start system is no longer used. The air-start system is a critical component of an aircraft's auxiliary power unit. The air-start system must be reliable and functional for the aircraft to be able to start its main engines. The air-start system is typically inspected and serviced regularly to ensure its reliability.

Brotherhood (The Chemical Brothers album) Brotherhood is the ninth studio album by English electronic music duo the Chemical Brothers, released on 3 June 2008 via Virgin Records. The album was produced by the Chemicals, with assistance from Michael Jackson, Hulusi, and Peter Kember. The album was mixed by Michael Brauer at Electric Lady Studios in New York City. The album was recorded in the band's North London studio, between January and May 2008. The album's title refers to the close relationship the band have with their fans, and the title track is a direct reference to this, featuring the sound of a crowd chanting the word "brotherhood". The track "Salmon Dance" uses a sample from an episode of the BBC's wildlife documentary series Planet Earth. The album was preceded by two singles, "Midnight Madness" and "Gettin' Up", released on 29 April and 27 May 2008 respectively. "Midnight Madness" was included on the band's second compilation album, Brothers Gonna Work It Out, released in 2009. Upon release, Brotherhood received generally favourable reviews from critics. It was also a commercial success, peaking at number nine on the UK Albums Chart, and number thirteen on the US Billboard 200. The album was certified gold by the British Phonographic Industry, and has sold over 200,000 copies in the United States. A music video for "Salmon Dance" was released in June 2008. The video, directed by Dom & Nic, was shot in Los Angeles, and features a group of synchronised swimmers performing to the track. The band toured the album across the UK, Europe, and North America throughout 2008.

St. Mary's Church (Dedham, Massachusetts) St. Mary's Church is an historic Catholic church at 201 Washington Street in Dedham, Massachusetts. The church is the fourth oldest church in the Boston area and the oldest in Dedham. The church was built in 1845, shortly after the peak of the potato famine in Ireland. At the time, Dedham was a major hub of the textile industry, and the church was built by Irish and French Canadian mill workers. The church was designed by Patrick C. Keely, who designed a number of Catholic churches in New England. By the 1970s, St. Mary's was in need of repair, and in 1975, a major restoration project was undertaken by the church's pastor, Rev. Francis W. Morriss. The project was supported by the local community, and included the repair of the church's windows, which had been covered over during the 1940s. In the late 1970s, the church was added to the National Register of Historic Places. Today, St. Mary's is part of the Archdiocese of Boston. The church is still active, and holds Mass every Sunday at 8:30 am.

Cheryl S. McWatters is a Canadian politician who was elected to in the Yukon Legislative Assembly in the 2011 election. She was the first woman to hold the position of Chief Minister in the Yukon, and the first Canadian First Nations woman to be elected as Chief Minister in Canada. McWatters was born in Whitehorse, Yukon and grew up in the Yukon. Her mother was born in Whitehorse and her father inConstructor, Yukon. She is a member of the Han citizens of the White River First Nation and a descendant of the Ta'an Kwäch'än citizens of the White TaigaDene Nation. McWatters was raised by a single mother and her grandmother. She has two siblings. Her mother was diagnosed with cancer at age 46, and died a year later in 1986. After her mother's death, McWatters and her siblings were raised by their grandmother, who was very active in the Native Brotherhood and the Yukon Indian Women's Association. Her grandmother's influence led McWatters to become involved in First Nations politics, and at age 19 she was elected to the White River First Nation Council. She served on the council for four years, and then worked for the Yukon Indian Women's Association for four years. In 1996, McWatters moved to Vancouver, British Columbia to attend the British Columbia Institute of Technology. She completed a two-year business course and then went to work for the First Nations Leadership Council. She also became involved with the British Columbia Treaty Commission, and worked on treaty negotiations for the First Nations Summit. After returning to the Yukon in 2000, McWatters was elected to the White River First Nation Council again in 2002 and re-elected in 2006. In 2005, she was elected to the Board of Directors of the Yukon Native Brotherhood. In 2006, McWatters was hired as the Executive Assistant to John Duncan, the Minister of the Environment and Member of the Legislative Assembly for the Yukon Party. She held this position until the 2011 election, when she ran for the Yukon Party and was elected to the Yukon Legislative Assembly. McWatters was elected to the Yukon Legislative Assembly in the 2011 election, defeating incumbent New Democratic Party MLA Kate White in the Yukon electoral district of Whitehorse Centre. She was the first woman to hold the position of Chief Minister in the Yukon, and the first Canadian First Nations woman to be elected as Chief Minister in Canada. As Chief Minister, McWatters served as the territory's Minister of Finance, Minister of Justice, Minister of Tourism and Culture, and Minister responsible for the Women's Directorate. In 2014, McWatters was re-elected to the Yukon Legislative Assembly, defeating New Democratic Party candidate Jan Stick in the Yukon electoral district of Whitehorse Centre. In 2016, McWatters was re-elected to the Yukon Legislative Assembly, defeating Yukon Party candidate Richard Cano in the Yukon electoral district of Whitehorse Centre. In 2018, McWatters was re-elected to the Yukon Legislative Assembly, defeating New Democratic Party candidate Kate White in the Yukon electoral district of Whitehorse Centre.

Lucien Grant Berry (March 31, 1889 – June 18, 1979) was an American lawyer, businessman, and politician from Memphis, Tennessee, who served in the United States House of Representatives from 1939 to 1967 as a member of the Democratic Party. He was also a member of the Ku Klux Klan. Berry was born on a farm near Memphis in 1889, the son of Thomas Jefferson and Martha Ann (Horn) Berry. He attended the public schools of Shelby County and the law school of the University of Memphis, receiving his law degree in 1911. He commenced practice in Memphis and became a businessman, owning a cottonseed oil mill and a sand and gravel business. In 1922, Berry was appointed assistant attorney general of Tennessee and served in that capacity for two years. He then returned to his private law practice. In 1939, he was elected to the United States House of Representatives, serving from 1939 to 1967. He was a member of the Democratic Party and served as the chairman of the Special Committee to Study and Survey Problems of Small Business Enterprises from 1941 to 1947. While serving in Congress, Berry was one of the few members to vote against the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In 1948, he was challenged in the Democratic primary by the African-American attorney and future judge Russell W. Dyer, who ran on a civil rights platform. Berry defeated Dyer by 5,730 to 3,458, winning 56 percent of the vote. In 1964, Berry was again challenged in the Democratic primary, this time by the African-American attorney and businessman George W. Lee, who also ran on a civil rights platform. Berry defeated Lee by 4,031 to 2,232, winning 56 percent of the vote. In the general election, Berry defeated the Republican candidate, William N. Dunn, by 60,32 to 39.68, winning by a margin of 20,84. In his later years, Berry was actively involved in the Democratic Party in Shelby County, serving as the chairman of the Shelby County Democratic Executive Committee from 1968 to 1972. He was also a member of the executive committee of the Tennessee Democratic Party from 1959 to 1972 and was the state party's chairman in 1968. Berry died at age 90 in 1979. He is buried in the Berry family plot in Elmwood Cemetery in Memphis.

Kim Jong-un bibliography Kim Jong-un (Korean: 김정은; Hanja: 金正恩,[3] Korean pronunciation: [tɕʰɛ.jʌn]; born 8 January 1984), also known by his pseudonym Pak Pong-nam (Korean: 박평남; Hanja: 伯平男,[4]), is a North Korean politician who has been the leader of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK) since 2011 and the leader of North Korea since 2013. He is the second son of Ko Yong-hui and Kim Jong-il; the younger brother of Kim Jong-chul and Kim Yo-jong; and the grandson of Kim Il-sung. Kim was designated as the successor to Kim Jong-il in the country's hereditary monarchy system around 2009, during which he was given the title of "Young Leader" (Korean: 젊은 리더).[5] He was publicly designated as the supreme leader in a ceremony in Pyongyang on 9 September 2010, after the death of his father on 8 July of that year.[6] He became the leader of the WPK at the 3rd WPK Congress on 26 September 2011.[7] Kim's rise to power was confirmed on 3 September 2013, when the WPK Central Committee issued a statement saying that "the dear respected Kim Jong-un is now the supreme leader of the KWP, the chairman of the Central Committee, the chairman of the Central Military Commission of the WPK, the leader of the KWP Central Military Commission and the supreme commander of the Korean People's Army.[8] After the death of Kim Jong-il, the WPK and the state of North Korea experienced a process of transition. The transition was smooth and stable, with Kim Jong-un gaining the immediate support of the WPK and the Korean People's Army. Kim has been the subject of much speculation regarding his personality and physical health, as well as his ability to lead the country.[9] There have been numerous unconfirmed reports that he has been in poor health since the early 2010s, and that he may have been suffering from various diseases, such as diabetes, cancer, or heart ailments.[10] In addition, there have been several reports of purges and executions of high-ranking officials close to Kim, which have further fueled speculation about his health and the stability of the country's leadership.[11] Despite the speculation, Kim has appeared in numerous public appearances since taking power, and has maintained a tight grip on the country's leadership structure. He has also been widely praised for his leadership, particularly for his handling of the country's economy, and for his efforts to improve the country's international relations. In addition, Kim has continued to pursue the country's nuclear and missile programs, despite international sanctions and condemnation.

Gangsta rap, also called gangsta hip hop, gangsta music, or simply gangsta, is a subgenre of hip hop music that is generally characterized by its use of explicit, and often violent, lyrics. Since the early 1980s, gangsta rap has been one of the most commercially successful subgenres of hip hop. The genre has been very influential in the mainstreaming of hip hop culture, as well as the proliferation of rap music in popular music. The development of gangsta rap was fueled by the emergence of several influential artists, such as N.W.A, Tupac Shakur, Snoop Dogg, and Ice Cube, who brought the subgenre to the mainstream and increased its popularity during the late 1980s and early 1990s. Since then, the genre has been a staple of popular music and has influenced numerous other subgenres of hip hop, such as grime, cloud rap, and trap music. The lyrics in gangsta rap are often characterized by their explicit and sometimes violent content, which can include discussions of drug use, sexual activity, and criminal behavior. The subgenre is also associated with the use of profanity and the depiction of misogynistic and homophobic attitudes. While some artists have been criticized for their use of explicit and violent lyrics, others have been praised for their creative use of language and their ability to convey complex social and political messages through their music.

Monarchy in Nova Scotia The Monarchy in Nova Scotia refers to the current and former sovereign states and their respective constitutional monarchies within the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. The present monarch, Queen Elizabeth II, is the head of state of Nova Scotia, and the province's longest-reigning monarch. The first European colony in what is now Nova Scotia was established in 1604 by French explorer Samuel de Champlain, on Cape Breton Island at a place called Port-aux-Basques. In 1605, de Champlain established the first permanent European settlement in North America at Port Royal in what is now the Annapolis Valley. The French colony was known as Acadia and, after 1627, as New France. The British established their first permanent settlement in 1749 on the Halifax Peninsula. The colony was renamed Nova Scotia in 1759. The city of Halifax was founded in 1749 and became the provincial capital in 1775. From 1713 to 1867, the British colony of Nova Scotia was a separate colony from New Brunswick. In 1867, the two colonies were combined into the single colony of Nova Scotia, which later became the province of Nova Scotia. From that time, the British monarch has been the head of state of Nova Scotia. The Scottish Jacobite leader Charles de Saint-Étienne de la Tour established the first permanent European settlement at Port Royal (Annapolis Royal) in 1632. La Tour was followed by his son Charles de Saint-Étienne de Saint-Étienne de la Tour, who was in turn followed by his son Pierre de Saint-Étienne de Saint-Étienne de la Tour. When Pierre de Saint-Étienne de Saint-Étienne de la Tour died in 1704, the house of Saint-Étienne came to an end and the French authorities assumed control of the colony. From 1713 to 1755, the British and the French were in conflict in Europe and North America. In 1713, the British colony of Nova Scotia was established. The British monarch was the head of state of Nova Scotia from this time until Canadian Confederation in 1867. The capital of the colony was established at Annapolis Royal in 1729 and moved to Halifax in 1749. From 1755 to 1783, the British were in conflict with the Mi'kmaq and the French. In 1755, the British captured Fort Beauséjour (near present-day Moncton) and established the colony of New Brunswick. The French were defeated at the Plains of Abraham in Quebec in 1759 and subsequently abandoned Acadia. In 1763, the British colony of Nova Scotia was expanded to include what is now Prince Edward Island and Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula. In 1867, the British colony of Nova Scotia became the province of Nova Scotia. The Canadian colonies of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec united to form the single colony of British North America in 1840. The British monarch was the head of state of British North America from this time until Canadian Confederation in 1867. The capital of the colony was established at Halifax in 1749 and moved to Ottawa in 1867. In the early 20th century, the British and the Mi'kmaq signed a treaty ceding most of the Mi'kmaq's land to the British. The treaty was never ratified by the British and the land was not surrendered. In 1999, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that the treaty was still in effect and that the British Crown was still in possession of the land. In 2009, the province of Nova Scotia adopted the Scottish tartan as its official tartan. The tartan was designed in 1953 by the Scottish weaver William Donald Alexander.

Pebble Mine is the common name of a mineral exploration project located in the Bristol Bay region of Southwest Alaska, near Lake Iliamna and Lake Clark, that was being considered for development as an open-pit gold and molybdenum mine. The proposal was controversial, because the mine would have been located near the headwaters of the Bristol Bay salmon fishery, the largest wild sockeye salmon fishery in the world, and the proposed mining method would have also disturbed a large area of the Earth's crust, possibly leading to earthquakes. The Pebble Partnership, a consortium of Canadian mining companies, proposed the project. The Pebble Mine site is located about 200 miles (320 km) southwest of Anchorage, Alaska. It encompasses 2,600 acres (11 km2) of the Alaska Peninsula, which juts westward from the mainland to form the southern boundary of Cook Inlet. The nearest communities are Tyonek to the southwest, and Soldotna to the northeast. The mine site is located about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) north of Lake Iliamna, which is fed by the Neacola, Pedro, and Kvichak rivers. The proposed mine site is located on the northern flank of a mountain called Nuyakuk. In 2007, the Pebble Partnership submitted a "Notice of Intent" to the US Army Corps of Engineers, stating their intention to develop the mine. In February 2010, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) listed the Pebble deposit as a "proposed action", and began an environmental impact assessment of the project. The EPA's assessment was expected to take several years. In September 2013, the Pebble Partnership voluntarily suspended its permit applications while it re-evaluated the project. In June 2017, the Pebble Partnership officially withdrew its permit applications. In November 2020, the EPA proposed to withdraw the proposed action status from the project, removing it from the EPA's list of projects for which it is actively considering a proposed withdrawal of a permit or license. The EPA stated that the decision was not a final decision on the project, and that the EPA would continue to study the project and could still determine that the project would have too much of an impact on the environment. In February 2021, the EPA announced that it would not withdraw the proposed action status from the project, and would instead prepare a supplement to the Bristol Bay Assessment that it had prepared in 2014. The decision was widely expected to lead to a lawsuit from the Pebble Partnership.

Nocturnal is the sixth studio album by the American death metal band The Black Dahlia Murder. The album was released on June 21, 2011, through Metal Blade Records. Nocturnal was produced by The Black Dahlia Murder and was mixed and mastered by James Murphy, known for his work with Death, Testament, and Obituary. Nocturnal is The Black Dahlia Murder's first album to be released on Metal Blade Records since their 2005 debut, Unhallowed. The band had previously been signed to Indianapolis-based label Rowe Productions, which released their 2007 album, Miasma. In 2009, the band was signed to Metal Blade Records, and released their EP, Warped & Decayed, through the label. Nocturnal was the band's final album to feature founding guitarist Mike Hodgin, who amicably left the band in early 2012 to pursue other musical interests. In July 2011, Nocturnal was released as a limited-edition double vinyl album. The album was re-released in June 2012, following the band's signing to eOne Music. The 2012 re-release was issued as a single vinyl album, and featured a slightly different track listing. The most notable difference was the replacement of the song "Satanic Panic (2009)" with a new track, "Mama". Nocturnal received generally positive reviews from critics. Review aggregator Metacritic, a review aggregate, gave the album a score of 72, indicating "Generally favorable reviews", based on four critical reviews. All About Jazz awarded Nocturnal five stars, and described it as "one of the best metal albums of the year". NME also awarded it five stars, and said that the band had "reinvented death metal for the new decade".

Round Oak railway station is a railway station serving the Round Oak area of east Birmingham, England. It is situated on the North Circular Road (A406) between the orbital ring road and the M6 motorway. It is the last stop on the Jewellery Line before it joins the West Coast Main Line and therefore is a useful station for visitors to the NEC and Birmingham International Airport. It was built by the London and Birmingham Railway in 1838, on their new route from the city to their proposed London terminal at Euston. The station was rebuilt in 1966 by the London, Midland and Scottish Railway during the electrification of the Jewellery Line. The station has two platforms, one for each direction. Platform 1 is for trains to Birmingham and platform 2 is for trains to London. It is served by Chiltern Railways, who operate the service between Birmingham and London Marylebone. The station is located about 1 mile (1.6 km) from the similar-sounding Birmingham Roundhouse railway station on the West Coast Main Line.

Wigglesworth Dole (April 17, 1841 – May 1, 1925) was an American lawyer, judge, civil servant, and politician from New York. Dole was born in Cambridge, New York. He was the son of David Dole (1809–1877) and Mary Merilla Wigglesworth (1813–1895), and the grandson of David Dole (1784–1855) and Lucinda Canfield (1787–1869), who were both born in Connecticut. The senior David Dole was a farmer and a member of the Connecticut House of Representatives. Dole was educated at Cambridge Academy and Cazenovia Seminary. He studied law, was admitted to the bar in 1864, and commenced practice in Albany, New York. He was an associate of Thomas J. Van Alstyne (1836–1917), a New York lawyer, politician, and businessman. In 1868, Dole was elected as a Republican to the New York State Assembly, representing Albany's 4th Ward. He served in the Assembly in 1869, 1870, 1871, and 1873. In 1871, Dole was appointed as private secretary to Francis C. Barlow (1825–1905), the Lieutenant Governor of New York. Barlow was elected Governor of New York in 1872, and Dole served as private secretary to the Governor from 1872 to 1873. In 1873, Dole was appointed as a justice of the New York Supreme Court to fill a vacancy caused by the death of John T. Sprague (1827–1873). He was re-elected in 1875 and 1880, and served until 1884. In 1884, Dole was appointed as a judge of the New York Court of Appeals. He was re-appointed in 1890, and served until 1895. Dole died in Albany, New York, and was buried at the Albany Rural Cemetery. Dole was married to Emma L. Noble (1845–1925), and they had three children, Grace L. (1877–1925), Paul S. (1879–1921), and James K. (1882–1883).

Slobodan Kaličanin (Serbian Cyrillic: Слободан Каличанин; born 11 January 1948) is a Serbian former politician and convicted war criminal. He was the founder and leader of the Serbian ultra-nationalist organization Tigers, which was responsible for a series of murders, torture and other crimes during the Yugoslav Wars. Kaličanin was born in 1948 in Niš, Serbia, in what was then the People's Republic of Serbia, Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia. He was a student at the Niš Faculty of Technology until the early 1970s, but dropped out in his third year. In the late 1970s, he formed the Association of Non-Conformist Students, which soon transformed into the Serbian nationalist organization known as the Tigers. The Tigers' initial goal was to unite the various Serbian nationalist groups in Yugoslavia and create a Serbian superstate, which would include all of Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and parts of Croatia. To achieve this, the Tigers conducted a series of murders, torture and other crimes against civilians, aiming to create a climate of fear and instability. The Tigers were also responsible for a number of political assassinations, including the murder of Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić. In the late 1980s, the Tigers began to cooperate with the Yugoslav government, and Kaličanin was appointed to a number of government positions. However, the relationship between the Tigers and the government began to deteriorate in the early 1990s, as the Tigers began to pursue their own agenda, and the government began to move towards a more moderate position. In 1992, the Tigers were banned, and Kaličanin was forced to go into hiding. In the late 1990s, Kaličanin was arrested and tried for a number of crimes, including the murder of Đinđić. In 2002, he was found guilty and sentenced to life in prison. Kaličanin is currently serving his sentence at the maximum security prison in Beograd.

Paul II Šubić of Bribir (born before 1283 – died between 1356 and 1360) was a Croatian nobleman and a member of the Šubić noble family who had possessions in Bribir, Omiš and other parts of Croatia, including the islands of Brač, Hvar, and Korčula. Paul was a son of Vladimir Šubić of Bribir, a nephew of King Andrew II of Hungary, and his second wife, a member of the Czech noble family of Hrabišic. Paul's father, Vladimir, was the son of Mihailo Šubić, the son of King Paul I Šubić of Bribir, who was, in turn, a son of Knyaz Matijaš of Bribir, who had been granted the title of king by the Holy Roman Emperor in 1325. Paul's half-brother was the famous Vladislav IV, Duke of Wallachia, who ruled Wallachia from 1330 to 1352. In 1322, Paul was granted the title of prince by King Charles I of Hungary. After the death of his father in 1324, Paul inherited Bribir and Omiš. He was also given the islands of Brač, Hvar, and Korčula by his cousin, King Andrew III of Hungary. Paul was married to Helen, a daughter of the Serbian king Stefan Milutin. They had three sons: Gregory, James, and Peter. In 1360, the citizens of Trogir appealed to King Louis the Great to confirm their earlier privileges. In the same charter, Louis also confirmed the possessions of Paul's sons in the islands of Brač, Hvar, and Korčula. A document issued by Louis in 1361 refers to Paul's sons as "the former Dukes of Trogir". It is therefore possible that Paul's sons had sold their possessions in Trogir to the King before 1360.

JibJab JibJab is an American digital entertainment company founded in 1999 by brothers Evan and Gregg Spiridellis, based in Los Angeles. The company's website is known for its personalized e-cards, which use its patented technology to integrate a digital photo with animated effects in a variety of templates, designed by the company's staff of artists. The company's products are oriented toward the holiday market, with a substantial portion of its revenue coming from Halloween and Christmas cards. The company has received $40 million in venture capital funding. In 2007, it was valued at $200 million, with more than 1.5 million active members and a revenue base of more than $20 million. In 2008, the company was valued at $300 million, with 2.4 million active members, and in 2010 it was valued at $650 million, with 3.8 million active members. In 2007, the company was ranked #33 on the Deloitte Technology Fast 50 list, with 5,698% growth over the previous five years. In 2008, the company was ranked #61 on the Deloitte Technology Fast 500 list, with 3,733% growth over the previous five years. In 2009, the company was ranked #43 on the Deloitte Technology Fast 500 list, with 3,000% growth over the previous five years. JibJab has produced numerous other entertainment products, including JibJab Jr. for children, JibJab Sports, and JibJab Music. In 2010, the company launched JibJab Photos, a tool for creating photo collages. In 2013, the company launched JibJab Video, a tool for creating video collages. In 2015, the company launched JibJab Kids, a collection of children's music.

The National Art Gallery of The Bahamas is a museum in Nassau, Bahamas. It is located in the former villa of a British colonial governor, which was purchased by the government in 1973. The museum was established in 1996 by the Bahamas Ministry of Youth, Sports and Culture, and is directed by a board of trustees. The museum's permanent collection includes works by artists from the Bahamas and other Caribbean countries. It also has a collection of works by European and Asian artists, including etchings and lithographs by Pablo Picasso. In addition to its permanent collection, the museum sponsors rotating exhibitions. It also maintains a reference library and a publication series. The museum is open Monday through Friday, from 10:00 am to 5:00 pm, and on Saturdays from 10:00 am to 2:00 pm. It is closed on Sundays, public holidays, and for three weeks in August. The museum is located at 18 Washington Street in Nassau. It is housed in a villa that was built in 1938 for Sir Harry Oakes, a Canadian goldsmith and investor who became a British citizen in 1939. The villa was designed by the British architect Edwin Sydney Cooper, who designed many buildings in Nassau. The villa has three floors and a basement. The main floor has a large living room, a dining room, and a kitchen. The second floor has three bedrooms and a bathroom. The third floor has two bedrooms and a bathroom. The basement has a wine cellar and a servants' quarters. The museum's collection includes works by artists from the Bahamas and other Caribbean countries, as well as works by European and Asian artists. The museum's permanent collection includes paintings, drawings, prints, and sculpture. It also has a collection of historical maps and documents. In addition to its permanent collection, the museum sponsors rotating exhibitions. It also maintains a reference library and a publication series.

Yang Fuqing ( traditional Chinese: 楊富清; simplified Chinese: 杨富清; pinyin: Yáng Fùqīng; born January 1957) is a Chinese politician and the current Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Yang was born in Linyi County, Shandong in January 1957. After the Cultural Revolution, he attended the Linyi Normal School, and then entered the Huazhong Normal University in March 1978. After graduating in August 1982, he became a teacher at the High School of Liaocheng City, and then was promoted to the position of principal in 1984. In 1985, he entered the Shandong Institute of Education and was promoted to the Deputy Dean in 1990. In 1992, he was appointed as the Dean of the Shandong Normal University. In June 1995, he became the President of the Shandong Normal University. In September 1999, he was appointed as the Party Secretary of the Shandong Normal University. In March 2008, Yang was appointed as the Party Secretary of the Shandong University of Technology. In August 2011, he was appointed as the President of the Shandong University of Technology. In March 2013, he was appointed as the Party Secretary of the Jining No.1 High School. In August 2013, he was appointed as the Vice Mayor of Jining. In July 2015, he was appointed as the Mayor of Jining. In January 2016, he was appointed as the Secretary of the Shandong Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China. In April 2020, he was appointed as the Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs.

History of Rockland County, New York (1798–1900) The county was created on January 15, 1798, by the New York State Legislature, after the Revolutionary War and the defeat of British Commander John Burgoyne at Saratoga. It was named in honor of theStack Rocks, a phenomenon of five erratic stacks rising from the Hudson River near its western boundary with New Jersey, in the area of Doodletown. The stacks are a major feature of the county seal. Rockland's early history is closely tied to the geography and history of the Hudson River. The river was the main transportation artery in the region, and Rockland's location along it gave the county its initial importance. The area that now includes Rockland was first inhabited by the Lenape natives, who lived in the region for thousands of years. In 1609, the Dutch voyager Henry Hudson explored the river and settled in the area. He and his crew traded with the local natives, and the river became known as the North River, as it flows north from the Atlantic Ocean to its source. In 1664, the English took control of the region. It was then that the Dutch name for the river, Noort Rivier, was anglicized to the Hudson River. The city of New York was founded as New Amsterdam at the southern tip of Manhattan in 1625, and grew to be an important colonial port. In the 18th century, the region that now includes Rockland was the western portion of Orange County. It included the towns of Newburgh, Wallkill, and Goshen. Rockland became its own county in 1798, when it was split from Orange. During the American Revolution, Rockland was the site of many battles and troop movements. The British military occupied the county for seven years, as they moved troops and supplies between New York City and the northern colonies. The main route of the British army was the King's Highway, which runs through the county from New Jersey to New York. In the 19th century, the opening of the Erie Canal across New York State in 1825 created a major new transportation route that connected the region to the west. As the canal ran through the length of the state, the importance of the Hudson River as an economic artery began to wane.

Orlando Peçanha (4 September 1905 – 21 June 1964) was a Brazilian poet and journalist. Orlando Peçanha was born in Cachapuz, São Paulo, in 1905. He moved with his family to Santos, where he attended the Colégio Santista from 1909 to 1917. He then attended the Liceu de São Paulo from 1917 to 1922. In 1922, he moved to Paris, where he studied law at the University of Paris. He returned to Brazil in 1927 and completed his law degree at the Escola de Direito da Universidade de São Paulo. In 1928, Peçanha joined the faculty of the University of São Paulo as a professor of legal theory. He became a full professor in 1942. In 1948, he was appointed Dean of the Law School, a position he held until his death. Peçanha was a member of the Brazilian Academy of Letters and the Brazilian Academy of Sciences. He was also a member of the Board of Trustees of the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). Peçanha was a recipient of the Gra思秋ndtner Foundation Prize, the Leo Tolstoy Memorial Prize, and the Neustadt International Prize for Literature. Peçanha died in São Paulo in 1964.

Efrem Hill (November 7, 1927 – April 6, 2004) was an American bass-baritone who had an active performance career in concerts and in opera from the early 1950s until the mid-1970s. Born in Atlanta, Georgia, Hill moved with his family to Detroit, Michigan at the age of 13. After finishing high school he served in the United States Army from 1945 to 1946. He then attended the Detroit Institute of Music where he studied voice with Helen Neilly. In 1950 he entered the Eastman School of Music in New York City where he studied voice with Arthur Craft and Malcolm Martineau. He graduated from Eastman in 1953 with a Bachelor of Music degree. In 1953 Hill began his professional career singing with the New York City Opera. He remained with that company for three years, singing such roles as Figaro in The Barber of Seville, Guglielmo in Così fan tutte, and Silvio in Pagliacci. In 1956 he began performing with the New York Metropolitan Opera, where he sang for the next ten years. At the Met he was a frequent performer in the Sunday afternoon broadcasts of live opera performances, and was heard in more than thirty different roles. These included such varied characters as Figaro in The Barber of Seville, Guglielmo in Così fan tutte, Silvio in Pagliacci, Sharpless in Madama Butterfly, Figaro in The Marriage of Figaro, Guglielmo in Le nozze di Figaro, and Belcore in L'elisir d'amore. He also sang major roles with most of the other opera companies in the United States and was a regular guest artist at the San Francisco Opera and the Lyric Opera of Chicago. In 1960 he performed the role of Figaro in The Barber of Seville with the Los Angeles Civic Light Opera. After retiring from the stage in the mid-1970s, Hill embarked on a second successful career as a voice teacher. Among his notable students were the sopranos Lauren Flanigan and Christinafrieda Clausen. He died in Naples, Florida at the age of 76.

Demon Gaze Demon Gaze is a Japanese visual novel developed by Japanese company Crea-Tech. The game was first released for PC as a first press bonus for purchasers of Compile Heart's PlayStation 2 game Saekano: bazooka shot. A port for the PlayStation 3 was released in Japan on December 18, 2008, via download from the PlayStation Store. The story takes place in the near future, and is set in a Japanese city that has been taken over by demons. The protagonist is a young man whose name and gender can be chosen by the player. The protagonist is an ordinary citizen who is caught up in the demon attack and, after managing to survive, is subsequently turned into a demon himself. The plot follows the protagonist as he tries to live a normal life despite his new circumstances. The game is divided into two main storylines. The first is the "Past" route, which follows the main character before he was turned into a demon, and the "Present" route, which follows the character after he becomes a demon. The game also features a "Human" and "Demon" route, which the player can choose between at certain points in the game. In the "Human" route, the main character tries to live a normal life as a human, despite being a demon. In the "Demon" route, the character embraces his demon nature and becomes a powerful being, but is shunned by other demons. The game also features a "Rebellion" route, in which the main character rebels against the demon world and tries to take back the city. Throughout the game, the player can choose between different dialogue options, which will affect the outcome of the story. There are also various minigames that can be played, such as a card game, a dice game, and a puzzle game. The game's graphics are in 2D, and the game is voiced by a cast of Japanese actors and actresses. The game's music was composed by Tomohiro Sato. Demon Gaze received a mixed reception. Some critics praised the game's concept and story, while others criticized the game's short length and lack of replay value.

Flexipop is a form of pop music designed to be played at discothèques, in contrast to the harder, more aggressive sounds of rock music. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, pop music was in a state of transition. The first generation of rock and roll stars were growing old, and a new breed of younger performers were starting to achieve stardom. The first wave of British Invasion acts, led by the Beatles, had already changed the face of popular music, and the second wave of British acts, led by the Rolling Stones, were starting to make their mark. At the same time, the early days of electronic music were producing a new sound, which was just beginning to make its way into popular music. The first electronic instruments, such as the therevox and the electric organ, were just starting to become popular, and the first electronic music composers, such as Karlheinz Stockhausen, were just starting to make their mark. The result was a period of experimentation and exploration, as musicians tried to find a new sound that would define the era. Flexipop was a result of this search. It was a fusion of pop and electronic music, designed to be played in discothèques, or dance halls. The music was usually upbeat and had a strong beat, designed to get people dancing. It was also usually associated with drugs, particularly MDMA (3,4-Methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine, or "ecstasy"). The combination of the upbeat music and the drug induced euphoria often created a feeling of unity and togetherness, and the music became a central part of the discothèque culture. The first flexipop acts were primarily European, and included acts such as the Rolling Stones, the Beatles, the Kinks, the Who, the Small Faces, the Doors, and the Seeds. However, as the genre grew, it began to include acts from other parts of the world, such as the United States, Australia, and Japan. Some of the more well-known acts from outside Europe include the Beach Boys, the Byrds, the Who, the Small Faces, the Kinks, the Doors, the Seeds, the Who, the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, and the Monkees. The flexipop era lasted from the late 1960s until the early 1970s, and was a major part of the discothèque culture of the era. However, as the 1970s progressed, the genre began to be replaced by a new form of electronic music, known as disco. Disco was a more commercial form of electronic music, and was designed to be played in a wider range of settings, such as clubs, parties, and radio. As a result, flexipop began to be seen as a more niche genre, and the number of new acts began to decline.

Shirala (Vidhan Sabha constituency) is one of the 243 Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) constituencies of Maharashtra state in western India. ## Overview Shirala constituency is one of the Vidhan Sabha constituencies of Maharashtra. It is a part of the Satara district and is known as the Chiplun Vidhan Sabha constituency. In 2009, it was renamed as Shirala from Chiplun after Chiplun got a separate constituency. Shirala is a taluka and a municipal council in Satara district in the Indian state of Maharashtra. It is located on the bank of river Venna. Shirala is well known for the Gaikwad royal family who ruled the place during the British period. The family had the title of "D unmet" and "Jadhav" and their surname was "Gaikwad". The family had a long history and was one of the oldest royal families in Maharashtra. The Shirala Palace is a well-known palace in the town. It was built bybdonations from the people of the town. The town has a population of about 30,000 and is known for its unity and cultural activities. Shirala has a wet climate with an average rainfall of 497 mm. June, July and August are the rainy months. Winter is in January and February. The cold waves from the Himalayas make the climate chilly. The economic condition of the people of Shirala is average. The main occupation is agriculture. The town has many rice mills. Shirala is connected by road to the cities of Pune, Satara, Kolhapur, Belgaum and Bangalore. It is on the Satara-Bangalore National Highway. The nearest railway station is the Karad railway station which is 25 km away from Shirala. ## Members of Vidhan Sabha | Year | Party | Picture | Member | | --

Mostyska is a village (selo) in Medvensky District of Kaluga Region, Russia, located on the left bank of the Oka River, 60 kilometers (37 mi) southeast of Kaluga, the district's administrative center. It is the second largest rural locality in Medvensky District. As of the 2010 Census, its population was 1,352. Mostyska was first mentioned in the 17th century as the village of Mosty. The name of the village derived from the Russian word mosty, meaning "bridge". In the 18th century, the village became the property of the Golitsyn family. In 1756, it was granted a status of a selo. In the 19th century, it became the property of the Lobanov-Rostovsky family. In the 19th century, the village became the center of the Bobrytskiye region, which included the lands of modern Medvensky and Peremyshlsky Districts. The Bobrytskiye region was a part of Vladimir Guberniya. In 1875, the Vladimir- Moscow railroad was constructed. The closest railway stations were in the villages of Bobrytsi and Korovinki. After the October Revolution, the Bobrytskiye region was included in the Moscow Oblast. In the early 1930s, the district was abolished, and Mostyska became a part of the Korovinskiye rural settlement of Moscow Oblast. In 1936, Moscow Oblast was abolished, and Korovinskiye rural settlement was included into Kaluga Oblast. In the 1990s, the district was re-established. Mostyska is located in the southern part of Medvensky District, on the left bank of the Oka River, which is the left tributary of the Volga. The distance from Mostyska to Moscow is 115 kilometers (71 mi). The area of the village is 3.23 square kilometers (1.26 sq mi). The length of the village from north to south is 2.6 kilometers (1.6 mi), from east to west is 2.8 kilometers (1.7 mi). Mostyska is a rural locality with a population of 1,352 people, 94% of whom are Russians, and 2% of whom are Ukrainians and Belarusians. The age structure of the population is as follows: youth (up to 19 years) — 24%, adults (20 to 64) — 56%, pensioners (over 65) — 20%. Mostyska's economy is based on the food industry. There are a meat processing plant and a milk processing plant in the village. The culture palace is located in the village. There are a children's art school and a school of culture in the palace. There is a local museum in the village. The museum's collection includes the works of the Russian painter and sculptor Alexander Golovin (1880–1945). Mostyska is a prominent tourist center of the district. There are several tourist routes in the village. The village is also a starting point for visiting the Knyazhe-Bogoroditskoye and the Pinkyosovka monasteries, which are located nearby. The people of Mostyska celebrate the Day of the Village on the last Saturday of April. The nearest rural localities are Korovino (2 kilometers (1.2 mi)), Korovinskiye (3 kilometers (1.9 mi)), and Novye Bobrytsi (4 kilometers (2.5 mi)). Mostyska is connected by roads to the settlements of Korovino, Korovinskiye, and Novye Bobrytsi, as well as to Moscow, Podolsk, and Ryazan. The nearest railway stations are in the villages of Bobrytsi (5 kilometers (3.1 mi)), Korovinki (7 kilometers (4.3 mi)), and Vereya (12 kilometers (7.5 mi)). The nearest urban localities are the town of Medvensky (12 kilometers (7.5 mi)), the town of Shchyokino (25 kilometers (16 mi)), and the city of Kaluga (60 kilometers (37 mi)). In the village there are two schools, one of which is a secondary school, and two kindergartens. There is a hospital in the village. The rural settlement of Mostyska is included into the category of rural settlements with a high level of social services. The village has a status of a rural tourist center. Death Magnetic is the tenth studio album by American heavy metal band Metallica, released on September 12, 2008, through Warner Bros. Records. The album was produced by the band and was recorded at Bay Area studios in California from January to June 2008. It is the first studio album by the band since St. Anger (2003), and the first since the death of their bassist, Cliff Burton, in 1986. Death Magnetic was announced on June 30, 2008, at the Revolver Golden Gods Awards, with a planned release date of September 15, 2008. However, the release date was later pushed up to September 12, 2008, to coincide with the band's twentieth anniversary. The album was released in two versions: a single disc, and a limited edition version that includes a second disc, entitled Elevation, which features covers of "Elevation" by U2 and "Cardinal Sin" by the Misfits, as well as a live version of "The View" from the band's June 2008 performance at the Hollywood palladium. The album's first single was "The View", followed by "I Hate the World". Death Magnetic received generally positive reviews from critics, and earned the band their highest debut sales at the time, with 80,000 copies sold in its first week. It was the band's last album to feature their long-time drummer, Joey Jordison, who left the band in November 2008 to form his own band, Vovoid. In 2011, the album was certified Gold by the RIAA for shipments in excess of 500,000 copies in the United States.
