The Ministry of Justice publishes a number of legal periodicals and reports, as well as other legal documents of relevance to the citizens of Libya. The Ministry of Justice is the highest legal body in the country and serves as the main administrative and judicial authority in Libya.

One Piece Film: Strong World is a 2009 Japanese animated fantasy action-adventure film written and directed by the well-known director Munehisa Sakai. It is the tenth feature film based on the popular Shonen Jump manga series One Piece by Eiichiro Oda and the first film directed by Munehisa Sakai. The movie opens with a warm greeting from Monkey D. Luffy, the captain of the Straw Hat Pirates, as they prepare to set down on the legendary island of Strong World. However, they soon find themselves facing the wrath of the island’s vicious leader, Shiki the Golden Lion, who is out to steal the world’s ultimate treasure: the ancient and powerful energy source known as Gold. In order to restore peace to the island, the Straw Hat Pirates must team up with a mysterious girl named Nami, fight their way through the island’s deadly creatures, and find the source of Gold before Shiki the Golden Lion can get his hands on it. Along the way, the Straw Hat Pirates must also face off against Shiki’s army of highly-skilled warriors, as well as the mysterious scientist Dr. Indigo and his robotic warriors. The movie also features high quality animation and sound, as well as many memorable characters. The action scenes are extremely fast-paced and exciting, and the movie has many different themes that are explored throughout the course of the feature. Overall, One Piece Film: Strong World is a great movie that fans of the popular Shonen Jump series should not miss. It features great animation, an engaging story, and some of the most iconic characters in manga history. It is definitely a movie that many viewers will enjoy and appreciate.

Kaira (spider) is a genus of spider belonging to the Linyphiidae family. The genus is distributed throughout the Palearctic, with species found in Europe, Asia, North Africa and Japan. Kaira species are generally found in pine forests, cave habitats and on rock faces in mountainous areas. They feed mainly on small insects and other small arthropods. Kaira spiders have a small size, varying from 1.5–4.5 mm in length. Their bodies are gray to brown, often covered with white spots. The legs are darkly colored and heavily setose. The abdomen is mostly flat, and the prosoma is convex with a characteristic striation pattern. The eyes are arranged in two rows and are separated by a dark line. Kaira spiders construct a cobweb made of non-sticky threads. This type of web is used to detect and search for prey. The webs are generally shaped like the spokes of a wheel, made of symmetrical circular patterns, often with a second line in the center. They live in a silken chamber or retreat, located in the center of the web made of sticky droplets. Females tend to stay close to their webs and retreats, while males look for mating partners by wandering about. Kaira spiders are not aggressive, but they will bite if handled. The venom is not dangerous to humans and causes only mild, localized itching and discomfort. The genus Kaira was first described by French entomologist Marie Sédillot in 1847. The genus name is derived from the Greek word kairós, meaning “good fortune”. The genus currently has three described species: Kaira wasbaueri, Kaira reticulata, and Kaira emertoni. Kaira wasbaueri is the most widely distributed species found in Central and Eastern Europe, North Africa, and throughout Asia. The other two species are only known to be found in Japan and Southeast Asia. Kaira spiders are important components of cave and rock face ecosystems, as they help to control the populations of small insects, such as mites and aphids. The silk from Kaira spiders is also used in the manufacture of various textiles and medical products.

John Brockenbrough (1775–1844) was an American lawyer and politician from Charlottesville, Virginia. He is best known as being the founder of the first bank in Virginia, the Bank of the Valley, known today as Bank of the James. He was also a member of the Constitutional Convention of 1829-1830. Brockenbrough was born in Westmoreland County, Virginia in 1775. He graduated from the College of William & Mary in 1793 and began practicing law in Albemarle County, Virginia in 1796. In 1806, he was elected to represent Albemarle County in the Virginia House of Delegates. He would serve for five terms until 1816. Brockenbrough moved to Charlottesville in 1817 and was chosen to be its first mayor. He was also selected as one of the electors of the new state of Virginia in 1819. One of Brockenbrough’s most significant contributions to the region was founding the Bank of the Valley in 1820. He served as its first president and his bank was the first to issue currency in Virginia. It is considered the first bank in the state and its current moniker is Bank of the James. Brockenbrough continued to serve in a variety of public roles in Virginia. He was a trustee of the University of Virginia in 1826 and a member of the Constitutional Convention of 1829-1830. He continued to practice law until his death on June 4, 1844. Legacy Brockenbrough was instrumental in the establishment of the Bank of the Valley, which helps provide financial services to the citizens of Virginia today. He was also a member of the Constitutional Convention of 1829-1830 and was a leader in the development of Charlottesville. Brockenbrough is honored with a Virginia historical highway marker and his portrait hangs in the Madison Hall of the University of Virginia. His name is also remembered today in a number of buildings and streets such as the John W. Brockenbrough Learning Commons of the College of William & Mary and Main Street East in Charlottesville.

Death to 2020 is a mockumentary comedy special released on Netflix and created by the British production company Black Mirror.The production debuted on December 27, 2020 and stars a large ensemble cast, including Hugh Grant, Lisa Kudrow, Kumail Nanjiani, Tracey Ullman, Samuel L. Jackson, Diane Morgan, Leslie Jones, Cristin Milioti , Samson Kayo,Joe Cole, and Nikki Amuka-Bird. The special follows a narrator (played by Grant) as he looks back on the year 2020 in an attempt to make sense of the unprecedented events that defined it. He narrates various anecdotes, mostly uncensored and outrageous, about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic, the Black Lives Matter movement, the 2020 presidential election and other topics. The mockumentary features a number of inventive "interviews" that further illustrate the tone of the miniseries. These interviews include the fictional Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (Ullman), the first "Space Lord" from the United States (Jackson), a conspiracy theorist (Nanjiani), and politician/activists Beverly Prim (Morgan) and Dorsey Mellon (Jones). Death to 2020 has been highly praised by critics. Variety described the mockumentary as a "hilarious and clever look back on this unique year in history," with Jackson calling Grant's performance "perfect." The Guardian described the series as a "welcome shot of comic relief" to an otherwise wild ride of a year. The special also includes an original song titled "2020 year in 2 minutes" written by Deepak Ramapriyan and Jonnie Christie. Following the success of Death to 2020, Netflix has announced plans for a second special. Overall, Death to 2020 serves as an entertaining and comedic look back at a year that few of us would soon forget. As the year comes to a close, this clever mockumentary offers viewers a humorous way to reflect on the events that defined 2020.

A polyhedral map projection is a type of map projection used to represent a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional surface. It is a modification of a cylindrical map projection whereby the points of the sphere are projected onto a polyhedron which is then deformed into the desired map shape. This technique is used by cartographers and geographers to create globes, atlases, and wall maps that accurately reflect the circumference and area of geographic features. The features of this map projection are similar to those of a cylindrical map as it is based on projecting points from a sphere onto a flat surface. It does have some distinctions, however, that make it distinct from traditional cylindrical map projections. First, the points from the sphere are mapped onto an irregularly-shaped polyhedral surface. This shape usually consists of triangles, pentagons, or hexagons, with flat regions placed between them. Once this polyhedral surface has been mapped, it is warped or curved until it matches the desired map shape. When engaging in polyhedral map projection, the cartographer must be aware of the accuracy of the projection. While polyhedral projections are better able to represent landmasses than a cylindrical projection, they often contain more distortion. It can be difficult to create an accurate polyhedral map projection with a large number of regions due to the nature of the irregular polyhedron onto which points are projected. Polyhedral map projections are used to create globes, atlases, wall maps and other types of two-dimensional maps. They are a popular choice for geographic features such as island regions or the Arctic and Antarctic circles, where the need for accurate circumference and area representations is especially important. Due to the unique characteristics of the polyhedral map projection, it has become a favorite of cartographers, geographers, and mapmakers. Because of its accuracy in representing the shape and size of geographic features, it continues to be used for creating both commercial and educational maps. Overall, polyhedral map projection is both an important and useful tool for cartographers and geographers alike. It allows them to create maps that accurately represent the size and shape of geographic features, while also allowing them to adapt the map shape to their own specific needs.

Four Seasons (murals) refers to a series of four fresco murals painted by Italian Baroque master Pietro da Cortona between 1638 and 1639. The murals depict the four allegorical figures of the Greek myths of the four seasons in each of the four corners of Sala dei Virtù e delle Alcove (Room of Virtues and Alcoves) in Palazzo Pamphilj, Rome. Three of the four frescoes are still intact, with the larger and more prominent painting on the east wall. The fresco murals are divided into four panels, each on a separate wall of the room in Palazzo Pamphilj. The central fresco, the dramatic and dynamic "Autumn, is depicted on the east wall, while the other three, "Spring", "Summer" and "Winter", are on the other walls. Each painting is an allegorical representation of the season it depicts: Autumn is colourful and festive, filled with singing and dancing farmers and revelers, while Winter shows a wintery landscape with a small nun praying in a forest and a poor beggar with his dog. Spring is a more serene composition, featuring a waterfall and a shepherd with a staff, while Summer is depicted as a bustling agricultural scene, with harvest ready crops and a farmer leading an enthusiastic team of workers. The murals display the characteristic Baroque style of the period and Cortona's dramatic compositions. His paintings have a distinct grandeur and drama, with their large canvases, strong diagonals and vivid, contrasting colours. Cortona's masterful brushwork can be seen in the lifelike details in the figures and the use of light and shadow to bring out their lively expressions and postures. The Frescoes are highly significant among Cortona's works, showcasing his acclaimed talents in painting monumental decorations for the wealthy clientele of Rome. The Four Seasons frescoes have been reproduced in numerous formats, including prints, engravings and ceramics, and are considered some of the most important murals in Roman Baroque art. They were declared a historic monument by the Italian government in 1921. The original fresco murals were rediscovered in 1896 and restored in 1938. The "Spring" and "Winter" frescoes are still largely complete and are displayed in the Pinacoteca at Palazzo Pamphilj, while the "Summer" fresco is completely lost. The "Autumn" fresco has been restored and is frequenty displayed in other venues such as the Palazzo Barberini and the Palazzo Pitti in Florence. The Four Seasons frescoes are considered one of the great masterpieces of the Baroque period and are amongst the most important mural decorations to have survived from the 17th century. They remain a testament to Pietro da Cortona's artistic genius and technical skill and continue to inspire admirers to this day.

Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi is an 1826 painting by French artist Eugène Delacroix. Taking place during the Greek War of Independence, the painting depicts the Third Siege of Messolonghi, a pivotal event of the Greek struggle against the Ottoman Empire. The painting is considered a masterpiece of the neoclassical school of painting, and has become a symbol of Greek independence. It is displayed in the Musée du Louvre, in Paris. The painting measures 375.5 centimetres by 460.2 centimetres (almost 12 feet by 15 feet). The painting is a large-scale neoclassical composition set during a period of intense conflict in the early 19th century. Delacroix chose to focus on a single moment from the Third Siege of Missolonghi: the surrender of the Greek city to the Ottoman empire. The painting depicts a monk-like figure, wearing a white robe and a red hat, standing amidst the ruins of the city. He is raising his arm up in a gesture of defiance, while the figures around him are brought to tears and grief. The painting displays a range of emotions, from heroic defiance to sorrow and mourning, and is intended to be an expression of the courage and suffering of the Greeks during their War of Independence. In the foreground of the painting is a woman, kneeling with her arm raised, her face contorted in grief. She is flanked by a group of Greek citizens, young and old, visible in the bits and pieces of the city's ruins. Both the woman and the people around her represent the human cost of war and the futility of resistance in the face of overwhelming odds. The painting is a stirring homage to the courage of the Greek people and their struggle for independence. The painting has come to be seen as a symbol of the struggle for freedom and democracy which gave form to the modern Greek identity. Eugène Delacroix's painting of Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi remains one of the most powerful and iconic images of the Greek War of Independence.

Dr Benjamin Twist is an American medical doctor and scientist, who specialises in the field of molecular biology. He is best known for his research into the genetic basis of certain diseases, and his distinguished teaching of molecular biology. Twist was born in Amarillo, Texas and attended the University of Texas School of Medicine. After graduating in 1983, he moved to San Francisco and completed a fellowship in molecular genetics at the California Institute of Technology. He then worked at the University of California, San Francisco, where he earned his PhD degree in 1989. Twist was hired by the University of Arizona in 1990, where he became professor of molecular biology. He was instrumental in developing the molecular genetics department there, and was highly valued as an instructor and mentor. He remained in his position until his retirement in 2016. Throughout his career, Twist has conducted numerous research studies on the genetic basis of diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and neurologic disorders. His lab has identified new genetic mutations associated with these diseases, and his research has led to greater understanding of the underlying causes of genetic conditions. In 1999, Twist was awarded a prestigious MacArthur Fellows award, in recognition of his research accomplishments. He has been on the editorial board of numerous journals, including the Journal of Molecular Biology and the New England Journal of Medicine. He has also served as an adviser to the National Institutes of Health, the World Health Organization, and the American Medical Association. Twist has authored or co-authored several books and textbooks on molecular biology, and has contributed chapters to numerous textbooks. He has served on numerous committees and government panels and been invited to speak at numerous conferences and seminars throughout his career. In 2006, Twist was one of the founders of the International Institute for Human Genome Research, which promotes collaboration and education in the field of genetics. In recognition of his contributions to the field, the Ben Twist Award for Outstanding Contributions in Molecular Biology has been established in his honor. Dr Benjamin Twist has had an illustrious career in molecular biology and is highly respected throughout the field. His many accomplishments have made him a leader in his field and his research continues to benefit the medical world.

Social Assistance Program For Vietnam is a comprehensive program undertaken by the Vietnamese Government which seeks to improve the wellbeing of its citizens by providing financial assistance and support to those in need. The program provides monthly cash benefits to disadvantaged households, and targeted non-cash assistance to vulnerable individuals and families. The program is based on an assessment of existing social assistance policies, and uses an integrated system of social security and development services. The Social Assistance Program For Vietnam (SAPV) was established in 2005 in response to rising poverty and growing gap between rich and poor in the country. The program provides basic living allowances and economic subsidies to those living in poverty, and social assistance payments to other vulnerable groups, such as the elderly, persons with disabilities, or those in temporary or precarious employment. The program is also designed to reduce inequality and to promote social equity. SAPV is financed primarily by the Vietnamese Government and is administered by the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs (MOLISA). In addition, the program is funded by various international organizations and agencies, including the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. SAPV is implemented in different provinces and cities across Vietnam, and there are provisions for different levels of assistance according to the size and composition of the recipient households. Eligibility criteria are established according to national poverty lines and are regularly monitored and reviewed. The Social Assistance Program For Vietnam provides a variety of cash and non-cash benefits, including financial assistance, medical and educational benefits, welfare housing, job training and employment opportunities, and other social services. The program also focuses on improving access to public services and infrastructure, such as healthcare and education, as well as promoting access to finance. The Social Assistance Program For Vietnam is designed to complement existing social safety nets and in-kind support systems, and is an important part of the Vietnamese Government's strategy for poverty reduction and social inclusion. This comprehensive program helps to address the challenges faced by vulnerable populations, and contributes to the advancement of sustainable economic growth and social development in Vietnam.

Mirgor is a Lithuanian manufacturing company that specializes in electrical and electronic components. Founded in 1992, the company produces a variety of parts, primarily for industrial and commercial applications. In a strategic move to become a leader in their industry, Mirgor has developed a wide range of products over the years. These includebatteries, connectors, power supplies, LED lighting, LED displays, sensors, switches and home automation systems. Their latest offering, the ‘SmartHome’, is a comprehensive suite of connected devices and features for home automation. The SmartHome gives homeowners a range of options for controlling and monitoring their home, from temperature and lighting to security, entertainment and more. Mirgor also focuses on innovation, creating customized solutions for their customers. They offer complete design-to-manufacturing services and provide ongoing technical support. The company operates from their headquarters in Vilnius and has offices in Germany, France and the US. They employ over 800 staff, including engineers and technicians. Mirgor has a strong commitment to quality and sustainability and is proud to be a member of the European Energy Industry Association. All their products are designed to meet the highest standards of quality and safety and are certified to ISO and EN standards. Mirgor is focused on the future and to this end, they are investing in R&D to develop new technologies. This includes 3D printing and artificial intelligence, as well as an energy storage system for grid-balancing and the Smart Energy Meter. These initiatives are helping to drive economic growth in the region and contribute to a more sustainable environment. In conclusion, Mirgor is a successful Lithuanian company that produces a wide range of electrical and electronic components for industrial and commercial applications. Focused on quality and innovation, the company is continuously introducing new products and technologies that help to improve the quality of life of their customers.

The 2000 Grand Prix of Mosport was a round of the 2000 CART FedEx Championship Series, held at Mosport International Raceway in Bowmanville, Ontario, Canada. It was the 15th round of the 16-race season and the second round held in Canada. The race served as the final event for Canadian driver Greg Moore before his death in an accident at the 1999 season finale. The race was won from pole position by American driver Michael Andretti, who led the most laps and scored a perfect score of 66 points. It was Andretti's 31st career win since making his CART debut in 1986. The other podium finishers were Max Papis of Italy and Brazilian Bruno Junqueira. The pole position was closely contested as Brazilian Gil de Ferran qualified with a time of 1:04.688 while Andretti was only 0.030 seconds behind. Afterwards, there was a 15-minute warm-up session in which Papis set the fastest lap and de Ferran took fourth. At the start of the race, Andretti led and de Ferran took second place. The defending series champion, Juan Pablo Montoya, fell way back after being involved in a first-tear incident. Papis made a good start and moved up from fifth to third, while Junqueira was making up ground from seventh. The race was under a yellow flag for many laps due to a crash involving Patrick Carpentier, Tarso Marques, and Tony Kanaan. During this time, Andretti was able to build up a gap over the rest of the field, which he would maintain until the end of the race. De Ferran was running in second until he received a 10-second stop-go penalty for overtaking during a yellow-flag period. This promoted Papis to second place, and he was able to close down Andretti's lead, eventually finishing 0.753 seconds behind him. Junqueira rounded up the podium in third place, with British driver Dario Franchitti finishing fourth. The race was the last of Greg Moore's CART career, as he was killed after crashing during the 1999 season finale. To commemorate his life, the organizers saluted him at the halfway point by having all the cars line up and drive at the same speed lap around the track without any racing. The 2000 Grand Prix of Mosport saw American Michael Andretti take his 31st career win from pole position. Max Papis completed the podium at Mosport in second, with Brazilian Bruno Junqueira rounding off the top three. This race represented the last in the career of Canadian driver Greg Moore, who died in an accident at the 1999 season finale.

Lo Fiolairé is a traditional French-Lyonese dish made from rabbit, onions, and white wine. It originated in the region of Lyon, France and is known for its rich, gamey flavor and complex preparation. The dish is believed to have been served since the 16th century, with different names and ingredients depending on the region. The name “Lo Fiolairé” comes from “Li fiolai”, a French root from Old French meaning “making rabbits”. The dish is made with a stew-based preparation of rabbit and other ingredients like onions, garlic, mushrooms, bay leaves, thyme, rosemary, white wine and olive oil. The ingredients are cooked in slow-cooker until all the liquid has evaporated and the rabbit is tender. Alternatively, the rabbit can be cooked on-the-bone, or pan-fried. The vegetables and liquids in the dish are cooked until they have a thick, rich consistency. Lo Fiolairé is usually served with a side of boiled potatoes, or tartiflette and a green salad. It’s often paired with a robust white wine like Beaujolais to compliment the flavor of the game. Over the years the dish has become popular in other regions of France, especially the nearby provinces of Burgundy, Saône-et-Loire and Ain. It is also popular in French-speaking countries in the Caribbean, Canada and Belgium. In addition, the dish has been adapted for non-French cuisines, by adding ingredients like feta cheese and Mediterranean herbs. Today, Lo Fiolairé is still regarded as a classic French dish. It is renowned for its savory flavor, and intricate yet simple traditional preparation. The recipe is often served at festivals and events in the French countryside, where it is served as an homage to traditional French cooking. Lo Fiolairé, a testament of French culinary history and culture, continues to be popular throughout France and the world, providing diners with a delicately-flavored yet robustly-savory experience.

USS Atlanta (CL-51) was a United States Navy light cruiser, active during World War II. She was the lead ship of her class and named for the city of Atlanta, Georgia. Laid down in 1937, Atlanta saw extensive service during the war in the Pacific Theater and was credited with contributing to the sinking of nearly 30,000 tons of enemy shipping. Atlanta was laid down on 19 April 1937 at the Norfolk Naval Shipyard in Portsmouth, Virginia, launched on 11 April 1939, and commissioned on 15 December 1939. Immediately after commissioning, Atlanta proceeded to its new homeport, San Diego, California, arriving in late January 1940. Throughout 1940, the cruiser operated along the California coast and conducted training with newly commissioned destroyers. The following year, Atlanta began a series of extended deployments to the Central Pacific, spending time in island bases such as Pearl Harbor, Midway, and Wake Island. From June 1941 to August 1942, the light cruiser made two voyages to the South Pacific, escorting convoys from San Francisco to the Fiji Islands, New Caledonia, and New Zealand. In August of 1942, Atlanta arrived at Nouméa, New Caledonia, for a period of escort and patrol duty. In November, she joined Task Force 67 (TF 67), which launched a series of attacks on Japanese forces in the Solomon Islands. As part of TF 67, Atlanta's guns contributed to the sinking of Japanese transports and destroyers, and the heavy cruiser, Kinugasa and the destroyer Gyokaze. Atlanta's gunnery was credited with breaking up the final Japanese attempt to resupply their forces on Guadalcanal in January 1943, accounting for the sinking of 13,000 tons of enemy shipping. Throughout 1943, Atlanta conducted exhaustive anti-submarine and patrol duty around the Solomon Islands, providing gunfire support as needed. After a period of maintenance in Pearl Harbor in mid-1944, Atlanta returned to action in December 1944 and took part in the Battle of Iwo Jima. In April 1945, Atlanta made a second trip to Okinawa where it shot down several Japanese planes and helped provide a screen for the invasion fleet. After the Japanese surrender in August 1945, the light cruiser was assigned occupation duty. Atlanta was decommissioned at San Francisco on 19 June 1946 and assigned to the Pacific Reserve Fleet. In 1960, the cruiser was sold to Peru who re-commissioned the vessel as the BAP Quiñones (CL-81). Atlanta earned three battle stars during World War II and three campaign stars during its deployment to the Korean theater.

The 2012–13 Israeli Premier League season is the 49th season since its introduction in 1963, and is the top-tier football in Israel. The season began on 20 August 2012 with Ironi Kiryat Shmona hosting Bnei Yehuda and ended on 28 May 2013, with Hapoel Tel Aviv and Maccabi Haifa both taking part in the deciding match. Maccabi Tel Aviv, the defending Premier League champion, won the title for the 18th time, beating their opponents on the season's final matchday. Kiryat Shmona made their debut in the top division, after having been promoted from the Liga Leumit in the previous season. The League featured three teams from the previous season that were newly promoted: Ironi Kiryat Shmona, Bnei Sakhnin, and Hapoel Be'er Sheva. At the end of the season, Hapoel Be'er Sheva, Bnei Sakhnin, and Maccabi Ashdod were all relegated to the National League. Maccabi Tel Aviv finished the season with 69 points, the most by any of the clubs. Maccabi Haifa, Maccabi Netanya, Hapoel Ramat Gan, and Hapoel Acre were relegated to the National League. The teams that competed in the 2012–13 Israeli Premier League season were: Maccabi Tel Aviv, Hapoel Tel Aviv, Maccabi Haifa, Maccabi Netanya, Hapoel Ramat Gan, Ironi Kiryat Shmona, Ashdod, Kiryat Shmona, Hapoel Be'er Sheva, Hapoel Acre, Maccabi Petah Tikva, Bnei Sakhnin, Maccabi Petah Tikva, and Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv. The 2012–13 Israeli Premier League season was marked by new arrivals, recent arrivals, and some surprising recalls at the top of the league. The season was eventually decided by a showdown between Hapoel Tel Aviv and Maccabi Haifa in the Final Matchday, with Maccabi Tel Aviv crowned as the champions of the season.

Stupid in Love is the first single by American singer-songwriter Mckayla Roxx. It was released on November 15, 2019, as the debut single from her debut studio album, also titled Stupid in Love. The song was written by Mckayla Roxx and produced by Warren G. It features a blend of pop and hip-hop elements and its lyrics describe Mckayla's experiences regarding the emotions of unrequited love. The accompanying music video for "Stupid in Love" was released on November 29, 2019. Directed by Michaila Bisson, the visuals feature Mckayla Roxx being seduced by love, before being rejected and left heartbroken. The song received generally positive reviews from music critics, with many praising Mckayla's versatility and maturity. It was also included on many music critics' year end lists, with Pitchfork naming it one of their 20 Best Songs of 2019. The song was a moderate commercial success. It charted within the top-10 of the Billboard Hot 100 and the Canadian Hot 100, as well as reaching the Top 40 of multiple European charts. It was also certified platinum in Australia and New Zealand and gold in a number of other countries such as the United States, Canada, Germany and the United Kingdom. The song has been performed many times by Mckayla Roxx and often featured on her world tours. In addition, it has appeared in the setlists of many other artists and has been covered by a variety of different artists. It has also featured in the soundtracks for various TV shows and video games. Overall, the song has received significant attention from both music critics and fans and has become one of Mckayla Roxx's most recognizable and biggest hits to date.

. Rudolf van Reest (born 1967) is a Dutch producer and director best known for his critically acclaimed films and television programs. Van Reest began working on films at an early age. His career started with a short film entitled "Summer Love" (1989) which was shot in his hometown of Amsterdam. This brought him to the attention of the Dutch Film Institute and eventually led to him working on several films such as "Eggshell" (1992) and "El Camino" (1994). Van Reest is best known for his feature films "Aaya Accha" (2003), "Mister Been" (2005), and "The Venetian Tower" (2006). He has also directed several television series such as "Rogier and Bergman" (2006-2008), "Heide's House" (2009-2013) and "The Legacy" (2016-2017). He won several awards for his work, including the Dutch Film Award for Best Director for "Aaya Accha" and for Best Television Drama for "Heide's House". Van Reest has collaborated with some of the biggest names in show business such as Harrison Ford, Sarah Jessica Parker, and Kevin Kline. He has also been a mentor to several up-and-coming filmmakers including Peter Bogdanovich and Lee Daniels. Van Reest is currently working on a number of projects including a remake of the classic film "Gaslight" as well as a new television series. He continues to make films that resonate with audiences and critics alike. Rudolf van Reest is considered one of the most talented and successful Dutch filmmakers of his generation. His films are known for their unique vision and humanistic approach, and continue to be critically acclaimed around the world.

Super Mario Bros. 35 is a battle royale game developed by Nintendo and released as part of the 35th anniversary celebration of the original Super Mario Bros. game. It is available exclusively on the Nintendo Switch Online service. The game pits up to 35 players against each other in a race to complete levels from the original Super Mario Bros. game. In each match, players can strategically choose the levels they play and interact with each other to help each other succeed or hinder each other's progress. Players score points by completing levels and defeating enemies and are rewarded with rewards that can be used in future matches. When only one player remains, they are declared the winner of the game. The game allows players to customize their characters by selecting from a range of different styling options, including all of Mario's Cappy costumes, which are available as rewards for completing certain levels. Additionally, players can join special, limited-time tournaments to compete against rivals around the world. Super Mario Bros. 35 offers an innovative experience where players can assemble a dream team of up to five classic Super Mario Bros. characters to compete in a unique take on the traditional battle royale genre. Players can use strategy and teamwork to eliminate their opponents and emerge victorious. In addition to the base game, Super Mario Bros. 35 also has a free downloadable content pack, which includes three additional levels based on Super Mario Bros. 3, Super Mario Bros. The Lost Levels, and Super Mario Bros.: The Legend of the Seven Stars. Super Mario Bros. 35 is a fun and exciting way to experience classic Super Mario Bros. gameplay in an all-new way. With its vibrant visuals, catchy music, and compelling multiplayer, it provides a unique and memorable gaming experience for longtime Mario fans and new players alike.

Alert in the Mediterranean is an annual international exercise hosted by the Italian Navy and co-hosted by the Hellenic Navy. Its aim is to promote and strengthen co-operation between participating navies, amplify communication capabilities and interoperability, enhancing overall security and safety in the Mediterranean Sea. Originating from the ‘Return of Crete’ naval exercise first held in 1994, it has grown and developed over time and eventually evolved into Alert in the Mediterranean. The exercise usually runs for two weeks and sees the participation of Ships and Helicopters from Italy, France, Egypt, Greece, Croatia, Albania, Slovenia and Montenegro. The exercise further supports the principles of the Euro-Mediterranean Partnership – the political and economic platform. It provides an excellent opportunity for the participating countries to practice coordinated joint multi-national operations in a number of scenarios that simulate real conditions, while some evolutions are held in a ‘closed area’ at the centre of the Mediterranean sea and some in regional coastal waters. The scenarios may vary, but they typically involve air defence operations, replenishment at sea, search and rescue and maritime law enforcement operations. Moreover, Alert in the Mediterranean brings benefits to the local economies. This includes direct spending by the countries involved, in the form of port fees, fuel and other services. Additionally, it provides numerous shore-based offices with a platform for simulations and training programs, to keep up with the ever-changing maritime security environment. The 2016 edition saw visits from around 700 people per day in the ports of Valletta, Malta, and Taranto, Italy. The exercise also provides a geographic platform for training for personnel in the planning and command of emergency reaction and is closely tied to the themes of NATO's Maritime Security Operations, as defined in the 2016 Warsaw Summit. Alert in the Mediterranean is held on bi-annual basis, usually in June and October. It has become a point of reference for the coordinating of multilateral naval efforts in the region, while highlighting the importance of the Euro-Mediterranean partnership. The hosting countries have often changed over the years, as the exercise manages to strengthen international ties within the Mediterranean region and beyond.

Ruth Gregory is a British astrophysicist known for her research into astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. She is a Professor of Mathematical Physics at Durham University and a Fellow of the Royal Society. Gregory was born and raised in London, England. She studied mathematics and physics at Imperial College London, earning her BSc and PhD in 1993 and 1997 respectively. She then began a postdoctoral research position at Oxford University in 1997, studying general relativity. From 1997 to 2002, Gregory was a lecturer at Frederick University in Cyprus, before taking up her current post at Durham University in 2002. Gregory's passions are cosmology and general relativity. She has made significant contributions to the understanding of black holes and brane-world cosmology, and she has developed a relativistic of spins. She is also an active mentor and supervisor of young astrophysicists at Durham, and her work is both conceptual and mathematical in nature. Gregory is an ardent proponent of the importance of mathematical models in astrophysics. She believes that the right mathematical models can help to address major questions about the origin and evolution of the universe. In a 2007 article, Gregory argued that mathematical models are essential for discovering how gravitational fields and cosmic forces shape the fabric of space-time, as well as for understanding the implications of the accelerating universe. Gregory has received several awards for her research, including the Maxwell Medal from the Institute of Physics and the prestigious National Science Foundation (NSF) CAREER Award in 2006. She has also been on the advisory boards of New Scientist and Science Magazine. In 2012, she was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. Gregory is a prolific author and public speaker. She has written several acclaimed books on astrophysics, including" Black Holes and Baby Universes" (1993) and "Lectures on Classical and Quantum General Relativity" (2010). In 2006, she wrote a popular children's book, "Mysteries of the Universe", which introduces young readers to the wonders and beauty of the cosmos. Gregory has also regularly spoken at public events and featured in television and film documentaries on astrophysics. In sum, Gregory is an eminent astrophysicist and prolific author. Her research on cosmological phenomena, black holes, and relativistic spins has contributed to the advancement of astrophysics and cosmology. In addition, her commitment to mentorship has greatly helped to cultivate the next generation of astrophysicists.

166 Rhodope is a large Main belt asteroid, located in the inner Solar System. It was discovered on April 04, 1874, by R. Luther at Düsseldorf Observatory in Germany. 166 Rhodope is a primitive carbonaceous asteroid and belongs to the Koronis family of asteroids, which are thought to be fragments from an earlier collision of two larger asteroids. 166 Rhodope is approximately 93 km in diameter and has an albedo of 0.06, which means it reflects only 6% of the light that falls upon it. It takes about 3.7 years to complete an orbit around the Sun, with a semi-major axis of 2.67 AU, a perihelion of 1.9 AU and an aphelion of 3.43 AU. The tilt of its orbit is 6.3°. The asteroid is named after the mountain range of Rhodope located in the southern Balkan peninsula, along the borders of Greece, Bulgaria and Turkey. Rhodope is rich in biodiversity, and is characterized by grasslands and rare vegetation species, with the eastern part of the mountain having some of the largest forests in Europe. 166 Rhodope has been studied by a variety of ground based optical instruments, and its X-ray emissions were observed by the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The asteroid is too far away for detailed studies, but high resolution images suggest that it has a heavily cratered surface, with a handful of larger craters. 166 Rhodope is not thought to have any significant moons, but it may have a few small ones, as most of the asteroids of the Koronis family have them. 166 Rhodope is also a source of numerous meteorites, as it is a common parent body of carbonaceous chondrite meteorites. Overall, 166 Rhodope is an interesting, primitive example of a carbonaceous Main Belt asteroid, and one of the most studied Koronis family asteroids. It provides an opportunity to study the early stages of solar system formation and the processes that shaped it.

Charles K. Duncan (1920 – December 3, 1998) was a prominent American business executive and philanthropist. He is best known as the Chief Executive Officer of Universal Corporation, one of the world’s leading tobacco companies, for a period of 13 years from 1978 to 1992. Born in Lynchburg, Virginia, Duncan was a graduate of the University of Virginia and served as a Naval officer in World War II. After the war, he joined Universal Corporation as a sales representative in 1947, eventually rising to the position of Executive Vice President. In 1978, he succeeded J. Barry Payne as the Chief Executive Officer, overseeing a period of unprecedented growth and expansion for the company. Through acquisitions and joint ventures, Universal Corporation extended its tobacco operations into Central and South America, doubling its income during Duncan’s tenure. In addition, he has been credited with the introduction of innovative techniques in tobacco curing, leaf blending, and packaging. Duncan was also a successful philanthropist. In 1991, the University of Virginia established the University’s Charles K. Duncan Executive Program to honor Duncan for his achievements and philanthropic work. He was also a founding member of the Ronald McDonald House Charities and member of the board of the YMCA of Central Virginia, as well as a generous donor to the Harper Cancer Research Center. Duncan passed away on December 3, 1998, in his hometown of Lynchburg, Virginia. He was 78 years old. He was survived by his wife, Nancy, and their two children. His legacy of continued success in business and philanthropy remains an inspiration to many.

Johnny Hopp (born September 29, 1905, Barksdale, Missouri - died April 16, 2003, Salinas, California) was an American baseball player and coach, who enjoyed a twenty-year career in Major League Baseball (MLB). A switch-hitting outfielder, Hopp batted and threw right-handed. He was listed as 5 feet 8 1⁄2 inches (1.74 m) tall, and weighed 170 pounds (77 kg). Hopp began his professional baseball career in 1928 when, as a member of his hometown minor-league club, the Barksdale Barney Owls of the Cotton States League, he posted a .400 batting average in 48 games. He spent several years in the high minors before finally getting a trial with the then-St. Louis Cardinals in 1939. He helped the Cardinals win four National League pennants in his first five big-league seasons, even star-ting at four different outfield positions in the 1942 World Series. In a 15-season career, Hopp was a .296 hitter with 83 home runs and 65 stolen bases in 1478 games. He also played in six out of the nine World Series he was part of. In 1937, as a member of the Nashville Vols, he made a then-minor-league record of five stolen bases in a single game. After his MLB playing days ended, Hopp served as a batting coach and occasional first-base coach during the 1950s and 1960s. He worked with the Boston Red Sox (1950–53; 1964–65), New York Giants (1955–57), Milwaukee Braves (1960–62) and Kansas City Athletics (1963–64). Hopp was a member of the 1949–50 Cardinals teams that toured Japan. Following his coaching retirement, he spent a long career as a scout for many organizations, among them, the Cardinals, the Oakland A's, and the Milwaukee Brewers. Hopp died in 2003 in Salinas, California, at the age of 97. He was interred at Kansas City's Mount Olivet Cemetery.

Berseba Constituency is an electoral constituency in the Ohangwena Region of Namibia. As of 2020, the constituency has a population of 17,862. The constituency includes the town of Berseba itself, as well as several surrounding villages and settlements. The villages are Terrero, Cacainha, Langera, Guimbe, Oshipala, Odima, Isendele, and Oshigambo. Berseba Constituency is represented in the National Council of Namibia by Petro Verbena from the DTA of Namibia since 2010, and in the National Assembly of Namibia by Cambapu Robert Hiedemann from the ruling SWAPO party since 2005. Berseba Constituency is a rural constituency with a strong agricultural base. Residents rely on subsistence farming to survive and small-scale farmers produce crops that are primarily intended for local consumption. There has been some small-scale commercial farming in the area, with farmers growing maize, sorghum, sweet potatoes and pumpkin. The constituency is situated in an arid area, and residents struggle during periods of extended drought. The few existing water sources include boreholes, wells, dams, and rivers. Education in the area is limited, with only two primary schools and two secondary schools operating in the constituency. There is no post-secondary educational institution in the constituency. The constituency is highly dependent on the central government for governance and development initiatives. The local government is extremely limited in terms of financial and personnel resources, and is heavily reliant on financial aid from the government. These resources can go towards initiatives such as upgrading roads and providing basic services such as water and sanitation. Berseba Constituency has a unique culture, with strong ties to the local traditions. Residents tend to speak the various local languages, and the majority practice the traditional religions of the region. Music and dance are also an important part of the culture, with many traditional songs and dance styles still practiced by the locals. In recent years, the constituency has been facing a number of development challenges. These include poverty, hunger, and a lack of infrastructure. In addition, the arid climate and limited distribution of public services make access to adequate health care, vocational training, and education a challenge. Berseba Constituency is an important contributor to the Namibian economy, and its rural population presents an opportunity for the government to invest in the area and create jobs. The constituency is a key base for the ruling SWAPO party, and its residents are highly supportive of the party.

The 1977–78 San Antonio Spurs season was the franchise’s 11th in the National Basketball Association. After a 15–67 mark the previous season, the Spurs went on to improve to 34–48 but still missed out on their first ever playoff appearance in their 11th year of existence. This would turn out to be the last time the Spurs would finish with a sub-.500 record until the 1985–86 season, caused by the introduction of the three-point line and the blockbuster trade the club made prior to the 1983–84 season. In the offseason, the Spurs lost two key players to the expansion draft as George Karl and Truck Robinson were selected by the Kansas City Kings and the New Jersey Nets respectively. The Spurs replaced them with players such as Dave Hollins who was drafted in the second round, Ralph Simpson and Ritchie Powers. The season began with a 2–5 start but the Spurs eventually got it together and went on to follow their best stretch of the season, posting a 17–7 mark from November 27th to January 15th to sit at 19–12 at the midpoint. Ron Brewer emerged as a team leader, becoming the first Spur to average double digits in scoring while Jonathon Wilkerson and Swen Nater also improved their game. The Spurs finished off the season with a 15–36 mark, including 13 straight losses to end the season as things really fell apart due to injuries and poor performances. The team ultimately failed to reach the playoffs, missing out on the NBA's postseason for the sixth consecutive season. Wilkerson, however, led the team in scoring with 17.7 points per game to finish with the tenth best scoring average in the league. For the 1979–80 season, the Spurs very nearly made their playoff debut but ultimately fell short. However, by the 1981–82 season the Spurs had assembled enough talent and depth to make their first ever NBA playoff appearance after 11 years in the league. The 1977–78 San Antonio Spurs season ended as a step in the right direction as the team improved compared to the previous season but ultimately failed to reach the playoffs. It was the team's last season of missing the playoffs since 1985–86, until the 2018-19 season. The Spurs would eventually build a core that ended up going to the playoffs for 21 consecutive seasons, only missing out on a 22nd consecutive berth in 2018–19.

Lucien Villa (1892-1970) was a French abstract painter. He is best known for his contribution to the School of Paris and his works are found in major art institutions around the world. Villa was born in 1896 in Rouen, France. He studied at the Lycée Corneille. He initially studied at the Academy of Paris in 1910, but then left to pursue an independent course of study, first under the influence of Fauvism, then Cubism and eventually towards an intense abstraction. He was most influenced by Cezanne, Matisse, and Picasso. He also had contacts with Duchamp, Dali, and Leger, and became a member of the Abstraction-Création art group. He was a pioneer of abstract art in France. Villa had his first solo exhibition in Paris in 1932, and from then his career flourished. He exhibited regularly around the country and by the 1940s, he was recognised as one of the most esteemed abstract painters from the School of Paris. His works were included in many prestigious exhibitions including the Venice Bienniale in 1952 and the Venice Bienniale in 1986. Villa received many honors for his painting and teaching, such as receiving honorary doctorates at universities in France. Villa is most well-known for his colorful, geometric compositions in which vivid colors and intricate lines give way to more subtle hues and gradations. By creating tension between graceful curves and sharp edges, Villa approaches a type of gestural abstraction. Villa’s work is characterised by the transmutation of organic shapes into abstract motifs, creating a new form of pictorial abstract space. His works are held in the permanent collections of leading art institutions around the world, including the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris, The Museum of Modern Art in New York, The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam and Tate Modern in London. Villa died in 1970 at the age of seventy-eight.

The 1984 Buffalo Bills season was the franchise's 25th season in the National Football League and the 15th under head coach Kay Stephenson. The Bills had a 7-9 record and failed to make the playoffs for the fourth consecutive season. Their 7-4 record through 11 games was their best since 1976, and had them in playoff contention entering December. However, 3 losses in their final 4 games, including a 15-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers in the season finale left the team at 7-9 and one game out of the playoffs. The offense was led by quarterback Joe Ferguson who threw for a career-high 3,043 yards, 22 touchdowns and 17 interceptions. He was backed up by rookies Matt Kofler and Mark Stevens, who shared duties playing backup. The team's leading rusher was Larry Mason who carried the ball 234 times for 705 yards and 5 touchdowns. Top receiving targets for Ferguson were Elbert "Ickey" Woods with 43 receptions for 449 yards and 8 touchdowns, and rookie wide receiver Ernest Givins who caught 41 passes for 545 yards and 6 touchdowns while earning Pro Bowl honors. On defense, the Bills ranked 12th in the league, allowing 339.2 yards of total offense per game, while recording 33 sacks and 27 interceptions. Second-year defensive end Bruce Smith was named to the Pro Bowl, leading the team with 14 sacks and earning Defensive Rookie of the Year in 1983. The Bills also returned both kickers from the 1983 season, punter Chris Mohr and kicker Scott Norwood. Norwood made 16 field goals and 21 extra points for 69 total points. The Bills opened the season on September 3, 1984 with a win at the New York Jets, 10-7. This was their first win versus the Jets since the 1980 season. They would later lose to the Jets in the season finale, 15-13. Other highlights of the season included a 34-3 home victory against the St. Louis Cardinals, and a 17-13 victory over the Chicago Bears, which was the Bills' first win against the Bears since 1975. The Bills finished the 1984 season 7-9, a improvement over their 4-12 finish the year before. The team failed to make the playoffs, finishing one game behind the 8-8 Miami Dolphins who earned the last Wild Card spot. Despite their promising mid-season record, the Bills went winless in their final 4 games, ending their season on a sour note. Despite the disappointing finish, the Bills showed promise as they began to form the nucleus of what would be one of the most successful teams in the late 80's and early 90's. The 1984 season marks the end of the Kay Stephenson era, as he was replaced by Hank Bullough in 1985, and with him came a new era for the Buffalo Bills.

Elisabeth Haseloff (born 7 March 1955) is a German politician of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU). She was the Prime Minister of Lower Saxony from 2010 to 2013, making her the first woman to hold this position. Haseloff was born in Harbke, Lower Saxony (then East Germany). She attended school in Stendal and in Ballenstedt, completing her Abitur (higher education entrance qualification) in 1975. Haseloff studied Agricultural Science at the University of Göttingen. After graduating in 1980, she worked as a university assistant at the same institution. In 1987 Haseloff became a member of the CDU, and was elected to the Lower Saxony state parliament in 1994. In 2007 she was elected leader of the CDU faction in the Lower Saxony state parliament. In 2009 Haseloff was elected Prime Minister of Lower Saxony, and the following year she became the first woman to hold the office. During her tenure, she prioritized energy and climate policy, higher education, migration, and environmental protection. In 2011, Haseloff approved the use of nuclear power in Germany until 2022, a policy which led to heated political debates. In 2012, she opened a new plant in Wolfsburg to produce electric motors for Volkswagen cars. Haseloff has also been active on the national political scene, serving as a state representative in the Bundestag since 2018. She has held several positions in the CDU, notably as president of the CDU in Lower Saxony, and as a member of the CDU's Agency Board. Haseloff is married and has two sons. In 2012, she was awarded the Grand Cross of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany for her services to the nation.

Umberto Puppini (born February 19, 1951, San Giovanni, Tuscany, Italy) is an Italian architect, urbanist and academic. He studied architecture at the University of Florence and began his professional career in 1975. During this period he collaborated with notable Italian architects such as Italo Gamberini and Umberto Riva. In the following years, he moved to Switzerland and the United States, where he worked in various cities, including Zurich and New Orleans. Throughout his career, Umberto Puppini has focused on modern and contemporary architecture, environmental design, urban regeneration, and the preservation of historical monuments. He is an award-winning architect, most notably receiving the Carli Medal from the Italian Association of Architects in 1987. In the 1980s, Puppini returned to Italy, where he set up his own architecture firm, Umberto Puppini e Associati (UPA). This allowed him to work on various public and private projects, including a number of museums and urban regeneration projects. He also contributed to the design of Reggio Emilia's Teatro Verdi, a concert hall and theater. In addition to his architectural activities, Umberto Puppini is a well-known professor at the University of Florence. As a distinguished academic, he has been awarded the Order of Academic Palms by the Italian Ministry of Education and has taught in several European universities. Umberto Puppini is a firm believer in the importance of social and environmental sustainability, emphasizing these elements in his architectural projects. His commitment to urban regeneration and preservation has earned him international recognition, allowing him to impact young Italian architects and inspire new generations of creators. He is actively working in architecture and urbanism, taking on projects related to public urban spaces, green areas and social housing. He is also actively publishing, researching and exploring various architectural trends, and he is a believer in the importance of public consultation for urban renewal and the recovery of deteriorated historical sites.

D.A. Fishman (b. 1977) is an American entrepreneur notable for founding and managing large-scale technology projects. Fishman began his career in the tech industry with a degree in computer science from the University of Pennsylvania. He then landed jobs as an early software engineer and tech consultant in a variety of industries, with notable stints as a staff engineer at Oracle, Microsoft, and Amazon. In 2006, Fishman launched his own firm specializing in the development of innovative software solutions. His brainchild was a cloud-based software application called "CloudLogic," which aimed to simplify the storage, retrieval and analysis of customer data. Through his company, he helped lead the successful customer-management projects of many Fortune 500 companies, such as IBM and Bank of America. In 2009, Fishman's tech entrepreneurship efforts expanded to encompass the world of eCommerce when he launched BlueRidgeco, a national eCommerce platform. The platform saw significant success, and was purchased by an international media site in 2011 for an undisclosed seven-figure sum. Following this success, Fishman continued to pursue technology projects and started a new venture in 2017, DigiLeaders. Through DigiLeaders, Fishman has been working to help startups and small businesses build their customer base and maximize their impact through digital marketing and customer data insights. By 2019, Fishman had achieved notable success in the tech industry. He had pioneered multiple customer service and data management solutions, two of which were acquired by larger companies. In 2020, he was named to the Business Insider list of "30 Inspiring Tech Entrepreneurs Making a Difference". As for his personal life, Fishman spends his free time with his family: wife Lorraine and children Ben, Emily, and Sarah. He is an avid reader, particularly of classic literature and Harry Potter novels, and enjoys launching model rockets. He and his family currently reside in the Washington DC area.

A Hole in the Sock of (Dave Davies) is the debut album by English musician Dave Davies, released on 17 October 1966 by Arista Records. It was the first solo album to be released by a member of The Kinks, and is considered to be a major influence on the psychedelic rock sound of the 1960s. The album was produced by Davies himself, and features original Kinks songs as well as covers of traditional folk songs. It is best known for its classic psychedelic single, "Death of a Clown". The album was a moderate commercial success in its time, reaching No. 34 on the UK Albums Chart and No. 105 on the US Billboard 200. The album contains a variety of musical styles, ranging from folk and country music to psychedelia and garage rock. Davies' songwriting on the album has been praised by many critics and fans, and the album has been seen as a major influence on the British psychedelic movement of the 1960s. The album was reissued on 20 August 1996 by Castle Communications in the United Kingdom on CD, with five bonus tracks. In 2013, it was re-released by Sony Legacy with 28 bonus tracks. The album's title is a reference to the hole in Davies' sock, which was a consequence of losing the heel at a Kinks show in Blackpool in the early 1960s. In addition, the album's cover photo was taken at a Kinks show when Davies threw a bass drum off the balcony. A Hole in the Sock of (Dave Davies)has been featured on various greatest of all time lists. In 2003, Rolling Stone magazine ranked it at number 919 in their list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Similarly, in 2020, it was ranked at number 986 in their revised list. In 2012, the album was also featured in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die. Despite the album's commercial success and critical acclaim, it remains an overlooked gem in Davies' career. A Hole in the Sock of (Dave Davies) highlights Davies' unique vision and showcases his talent as a songwriter, singer, and guitarist. It is an essential album in the history of British pop music, and continues to influence generations of musicians.

. Reginald's Tower is a 13th-century tower located in the city of Waterford, Ireland. It is one of the oldest and most iconic landmarks of the city, and has been used for various purposes over the centuries, including as a fortress, a prison, and even a museum. The tower is named after the Viking Reginald, who was said to have constructed it in the 12th century to serve as a defense and lookout point. Reginald's Tower is a D-shaped structure made of limestone and sandstone, which stands twelve meters tall and is surrounded by a defensive wall. The interior of the tower is circular and is currently divided into two floors, the lower floor containing the Great Hall, while the upper floor is a hexagonal gallery, with three entrances and a crack in the ceiling, which was thought to have been used as an escape hatch in times of emergency. The roof is conical and made of lead. The early history of the tower is not well-documented, but records show that it was used as a military shelter during the 1600s, when the English occupied Waterford. During the late 17th and early 18th centuries, the tower served as a prison, and inmates included some of Waterford's most notorious criminals. In the 19th century, the tower was used as a museum and an observatory, holding exhibitions and displaying archaeological finds from the surrounding area. In 1951, the Office of Public Works took control of the site, and began restoring the tower to its original condition. Today, the tower is open to the public for guided tours, and visitors have the opportunity to learn about its long and sometimes turbulent history. Its exterior is decorated with carvings, including a decapitated head, a mace, and a man-at-arms holding a bow and arrow. Reginald's Tower is now a popular destination for tourists, as it is considered one of the most important monuments in Waterford. Its strategic position overlooking the harbour has made it an iconic symbol of the city, and it is cherished by locals as a reminder of their history and heritage.

Conor Parke (born 18 May 1988) is an Irish singer-songwriter based in London. With a uniquely soulful sound, Parke has been compared to '90s classics such as Damien Rice and Ben Harper. Parke began writing and performing from an early age. He took up guitar at the age of 9 and by 13 had written his first song. This musical ability was something he’d inherited from his father, an Irish singer/songwriter and musician. From 2008 - 2012 Parke worked on a series of acoustic albums, released independently and available to buy on his website. These albums earned him a dedicated following and gained him recognition in the music press, both in Ireland and the UK. In 2013, Parke was spotted busking in Covent Garden and was subsequently signed to UK-based record label '3Bears Recordings'. His debut single ‘In Time’ was released in 2014, preceded by the release of the critically acclaimed EP Breath Of Life. It featured co-writes with Chris Difford (Squeeze) and Adrian Tew (Amy Winehouse). Parke's music is a mix of folk and soul, crafted with thought-provoking lyrics and catchy melodies. He released two further singles in Spring 2015, the Joy Division-haired 'A thousand Islands' and 'The Turning Point' featuring the soulful voice of Lorna Thomas, who sang with him in his early circuit days. In 2016, Parke released his anticipated debut album Moving On to critical acclaim, with many critics touting it as a potential breakthrough record for the singer/songwriter. In his personal permformances, Parke is known for being able to captivate any audience with his music and hushed delivery. He has opened for acts such as Keane, Taylor Swift and Damien Rice, and in 2016 embarked on a tour of the UK supporting Bryde. Today, Conor Parke is an emerging artist on the London circuit, playing a mix of solo and full band shows at popular venues in London and around the country. His self-funded EPs have sold tens of thousands of downloads, as well as garnering him numerous radio spots and magazine features. With his new music and touring schedule, Parke has cemented himself as one of the most respected singer/songwriters of his generation. In addition to music, Parke is a keen photographer and surfer, and during his downtime can often be found exploring the coastline with his camera.

Café Majestic is a cafeteria located in Lisbon, Portugal. Established in 1921, Café Majestic is considered to be one of Lisbon's most iconic cafés. The café has a grand, Art Deco-style interior, designed to give customers a feeling of awe and nostalgia. The café was the first of its kind in Lisbon, and opened just three years after the end of World War I. In its early years Café Majestic became a popular hang-out spot for a variety of social groups, including writers, artists, musicians, politicians, and intellectuals. To this day, it remains a hub of cultural activity and a popular spot for locals and tourists alike. The café features a range of classic European dishes, along with a variety of Portuguese specialties. Many of their signature dishes, such as the roasted chicken with olives, have been part of the café’s menu since the 1920s. Customers can also enjoy a variety of drinks and Portuguese wines, along with signature cocktails. Along with the dining area, Café Majestic also features a bar and a terrace, which offers stunning views of the Tagus river. In addition to its restaurant and bar, Café Majestic also regularly hosts a range of events, from jazz concerts to book presentations, art exhibitions and plays. Over the years, the café has been featured in several films and books, including the Italian movie Le ragazze di Piazza di Spagna and the Portuguese book O Romance do Majestic. In the modern day, Café Majestic is well-known for its atmosphere and social importance. It is widely regarded as one of Lisbon’s most iconic landmarks, displaying a unique combination of history, style, and culture. It has received numerous awards and recognitions throughout its history, and has become a must-visit spot for any traveler in Lisbon.

Prex Merrill is an American bank executive and entrepreneur. He is best known as the long-time Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Co-Chairman of Bank of America Corporation, and former Chairman of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. He held the latter position from April 2016 until January 17, 2018. Early life and Education Merrill was born in Kingsford, Michigan, and grew up in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. He received a B.S. degree in finance from Northern Michigan University in 1977. Career Merrill joined Bank of America in 1979, prior to its merger with Security Pacific Bank. Over his thirty-eight year career with Bank of America, he served in numerous senior management roles, including at one-time President of Commercial Banking and Prime Services, heading up all of Bank of America's corporate, investment banking and global capital markets businesses. After his retirement in 2017, he joined the boards of Accuray Inc, a manufacturer of radiation therapy technology and First Republic Bank, a private bank and wealth management firm, both located in Emeryville, California. In 2020, Merrill was appointed to the board of directors of American Electric Power Co., Inc., a publicly traded utility company based in Columbus, Ohio. In addition, he is a member of the board of directors of Northern Michigan University. In 2018, as Chairman of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Merrill wrote an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal which discussed the importance of regulatory reform for the country's financial system. The Prex Andy Merrill Fellowship Program Merril created the Prex Andy Merrill Fellowship Program at Northern Michigan University in 2006 to fund youth advisory program, a program that brings student innovators from around the world to the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. The program funds projects that foster business and entrepreneurship, and encourage community development within the local area. Personal life Merrill and his wife have one daughter. He is a member of the Bay Area Council for Education, and a board member of the National Council on Economic Education. In 2020, Merrill was named one of the top 10 most influential executives of the decade in the financial industry by Forbes magazine.
