Sašo Mijalkov (born 26 August 1969) is a Macedonian businessman, the owner and a former CEO of Makedonski Telekom, one of the largest Macedonian companies. He was the director of the Macedonian Intelligence Agency from 2008 to 2011. Mijalkov was born on 26 August 1969 in Ohrid, Macedonia. He graduated from the Faculty of Electrical Engineering at St. Clement of Ohrid University in Skopje in 1992. He then earned a degree in Business Administration from Ss Cyril and Methodius University in 2006. Mijalkov started his business career in 2002 when he joined Makedonski Telekom as CEO and later as chairman and major shareholder in 2004. Under his leadership, the company increased its market share from 2% in 2002 to over 60% by 2010, becoming one of the most successful companies in Macedonia. At the same time, Mijalkov was appointed director of the Macedonian Intelligence Agency in 2008. He resigned from that position in 2011. Outside of his professional activities, Mijalkov is a keen sportsman. He is a member of the National Soccer Association and the National Basketball Association, and participates in various local tournaments. He is also an active philanthropist and a patron of several charity organizations in Macedonia. In recognition of his contributions to the success of Makedonski Telekom, Mijalkov was given the Skopje Award in 2010. He is regarded as one of the most successful entrepreneurs in Macedonia, and is often called upon to give lectures and keynote speeches at business conferences and universities.

The Alhambra Theatre of Variety was a prominent theatre located in London's East End that opened in 1879 and stood until 1959. It was known as the "home of variety" and produced music hall and vaudeville performances. The theatre was built by entrepreneur Edward Moss who owned many other theatres in the area, including the nearby Oxford Music Hall. His brother, Alfred, had previously owned the small Hoxton Hall before they moved to the Alhambra's large premises. Moss created a grand theatre, complete with lavish decorations, an ornate entrance hall and a staircase designed by architect William Bonython Moffatt. The Alhambra is often associated with the great music hall stars of the time, including singer-songwriter Marie Lloyd and comedian Dan Leno, who both performed on the stage. Other big names who graced the Alhambra's boards included Arthur Lloyd, George Formby Sr., Little Tich, and Mark ''Spud'' Murphy. These big-name stars attracted large audiences who, on occasion, even spilled out into the streets. At the start of the twentieth century, the theatre underwent major renovations, which included a complete redesign of the main auditorium area and the addition of two upper balconies. The Alhambra Theatre was an important stop on the circuit for most vaudeville and music hall acts, who made regular tours of Britain and Ireland. It was also an important proving ground for young and aspiring performers, who could perform in front of a large and enthusiastic audience. The theatre's heyday faded eventually, as the popularity of music hall and variety shows began to wane. The Alhambra closed in 1959, when music hall performances had become a rare occurrence in London's East End. The theatre was demolished soon after its closure and the area has since been redeveloped. Today, the Alhambra Theatre is remembered fondly by theatre aficionados and East End locals alike. It was a unique, colourful and vibrant venue, where many great performers began their careers and where entertainment was provided to thousands of Londoners each week. A blue plaque outside the building commemorates its existence and remembers the great performers it once housed.

Bluegrass Warhorses is an American bluegrass band founded in 2014 in Richmond, Virginia. The band is composed of four members: Andy Bailey on banjo, Tom Nowell on mandolin, Hank Hunt on guitar and John Price on bass. Their music is an eclectic mix of traditional Appalachian bluegrass, modern country, folk, and blues. The band is known for their high-energy performances and has become a staple of the Richmond music scene. They have released two albums, Ride the Wave (2016) and Startin’ Over (2019), to much critical acclaim from a variety of sources, including fans, bloggers and reviewers. Their work has been featured in a number of film and television projects. The members of the band have a long history in the Richmond and surrounding areas. Bailey, Nowell, and Hunt have been playing music together since 2007, playing locally in and around Richmond. When Price joined the trio in 2014, they felt the need to give the project a name, which lead to the creation of Bluegrass Warhorses. Bluegrass Warhorses has built a reputation best described as “innovative traditional”, playing a unique style of bluegrass music with a mix of old and new elements. Drawing on old-time roots, they call on a wide range of Americana and folk influences as they craft and perform their songs. The band has toured extensively, playing festivals, clubs and other venues all around the eastern United States. They have shared stages with some of the premier artists in the bluegrass and Americana genres, including Del McCoury, Sam Bush, and Dead Leaves Rising. Bluegrass Warhorses is widely considered one of the most exciting young bands to emerge in the U.S. bluegrass scene. The band delivers passionate and energetic live performances and are sure to keep you entertained from start to finish.

Sempronius Densus (born c. 361 AD) was a Roman soldier and part of a military unit known as the Protectores, who served the Roman Empire during the 3rd and 4th century AD. Densus is known for being the only member of his unit to survive the Battle of Adrianople, in which the Romans were defeated by the Goths in 378 AD. Densus was from the ancient city of Spalatum on the Adriatic coast of modern-day Croatia. He was part of the Protectores, a unit formed from Constantine's bodyguard, the Scholae Palatinae. Densus rose to prominence in the reign of Constantine I (306-337 AD). His unit was an elite, professional force that rode to battle in wagons, and wore white cloaks in battle, which served as a psychological deterrent. In 378 AD, the Roman army, under Emperor Valens, was defeated at the Battle of Adrianople, by a large army of Goths. Valens himself was killed leading the charge. Only Sempronius Densus and another soldier, Himilco, managed to survive the battle. It is believed that both men made their escape by hiding in a chariot and merging with the victorious Goth army. After the battle, it is believed that Densus and Himilco went their separate ways and no more is known of their ultimate fate. Densus appears to have survived long enough to be remembered in the writings of Ammianus Marcellinus, who mentions that he escaped the Battle of Adrianople and tells the story of how Densus and Himilco saved themselves. Densus’s courage and bravery were widely praised for centuries. As late as the 6th century AD, this courageous soldier was remembered as an example of courage and faithfulness to the Roman Empire. He was not just praised for surviving the battle, but was also respected for his courage and loyalty in a desperate situation. Today, Densus is remembered as a heroic figure, an example of bravery and true Roman spirit in a very dark period of history. He is an inspiration to everyone who faces a seemingly impossible task and is a reminder of the determination and courage that can enable a person to overcome even the most unfavourable circumstances.

Richard Trenkel (born June 16, 1989) is a German professional soccer player who currently plays for Schalke 04 in the German Bundesliga. He is a defender who can also play in mid-field and has been a regular for Schalke since 2013. Trenkel began his career in 2007 with FC Bruchsal in the fifth division of German soccer. He then joined the U-19 team of 1899 Hoffenheim and soon after signed his first professional contract. During his tenure at Hoffenheim, Trenkel made 73 appearances, scoring five goals. In 2012, Trenkel signed with Schalke 04, a club playing in the first division Bundesliga. He made an immediate impact in Schalke's midfield and quickly established himself as a regular starter. In 2013, Trenkel was voted Schalke's Player of the Year. Prior to joining Schalke 04, Trenkel was also invited to take part in the German U-19 team, eventually making nine appearances and scoring one goal. His impressive displays earned him a place in the German Under-20 side in 2012. Trenkel has made upwards of 172 appearances for Schalke 04 since joining the club, and has scored three goals. He has become an integral part of the team and has played in both major European tournaments, the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League. Trenkel's playing style is that of a defensive midfielder which he has adapted over time to become more versatile. He is known for his excellent passing and aerial capabilities, coupled with good defensive positioning. His performances at Schalke have made him a fan favourite, with many labelling him as "The Man of Steel" for his work ethic and leadership in the field. Outside of football, Trenkel is a proponent for youth development in Germany, regularly taking part in coaching clinics and academy classes. Away from soccer, Trenkel is a keen athlete and participates in various running and cycling activities. In the summer of 2016, Trenkel signed a new four-year contract with Schalke 04, keeping him with the club until 2020. This extension established Trenkel as a cornerstone of the Schalke squad, with his performances and leadership in the field being a major factor in convincing the board to extend his stay with the club.

The 2013–14 FC Anzhi Makhachkala Season was a season in the Russian Premier League, the top flight of professional football in Russia. The season saw Anzhi Makhachkala, the reigning champions of the Russian Premier League, finish in 10th place. The season began under new Anzhi Makhachkala boss Rene Meulensteen following the departure of Guus Hiddink at the end of the 2012–13 season. Anzhi kicked off the season with a 1–0 home win over FC Kuban on April 20, 2013. Anzhi had a strong start to the season with wins over Kuban, Dynamo Moscow and Krylia Sovetov Samara giving them a tally of seven points from the opening three games. Anzhi would soon find their feet and began to creep up the table. On 3 February, just after the winter break, they played their biggest game of the season against city rivals Dinamo Moscow. The game ended in a 2–1 defeat, but Anzhi still ended the game in 5th place. Anzhi won the Russian Cup on 27 May 2014. This meant that the club qualified for the UEFA Europa League for the 2014–15 season. On the league front, Anzhi fell away from the top three after a poor run of form, culminating in a defeat against FC Rostov in the 40th game of the season. Anzhi then dropped as low as 12th place, before ending the season in 10th place. Despite their league finish, Anzhi’s qualification for the Europa League meant that the season was seen as a successful one for the club. In the UEFA Europa League, Anzhi were knocked out in the group stages after finishing third in their group. They earned four points, with a 5–0 win over Litex Lovech the highlight of their campaign. The season saw the emergence of several key players, including Oleg Shatov and Aleksandr Bukharov. Shatov was the club’s key attacker, scoring nine goals, while Bukharov scored seven. Overall, the 2013–14 season was a successful one for FC Anzhi Makhachkala, as they ended the season with a Russian Cup win and qualified for Europe.

La Roche-en-Ardenne Castle is a medieval castle located in the town of La Roche-en-Ardenne, in the Province of Luxembourg, Belgium. The castle is one of the most renowned and beautiful castles in the country, characterized by its typically medieval towers and walls. The exact date on which La Roche-en-Ardenne Castle was first built is unknown, though some sources estimate it to the 9th century, during Carolingian Empire rule. At first, it served as an initiative of local counts who depended on the town’s strategic position near the rivers Ourthe and Lomme. In the 11th century, the castle was seized by the count of Luxembourg and later, it passed on to the earls of Bouillon. In the 15th century, the castle was severely damaged during the Burgundian Wars, and during the 16th century, it was rebuilt. However, it was once again destroyed in 1677, when Louis XIV of France sent an army to take over the castle. It was then reconstructed yet again, this time in a more modern appearance, with a tower and two massive bastions. Another restoration was made in the 20th century. Today, the castle remains a beautiful attraction and is open for tours year round. Visitors can explore the castle and visit the old armory and chapel, built in the 13th century. Additional facilities such as a hotel, restaurant and shop are also available for visitors. The castle also hosts a number of cultural events throughout the year, including music festivals, plays, and other social gatherings. La Roche-en-Ardenne Castle is a beloved tourist spot, and is widely admired for its grandeur and history. It remains a reminder of the turbulent past of Belgium, and a testament to its perseverance and strength.

Waltham on the Wolds is a small village located in the Vale of Belvoir, Leicestershire, England. It is around 6 miles from Melton Mowbray and part of the civil parish of Somerby. The population of the village is around 500 people and is known for its bucolic atmosphere, typical of rural England. The name Waltham originates from "walda ham", which translates as "forest home". The village itself is situated in the eastern fringes of the Forest of Belvoir, and is surrounded by much of the surrounding area being farmland. The village has four public houses: The Royal Oak, The Hand & Heart, The Bell and The Poacher. The village was established in 1086, when it was mentioned in the Domesday Book as "Waletona". It was recorded as having five families, two ploughs and enough woodland for two pigs. Waltham on the Wolds appears in the 1831 Gazetteer of England and Wales, described as an insignificant village but having an extensive parish of 2,820 acres with a population of 1,071. Waltham Parish Council was formed at a meeting held in the village on 27th January 1899 which was attended by twenty-one parishioners. The council operates with the incorporation of Waltham on the Wolds among its responsibilities. Committees of the parish council include assets, finance, planning and environment and tourism. The village of Waltham on the Wolds also has two Church of England churches; St.Peter & St.Paul's Church and Christ Church. The primary school for the village goes by the name of Waltham on the Wolds Primary School and the village has a local tennis club which is called the Waltham Tennis Club. The village is known for its occasional festivals and events, such as the village fete, which takes place in the summer. These events are mostly organised by the parish council or the residents' association. The village also has an active gardening club, which meets every month and discusses various aspects of gardening and gardening techniques. Waltham on the Wolds is largely a residential area, with many of its inhabitants commuting to Leicester, Nottingham and further afield. It contains a range of period property including large houses, many of which are listed buildings. It also includes the woods, meadows and farms typical of the area.

Else Holmelund Minarik (August 24, 1920 – April 12, 2012) was a Danish-American author, best known for her Little Bear series of children’s books. First published in 1957, the Big Little Bear series consists of numerous titles with Minarik’s story and illustrations about Little Bear, a lovable young polar bear who has exciting adventures in the wilderness. She has written more than 60 books for children. Else Holmelund Minarik was born on August 24, 1920, in Denmark, to Holger and Ægidia Holmelund. In 1928, the family emigrated to the United States. They eventually settled in the Bronx, New York, where Minarik attended grade school and Hunter College. After school, she worked as a secretary in a Manhattan bank before trading it in to pursue authorship as a full-time career. Minarik wrote heavily for children. In addition to the Little Bear series, she wrote books about dogs and cats, a series about the Robinson family, stories about familiar childhood characters, the Charlie Smiff series, and books about animals from other parts of the world. She also ghosted Dr. Seuss' first book, To Think That I Saw It On Mulberry Street. With its simple text and sly illustrations, this book Mr. Brown Can Moo! Can You? sold over one million copies in a number of languages. Minarik was a worthy addition to the world of literature for children. She was one of the first authors to combine short gracefully written text with intimate and precise explanation of emotions. Apart from books, she wrote television scripts, wrote essays and magazine articles related to writing and children’s literature. Her other works have been adapted into an animated movie, Little Bear (2001), and animated TV series based on her books. Three of her books have also been adapted into live-action plays. Minarik received numerous awards in her commendable career. The Little Bear books were given the Lewis Carroll's Shelf Award and the Children’s Book Council Award. She received lifetime achievement awards from the American Library Association and the Bank Street College of Education. Minarik married Peter Minarik, a Czech-American artist, in 1947. The couple had two sons, David and Adam, in 1951 and 1956 respectively. She passed away on April 12, 2012. I The children’s literature world will remember Minarik forever for her timeless stories about Little Bear and her many other brilliant and charming works that young readers will always enjoy. To this day, Little Bear books still remain popular among children, giving a modern twist to the classic stories that were penned by Minarik decades ago.

Saint Rose (d. 1310) was a German nun and mystic who is now venerated as a saint. She was born near Basel, and joined the Poor Clares at Altshausen Abbey in 1283. She is credited with a number of miracles, including the healing of lepers, the cure of infertile couples, and the recovery of lost items. Saint Rose's mysticism was largely focused on visions and inner contemplation. She was known to enter a state of ecstasy when praying, and to this day her writings remain widely read among Christian mystics and contemplatives. She is believed to have had a number of profound spiritual experiences, including a vision of the Crucifixion. In 1294, Pope Boniface VIII declared her a saint of the Catholic Church. Later in the same century, two of her followers, Kilian Sprecher and John Wolf, wrote a book about her life and mysticism called "The Life of Saint Rose". This book recounts her life story, her commitment to a life of poverty and prayer, and her various miracles. Today, Saint Rose is venerated by many in Europe. She is often depicted in religious art, including altarpieces and stained glass windows. On her feast day, October 30, which also happens to be her birthday, churches throughout Europe celebrate in her honor with special services and prayers. In addition to being venerated as a saint, Saint Rose is also acclaimed as a great Christian example. Her commitment to a life of prayer and contemplation, her dedication to serving the poor, and her efforts to convert the pagans of her day are highlighted in many biographies. Several churches and schools have been named in her honor in Germany. Saint Rose is remembered today as an example of Christian holiness and communion with God. Her healing miracles, her spiritual writings, and her commitment to serving the poor are lasting examples of faith and devotion for people of all walks of life.

The Yamatogoto (山取) is a bowed string instrument from Japan dating back to around the 9th century CE. It is part of the classical tradition of Japanese instruments. The Yamatogoto is a 7-string instrument made of wood, with frets and a bridge similar to the Shamisen. It is often tuned in a major pentatonic tuning with perfect fourths between the strings. The Yamatogoto has a large resonator, resembling a half-moon shape on which the strings are strung. It is held between the legs when playing and the player plucks the strings with a bachi (plectrum). The Yamatogoto is used in a variety of musical contexts, from classical concerts to modern pop. It plays an important role in Japanese noh, a form of classical Japanese musical drama. Here, a Yamatogoto accompanies the actors and narrators as they perform their chants and songs. The instrument also plays a role in traditional and folk music, often accompanying chants, ceremonial music, and storytelling. It is also heard in gagaku, Japanese court music for ritualistic ceremonies. Gagaku is made up of ancient Asian traditions and modern Near Eastern influences, and the Yamatogoto is one of the instruments used to create this fusion of sound. Given its long history and associations with traditional culture, the Yamatogoto is sometimes used in accompaniment with shamisen and koto to depict an image of traditional Japan. In modern times it has been played by popular groups such as the Min'yo Connection, who give new life to traditional instrumentation. The Yamatogoto is a fascinating instrument, combining classical sounds with modern interpretations. Its use in a variety of musical styles and contexts makes it a fascinating instrument to explore and a vital component of the broader Japanese musical tradition.

Ming Shilu, or the Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty, is a collection of documents compiled during the Ming Dynasty of China (1368–1644). It consists primarily of imperial edicts, court verdicts, local and provincial regulations, and other administrative information written in Classical Chinese. The collection was ordered by the Yongle Emperor and compiled by his Chancellery officials between 1402–1424. The Ming Shilu is recognized as one of the most important and authoritative works of the history of the Ming Dynasty. It covers a vast range of subjects, from astronomy and geography to international relations and philosophy. It is an invaluable source of information for understanding not only the governing practices of the period, but also the religious, literary, and economic policies of the dynasty. In particular, it marked a transition from recording only major events to including smaller-scale details of daily life in the emperor's court. The Ming Shilu is organized into nine chapters, each focusing on a different aspect of the Ming Dynasty. The chapters are: 1. Documents relating to the imperial court and government officials 2. Decisions and regulations issued by the government 3. Reports of court cases 4. Records of natural disasters and wars 5. Memorials submitted to the court 6. Proclamations and edicts issued by the court 7. Local administration and customs 8. Documents concerning foreign affairs 9. Other miscellaneous documents Each chapter is subdivided into individual entries and divided into categories, such as tributes, taxation, or religion. The title for each entry is followed by the purpose of the document and the written text. Aside from the Yongle Emperor's compilation, two other editions of the Ming Shilu were commissioned by the Qing dynasty in the late 17th century. The revisions changed some editorial content, though the fundamental structure, categorization, and authorship of the original collection remained largely unchanged. Today, the Ming Shilu is widely respected and held to be an invaluable source of information for researchers and scholars of Chinese history. It is cited in many books and articles on the dynastic period and is also used as a reference in modern translations of Chinese literature that originated during the Ming Dynasty, including Ān Lànzhǐ's Dream of the Red Chamber and the Plum in the Golden Vase.

Iran first competed at the 1970 Asian Games, held in Bangkok, Thailand, from December 9 to December 20. The country sent at least 7 representatives to compete in 6 different sports and won no medals. Iran debuted at the 1970 Asian Games in the sport of weightlifting. Ali Rafei, Farhad Mousalli and Morteza Jahanbakhsh all represented Iran in the sport. Rafei competed in the 59kg event, Mousalli in the 67 kg event and Jahanbakhsh in the 75 kg event. All three athletes competed in the clean and jerk event but none of them placed in the top three. In the sport of judo, Korea Sojteh represented Iran in the event. He competed in the men's 66kg event and won no medals, despite his performances. Iran also had representatives in the men's 1500 metres event at the 1970 Asian Games. Jalal Tahmasebi and Seyed Reza Pourmousavi were the country's representatives and they competed against each other in heat two. Tahmasebi finished fourth in the heat and Pourmousavi finished sixth. In table tennis, Iran competed in the men's doubles event. Majid Dotanloo and Khosro Seyed Shokri were the country's representatives and they competed in the first round of the event, against the team from Thailand. The Iranian team lost the match and thus were eliminated from the event. In addition, Iran also competed in the men's basketball and men's volleyball events. The basketball team was composed of an all amateur roster, however, the team would go on to finish fifth in the event, after losing to Thailand in the semi-finals. Meanwhile, the volleyball team failed to reach the quarter-finals and were likewise eliminated from the competition. Overall, Iran participated in 6 events at the 1970 Asian Games and failed to win any medals. Though the country managed to perform quite well in the basketball and judo events, their lack of success across the other events indeed limited their medal tally. This concluded the nation's debut at the Asian Games, with Iran failing to place any athlete on the podium in the event.

Mannford is a city located in Creek County, Oklahoma, United States. As of the 2010 census, the city had a population of 2,044. It is 30 miles (48 km) west of Tulsa. The city is named after Henry Mann, a local rancher who started a post office in 1901. The city of Mannford is located in a rural agricultural area and borders the shores of Lake Keystone. Mannford experienced a large population increase between 2000 and 2010 with a growth of nearly 400%. This growth was largely attributed to the city's proximity to Tulsa, the outdoor recreational opportunities available at Lake Keystone, and other nearby lakes and rivers. Once a small ranchers and farmers community, Mannford is now becoming known for its lakeside resort area, featuring luxury condominiums as well as marinas, campgrounds, restaurants, and convenience stores. The town's most popular activity is waterskiing, but camping, hiking, fishing, boating, and swimming are also common. Mannford is also home to the Oologah-Talala Historical Society and Museum, which preserves the heritage of Creek County and its surrounding areas. Mannford is served by the Mannford Public School System, which consists of four schools: Mannford High School, Mannford Middle School, Mannford Elementary School, and Mannford Special Education Center. In 2016, the high school was honored with recognition from the U.S. Department of Education and the National Blue Ribbon Schools Program. The City of Mannford is governed by a Mayor and four City Council members who are elected to four-year terms. The current Mayor is Robert L. Tolbert, and the City Council consists of Monica Beal, Jake Albritton, Chad Custer, and Carl McFall. Mannford is also home to an Indian Health Service hospital, the Mannford Rural Health Clinic, and is part of the Okemah-Mannford-Catoosa Fire Protection District. The community is also served by the Mannford Post Office, Amtrak Train Station, and regional bus service. In conclusion, Mannford is a rapidly growing city located in Creek County, Oklahoma. The city is home to many outdoor recreational opportunities, a thriving business district, and highly-recognized school system. With its small-town feel and big city amenities, Mannford is a great place to live, work, and play.

Curtis Staples (born December 21, 1974) is an American professional basketball player and current coach. A 6-foot-2-inch guard from Roanoke, Virginia, he was selected by the Chicago Bulls in the second round (25th overall pick) of the 1998 NBA Draft. Throughout Staples' basketball career he has been a journeyman, playing for multiple NBA teams, including the Bulls, the Los Angeles Lakers, the Toronto Raptors, and the Sacramento Kings. In addition to his NBA career, Staples was also a member of the Orlando Magic in the NBA's summer league in 2002 and played for the Fayetteville Patriots (formerly the Raleigh Cougars) in the National Basketball Development League (NBDL). In April of 2007, Staples was hired by the Boston Celtics as an assistant coach. He then spent the next three seasons with the Celtics, helping them win the 2008 NBA Championships. In 2010, he joined the coaching staff of the New Jersey Nets. After two seasons with the Nets, Staples was hired by the Atlanta Hawks in July 2012, where he served as an assistant coach and player development coach for the next three seasons. Most recently, Staples held the role of director of player development for the Houston Rockets from 2015-18. While in Houston, the Rockets went to the Conference Finals and clinched back-to-back playoff berths. Aside from his coaching career, Staples is known for his individual achievements as a basketball player. He is the all-time leading 3-point shooter in the history of the Atlantic 10 men's basketball conference. He holds the school record for 3-pointers made in a game and is also the all-time leader in steals and 3-pointers made at the University of Virginia. In 2011, Staples was inducted into the Virginia Sports Hall of Fame. He was also inducted into the University of Virginia Sports Hall of Fame and the Roanoke Valley Sports Hall of Fame in 2016. Today, Staples continues his involvement in the game as a coach and mentor in the NBA as well as a keynote speaker, sharing his wealth of basketball knowledge and offering advice to aspiring players and coaches.

Sportpaleis is a multipurpose indoor arena located in Antwerp, Belgium. It is regularly used for concerts, family shows, sport events and other activities. The arena was originally opened in 1933, and later renovated in 1989, today has a seating capacity of 18,000. The arena is owned and operated by the N.V. Group Sportpaleis, which runs several entertainment venues and events in the country, including the Ethias Arena and the Lotto Arena. The history of Sportpaleis goes back to 1933 when it was opened as an ice hockey venue, known as U-Rink. During the Second World War, it was damaged by Allied bombing, but was able to be repaired and reopened shortly after the war. In 1962, the arena was renovated and expanded to accommodate up to 10,000 spectators, and became known as the Sportpaleis. In 1989, the arena was renovated once again, and now has a seating capacity of 18,000. The building is split into four levels, with the ground floor devoted to sport, the upper mezzanine views for concerts, the Royal Box for VIP guests, and the corporate suites for the more discerning audience. The arena has hosted a number of highly prestigious events since its opening, such as both the 1987 and 1995 Eurovision Song Contests, 1990 Davis Cup and the 1998 World Ice Hockey Championships. The venue is also regularly used for various sports events, including basketball, volleyball, karate and even sumo wrestling. It is also used for rock, pop and classical music concerts, as well as comedy and other family entertainment shows. In recent years, Sportpaleis has seen an increase in the number of non-traditional events, such as the Michelin Star Chef Test Restaurant Series, the Glow Run and the Ninja Warrior. There are also a number of restaurants located in the arena, which offer a range of cuisine, including Italian, Thai, Mexican and Greek. Sportpaleis is a modern day entertainment hub in the heart of Antwerp and serves as a prime example of the city’s commitment to providing first class entertainment experiences for all. Whether you’re looking for a sporting event, a concert or a family show, Sportpaleis is the perfect venue to visit.

The List of Qazis of the Maldives contains the names of the Islamic jurists of the Maldives who managed the religious affairs of the island nation. For the majority of the Maldives' history, the qazis were appointed by the sultan and were responsible for the administration of justice, and adjudicating legal cases under both Islamic and local law. A qazi or kazi is an Islamic jurist or judge, responsible for judging matters relating to Islamic law such as marriage, inheritance, sale and other legal agreements in a Muslim community. The qazis in the Maldives were primarily responsible for implementing Islamic laws, but also dealt with local customary laws when relevant. The first qazi of the Maldives was appointed in the 11th century by the first sultan of the Maldives, Sultan Abu Bakr. Since then, there have been qazis appointed by subsequent sultans, with some serving as qazis for more than a decade. The most prominent qazis from the 12th century to the 19th century include: * Abu Bakr al-Qasim (fl. 12th century): The first qazi appointed in the Maldives, appointed by the first sultan. * Abd al-Rahman ibn Mara al-Munayyar (fl. 13th century): An Arabic scholar and qazi, appointed by Sultan Al-Ghazan. * Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Amra’i (fl. 13th century): An Arabic theologian and qazi, appointed by Sultan Al-Ghazan. * Sayyid Ahmad Shamsuddin ibn ‘Abd Muttalib (d. 1314/1315): A Yemeni-born qazi, appointed by Sultan Shams ad-Din I. * Muhammad ibn Ahmad (d. 1431): An Indonesian-born qazi and Islamic scholar, appointed by Sultan Ahmad Taj ad-Din I. * Muhammad al-Habashi al-Muntasir (fl. 15th century): An Ethiopian-born qazi, appointed by Sultan Saif ad-Din I. * Ishaq ibn Hasan ibn Adam (fl. 17th century): A qazi who served under Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar I and Sultan Banun ‘Abd ar-Rahman. * Mohammad Ismail sarraf (fl. 19th century): A prominent qazi, appointed by Sultan ‘Ali Hasan. Throughout its history, the Maldives has had many qazis and each one played a pivotal role in administering justice to the people. The position of qazi holds religious significance, being responsible for adjucating legal cases and decisions according to Islamic law.

. Malcolm Patrick Galt (September 3, 1866 – December 17, 1948) was a prominent American engineer, entrepreneur, and industrialist. He was one of the pioneers of the modern industrial revolution, credited with inventing and applying revolutionary technologies that had a major impact on the development of the 20th century manufacturing industry. Malcolm was born in California in 1866, the son of a well-to-do merchant family. As a young man, he was trained in art and science at The California School of Arts & Sciences. He went on to learn about mechanical engineering and machining technology at the University of California, Berkeley. Following his studies, he was employed as a machinist for the state government. He eventually established his own machine shop in San Francisco. In 1895, Malcolm founded the firm of Galt Engineering, which specialized in the making of industrial machinery. Through his successful implementation of new technologies, Galt's business prospered, and additional factories were constructed. During his peak, Malcolm Galt was called "the King of the Machine Tools." He earned recognition for his pioneering efforts in the precision tools industry, and went on to gain important contracts in the automotive industry and established machine tool factories all over the United States. He also had major influence in the development of modern petroleum technology. Galt was active in the American Institute of Mining, Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineering, eventually becoming its president in 1925. During his term, he was instrumental in the founding of the organization's journal, Mining and Metallurgy. He served as editor-in-chief of the journal for 30 years until his retirement in 1947. Malcolm Galt died in 1948 in San Francisco. He was highly regarded by his peers and is remembered as one of the great innovators of industrial engineering. In his lifetime, Galt received numerous accolades, including several honorary doctorates from notable universities.

Val was a Canadian sculptor, whose works are notable in the art world for capturing moments of joy, love, and other content feelings. From the late 1950s to the early 1990s, Val created sculptures from wood, metal, and stone that explored the subtleties of everyday life. Born in Toronto, Val was first exposed to art as a youth in her parents' eclectic decor and folk art collection. Val showed a keen interest in art from a young age, taking art classes and summer camps. During university, she began to dabble in sculpting and soon developed her own distinct style. Val's sculptures were characterized by their vibrant colors and curved shapes, a style that was both aesthetic and conveying emotion. Val often used human and animal figures, creating bold and cheerful images. Her artwork was a natural expression of the joy in her life, reflected in her choice of materials. She favored beautiful and durable types of wood, such as white birch and rosewood, to match the vibrant textures of her sculptures. Throughout her career, Val exhibited her work in galleries across Canada. However, in the mid-1990s, she withdrew from the art world and ceased all sculpting. Val sadly passed away in 1998. Nevertheless, Val's work has left a lasting mark on the art world. Val's works are now housed in numerous galleries and museums, celebrated for their cheerful and optimistic outlook. Val is remembered as a beloved Canadian artist who celebrated the joy of everyday life in her work.

Paul Schuitema (1897 – 1968) was a Dutch graphic designer, who is known for his modernist influences and advanced typographical innovations. He is considered to be one of the pioneers of modern graphic design and is renowned for creating iconic logos and posters. He was born in Zaandam, Netherlands, and studied at the Art Academy in Amsterdam. In 1924, he joined his father's company, the Schuitema Andijk Advertisers Corporation, in which he worked as a graphic designer until it closed in 1927. During this time he developed a modernist design style and prefigured Dutch graphic design. In 1931, he founded his own studio, Schuitema Grafisch Seminarium, in Amsterdam. He focused on modernist book designs, logos, labels, and posters and soon became a leader in the Dutch graphic design industry. Throughout the 1930s and 1940s Schuitema designed many logos and posters, which embodied his distinct style of abstract shapes, basic geometric forms, limited colours, and sans-serif typefaces. He is best known for his "DAF" logo, which he designed in 1933 for the Dutch automaker's first car. His logo for the Departement of Social Affairs consisted of three bars in black, yellow and blue and became widely utilized throughout the Netherlands. He also created a logo for the Dutch Civil Aviation Authority, which featured an airplane and horizontally striped wings, as well as a logo for Air France, which combined two short horizontal lines and an 'A' in the centre. In addition to playing a major role in influencing American and International design firms, Schuitema's work was integral in launching the modernist movement in Dutch graphic design. He was named the president of the Council for Art and Industry, which sought to promote modern art, design and architecture. In the 1950s, Schuitema was a major figure in the Amsterdam Art Group, an organization devoted to the promotion of graphic design and its role in visual communication. Schuitema's legacy has been widely celebrated and in 2006 he was inducted into the Dutch Hall of Fame for Graphic Designers. His contributions to the field of graphic design continue to inspire and influence modern practitioners.

Teletubbies: The Album is the first album by the British children's television series Teletubbies. The album was released on July 13, 1998, by Universal Music Group (UMG) and features music from the original show and songs inspired by it. The album was produced by Simon Driscoll and Mike Crowther and features the vocal talents of the original show's voice cast. It was the first Teletubbies album released and was quickly followed by Teletubbies: Sing-a-Long in 1999. The album contains a variety of tracks, including the theme song Tubby Bye Bye, instrumental versions of each of the four Teletubbie's theme tunes, some spoken lines from the show's popular characters, and five original songs written specifically for the release. These songs include Big Hugs, In the Night Garden, Among the Clouds, and The Wonder Walk. The album was a critical success, with many praising the production quality and catchy songs. It was also popular with children, with its lead single Big Hugs reaching number eight on the UK Singles Chart. It would also go on to win the 1998/1999 Parents' Choice Award for Best Music Album. Although the success of Teletubbies: The Album was not replicated by subsequent releases, the album is seen as highly influential in paving the way for subsequent children's television music releases and as helping to establish Teletubbies as a prominent part of 90's pop culture. It has been referenced in popular culture, with the album's artwork appearing in the 2018 film Eighth Grade. The album is available to stream on various services as of 2021.

Ascot Chang (born 1935) is a Hong Kong-based tailor, best known as the founder of a luxury bespoke tailoring house, Ascot Chang. Ascot was born in Hong Kong to a prosperous family in the clothing business. Growing up, he developed a deep interest in bespoke tailoring and honed his skills by working alongside local tailors. In 1962, he set up his own small tailoring business, which quickly gained a cult following due to the exceptional craftsmanship of his creations. His clientele included celebrities such as Bruce Lee, rock stars like Elton John, and renowned chefs like Paul Bocuse. In 2002, Ascot opened the doors to his flagship store in Hong Kong's Happy Valley. The space houses a tailoring team of 40 members and it is the only Ascot Chang store opened to date. The store is a new interpretation of the traditional Chinese tailor's shop, with 20 fitting rooms dedicated to custom tailoring. Ascot himself can be found in the store, offering his exclusive craftsmanship and design to clients. Ascot has won multiple awards for his extravagant tailoring and dedication to quality. Most recently in 2020, he won the prestigious Men's Fashion Award in the tailoring category. Ascot's designs are recognized for their exquisite craftsmanship, exquisite fabrics and attractive silhouettes, which have been modernised to fit the taste of a global audience. Ascot Chang has been recognized as a leader in modernizing classic tailoring. His work has gained a cult following and is seen as a benchmark for excellence in the industry. His designs feature in numerous editorials and can be found in luxury stores around the world. Ascot remains one of the last pioneers of traditional tailoring and leads a movement of modern artisans, preserving an elegant and timeless aesthetic.

WDRB (sometimes referred to as WDRB-TV or WDRB 41) is a full-service television station in Louisville, Kentucky, broadcasting a local newscast, weather updates, and sports programs on digital channel 41 (UHF frequency 22) for the Louisville, Kentucky and Southern Indiana area. The station is affiliated with The WB Television Network and is owned by Block Communications, a telecommunications holding company located in Cincinnati, Ohio. WDRB first went on the air on August 15, 2001. Prior to being acquired by Block Communications, WDRB operated as an affiliate of the United Paramount Network from 2003 to 2006. Since August 1, 2006, WDRB has broadcast its digital signal on Channel 41, providing a 6-megawatt signal over a 35-mile coverage area. It also transmits through cable and satellite providers in the Louisville area. WDRB features 24 hour programming including syndicated programming such as True Crime Files and CSI, network news and entertainment programming including The Ellen DeGeneres Show, and local news, weather and sports. The station covers local, national and international news and has a wide variety of sports programming including University of Louisville, Louisville Bats, Louisville City FC, and other local high school, college and professional sports. The news and sports departments have been honored with Emmy Award nominations. WDRB airs the Fox network's primetime programming, and is the only television station in the Louisville DMA (Designated Market Area) to have gained the rights to air most of the NFL Sunday Ticket package from DirecTV in fall 2010, though WDRB does not air the Sunday Ticket games–they are simply offered via DirecTV to viewers in the Louisville DMA. In July 2013, WDRB and WHAS-TV launched The NOW Louisville, which provides live traffic, weather, news and other up-to-the-minute media updates framed within 30 minute intervals airing twice daily. Along with WDRB, WHAS-TV (ABC) and WAVE-TV (NBC) form the largest network of news teams in Kentucky and Southern Indiana. WDRB also offers streaming live newscasts on the internet on both the web and mobile platforms. In July 2017, WDRB was acquired by Block Communications, a media and communications holdings company, as part of its $105 million purchase of Ohio television stations, which included Louisville-based WDRB-TV. Block Communications also owns The Blade, a daily newspaper in Toledo, Ohio and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. WDRB is known for its commitment to local programming, for its access to the Kentucky Derby and the Kentucky Oaks, and for its extensive coverage of sports in Louisville.

CT Rei Pelé is a term playfully used to describe a renowned Brazilian soccer player, Edson Arantes do Nascimento, better known as Pelé. The term literally stands for "Football King Pele Center" in Portuguese, and references the incredible success Pelé achieved during his career. Playing professionally since the age of fifteen, first with Santos Futebol Club and then with New York Cosmos, Pelé is widely considered to be one of the greatest soccer players of all time. By the end of his career, Pelé had scored 1,282 goals in 1393 appearances, breaking many records and creating countless new ones. He was recognized at the international level for his skill, playing for the World Select Team on four separate occasions and becoming the top scorer at the 1970 FIFA World Cup. In addition to his successes on the soccer field, Pelé has been a strong advocate for social change and sportsmanship initiatives. In 1971, he became an ambassador for the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF); his ongoing commitment and service to that organization eventually led to him receiving the Peace and Sport Award in 2011. Pelé has also received countless honors, such as being named FIFA Player of the Century, a three-time South American Footballer of the Year, and having both a Portuguese and Brazilian stamp issued in his honor. Perhaps, however, the greatest acknowledgement of Pelé’s soccer prowess came in November 2017 when the City of Santos in Brazil inaugurated the Centro de Treinamento Rei Pelé (CT Rei Pelé), or King Pele Training Centre. This facility was established to recognize the Brazilian soccer legend and his legacy, as well as his contribution to the development of youth soccer in Brazil. The official opening of the center included a ribbon cutting ceremony featuring Soccer Hall of Fame members, and featured remarks from Pelé himself. Overall, CT Rei Pelé is a term used to honor Edson Arantes do Nascimento and his fantastic achievements in the world of soccer. His name has become synonymous with incredible skill, passion and dignity, and his drive and commitment to the game has earned him a place in the history of this beloved sport.

Oklahoma State Highway 71 is a north-south highway in the US state of Oklahoma. It travels from US Highway 69 near Iron Post, in McCurtain County, to US Highway 62 near Pawnee, in Pawnee County. It is a major east-west Route in northeastern Oklahoma, and is part of the Indian Nation Turnpike system. The highway begins at a junction with US 69 near Iron Post and travels northwards through rural McCurtain County. As it approaches Idabel, the highway passes through residential areas before intersecting US 259 in the east side of Idabel. From US 259 the highway continues on a northwesterly route through rural parts of McCurtain County, passing several towns and small settlements. In Pawnee County, OK-71 intersects State Highway 18, before reaching its northern terminus at US 62 just east of Pawnee. Overall, OK-71 runs for approximately 95 miles (152.89 km). It serves as an important connection between two major routes, US 59 and US 62, and is an important route for local commuters, freight carriers, and tourists. A nearby section of the road is one of the few places in Oklahoma where the original pre-1920s road still remains, and this section is known as the Old Oregon Trail. OK-71 has been a continuous route since at least 1922 when it was originally designated in the state of Oklahoma. In the mid-1990s the road was improved by resurfacing and was also widened in a few places. The road also underwent several bridge improvements in recent years. OK-71 is clearly marked along its entire route, and provides reliable transportation for residents of the area. The highway also serves as an important link to a number of popular tourist destinations, including the Red Slough Wildlife Management Area, the Ouachita National Forest, and Lake Wister State Park. Overall, Oklahoma State Highway 71 is a key transportation route for the northeastern-most part of the state. It provides an important connection for local commuters and travelers, as well as an important link to several tourist destinations.

Medusa is the fourth studio album by the British progressive rock/hard rock band Trapeze. Released in 1974 by Threshold Records, it is named after the mythological Medusa and is known for its jazzy sound. The band themselves were known for their jazzy rock sound, blending hard rock features with winding, complex instrumentals to form an interesting and unique sound. This album specifically is seen as a more proggy work than their previous endeavors, but still largely holds true to the hard rock background of the band. The album was composed of six tracks, two of which were distributed as singles. "Medusa" was the longer of the two singles, clocking in at 6m 22s, and released with the song "Coast to Coast" as the b-side. The other single was the leadoff track on the album, "Your Love is Alright", which was released with "Cradle Rock" as the b-side. There was a remastered, single-CD version released in October 2003, which included the bonus tracks "Coast to Coast (Single Edit)" and "Cradle Rock (Single Edit)." Most reviews of the album praise it for its innovative sound and mix of genres. AllMusic's critic Bruce Eder in particular hailed it, giving it a full five star review. In his review, Eder writes that "Medusa stands as one of the most ambitious, idiosyncratic progressive rock albums of the early Seventies, and it still sounds fresh to the ear nearly 30 years on." The album has since been recognized as a Classic Rock and Prog Archives' Essential for Progressive Rock albums. In 2017, Rolling Stone named "Your Love is Alright" as one of the 100 Greatest Prog Rock Songs of All Time. The lineup for the album featured Glenn Hughes on vocals and bass, Mel Galley on guitar, Dave Holland on drums, and John Jones on keyboards. The album was a success, reaching number 22 on the UK Albums Chart.

Lester Afflick (born June 1, 1940) is an American author, scholar, and sociologist who has written extensively on racial, economic, and social justice. Afflick received a doctorate in sociology from Columbia University in 1971, and has worked and taught in both the United States and Canada for over fifty years. Afflick is best known for his books Race and Social Problems (1988) and Reconstructing Social Problems (1994). In these books, he examines racial and social issues using an interdisciplinary approach, often involving references to literature, sociology, philosophy, history, and economics. He uses this interdisciplinary approach to explore the concept of 'race' and examine our understanding of a racial hierarchy. His goal is to challenge assumptions and to move beyond the traditional boundaries of social science research. In Race and Social Problems, Afflick sets out to explore the relationship between 'race' and social problems, looking at how these problems have evolved over time, how they are shaped by the power of society, and what can be done to address them. He argues for a more nuanced understanding of social problems, and calls for a shift from racially-based solutions to ones that take into account the related issues of class, gender, and other social distinctions. Afflick also emphasizes the need for reflection and action in the areas of racial and social justice. He encourages readers to consider the shortcomings of traditional social theories, and to think critically about structural inequities that exist in society. Moreover, he argues for a more holistic approach to social problems, recognizing that any solutions must involve ongoing dialogue, action, and education. In addition to his books, Afflick is a frequent contributor to journals and magazines, and he has been published in newspapers such as The New York Times, The Guardian, and The Wall Street Journal. He is also a sought-after public speaker, delivering lectures and workshops at universities and conferences. Throughout his career, Afflick has been a strong advocate for social and racial justice. He believes that change can be achieved through direct action and education, and through creating dialogue and developing meaningful partnerships with people of other backgrounds. His work has been widely praised, and his contributions to the field of sociology and social justice continue to inspire students, activists, and scholars around the world.

Olbia Costa Smeralda Airport (IATA: OLB) (former name Olbia-Tempio Airport) is an international airport in Olbia, Sardinia, Italy. It is the main airport in the north-east of the island and the main gateway to the popular beach resort of Costa Smeralda. The airport is operated by GE.S.A.C. (Società di Gestione dell'Aeroporto di Olbia-Costa Smeralda), which also handles traffic for other Sardinian airports such as Alghero Airport and Cagliari Airport. Opened in 1964, the airport is located 5 km (3.1 mi) north-east of Olbia and covers an area of 330 hectares (820 acres). It is connected to the city centre of Olbia and to the nearby town of Golfo Aranci by a taxi and shuttle services. The airport has one runway, 16/34, which is 2,300 metres (7,546 ft) long and paved in asphalt. The arrival hall of the airport has been recently renovated in order to provide passengers with improved services and comfort. It is equipped with multiple shops, restaurants, bars and duty-free outlets. The departure lounge is located on the first floor and is equipped with modern facilities. Furthermore, it provides passengers with car rental services, a parking area and a VIP lounge. In terms of air traffic, the airport boasts direct flights with major Italian destinations such as Rome, Milan, Turin and Florence. Moreover, there are domestic and international flights operating to major European countries such as Germany, Spain, France, Portugal, Belgium and the United Kingdom. In 2020, the airport handled 2.76 million passengers. Furthermore, in the same year it was recorded a total of 8,922 aircraft movements and managed to record a total of 72.608 tons of goods. The airport is served by many airlines, often in partnership with partner airlines. Some of the carriers operating out of Olbia include: Alitalia, Blu-express, Easyjet, Ryanair, Vueling, Wizz Air and Neos. In addition to the regular scheduled flights, the airport also serves seasonal and charter flights which operate during summer. Overall, Olbia Costa Smeralda Airport is a major gateway for passengers wishing to visit the north-east of Sardinia and the beautiful Costa Smeralda. In the future, the airport is plans to expand the existing facilities to provide passengers with a better experience.

Rodovia Floriano Rodrigues Pinheiro, also known as BR-402, is a federal highway in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. The highway connects the cities of Pelotas and Capão da Canoa, spanning a total of 140 kilometers. The highway is named after Floriano Rodrigues Pinheiro, a Brazilian lawyer, politician and writer born in 1852. The highway was inaugurated in 1939, but wasn't asphalted until 1978. The asphalt was placed in two bands of 7 meters width, having a signaling line in the center of the bands. The improvement works in the highway were carried out by the military government, which was in power from 1964 to 1985. Since its inauguration, the highway has witnessed the growth of two large cities, Pelotas and Capão da Canoa, now being vital for the economic development of the area. BR-402 is known for its majestic vistas, and serves as a major route of transit for trucks, buses and passenger vehicles between Rio de Janeiro and the cities of the South of Brazil, including Rio Grande do Sul. In recent years, BR-402 suffered from lax supervision and laws, leading to an increase in traffic fatalities and cargo banditry. In an effort to reduce the number of accidents, the Brazilian government implemented new safety standards in the highway in 2008, including better supervision of cargo haulers, greater speed limits and more frequent patrols by police. Despite these ongoing efforts to improve the highway, BR-402 remains one of the most dangerous roads in the country, with more than 450 fatalities reported in the region between 2017 and 2018. The Brazilian government and the state of Rio Grande do Sul are constantly working on improving the condition of the highway in order to reduce the number of fatalities, as well as increase the access to the important cities it connects. BR-402 is currently one of the most important highways in Rio Grande do Sul, connecting some of the most important cities in the region, including Pelotas and Capão da Canoa, as well as providing access to Rio de Janeiro and other states of the South of Brazil. Despite its issues and accidents, the highway remains an important route for cargo haulers and passengers.

Vladimir Janjgava (born 27 April 1971) is a Georgian politician and member of United National Movement political movement. He is the leader of the Gori branch of the United National Movement since 2006 and a member of the party leadership council since 2009. Janjgava is a former Deputy Minister of Defense of Georgia and former Georgian Army Specialist from 1993 to 2006. Janjgava was born in Tbilisi, Georgia and graduated from the Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University. He further studied at the Academy of the Ministry of Defense of Georgia and received the military rank of alternative lieutenant-colonel. From 1993 to 2006, Janjgava worked for the Ministry of Defense for 13 years and was military specialist in mobilisation, armaments and ammunition. In 2006, he was appointed as a Deputy Minister of Defense of Georgia, and in 2007 he was involved in a conflict between the Georgian army and the breakaway province of Abkhazia. During this conflict, Janjgava served as a commander of the mission to defend Georgian villages invaded by Abkhazian troops. In 2009-2012, Janjgava was a member of the Parliament of Georgia, where he was Chairman of the Anticorruption and Judiciary committees. In 2011, he was elected one of the 5 leaders of the United National Movement. He served on the National Security Council and National Consultative Council and was a frequent member of the European Delegations. Later in 2012, Janjgava joined the opposition party European Georgia and established their Gori branch. In 2020, Janjgava was elected as the Mayor of Gori. As Mayor of Gori, he has promised to fight unemployment, poverty and corruption in his region. Janjgava is married and has one son. Change is an album by trumpet player and pianist Chick Corea that was released in September 1978 by Polydor Records. The album won Down Beat magazine's Album of the Year award and was nominated for two Grammy Awards: Best Jazz Instrumental Performance, Group and Best Jazz Instrumental Performance, Soloist (for Corea's "Spain"). It is considered one of Corea's best-known albums. Change features Corea on Fender Rhodes electric piano, bass, drums and acoustic piano, and includes contributions from Airto Moreira (percussion and vocals), Joe Farrell (woodwinds), and Joe Henderson (tenor saxophone and flute). The album's title track, a fifteen-minute song suite, is one of Corea's best-known compositions. The album includes three other compositions by Corea: "I'm Your Pal", "Time Track" and "Armando's Rhumba". The other pieces are covers, including Dizzy Gillespie's "A Night in Tunisia", John Coltrane's "Moment's Notice" and Wayne Shorter's "Etcetera". The closing track, "Señor Mouse", combines pieces by Corea and Shorter. Change has been praised as a classic of jazz fusion and has been cited by many as a major influence in jazz, pop and rock music. Rolling Stone magazine placed it at number 63 on its 2020 list of the 500 best albums of all time. The album has been reissued multiple times, including on CD (in 1994) and as a two-disc set (in 2001). Corea has often performed songs from the album in live performances. Change has been featured on several of Corea's career-spanning collections, including Ultimate Corea (2006) and The Musician (2020). In 2017, Corea, Moreira and Henderson reunited to perform songs from the album at the Hollywood Bowl.

Candidates of the 1975 Australian federal election was part of the process for electing members to the 34th parliament of Australia. The election was held on 13 December 1975, and produced a landslide victory for the Labor Party led by Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, who defeated the Liberal-Country Party Coalition led by opposition leader Malcolm Fraser. Nominations for candidates for the election closed on Friday 5 December 1975, with a total of 1145 candidates nominated in the House of Representatives and 96 candidates nominated in the Senate. The main parties were the Australian Labor Party, the Liberal Party and the Country Party. In the House of Representatives, the Labor Party had 413 candidates, while the Coalition had 365 candidates. Independent candidates numbered 75 and there were smaller numbers of candidates from other minor parties. The Senate was mostly a contest between Labor and the Coalition, with Labor fielding 35 candidates, the Coalition 23 and smaller parties the remaining 38. Labor candidate Neville Wran went on to win the election as New South Wales Premier, while Malcolm Fraser also recorded a 12-year political career as Prime Minister of Australia. Fourteen other first-term candidates were elected, including future Prime Minister Bob Hawke and future Deputy Prime Minister Brian Howe. The 1975 election was the first one to use preferential voting for the House of Representatives. This system enables voters to number the candidates in the order of their preference. This is thought to be an important factor in the election result, as it allowed a greater proportion of Labor votes to be accumulated than under the simple majority system used in 1919 and prior to 1920. Also of note were the increasing number of women contesting the election. Among the new female candidates were Flo Bjelke-Petersen, who would go on to become the first female Queensland Premier, and Rosemary Crowley, who became the first South Australian female minister. The election resulted in a Labor landslide, with the Party claiming 67 of the House of Representatives seats and 32 of the Senate seats. The Coalition could only claim 28 lower-house seats and eight Senate seats. This result was the first in a series of major Labor victories which marked the end of 23 years of Coalition rule. The election of 1975 was a significant milestone in Australian political history, and the success of many of its first-term candidates, such as Neville Wran and Bob Hawke, ensured its place in the nation's collective memory.

Formyl peptide receptor, also known as formyl peptide receptors (FPRs), are a family of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that bind to and respond to formyl peptides. Formyl peptides are small peptides of varying length (3-29 amino acids) and are mostly found in bacteria. Formyl peptides are structurally distinct from their mammalian counterparts, yet their ability to function as signaling molecules suggests they have a common evolutionary origin. FPRs were first identified in 1983 in the sea hare, a marine mollusk, where they were found to be involved in the recognition of bacterial-associated formyl peptides. They are now known to be found in a variety of animals and are involved in multiple physiological processes. The discovery of FPRs has led to a better understanding of the importance of formyl peptide recognition in the innate immune system and its potential as a therapeutic target for treating inflammation and infectious diseases. FPRs are members of the large family of GPCRs that have seven membrane-spanning domains and are formed from the α-helix structure. There are three different classes of FPRs with several members within each class. FPR1, FPR2, FPR3, and FPR4 are considered the classic formyl peptide receptors, and they respond to bacterial-associated formyl peptides. FPR5 and FPR6 are considered divergent FPRs and are activated by eukaryotic formyl peptides, such as peptides derived from mast cells. FPR7 is an orphan receptor and its expression and function has yet to be determined. FPRs are characterized by their recognition of specific formyl peptides, as well as their differential signaling pathways. FPR1, FPR2, and FPR3 recognize several bacterial formyl peptides and are coupled with Gαi upon activation. Upon activation, this leads to the production of intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), which will then activate a response such as an inflammatory response. FPR4, FPR5, and FPR6 all recognize eukaryotic formyl peptides and are coupled to Gαq, which leads to an increase in intracellular calcium levels. These formyl peptides receptors have been found to be involved in several physiological processes, including the recognition of bacterial pathogens and the activation of an inflammatory response, phagocytosis, wound healing, and angiogenesis. FPRs have been studied for their potential as a target for treatment of infectious diseases and inflammatory disorders. Inhibition of FPRs has been found to reduce inflammation, while activation of FPRs has been found to reduce infectious disease. Research is continuing to further our understanding of how FPRs recognize and respond to formyl peptides and their potential as a therapeutic modality.

Peter Pascoe is an English physician, historian, and author born in Bristol in 1964. He attended the University of Cambridge and was elected a research fellow in history at Trinity College. He is best known for his widely acclaimed study of the history of medicine and medical ethics, Patients or Consumers? A History of Health Care in Britain. Pascoe has authored several works and is a regular contributor to a range of medical journals, including the British Medical Journal, the Lancet and the British Journal of General Practice. His books have covered a range of topics, such as the history of hospitals, the involvement of the Church of England in health and illness in Britain, and the care of the elderly in the United Kingdom. He is also the author of The History of British Migration (2006) which is a comprehensive look at the history of British migration from the 16th century to the present day. His research has also helped to shape healthcare policies in the UK, including the reform of the NHS from a monolithic public health service to a consumer-driven one. Pascoe is also the editor of Health Care in Britain: A Documentary History (2006), which provides an in-depth analysis of the key elements that have shaped health policy in the UK over the past two hundred years. In 2008, Pascoe was appointed a visiting professor at Liverpool University’s School of Medicine, a post he held for five years. During this period, he undertook research into health inequalities in England, a project which helped inform the Government’s response to poverty and deprivation. His expertise in medical history was recognised when he was appointed as a member of the Royal College of Physicians’ Ethical and Performance Committee in 2016. Pascoe has received numerous awards in recognition of his work and contributions to the history of healthcare in Britain. These include the Wellcome Medal for Outstanding Contributions to the History of Medicine in 2016 and a Fellowship of the British Academy in recognition of his exceptional contributions to the study of the history of health care in 2018. In addition, he has been awarded an honorary Doctorate of Science from the University of Bristol in 2019. He remains active in the study and promotion of healthcare in Britain and recently published a thought-provoking book entitled Health Care Beyond Borders: A Global Perspective. Overall, Peter Pascoe has made a significant contribution to the understanding and improving healthcare in the UK. Through his detailed research, inspiring lectures and engaging writing, he has shown himself to be an important figure in the field of medical history, health policy and health care.

Magrahat I is the name given to a large collection of ancient relics and artifacts located in the Hooghly district of West Bengal, India. The collection includes pieces from the late Harappan period and the early Iron Age, around 2500 BCE. It also encompasses remains from other cultures of the time, including the late Vedic period, Jaina period and Buddhist period. The collection was discovered in 1919 by B.N. Sen and first excavated by a team of archaeologists, headed by Sri P.C. Malik, in 1931. The team uncovered several stones, bricks, pottery, terracotta figures and tobacco pipes. These pieces were carefully catalogued and stored at the Indian Museum, Kolkata. The pottery pieces include some of the earliest instances of rice cultivation, as well as early examples of Indian ceramics and glass work. At least two distinct pottery styles were discovered - one in which the use of locally made and fired clay was prominent, and another in which fired terracotta from nearby states was dominant. The terracotta figures found at Magrahat I are exceptionally well preserved and depict everyday scenes from the time. Many of them depict humans and animals and some have been interpreted as showing activities associated with a fertility cult, while others are modeled after Lord Shiva. The figures are generally associated with the late Harappan period but may also be representative of the early Iron Age. The stone structures found at Magrahat I may have been used for ritual purposes or for erecting a temple. This is evidenced by the presence of phallic symbols and ritualistic carvings. There are also stonework structures of a drainage system and other artefacts, such as stone weights, stone grinders and edged tablets. The discovery of this ancient collection has provided significant insights into the culture of the time, particularly the use of more sophisticated tools and technology than had previously been thought available to the people of this region. It has also offered evidence for the use of rice in ancient India, as well as an opportunity to examine the roles of craftsmen and women in the production of the ceramics and glass items. The Magrahat I collection contains a wealth of archaeological and cultural information and serves as an invaluable resource for understanding the history and culture of early India.

Philip Read (born September 4, 1920) is a British author and historian, best known for his biographies and works of popular history. Philip was born in Leeds, England to parents Robert and Winifred. He was educated at Earlham College, in Norwich, where he gained a B.A. in History and Classical Studies in 1941. After graduating, he worked as a tea-packer in Glasgow, then joined the Royal Navy. He took part in the Battle of the Atlantic and of the Mediterranean. After the war, Philip studied in Paris, then returned to England and did a post-graduate course at St John's College, Oxford. Philip began his career as a publishing editor, working with firms including Longmans and Penguin Books. He has edited many books over his career, including works by Mary Shelley and Thomas Hardy, and a volume of volume of Victorian mock-heroic poetry, the “Epics of the Age”. In 1964, he released his first biography, A Short Life of Charles Dickens. It quickly became a critical and popular success. He followed this with nine more biographies, including books on Percy Bysshe Shelley, Robert Frost, and Arthur Conan Doyle. He has also published works of history, including The Making of Victorian England and From Socrates to Croesus: A Social and Economic History of Ancient Greece. Philip has won numerous awards over the course of his career, including a Whitbread Prize in 1969. He won a lifetime achievement award from the British Biographical Society in 2004, and was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2017. Philip is also a prominent public speaker, having delivered lectures at Cambridge, Edinburgh, and Harvard. He also serves as a mentor to young writers and historians. Philip still lives in Findhorn and Oxford. He remains a dedicated writer and historian, and continues to produce and publish acclaimed works of history and biography.

Herbert Lankester (4 May 1912 – 15 June 1994) was a British silversmith, jeweller and coin designer. He was born in Woolwich, London and attended the Lambeth School of Art from 1929–31. Lankester specialised in the restoration of silver, often working on replicas of antique pieces. He was particularly interested in the work of medieval silversmiths and jewellers, resulting in a series of pieces replicating their designs. He also created wrought-iron stands for pieces of silver. Lankester was also an experienced coin designer. His coins were widely circulated and used for change in the shops of the British currency. He designed coins for the United Kingdom, Canada, British West Indies and Gibraltar, as well as some of the coins found in the Royal Collection. Lankester was awarded the Royal Society of Arts/Wolfson award for design excellence and the Harrison Prize for creative work in metalwork. He was a fellow of the Royal Society of Arts, the British Jewellers' Association, the Goldsmith's Company, and the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths. Lankester was married to Lillian and had four children. He died on 15 June 1994 in Southend-on-Sea, Essex. Lankester's legacy lives on through the pieces he created, which have been featured in a number of museums and galleries around the world, including the Victoria and Albert Museum and the National Museum of Scotland. In 2014, the British Museum ran an exhibition of Lankester's work entitled 'Herbert Lankester 1912-1994: The Silverworker'.
