Greenland Township is a civil township of Grand Traverse County in the U.S. state of Michigan. The population was 2,062 at the 2010 census. Greenland Township was organized in 1906, although settlers had already been in the area since the late 19th century. It is served by several communities, including Honor, McBain, and Mayfield. The Lansing and Lake Michigan Railroad once served the township. Land in the township is generally flat, due to its low elevation, and is used for mostly agricultural reasons. Much of the land also lies within the Brady Creek Natural Area, home to a variety of flora and fauna. Greenland Township contains its own rural fire department, as well as a few stores. Greenland Township is home to several churches, such as the Greenland Mennonite Church and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Visitors interested in the area can enjoy hiking and birdwatching at the Brady Creek Natural Area, or partake in some of the many fishing opportunities found in the County. Greenland Township also houses the Mayfield Township Hall, an historic building erected in 1908. The Hall is now home to a variety of community events such as the Firemen’s Ball, rummage sales, and other activities. The building is also on the National Register of Historic Places. In addition to the many recreational and government buildings in the township, Greenland also has a representative in the Michigan House of Representatives, Leighton Schubert, who has served since November 2018. Greenland Township serves as an important part of Grand Traverse County, and continues to be a destination for residents and visitors alike. Its rural location, recreational activities, and government services make it a popular destination for those looking for a rural respite close to town.

The 154th meridian west is a line of longitude that approximately passes through the U.S. states of Colorado, Kansas, and Oklahoma, as well as the countries of Mexico and Canada. It forms a great circle with the 126th meridian east. The meridian 154° west of Greenwich is a line of longitude that passes through the following areas: Mexico: Baja California Sur United States: Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma Canada: Alberta In the United States, the meridian defines the western boundaries of the cities of Limon, Colorado; Liberal, Kansas; and El Reno, Oklahoma. In Canada, the meridian marks the northern boundary of the Foothills Natural Region of Alberta. It is 30 minutes of arc and 1500 statute miles in length. To the east, the line passes through the eastern borders of the states of Colorado and Kansas, crossing the lower portions of the Oklahoma panhandle. To the west, the meridian intersects the Mexican states of Baja California Sur and Sonora. In Canada, the meridian intersects the province of Alberta, passing just east of the city of Calgary. The 154th meridian west is the basis for measuring time zones in parts of Canada and the United States. In these areas, the time is based on the local mean solar time at the meridian. In the United States, these time zones are known as Mountain Standard Time for areas near the Rocky Mountains, and Central Standard Time for other states. In Canada, the time zone at the meridian is known as the Mountain Time Zone. In aviation, the meridian is the divider of high altitude airspace between the two countries, with flights at or above this altitude needing to request clearance from the controlling agency of the country they are flying into. The 154th meridian is also the divider of International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) flight information regions between the U.S. and Canada. The 154th meridian is located to the east of the Rocky Mountains, and to the west of the Great Plains. It follows the course of the lower portion of the Arkansas River, and it intersects the Rio Grande near El Paso, TX. The 154th meridian is also close to the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, which passes through parts of the states of Kansas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas. The 154th meridian passes through several national parks, such as Big Bend National Park in Texas and Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado. It also intersects the Wichitas National Forest in Oklahoma.

Oona Chaplin (born 4 June 1986) is a British actress and dancer best known for playing Talisa Maegyr in HBO's Game of Thrones and other roles in BBC's The Hour, Taboo, and Sherlock. Chaplin is the granddaughter of Charlie Chaplin and was born in Madrid to Geraldine Chaplin and Chilean cinematographer Patricio Castilla. Her parents separated when she was young, and she was raised predominantly by her maternal grandmother, Annette. Chaplin studied dance and theatre at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama in London before embarking on her acting career. Her first role was in the 2009 short film Aurora, for which she won the Best Electronic Movie award at the Galway Film Fleadh. She then went on to appear as Marnie Madden in the BBC production of The Hour (2011-2012). In 2012 Chaplin was awarded the Nuevo Talento Award at the San Sebastián International Film Festival for her performance in the Spanish film Empty View. In 2013 she was cast as Talisa Maegyr, a medical student and wife of Robb Stark, in the HBO series Game of Thrones. Her performance in the show earned her praise from both critics and fans alike. Chaplin went on to receive roles in the BBC miniseries Taboo (2017) alongside Tom Hardy, and the Netflix series Heading Out (2018). She also reprised her Game of Thrones role for the all-star recreations in Jimmy Kimmel Live, Late Night with Seth Meyers, and The Stand Up Sketch Show. On the stage, Chaplin performed in Under the Skin at the Finborough Theatre in 2017 and won positive reviews for her performance in the West End musical Gypsy (2018). Film and TV aside, Chaplin also has experience in stunt-work and performed several of her own stunts in BBC's The Hour, Taboo and Sherlock. Chaplin currently lives in north London. She is an ambassador for Oxfam, which works to alleviate poverty and suffering around the world. Oona is also a degree holder in anthropology, specializing in global migration. In 2019 Chaplin received overall praise for her performance as a top official in the Netflix science fiction mini-series Warrior Nun. She is presently filming the Brazilian series A Vida Invisivel De Euridice Gusmao.

The 1988 Hall of Fame Tennis Championships and the Virginia Slims of Newport were tennis tournaments played in Newport, Rhode Island and Boston, Massachusetts respectively from July 11 to July 17, 1988. Both tournaments were Tier IV events on the WTA Tour and were played on outdoor grass courts. The Hall of Fame Tennis Championships, which replaced the New England Classic, were sponsored by Citizen Watch Co. and the Virginia Slims of Newport were sponsored by Virginia Slims. The singles titles were both won by American Pam Shriver, who started the tournament by defending her title in Newport, defeating Natasha Zvereva of the Soviet Union in the final in straight sets. She then went on to win her second consecutive Virginia Slims of Newport title without dropping a set, defeating Dinky Van Rensselaer in the final. In the doubles competition, Shriver teamed with Zina Garrison and won the title in Newport, defeating Gigi Fernández and Robin White in the final in three sets. The team then moved on to the Virginia Slims of Newport, where they repeated their feat and won the doubles title, defeating Helena Suková and Barbara Potter in the final. The men's tournament was won by American Jay Berger, defeating Brad Gilbert in the final, 6–3, 6–3. The doubles event was won by Luke Jensen and John McEnroe. These two tournaments formed the first of five events in the 1988 Harvest Classic series, challenging the players to win four or five events consecutively, in a round-robin format. The uniqueness of the Harvest Classic was a new and innovative way to promote a series of tournaments at the time, and was quite successful. The Hall of Fame Tennis Championships and the Virginia Slims of Newport were two of the most important tournaments of the season and represented the start of the Harvest Classic series. They brought together some of the top players in the world and promoted tennis as a major sport in two iconic locations.

The 2021 The Spring League season was the fifth season of The Spring League, a developmental football league. The season began on April 17th and concluded on May 13th, with the Spring Showcase championship game at The Greenbrier. The Spring League is composed of four teams: Southland, Conquerors, Jousters and Alphas. The Spring League provides an opportunity for athletes to develop and showcase their skills to potential employers, including NFL and CFL teams. Over 250 athletes from 40 countries were part of The Spring League's 2021 season. Many NFL scouts, personnel executives and coaches attended The Spring League’s live practices and scrimmages, giving players an opportunity to get noticed and compete for jobs in the professional leagues. The Southland team was coached by Steve Hewitt and included players such as former CFL quarterback Chase Klivating, former Grambling State signal caller DK Metcalf, former Miami Hurricanes safety Jaquan Johnson, former Duke Running back Shaun Wilson and former New Mexico State signal caller Tyler Rogers. The Conquerors, who were coached by former Laguna Beach High School coach Scotty Walden, included players such as former Nebraska standout defensive end Freedom Akinmoladun and former Heisman Trophy finalist Zac Stacy. The Jousters, led by head coach former Martys Head Coach Jonathan Hayes and linebackers coach Matt McGloin, featured former USC quarterback Sam Darnold, and former Wake Forest signal caller John Wolford. Alphas were coached by former Delaware Head Coach Danny Rocco and featured former Virginia Tech quarterback Josh Jackson. The 2021 Spring Showcase championship game saw the Jousters led by Sam Darnold defeat the Alphas, coached by Danny Rocco, 24-18, with Wolford throwing a 14 yard touchdown pass to Iosua Opeta in the fourth quarter. Southland defeated the Conquerors to take third place in the tournament. The 2021 Spring League season was overall successful as players had an opportunity develop and demonstrate their talent to potential employers. It was a great opportunity for players to prove their worth and make an impression. Although the season was shorter than usual due to the pandemic, it still provided a great opportunity for players to shine.

Buffalo Springs National Reserve (BSNR) is a protected area in the Eastern Rift Valley region of Kenya, located close to the town of Maralal in Samburu County. It is a contoured, 9,000-hectare national reserve which hosts one of the most biologically diverse habitats in the region, including grassland, woodland and bushland, which are home to numerous species of flora and fauna. BSNR is home to a wide selection of animal species, including antelopes, wildebeest, elephants, lions, cheetahs, and giraffes. The area is also renowned for its numerous bird species, such as guineafowl, hornbills, starlings, waxbills, and sunbirds. One of the reserve's most important predators is the African Wild Dog which is listed as an endangered species by the IUCN. Buffalo Springs National Reserve was established in 1989 and forms part of the Samburu-Buffalo Springs-Shaba ecosystem, which stretches over some 350,000 hectares. The reserve is managed by the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) and is run in partnership with the Northern Rangelands Trust, which works with the local communities to ensure the sustainable use of the area's natural resources. The main natural attraction for visitors to Buffalo Springs National Reserve is its abundance of wildlife. The area also provides a number of activities for visitors to enjoy, such as bird watching, game drives, and guided hikes. There are a number of accommodation options for visitors which include tented camps, lodges and self-catering cottages. In addition to wildlife attractions, Buffalo Springs National Reserve is home to a number of archaeological sites, which provide evidence of human settlements dating back to the late Stone Age. There are also a number of archaeological sites located within the reserve, including rock shelters and mounds that are believed to be graves. The reserve provides an important habitat for many species of flora and fauna, and as such, it is a crucial part of conservation efforts in the region. The area is being developed as a national ecotourism destination in order to promote the conservation of the area's natural resources and to ensure the long-term sustainability of the area. Overall, Buffalo Springs National Reserve is a stunning region within Kenya's Eastern Rift Valley. The area provides visitors with access to a diverse array of flora and fauna, with plentiful wildlife and archaeological sites, making it a popular destination for visitors to explore and enjoy.

Kehkashan Basu is an environmental activist and global leader for sustainability. She is the Founder and President of the environmental initiative, Green Hope, an international organization that works on environment and sustainability issues. Kehkashan was born in Dubai, United Arab Emirates on 13 August 2001 and was the youngest ever to participate in the World Future Council's Global Parliamentary Forum on the Environment held in 2008. She held the post of Chairperson for the event. Since then, Kehkashan has been a leading voice in the international movement towards a more sustainable future. Kehkashan has devoted much of her time to raising awareness of the current global environmental crisis through media campaigns and forums. In 2016, she founded Green Hope and has since been engaged in numerous international campaigns to raise awareness of global sustainability issues and initiatives. Green Hope, which is now active in over 15 countries, is focused on empowering youth to take action on climate change and create sustainable solutions for a global community. Kehkashan believes that young people and communities should play an active role in shaping the future of their environment and society. She advocates for investing in youths and for the recognition of their role as experts. Kehkashan is involved in multiple environmental projects around the world. She holds the position of Goodwill Youth Ambassador of UN Environment and sits on the Thematic Advisory Group for the UN's Global Education and Skills Forum. In addition, she is a Global Representative from UNFCCC and she is currently a member of their Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation community. Despite her young age, Kehkashan has received numerous awards for her work, such as the International Children’s Peace Prize and the Children of the World Award. In 2018, Kehkashan, along with Green Hope, was recognized by the World Economic Forum’s Sustainable Development Impact Award. In 2019, she was selected as one of Forbes' 30 Under 30 Social Entrepreneurs. Kehkashan Basu has proven to be a growing leader for sustainability through her environmental activism and initiatives. She serves as a role model to many young environmentalists and is continuing to create sustainable solutions for global communities with her organization, Green Hope. Through her efforts, she is making a large impact in the world and inspiring many youth to take small, everyday steps to make their world a better place.

Ferdinand IV, King of the Romans (also called Ferdinand IV of Habsburg) was a member of the House of Habsburg and King of the Romans from 1491 until his death in 1564. As King of the Romans, Ferdinand was the head of the Holy Roman Empire, and his rule oversaw many of the political and religious conflicts in Europe during the Reformation and Counter Reformation eras. Ferdinand was born in 1473, son of Emperor Maximilian I and Mary of Burgundy. As a child he was known as 'Ferdinand the Learned' due to his aptitude for languages, although he was not originally seen as a potential successor to his father as emperor. He was only named heir after his elder brother, Philip the Fair, died in a riding accident in 1492. Ferdinand succeeded Maximilian as emperor at the Diet of Worms in 1493, becoming King of the Romans and simultaneously Archduke of Austria and King of Bohemia. In the beginning of his reign he concentrated much of his energy on the repression of the growing Protestant movements in the Holy Roman Empire. His army, led by his cousin and eventual successor Charles V, was successful in stopping the spread of Lutheranism, most notably their victory at the Battle ofAugsburg in 1530. On the international stage, Ferdinand's rule was marked by conflict with other European powers, particularly France, with whom he was engaged in a series of wars for control of northern Italy. Though the wars, begun in 1494 and ending in 1559, proved costly for all involved, Ferdinand ultimately emerged with more territory in northern Italy and increased influence in the region. Finally, Ferdinand's reign was important in setting the foundations for the eventual dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Ferdinand abdicated in 1558, leaving the throne to his son Karl II, who in turn passed the title of Holy Roman Emperor to his brother, Charles V the following year. Without Karl's claimed right to the throne, the concept of a universal Roman Empire quickly faded. In conclusion, Ferdinand IV of Habsburg was a key figure in the Reformation and Counter Reformation eras of European history. His rule as King of the Romans from 1493-1558 was marked by religious and political conflicts, as well as his campaigns for control of northern Italy. After his death in 1564 his title of Holy Roman Emperor was passed on to his eldest son, Karl II, and his legacy to the eventual dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.

She Knows Me Too Well is a song by the American rock band The Beach Boys, released in 1965 on the album The Beach Boys Today!. Written by Brian Wilson and Tony Asher, the song is an up-tempo ballad about a young man's dilemma in that his lover knows everything about him, including his flaws and shortcomings, and the potential difficulty of hiding them. Wilson's creative ambitions instilled into the track an unusual musical structure and an assumed influence of a symphonic-like sound. The track is a fusion of rock style instrumentation and classical aspects, with the inclusion of strings and a baroque-style harpsichord playing. It centres around a chord progression of F major, G minor, and C major, around which the rest of the instrumentation derives its tonal construction. The track features various Beach Boys layered vocal harmonies ranging from bass harmonies to falsetto, that accompany the lyrical themes of humiliation and vulnerability. The track was generally well-received, with American music writer and critic Bruce Eder writing “it was an incredible song, with an ethereal violin line adding an intense contrast to the bright major-key melody line.” It has been cited by various writers as a favourite recording of the band’s, with Joseph Lanza referring to the track as “Brian’s first adult song with a dramatic lyric”. The song has been included on various compilations and compiles of the band’s work, such as Stack-o-Tracks in 1968, Endless Summer in 1974, and Made in USA in 1986. The song has been used in various films and other media such as the Stanley Donen musical Two for the Road. In 1975, The Beach Boys performed the song on Welcome Back, Kotter, and a live version was included on their Beach Boys Live in Concert in 1976. The song continues to be included in the setlist of live tours of the band, with a live performance of the track being included on the band’s Live in London album, released in 2009.

The Constitution of Uruguay is the supreme law of Uruguay, the country's most important source of law. It was adopted in 1967 and is the tenth constitution in the country's history. The Uruguayan Constitution is one of the most advanced within Latin America as it establishes a social and democratic state of law. Its primary objective is to promote citizens' well-being and protect their rights and freedoms. The Constitution has been an inspiration for many other countries in the region who have sought to adopt a more progressive outlook. The Uruguayan Constitution is divided into 15 parts, known as titles. Among these titles are a chapter on fundamental rights and duties (Title IV), a chapter on government organization (Title VII) and one on the government's economic and financial control (Title XI). The Constitution also sets out the principles of constitutional revision, which can take place by referendum or by parliamentary decision. The Constitution establishes Uruguay as a unitary republic with a centralized government and a single-chamber Parliament, made up of two houses: the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. The President of Uruguay is the head of state and exercises executive power. The Constitution also creates the Supreme Court, which is composed of five judges. The Fundamental Rights and Duties chapter guarantees and respects civil, political, economic, and cultural rights. These include the right to life, liberty and security of person, the right to vote, the right to privacy, and the right to education. Other fundamental rights established by the Constitution include freedom of expression, the right to participate in elections, and freedom of association. The Constitution also establishes the country’s socio-economic system, which seeks to achieve social justice through equitable redistribution of wealth created by the state. This includes the protection and promotion of entrepreneurship, and the gradual integration of uruguayans into the work force. In addition to the Constitution, Uruguay also has an Electoral Code and a Civil Code. The Constitution is considered ''inviolable'' by the country and any amendment to the text must be approved by referendum. It is an important symbol of Uruguay's commitment to human rights and the rule of law.

A regular graph is a graph in which all the vertices or nodes have the same degree. The degree of a vertex of a graph is the number of edges incident to the vertex. A regular graph that has n vertices each of degree k is often denoted as kn. Regular graphs generalize the notion of an n-dimensional hypercube and can be used to generate constraint satisfaction problems with finite domains. Regular graphs are important in the conception and analysis of networks, as many real-world networks are believed to be well-approximated by regular graphs. They are also known to be highly symmetric and self-dual, which makes them easier to analyze and visualize. In graph theory, a regular graph is called a k-regular graph or k-1-regular graph, denoted by Kn or K1n, respectively. All graphs with the same degree on all vertices are called regular graphs. Depending on the degree, the regular graph has different properties and properties of the underlying combinatorial objects. Regular connected graphs are also known as regular subgraphs. A k-regular graph is a graph in which every vertex has exactly k edges connecting it to other vertices. If we denote the number of vertices by n then we can calculate the number of edges, e, as follows: e = kn/2. As an example, the complete graph K3,3 is a graph with 6 vertices and 9 edges with degree 3 on each vertex. Examples of regular graphs include complete graphs, where every vertex is connected to every other vertex, bipartite graphs, where each vertex is connected only to vertices of the opposite group, and cycles, where each vertex is linked to its two adjacent neighbors. All regular graphs are planar and Eulerian. In some cases, though, a regular graph may not be Hamiltonian. Examples of non-regular graphs include wheel graphs and star graphs, which are both highly symmetric but neither is a regular graph. Wheel graphs contain two regular subgraphs, a cycle and an additional vertex of degree 2. Star graphs are similar to wheel graphs, but in these the additional vertex is of degree n − 1, where n is the number of vertices in the graph. In some cases, regular graphs may have multiple edges between two vertices, which are called multigraphs. Multigraphs are useful when some information needs to be encoded in the edges, as in programs such as weighted graph coloring. For example, in a weighted graph coloring problem, each vertex of the graph is assigned a color, and its edges are assigned weights that depend on the colors of the vertices they connect. Regular graphs are an important type of graphs that have many applications across a wide range of fields, including computer science, network analysis, and graph theory. They are useful in solving a variety of graph-related problems, such as Hamiltonicity, colorability, and graph isomorphism.

List of Hong Kong Twenty20 International cricketers is a list of all the cricketers who have played Twenty20 International cricket for Hong Kong since the team made its Twenty20 International debut in 2014. This list is correct as of 28 November 2020. The only men to play for Hong Kong in T20 Internationals are Anshuman Rath, Babar Hayat, Waqas Khan, Nizakat Khan, Tanveer Ahmed, Ehsan Khan, Kinchit Shah, Aizaz Khan, Kyle Christie, Aftab Hussain, Waqas Barkat, Simandeep Singh, Haroon Arshad, Aarush Bhagwat, Ehsan Nawaz, Scott McKechnie, Nadeem Ahmed, Jhatavedh Subramanyan, Asad Mohammadi, Hoison Mckay, Scott McKechnie and Ayush Shukla. The team is captained by Anshuman Rath. Hong Kong have so far played thirteen T20 International matches, winning 5 and losing 8. In their most recent match, Hong Kong lost to Iraq by six wickets. The Desert Locust Control Organization for Eastern Africa (DLCOEA) is an international organization dedicated to the control and eradication of desert locusts in Eastern Africa. It was founded in 1992 by nine African countries of the region, including Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Sudan, and South Sudan. DLCOEA is a joint commission of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). DLCOEA works to implement protective measures against locust breeding and keep the locust population at an acceptable level within the area of responsibility. Its main focus is to reduce the effects of locust infestations on the region's food security. The organization provides financial and technical assistance to member states in their effort to control locusts. It develops strategies for control and management, conducts field research, and works with agricultural projects that focus on locust infestations. In order to fight the desert locust infestations, the organization works closely with regional government authorities, local agricultural research institutes, and international development agencies. DLCOEA is involved in data collection on the state of locust infestations and also provides training on preventive and curative control operations. Furthermore, it collaborates with non-governmental organizations, such as UN Food and Agriculture Organization, to provide information materials on desert locusts. DLCOEA's projects have been successful in reducing the risk of locust infestations and contributing to improved food security in the region. The organization's most notable project was the "Desert Locust Management Programme for East Africa", which has helped reduce locust infestations in many countries in the region. The program has provided training to over 160,000 farmers and helped to build capacity on locust control. DLCOEA was formed to support its member countries in their efforts to prevent and control locust infestations. The organization has achieved a number of successes in the region, which have led to improved food security and increased locust safety for the population.

Hollis Gillespie is an American journalist, author, and radio show host from Atlanta, Georgia. She has typically been seen impressing her audience with her unique style in writing and reporting. Gillespie's flair for edgy humor and often irreverent takes on serious topics has been praised by renowned publications such as New York Times, LA Times, and Rolling Stone. Gillespie began her career as a magazine writer for Creative Loafing, a free weekly paper in Atlanta. After she developed critical recognition for her style in the paper, she went on to write for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution and then author the popular “Shocking & Awful” column for The Atlanta Quarterly. In addition to being a successful writer, Gillespie is also an accomplished radio show host. In 2000, her show, “LifeasWeirditGets” debuted on public radio station, WABE. The show gained her further recognition for her style, which often coalesced political wit with dry yet biting humor. Since her radio show debuted, Gillespie has branched out to other fields such as television. She's made appearances on Good Day Atlanta, CBS Early Show, NBC’s The Today Show. She also hosted an online show titled, "Hollis’ World" for two seasons, which was a serial comedy on ULive, a sponsored-content website of NBC Universal. Gillespie’s popularity further grew thanks to her award-winning book, Bleachy-Haired Honky Bitch: Tales from a Bad Neighborhood (2005). The book is a blend of anecdotes, revelations, and sharp-witted humor which was said to offer a brutally honest and immensely humorous glimpse into her life. Additionally, she has penned numerous other books such as Trailer Trashed: My Dubious Efforts to Haul Myself Up the Economic Ladder. Gillespie has been praised for her dry and often profane writing that reflects her roots in the South. She has become known for her frank and humorous takes on current and social issues, and is also highly active in the fight for animal rights organizations. Her writing and shows continue to receive praise, and she also regularly opens up about her experiences as a mother, an Atlanta native, and an animal rights advocate.

A seismometer, also known as a seismograph, is a device used to measure, record, and detect seismic activity. The device is typically composed of a strong base and a seismometer, which typically uses a weight and pendulum to detect vibrations in the ground. Seismometers are important tools in seismology, a branch of geophysics that studies earthquakes and their waves. Seismometer readings are used to understand more about the nature of earthquakes and other seismic events, and to predict potential disasters. The earliest seismometers were based on a tilt sensor that measured the angle of the ground relative to the horizon, then converting the measured tilt into a proportion of the intensity and magnitude of an earthquake. This type of device was used by the ancient Chinese to measure earthquakes in the second century BC. Modern seismometers, however, have undergone a significant evolution. Digital seismometers, also known as digital seismographs, are much more advanced than their predecessors. They utilize a variety of methods, including motion sensors and accelerometers, for measuring ground motion generated by seismic waves. Different types of digital seismometers have various capabilities, with some being able to measure both horizontal (from side to side) and vertical (from top to bottom) motion. Modern seismometers are also very sensitive in order to accurately measure motion, and can detect vibrations that are partially caused by human activities such as construction and traffic. They can also detect ground tremors caused by natural phenomena such as landslides and earthquakes. This information can be used by seismologists and engineers to understand more about the underlying causes of an earthquake and to make predictions about future seismic events. Seismometers are also helpful in detecting underground nuclear tests and other activities of humans. The data collected by the seismometer can be used to detect any potential nuclear tests that are conducted underground, therefore helping to reduce the chance of an international nuclear incident. In addition to providing seismic information, seismometers can also be used in energy exploration. By detecting vibrations from deep beneath the surface of the Earth, seismometers can help detect underground deposits of oil and gas. This type of data can be used for geologic mapping and for locating areas of high petroleum potential. Seismometers are an invaluable device for usage in research, energy exploration, and for predicting the effects of seismic activity. As technology develops and becomes more advanced, the capabilities of seismometers have also greatly improved. They have become an essential tool in the fields of geophysics, energy exploration, and in helping to protect humans from harm caused by natural phenomena such as earthquakes.

Toby Township is a rural township located in Clarion County, Pennsylvania. It was established in 1829 from parts of Richland Township and Piney Township. The area comprises four villages: Tobyville, Lilyburg, Port a Town, and Sweeney's Corners. The township is home to two Clarion County parks, Tobyhanna Creek Lake and Longshore Lake, which are popular destinations for fishing and boating. The unincorporated community of Tobyville is the largest in the township. It was founded in the late 1700s by Benjamin Toby, a farmer from New Jersey, and is named after him. The settlement is mostly residential and provides amenities such as a post office, library, and general store. Other villages in the township include Lilyburg, Port a Town, and Sweeney's Corners. Lilyburg was founded in 1835 by Daniel and Rebecca Lily. Today, the settlement consists of a United Methodist Church and several residences. Port a Town is another unincorporated community in Toby Township. It was established in the early 1800s by the Port family and is mostly residential. The residents of the community are primarily descendants of the Port family. Sweeney's Corners is a commercial area with several businesses serving Toby Township and the surrounding area. Toby Township has a total area of 38.4 square miles and is bordered by Richland Township and Piney Township to the north, Elk Township to the northeast, Clarion Township to the southeast, Perry Township to the south, and Jefferson Township to the west. The Clarion River and Tobyhanna Creek flow through the area, along with several smaller streams. The area is predominantly wooded, with some agricultural use in the valleys. Overall, Toby Township is a quiet, rural area with a small-town charm. It has a number of attractions including Tobyhanna Creek Lake, Longshore Lake, and the scenic Clarion River. There are numerous recreational activities to enjoy, as well as some unique businesses located in the area.

Lietava (Neris) is a small village in Šakiai district municipality located in northern Lithuania, at the intersection of the main Četegiris-Šakiai road and Dovainonys-Rastoniai road. It has a population of approximately 406 people. The name of the village first appeared in written documents sometime in the 18th century. Initially, it was called “Šakių Girdinių Meilandas”. Later it changed to “Lietava” as its current name. Its name translates to “wet land” in Lithuanian, as the neighborhood is mostly wetland and swamp. Most of the people of Lietava are engaged in farming. They grow various types of crops, such as potatoes and grain, as well as raising animals such as pigs, cows and chickens. In 2003, the village decided to make a construction project to improve the condition of its streets. An asphalt road was built from Četegiris to Šakiai, which covers the entire distance from Lietava up to the Šakiai boundary. Lietava also provides a number of services to the nearby villages. It has several retail stores that offer basic items, as well as a barbershop and a small restaurant. There is also a post office and a library in the village, which enables people to keep in touch with their relatives and access the latest news. The village also has a small church, which is used mainly by the inhabitants of Lietava and the surrounding region. The celebration of the Catholic Easter is very important to the people of Lietava, as it is a sign of the new year's resurrection and the difficulties of the preceding year. Lietava is a small but vibrant village, full of life and culture. Despite the simple facilities, it has become a wonderful place to raise a family. The villagers are very friendly and welcoming to visitors, which is what makes the village so attractive to tourists.

Andreas Heusler (1848-1923) was a Swiss historian and lecturer, best known for his seminal work on medieval Switzerland. He was born in Zurich and studied at the University of Zurich, earning his doctorate in 1880. His work on Swiss history, specifically the period between 1250 and 1450, changed the approach of early modern Swiss historiography, diverging from the nationalist trend of his predecessors and instead focusing on religious and political changes. Heusler's early writing focused on his dissertation on the city of Zurich in the years 1250–1350, which he published in 1881. He then moved on to write a series of monographs on Swiss history and archaeology, including works on the Swiss Confederacy from 1350–1450, and the history of the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. He also wrote on Swiss judiciary, ecclesiastical, and economic history. Through his works, Heusler helped create an academic language for the study of Swiss history, and his research was often used in both the academic and wider contexts. Heusler served as an associate professor of Swiss history at the universities of Zurich, Basel and Berne, and worked for many years as the curator of the Swiss National Archive. He was elected to a number of scholarly societies, most significantly the German Historical Institute. In 1898, he was given an honorary degree from the University of Oxford, in recognition of his work. He was a founding member of the Swiss National Museum, and served as its first director from 1904-1923. His work on the development of the Swiss nation has greatly shaped the way modern historians view history. Heusler was known for his expansive knowledge of Swiss history, again steering away from the nationalist trends of his predecessors. His views on the history of medieval Switzerland have been described as profoundly and fundamentally different from the prevailing historiography of the time. He critiqued the use of legends and myths in historical accounts, and instead encouraged the use of primary source material. Heusler also wrote several books arguing against religious persecution and persecution of the Jews, and in favour of the separation of Church and State. Heusler died in 1923, and is remembered in Switzerland as the grandfather of modern historiography. His work has greatly shaped the study of Swiss history, and his approach to historiography is still in use today.

Clarence Drive is a major arterial road in New South Wales, Australia. The road serves as an important link between the towns of Grafton and Yamba. It is one of the longest roads in the region, stretching for 53 kilometres (33 miles). Clarence Drive, which is a two-lane highway, was constructed in the 1960s to improve access between Grafton and the nearby towns. It is often used by tourists visiting the region as it passes through some of the most picturesque coastal scenery in the area. During the holiday season, the road can become congested due to its popularity. The road is named after the nearby Clarence River, which runs alongside the road for most of its length. It passes through many rural and settlement areas, including the towns of Coldstream, Seelands, Cowper, Brushgrove, Ulmarra, Lawrence, Maclean, Sandon, and Lawrence. Many parts of the road feature rolling hills and winding curves as it passes through the lush landscape. Clarence Drive has a number of notable landmarks located along its route. The most prominent of these is the Maclean Bridge, a three-span bridge which was opened in 1973. The road also passes through two state forests, Cougai-Munmorah and Bundjalung, as well as a number of small parks. Clarence Drive is considered an important regional road and is regularly maintained by the Roads and Maritime Services. It is a popular recreational driving route for motorcycle and car enthusiasts. The road has also been recognised by various organisations including the Keep Australia Beautiful Council, which awarded it a "Most Scenic Drive" in 2008. In addition to serving as a major arterial route, Clarence Drive is also a vital link in the local economy. It provides access to local businesses in the towns it connects, as well as providing local farmers with access to markets. Clarence Drive is a popular tourist destination, with many visitors taking the opportunity to enjoy the scenery and take in the sights in the area. As one of the main routes between Grafton and Yamba, the road sees an increase in traffic during the holiday months. This has led to the implementation of several additional safety measures, such as the construction of a number of passing lanes and designated rest areas for drivers. Overall, Clarence Drive is an important road in the region, providing key links between towns and providing access to the stunning scenery of the Clarence Valley. Its long history has earned it recognition as a scenic drive, making it an area of interest for both residents and visitors alike.

New London Harbor Light is a lighthouse located in New London, Connecticut, United States. It features a white conical tower that stands 45 feet tall, and is the second oldest lighthouse in Connecticut. It is the oldest lighthouse which is still active on the Connecticut coast. The construction of the lighthouse was started in 1761 and it was first lit on May 30th 1801 with an array of five lamps, set in 21-inch reflectors. The light was originally powered by lard oil, which was later changed to kerosene. The tower has been described as having "spider-like" steps, with its walls having the thickness of two feet. In 1838, a lightning strike destroyed the lighthouse; it was then rebuilt and relit. During World War II, the Coast Guard added a three-mile radius of surveillance around the lighthouse. In 1965, the light was automated and maintained by The United States Coast Guard. On June 20th, 1984, the National Park Service added the New London Harbor Lighthouse to the National Register of Historic Places, and acts as the caretaker of the lighthouse today. The property is managed by New London Maritime Society, which operates the facility and provides interpretive programs about the lighthouse and the maritime history of New London. A fee is charged for visitors wishing to climb the tower to get a better view of the harbor. The current light is an automated aerobeacon which emits a white light every three seconds, visible up to 8 nautical miles. The lighthouse is also displayed on the New London Flag as a symbol of the city. The New London Harbor Light is a historic and iconic site of the city, offering a unique view and glimpse of New London’s rich maritime heritage. It stands as a testament to the city’s importance as a maritime port of the United States.

Toy soldier (disambiguation) is a term which can refer to multiple related topics. The most common definition of toy soldier refers to a miniature figurine that resembles an actual soldier in either a historical or fictional setting. Toys of this type have been around since the early 19th century, and can range from simple plastic figurines to highly intricate metal models. Toy soldiers are often used in wargaming, and can also serve as a collectible item. Another usage of the term "toy soldier" refers to the military action figures and playsets which have been made available since the 1970s. These are typically marketed towards children and come in both historic and contemporary styles. Action figures often come with a range of accessories such as weapons, vehicles, and buildings, and are commonly used to recreate battles from both real life and fantasy settings. The term "toy soldier" is also used in reference to a style of dance that gained popularity in the early 20th century. Toy soldier dances typically involve soldiers (often seen in minstrel shows of the time) marching and dancing in synchronized patterns and formations. This type of dance is still performed around the world in both traditional and modernized forms. Finally, the term "toy soldier" can also refer to a song written and recorded by British band Coldplay in 2000. The track was the third single off their debut album, Parachutes, and reached number 11 on the UK Singles Chart. In conclusion, the term "toy soldier" has multiple meanings, the most popular being the miniature figurines which either represent real or fictional soldiers, and the associated action figures and playsets. The term is also used in reference to a style of dance which was popularized in the early 20th century, as well as a song by Coldplay which was recorded in 2000.

Hugh Otter-Barry, MNRSA (1850–1925) was a British architect, civil engineer and conservationist who gained particular recognition for his contributions to the restoration of Westminster Abbey, Westminster Hall and Westminster Hall’s Great Clock. Otter-Barry was born in 1850 and became a Fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1878. He was employed as an architect to the London County Council, where he oversaw the construction of a number of public buildings including Montagu House, now the Library of the University of London, and Holloway Sanatorium. From 1895 to 1898, Otter-Barry was Engineering Surveyor for Westminster Abbey, where he developed a close relationship with the Dean, Rev. Arthur Richard Everard, who requested he be engaged in the long-term restoration of Westminster Hall. In 1900, Otter-Barry was appointed surveyor to Westminster Hall, a post he held until 1923. During this time, Otter-Barry was responsible for a wide range of restoration and conservation work, including the restoration of its thirteenth-century hammer beam roof. He also supervised the construction of a new clock chamber and helped to install the eleven-ton turret clock, known as 'Big Ben', at the north-west corner of Westminster Hall in 1912. In addition to his restoration work in Westminster, Otter-Barry undertook repair and conservation projects at other important London buildings, including Tower of London (1908-1910) and Whitehall Palace (1911-12). He also carried out extensive work across Britain, including at the Chapter House at Ripon Cathedral (1909-11) and Wycombe Parish Church in Buckinghamshire (1914-15). Otter-Barry was a lifelong conservationist, writing on the need for the protection of our ancient buildings and monuments, and was one of the first to champion the use of photogrammetry for the accurate mapping of sites and structures from photographs. He was also an active member of the Royal Society of Antiquaries and was awarded the society's Medal of Service for recording ancient and historical sites for posterity. Hugh Otter-Barry died in 1925 and was buried in Kensal Green Cemetery. He is remembered as an architect and civil engineer who played a major role in protecting and restoring Britain's endangered historical sites.

Ivan Sertić (born October 12, 1979) is a Croatian former professional basketball player who played as a center and power forward. He was born in Split in the former Yugoslavia, and attended high school in his hometown. He made his professional basketball debut in 1999 with the Croatian basketball club KK Split, with whom he won the Croatian championships in 2000, 2002 and 2004, as well as the FIBA Saporta Cup in 2003. Sertić played for the Lithuanian team BC Žalgiris for the 2003-2004 and 2004-2005 seasons, and for Spanish side TAU Cerámica for the 2005-2006 season. In the 2006-2007 season he returned to Croatia and played for Cibona Zagreb. He represented the Croatian national basketball team in the Eurobasket tournaments of 1999, 2003 and 2005, helping his team to win the silver medal in 2003. In 2008, Sertić moved to the United States, where he signed with the Los Angeles Lakers and played one season in the NBA. After the 2010-2011 season, Sertić retired from professional basketball and moved back to his hometown of Split. In 2012, Sertić opened a basketball school in his hometown, named after a former Split basketball legend, Goran Sobin. The school has since become a major basketball organization in Croatia and accepts students from all over Europe to study and play basketball. Sertić has been inducted into the Croatian Basketball Hall of Fame for his numerous contributions to the game over the course of his career. He is also held in high esteem by his former teammates and coaches on account of his dedication and commitment to the sport.

Fireworks Entertainment is a Canadian film and television production company. The company was founded in 2003 by co-chairmen and co-CEOs Jay Firestone and John Morayniss with offices in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The company produces feature films, dramatic television series and reality shows, along with original content for streaming and other digital media outlets. Fireworks produces for the domestic and worldwide television markets, and its programs have been sold to broadcasters in over 180 countries. Its library consists of over 1,000 hours of television including such series as Queer as Folk, Hex, Mutant X, Train 48 and Ready or Not. The company's theatrical release credits include Stick It, the 3-D remake of Journey to the Center of the Earth and the 2010 remake of The Clowns. Fireworks is also involved in a variety of digital media projects and content creation for mobile phones, Xbox Live and Apple iTunes. Fireworks also continues to develop feature film projects and pursue even more exciting opportunities in the interactive, new media and gaming arenas. Fireworks works with a variety of partners and produces programming for networks in Canada and around the world. In 2017 Fireworks partnered with Academy Award winner Morgan Freeman to launch his Mad Rabbit Entertainment production company. This partnership has enabled Fireworks Entertainment to develop original scripted and unscripted content for film and TV. In addition to their long list of producer credits, Fireworks Entertainment also houses the distribution company Matador Content, which owns rights to several drama and comedy television series. Matador has distributed content in over 130 countries and its titles have been nominated for several awards, including three Emmy Awards. The company also boasts an impressive list of awards for its programming, including Gemini Awards, Canadian Screen Awards, a Golden Globe nomination and an Emmy win. Fireworks Entertainment takes pride in its ability to identify and develop original concepts for entertainment.

Helga Stephenson (born 1943) is a Canadian film producer, writer, and festival administrator. She is currently the CEO of the Academy of Canadian Cinema & Television. Helga's career began in the 1970s, when she worked as a production consultant and writer on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) application process for feature film production. In 1975 Helga produced and wrote her first feature film, I Know Who Killed Me, which was followed by The Sex Diaries (1977) and Little Moscow (1978). In 1979 she established the discotheque in Toronto, Ontario, called Nuit Blanche, which attracted various nightclub aficionados. Stephenson starred in the short film Sunset Limousine, which won a Genie Award for Best Short and was nominated for a Golden Zeppelin at the 1982 Berlin International Film Festival. She also produced and wrote the film Ballet Triste (1984). From 1989 to 1992, she served as the Executive Director of the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). After leaving TIFF, Helga joined the Ontario Film Development Corporation (OFDC), now known as the Ontario Media Development Corporation (OMDC), as Director of Festival Programming. In 2003, she became the founding Executive Director of the Academy of Canadian Cinema & Television. She was appointed Chief Executive Officer in 2013, a role in which she served until 2020. Throughout her career, Helga has received a number of awards and honours, including the Outstanding Achievement Award from both TIFF and the OMDC. In 2007 she was inducted into the Canadian Association of Broadcasters Hall of Fame, and in 2010 she was made an Officer of the Order of Canada. Most recently, Helga was the National CBC Ambassador for International Women's Day and served as a juror for the Banff World Media Festival and the RBC Canadian Documentary Film Festival.

John Baumgartner (born October 15, 1950) is an American entrepreneur and business executive who has served as the president and chief executive officer of several companies, including Digital Equipment Corporation, Oracle Corporation, Siebel Systems, and most recently Teradata Corporation. Baumgartner grew up in a small farming town in Kansas. He attended the University of Kansas and earned a degree in Computer Science. After graduating he quickly advanced in the computer industry, working for Illinois Computer Services, Inc., later spending four years at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) where he held various managerial positions. In 1988, Baumgartner joined Oracle Corporation, eventually becoming President and Chief Operating Officer. At Oracle, Baumgartner played a significant role in its growth from a $140 million to a $2 billion software company. In 1996 he became President and CEO of Siebel Systems, taking the company from having fewer than 60 employees to a $1 billion company in under five years. Baumgartner then served as President and CEO of Teradata Corporation from 2002 to 2006. He is currently on the board of several companies, including Oracle and Lufthansa. He is also on the university advisory board at his alma mater, the University of Kansas. John Baumgartner is widely recognized for his leadership and is credited with helping many organizations transition from the traditional hardware-based computing era to the world of digital computing. He has a long record of successful acquisitions and strategic collaborations, and he has been recognized for his expert management of technology transitions. In recognition of his outstanding business accomplishments, Baumgartner was awarded the Oregon Collaborative Leadership Award in 2001. He has been inducted into the Kansas Business Hall of Fame and has received several lifetime achievement awards from various organizations including the Software Council of Southern California, the San Diego Software and Internet Council, and the San Francisco Software and Internet Council. John Baumgartner is an example of modern business success, having held the positions of president, CEO, and board member for some of the largest technology companies in the world. His successes have been remarkably consistent amongst the companies he has lead, and his legacy as a businessman will not soon be forgotten.

Josh Ginnelly (born October 5th, 1996) is an English professional football player who plays as a winger for Floriana F.C. in the Maltese Premier League. Born in Stourbridge, West Midlands, Ginnelly began his career with Wolverhampton Wanderers before signing a professional contract with League One side Shrewsbury Town in 2013. Ginnelly made his debut for The Shrews in a 1–1 draw with MK Dons on 15th August 2015. Ginnelly helped the club gain promotion to League One in the 2016/17 season, during which he scored 8 goals and provided 8 assists in 50 appearances. He also scored the winner in their 4–3 win over Northampton Town on 17th February 2017, a goal which was ultimately nominated for the Sky Bet League Two Goal of the Season. Ginnelly left Shrewsbury in July 2018, transfer to Preston North End, who had been tracking his progress since his Shrewsbury debut. He was a regular in the Preston side over two seasons and was part of the team which reached the play-off semi-finals in 2020. In August 2020, Ginnelly moved abroad for the first time, joining Maltese Premier League side Floriana F.C on a two-year contract. Ginnelly scored on his debut in a 2–1 win over Tarxien Rainbows in November 2020, and he scored again in a 2–0 victory over Gzira United in February 2021. He has become an important player in Cristiano Lucarelli's squad, providing width and attacking threat to the team. Away from his football career, Ginnelly has also been involved in charity work. In October 2020, he raised money for The James Wilkie Ginnelly Foundation which was set up in memory of his cousin who died in a house fire in 2019. The charity aims to raise money to buy and install smoke alarms in homes. Ginnelly is currently injury free and looking forward to helping Floriana finish the season strongly. He will be hoping to pick up his fifth promotion from the fourth tier in 2021-22.

Bitch, Don’t Let Me Die! is an anthem of resilience, resistance and solidarity that was created in response to the call for Black Lives Matter and other racial justice movements around the United States. The song, written and performed by Rahbi and featured artist JohnBoy, was released on July 4, 2020 in the wake of national protests and outcry of racial injustice sparked by the police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. Yalonda Johnson-Gutierrez, also known as Rahbi, reported that the emotional and passionate song was created as a cry out for help and support for those who were hurting in response to the ongoing crisis surrounding police brutality and systemic racism across America. The song was created in collaboration between Atlanta-based artist Rahbi and American hip hop recording artist and storyteller, JohnBoy. The lyrics of the song provide a candid look into the escalating urgency of the Black Lives Matter movement and its intent to uplift Black and Brown individuals in the United States. JohnBoy and Rahbi’s song blends R&B, hip-hop and soul elements, creating a powerful and moving musical accompaniment to the strength and resilience of justice-seeking protestors in the nation’s streets. The two artists sought to use their platform to spread a message of unity, love and inclusivity by staying true to their craft and delivering honest soundscapes. The song has since had support from press outlets such as NBC’s The Grio and The Shadow League, which praised the tune for its “message-driven lyrics and strong emphasis on positivity.” Since its release, the song has gained over 70,000 streams and millions of impressions as it continues to spread throughout streaming platforms. As JohnBoy and Rahbi continue to spread their message of love, justice and solidarity, their mission will ring louder than ever in their anthem, "Bitch, Don’t Let Me Die!"

The Phantom Freighter, also known as the Flying Dutchman, is a legendary sailing ship believed to be cursed and doomed to sail the seas for all eternity. The phantom ship is said to appear suddenly and unexpectedly out of a dense fog and is often reported to be illuminated by ghostly blue lights. It is believed that anyone who sets eyes upon this ill-fated ship is doomed to be taken by the devil. Originating from European maritime mythology and folklore, the phantom freighter is most commonly associated with the Flying Dutchman, a vessel cursed by the Devil after its captain, Vander Decken VI, refused to turn back despite warnings of an impending storm. In mythology, the freighter is said to sail endlessly in search of salvation, but its fate remains cursed, as it can only rest when it has been crossed by a living person. Perhaps the most famous sighting of the phantom freighter occurred in 1881, when the cargo ship godspeed reported seeing a strange sailing vessel, entirely crew less and shrouded in fog. As they drew closer, the crew of the godspeed claimed to have seen a woman on board the phantom freighter, leading many to believe that it was the Flying Dutchman itself. The legend of the phantom freighter has been featured in countless works of literature and film, from William Hope Hodgson’s 1904 novel The Ghost Pirates to Disney’s 2003 film Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl. It has also inspired songs, such as The Dubliners’ “The Flying Dutchman” and Iron Maiden’s “The Phantom of the Opera.” Today, the Phantom Freighter remains a captivating figure of folklore and mythology, and continues to be a source of fascination for sailors, adventurers and authors alike. Despite the mysterious and ghostly reputation it has built up over the centuries, it is a reminder of the power of the natural world and a warning against the dangers of ignoring it.

James Gisborne (1758–1846) was an English lawyer and man of letters, remembered for his book Travels in the Interior of Brazil and for editing the Morning Post. Gisborne was the son of Roger Gisborne, a Reform Club member who was one of the first Englishmen to visit Switzerland. He was born in England and travelled extensively in Europe and the Americas. Gisborne studied law at King's College London and at Lincoln's Inn, eventually becoming a barrister. He was a close friend of Pitt, a member of the Pitt Club, and a noted wit and conversationalist. Gisborne published several books, including The Pleasures of Memory (1796), Essays, Critical and Satirical (1798), and Italy But Not as I Trustriced It (1801). However, his most significant work was Travels in the Interior of Brazil (1810). This book describes Gisborne's extensive travels in Brazil and his encounters with the French naturalist Aimé Bonpland. After returning to England, Gisborne edited the Morning Post, overseeing such unprecedented additions as the Athens Correspondent and an Agricultural Reporter. He also contributed a number of articles, primarily devoted to foreign and law stories. Gisborne died in 1846 in London. Gisborne's legacy continues in two ways: his works remain important sources of knowledge and detail regarding Brazil in the early 19th century and his work on the Morning Post stands as an early example of a major newspaper undertaking substantial foreign and specialist coverage.

Nicholas Raymond Altrock (born June 8, 1876 - December 14, 1965) was an American left-handed pitcher in Major League Baseball (MLB). He was also an occasional first baseman and long-time coach for the Washington Senators/Minnesota Twins franchises. Altrock was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, on June 8, 1876. He made his big-league debut with the Chicago Orphans in 1898 and spent four seasons with them before spending 1899 with the Louisville Colonels and 1901 with the Cincinnati Reds. In 1902 he joined the Washington Senators for a nine-season tenure with the club as a player/coach, during which he led the American League in ERA (earned run average) in 1907 and established himself as one of the game's humorous characters. He also managed 13 games for the Senators in 1910, compiling a 5-8 record. After completing his initial major-league career with the Boston Rustlers of the National League in 1914, Altrock returned to his old club in 1915 as a coach, becoming the long-time assistant to Senators/Twins manager Bucky Harris—except for a two-year stint as Miami Marlins manager in the Florida State League (1939-1940). His mediocre record as a major-league manager was due in part to the fact that he had no real coaching experience, despite working for many years as an assistant. altrock Altrock was also an accomplished artist, for which the sports world is thankful. The room in which the Washington Senators hosted their post-game banquetsused his cartoon artwork to adorn the walls. He was also a great practical joker, so much so that Sport Magazine named him "king of clowns" in 1941. Nick Altrock was so popular in Washington, D. C., that Congress granted him a $1,000 salary in recognition of his services to the game. Altrock decided to return to the Senators in 1921 and spend the rest of his life in D. C. After 54 years as a coach and an additional 14 years as a scout, he retired from the Twins organization in 1969 at the age of 93. On December 14, 1965, Altrock died of a heart attack at age 89 in a Washington hospital. He was posthumously elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2005 with the Veterans Committee award. Altrock is the only person in baseball history to address the crowd at the Hall of Fame induction ceremony. He was inducted in 1947 and told the audience, "It is a great honor to be here today. I'm glad I made it." Although he did not personally receive the award, he was honored posthumously.

The Flying Tigers is a 1942 film directed by David Millar and produced by First National Pictures. The film stars John Wayne and John Carroll as two members of the 1st American Volunteer Group (AVG), an air group working with the Chinese Air force against the Japanese during World War II. The film begins with the AVG being formed in 1941, with pilot Jim Gordon (Wayne) joining the group to avenge the death of his brother, who had been killed while serving in the Chinese Air Force. Gordon is joined by John Tex Riddle (Carrol), a tough Texan who is eager to fight. The AVG set off for China and begin to launch raids against the Japanese, but the enemy proves to be too strong for the increasingly outnumbered Tri-colored forces and their planes. With the help of Chinese ground forces, the AVG manages to turn the tide in the battles. The Japanese finally launch a major attack on Rangoon, but the AVG manage to repel the attacking forces. After several successful missions, the AVG is finally forced to abandon China as the Japanese forces overrun the country. Gordon and Riddle return home to America as heroes, but with the knowledge that the Trip-colored forces were ultimately unsuccessful in their mission. The Flying Tigers is a classic World War II action movie with excellent performances from Wayne and Carroll and thrilling aerial-combat scenes. It is widely considered to be one of the best films of the genre and was a box-office success, grossing over $3 million. The Flying Tigers was added to the National Film Registry in 1995, recognizing the film as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant". The film has had many positive reviews, with Guy Flatley of The New York Times writing that it was "a good solid job of action entertainment". The Flying Tigers is an important and exciting film that captures the heroism of the AVG as they battled against overwhelming odds in an effort to save China from Japanese invasion. It is a classic example of late-war production and celebrates the courage and dedication of the brave pilots and their Chinese allies.

Deatsville, Alabama is a small town in Elmore County, Alabama, United States. The population was 1,317 at the 2010 census. Deatsville was founded in 1870. The town was named for its first postmaster, Joseph Deats. Deatsville is located in a rural area of Elmore County, about 50 miles south of Montgomery, Alabama. Deatsville is a vibrant community with a growing population of people from all over the world. The town is made up mostly of families, who are supported by local businesses, schools, parks, and other services. The town is known for its friendly people and a historic downtown area. Deatsville's economy is largely based on agriculture and timber. The city is home to several large farms and timber companies that are active in the area. In addition, the town is home to several small businesses and local restaurants. The town is served by Elmore County Schools and has three elementary schools and one middle school. The town is also home to one private school, Deatsville Christian Academy. Deatsville is home to a variety of recreational and entertainment opportunities. The city is home to the Deatsville Community Park, which features several athletic fields, a playground, and a walking trail. There are also several fishing and hunting areas nearby, as well as a nature preserve. The town is also home to several small lakes and a public swimming pool. In addition, the city has a variety of religious congregations, ranging from Baptist to Catholic. The town is also home to two freestanding churches: Deatsville Presbyterian and Deatsville Baptist Churches. Deatsville is a charming and welcoming community with a growing population, diverse workforce, and a variety of businesses, activities and amenities. The town is a great place to live and work and offers something for everyone.

Gabriele Münter (February 19, 1877 – May 19 ,1962) was a German Expressionist painter, printmaker and lyrical abstractionist. She was a member of the Blue Rider, a group of expressionist artists in pre-World War I Germany, and a mentor to the Bauhaus Movement. She had a deep influence on the early years of European modernism. Münter was born into a wealthy family in Berlin. She was an able student and a talented pianist, and it was expected that she would pursue higher education in pursuit of a music career. However, when she was eighteen, she met the French painter Jacques Marquet and fell in love with him. Inspired by Marquet, she began to attend drawing classes. She then moved to Munich to continue her studies under the painter and printmaker Lovis Corinth. Münter's artistic career began during her time in Munich. Her teacher Corinth introduced her to a number of influential artistic circles. Among them was the avant-garde group Blaue Reiter, which she joined in 1911. The group included the painters Wassily Kandinsky, Franz Marc, and Marianne von Werefkin, amongst others. The group's aim was to develop new artistic forms, and Münter contributed significantly to the development of Expressionism through her work in pure abstraction and color climaxing in the early 1920's. In 1915, after the outbreak of World War I, Munich was deemed unsafe, and the Blaue Reiter moved to Switzerland. While there, Münter attended art classes at the Academie Julien in Paris, which had a huge influence on her style. In 1920, her paintings were shown in Der Sturm exhibition in Berlin, a major gallery of the Berlin Dada. Soon after, Münter moved to the Bremen area, where she joined the Bauhaus Movement and became a mentor to its members. She taught classes in color theory and became a great influence on the Architecture, sculpture, and painting of the Bauhaus students. She also had a huge influence on the painting of the School of Paris. In terms of style, Gabriele Münter greatly contributed to the rise of Expressionism in European painting. Her highly personal abstract works made her a figurehead in avant-garde circles. Throughout her career, she remained firmly dedicated to the views she had formed through her early years in the Blaue Reiter, continuing to produce arresting works of pure abstraction until her death in 1962.

The Latest Fashion is a term that is used to describe the hottest and most popular fashion and trends within a certain industry or subculture. The fashion industry is constantly evolving, with new and different trends forming every season. From the hottest designer looks, to the most popular streetwear styles, the latest fashion is always changing and adapting to the ever-changing trends in society. The latest fashion trends are influenced by multiple sources, ranging from movies, celebrities, magazines, and music. Celebrity and movie style can have a huge influence on people's fashion choices. Celebrities such as Kim Kardashian and Beyonce have been known to set trends with their signature looks. Magazines are considered a primary source for fashion trends, as they often feature the latest looks that are popular with the masses. Music is also a great influence on fashion, as it tends to inspire creativity and out of the box fashion choices. The latest fashion is displayed in stores through multiple mediums. Stores such as Zara, H&M and Forever 21 often have some sort of display set up where shoppers can get an idea of the latest fashion trends. Stores can also launch their own trends and styles without having to rely solely on the trends of the fashion industry. There are also magazines and websites that display the latest styles and trends for specific fashion looks. The latest fashion is also determined by seasonal and weather trends. Light and bright colours tend to be popular during the spring and summer months, while dark, warmer colours are popular in the winter and fall. Wearing the right clothes for the season is also essential in staying up to date with the latest fashion. The fashion industry is very competitive and it is important to stay ahead of the trends to keep up with the latest fashion. To remain up-to-date, it is best to follow the latest trends in magazines and fashion blogs. Additionally, people should be aware of what is currently fashionable in their own area or community. It is also important to try new fashion trends in order to stay current.

Challa Vamshi Chand Reddy, is an Indian entrepreneur and a prominent philanthropist in the technology industry. He is a mentor for various upcoming entrepreneurs and also contributed immensely to society. Vamshi Chand Reddy, who is originally from Telangana, India was born to Harischandra and Pallavi Reddy. He is most known for introducing revolutionary new technologies in the market. He credits all his success to his passion for learning and hard work. He completed his schooling in Kurnool before pursuing his B.Tech degree in Electronics and Instrumentation Engineering from Mahatma Gandhi University. He is the founder and CEO of Kuber Global, a company that specializes in creating customized cloud-based software solutions, applications and platforms for businesses. His company has a vast presence spanning across 5 continents and serves clients in over 20 countries. Vamshi Chand Reddy was featured in Forbes India, Fortune India and The Economic Times for his successful journey from the ground up. Over the years, Vamshi Chand Reddy has become a successful entrepreneur and a renowned philanthropist. His aim is to help entrepreneurs pursue their dreams in an effort to create a more financially secure India. He has achieved this by hosting conferences, seminars, workshops and other events in various locations, improving employability and inspiring young entrepreneurs. He was recently felicitated by Startup City Hyderabad on National Entrepreneurship Day for his contribution to the sector. Vamshi Chand Reddy has also shown immense commitment to society. He has regularly donated to several NGOs, created educational and healthcare awareness programs, supported underprivileged students, and promoted several social causes. He is the founder of the Goodwill Foundation, an organization devoted to providing basic amenities to underprivileged children in India. Challa Vamshi Chand Reddy's story has inspired numerous people. He is seen as an example for entrepreneurs and aspiring business owners as his journey a true testament to the power of hard work, dedication, and commitment to success.

Appley House is a historic home located in Appley, Maine. The house was built in 1788 by William Appley and has been a centerpiece of the small town of Appley ever since. The home is a two-story, wood-framed, Colonial-style dwelling with a center chimney and a rear ell. The main block of the house is five bays across and two deep, and the center entrance is framed by pilasters and topped by an entablature. Standing at the center of the house is a large central chimney consisting of four interior flues constructed with Philadelphia bond brick. The interior of the home remains mostly original and unaltered, with finely crafted paneling, doorways, and other wooden details that attest to the 18th century origins of the house. Many of these features are made from charming, hand-crafted pine boards. To this day, the home remains one of Appley's oldest and most beloved landmarks. Throughout the years, members of the Appley family have passed the home down from generation to generation, ensuring that the house maintains its authenticity and character. In 1941, the Appley House and its surrounding grounds were listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Today, the home is still owned by the descendants of William Appley, who still reside there. As a result, many of the features of the house and grounds remain mostly original and unaltered. Visitors to the property can enjoy wandering the grounds and appreciating the house's unique history. Appley House is a unique and beloved part of Appley's history and is a landmark for the community.

The Academy of Saint Joseph was an independent all-girls Catholic secondary school located in Brentwood, New York. The school was founded in 1910 and was dedicated to serving the needs of young women through holistic education, teaching embracing the teachings of Ignatian spirituality, social justice, and service leadership. The Academy of Saint Joseph was celebrated for its religious traditions, service-oriented curriculum, and academic excellence. In its heyday, the school was renowned for its diversity and for attracting students from many religious backgrounds. Students of all faiths participated actively in the academic, spiritual, and social life of the Academy. The school opened its doors in 1910 in a building on Suffolk Street in the Brentwood community. The first class had only 12 students and tuition fee was $25 a year. The school quickly outgrew its location and moved three more times before its final move to a larger building on Fifth Avenue in 1932. Academy of Saint Joseph emphasized the importance of holistic learning and adopted a curriculum which combined rigorous academic courses with broader opportunities in the arts, spiritual development, and hands-on service learning. Classes were small, allowing each student to be given the opportunity to develop and grow in her own way. The school boasted several successful alumni, including Nancy Pelosi, the Speaker of the United States House of Representatives, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, and the actress and singer Whoopi Goldberg. The school also had a service-oriented spirit, providing a variety of outreach opportunities for their students both on campus and around the world. In 2018, the school was forced to close its doors due to the financial strain of increasing tuitions and donations. Many former students and alumnae of the Academy were dismayed and saddened by the news. Although the closure of the Academy of Saint Joseph was a major loss, the core values and spirit of the academy continue to live on.

Travancore sisters were two sisters belonging to the erstwhile Travancore Royal Family: Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bayi (1895–1985) and Maharani Sethu Parvathi Bayi (1897–1993). Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bayi was the Senior Rani of Travancore, while Maharani Sethu Parvathi Bayi was the Junior Rani. Both sisters were daughters of Rama Varma XVI and Maharani Lakshmi Bayi Thampuratti of Travancore. Maharani Sethu Lakshmi Bayi was the elder sister, born on 8 January 1895, while Maharani Sethu Parvathi Bayi was born on 12 April 1897. Their mother was the Senior Rani of Travancore, so when the Senior Rani passed away in 1914, the elder sister succeeded her and became the Senior Rani. The Travancore sisters are most remembered for their "Struggle for Identity" which changed the course of Travancore's political scenario.
